The method satisfies all the basic Shapley axioms by construction. Automated tests check whether explanations are necessary and sufficient for the ranking produced. For most query types, CQD-SHAP explains answers more effectively than the baselines compared.
arxiv-2510-15723:
RR Lyrae stars are old pulsating stars, and almost none show heavy-element enrichment from slow neutron capture. V. D'Orazi leads a nineteen-author team reporting two such stars in this 2025 arXiv paper. Until now, TY Gruis was the only known example of this rare class. The team used high-resolution spectrographs in Australia and Chile to measure detailed abundances. Gaia data supplied motions and orbits, letting them classify each star's Galactic population.

Both stars show strong overabundances of barium and lanthanum compared with lighter s-process elements. The pattern fits pollution from a companion that once passed through its giant phase. Mismatches in dilution factors suggest low-metallicity giant models still need refinement.
arxiv-2510-15923:
Ivan Bortnovskyi heads a team of ten authors improving the algorithms that write vectors as sums of generalised Fibonacci vectors. Zeckendorf's theorem says every non-negative integer is a unique sum of distinct k-bonacci numbers with no k in a row used. Anderson and Bicknell-Johnson extended that uniqueness to vectors built from k-bonacci vectors.

The team presents two faster algorithms for finding a vector's representation and compares their efficiency. A projection map reduces the vector problem to the number problem, once a lower bound on the most negative index used is secured. Through that map and a bijection with the non-negative integers, they show counts and gaps of summands behave exactly as in the number case. The vector representations also enjoy summand minimality, needing no more pieces than necessary.
arxiv-2510-16123:
Federico Malato and Ville Hautamäki test a shortcut for world models. A world model is an inner map that lets an AI agent guess what happens next in a game-like world. Most world models, like the well-known Dreamer family, need long training runs. Their model skips training and instead searches a memory of past scenes for ones that match the present.

They compare their search-based model with PlaNet, a trained model from the Dreamer line. Both are judged on how well they rebuild scenes and how well they predict the next steps and far-off steps. The search model matches the trained one on most tests. It even does better at long-range forecasts across several unlike worlds. That hints training-free models may suit agents that must adapt fast with little data.
arxiv-2510-16223:
Kate Glazko and five co-authors report a hands-on experiment: using generative AI to design embroidery patterns that real machines can stitch. Making embroiderable art is intricate work involving detail limits, color choices, and cultural relevance, and the disabled-led team explores the tool as assistive technology for makers.

Through an auto-ethnographic case study, they describe iteratively engineering prompts for custom GPTs tuned to produce stitch-ready images, and the friction of coaxing outputs that respect real embroidery constraints. Results were mixed: the AI widened creative access and supported inclusion, yet its designs could be unpredictable and hard to steer. The authors plan refinements aimed at more dependable, accessible tools for creative making.
arxiv-2510-16923:
Mansi Phute leads eight co-authors in building a new attack-testing tool in a 2025 paper. Self-driving systems are tested in photo-like simulators for safety. Attackers can fool such systems with carefully changed objects. Real simulators, though, cannot be tuned step by step by math.

Their framework, UNDREAM, links a realistic simulator with a tunable renderer. Tunable here means every small change gives usable feedback for improvement. Users control weather, lighting, backgrounds, camera angles, and movement. They can then shape physical objects that still look plausible. Tests produced many distinct objects that fooled vision models. The tool helps researchers probe failures before real roads do. That makes safety checks for driving systems much stronger.
arxiv-2510-17023:
Shraman Pramanick leads five co-authors in sharpening video moment search in a 2025 paper. Temporal grounding finds where a described moment occurs in video. User queries often omit details needed for precise matching. Their method first enriches the query before locating it.

A multimodal language model rewrites queries with missing cues added. A lightweight decoder then predicts the moment's boundaries. Training uses a multiple-instance objective to fight noise. That objective picks the best query version for each example. It also limits damage from model-invented details. Results set new best scores on several grounding benchmarks. The method beat every earlier language-model approach clearly. It also matched or beat specialized grounding models overall.
arxiv-2510-17223:
Ivan Arzhantsev and Mikhail Zaidenberg sort special subalgebras of vector field algebras in this 2025 paper. Vector fields act as smooth flows on affine spaces, which are flat algebraic shapes. A Borel subalgebra is a largest solvable part of such an algebra. The authors call such a part integrable when it comes from a group.

They prove integrable parts are just the tangent algebras of Borel groups. Past work found those groups for affine toric surfaces, a class of ruled shapes. The pair now sort all integrable parts for those surfaces. The affine plane and its cyclic quotient shapes get full lists. The work ties group acts and algebra forms in a tight way.
arxiv-2510-17423:
BULLKID is a cold silicon detector built to hunt for light dark matter particles and to catch neutrinos scattering off atomic nuclei. M Folcarelli, leading a team with forty-one co-authors, reports on how the detector energy scale is set for events that happen deep inside its silicon dice, rather than at the surface. Earlier checks used bursts of light, which stop within a hair of the surface.

The team instead used gamma rays from an americium source, which pass through the bulk of each die and better mimic a real dark matter hit. The measured peak stayed close to the light based calibration, and its sharpness doubled when signals from neighbouring dice were combined. Folcarelli and the large team take this as confirmation for the planned dark matter search.
arxiv-2510-17623:
Christiane K. M. Klein reviews quantum fields near spinning black holes in a 2025 arXiv paper. The setting is a Kerr-de Sitter black hole, which rotates and sits in a universe with a small outward push. Klein studies a special quantum state of a free field around such a hole. That state, called the Unruh state, is the natural choice for a hole formed by collapse.

Earlier work proved the state has the smooth local behavior physics requires, but only for slow spin. Klein shows the proof extends to any spin below the extreme limit. The key step widens a geometric study of trapped light paths. She also discusses numerical work on quantum effects at the inner horizon. A related result shows those effects take a universal form.
arxiv-2510-18123:
Xiangbo Gao, with eight co-authors, maps the safety holes that open when self-driving cars talk to each other in plain language. Shared language promises rich meaning at low bandwidth, but it also invites lost messages, made-up content, manipulation, and attacks. Their SafeCoop study claims the first full-stack look at this shift.

The work builds a taxonomy of threats across the whole communication stack. Each layer, from message transport to shared decisions, gets its own failure modes. Vehicle network designers get a checklist for a young technology whose safety case cannot rest on bandwidth savings alone.
arxiv-2510-18623:
Moein Ivaki works with Matias Karjula and Tapio Ala-Nissila. They ask how to tune a quantum reservoir computer. The reservoir must stay learnable as it grows. In reservoir computing, a fixed circuit processes time signals. Only the readout is trained. Their circuits mix two gate types. Clifford gates can be simulated by classical computers. Conditional T gates add real quantum power. The mix is set by a chosen chance.

Raising that chance shifts the reservoir's character. It moves from classically easy to fully quantum behavior. The authors link task performance to two things. One is the circuit's entanglement pattern. The other is its stock of non-stabilizer resources. They also track a flatness measure. It signals when learning may seize up at large size. Performance and scalability tuned smoothly with the gate chance. Designers gain a dial between cheap simulation and maximal quantum power.
arxiv-2510-18723:
Enes Yavuz Ugan works with Ngoc-Quan Pham and Alexander Waibel. They adapt large speech models to new speaking styles. The risk is losing what the models already know. Direct fine-tuning can overfit the new domain. It can overwrite broad skills, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Their method uses Bayesian factorized adapters. These are small trainable matrices held near zero by priors. The changes to the model stay sparse.

The adapters were applied to the Whisper speech model. Tests covered code-switching, where speakers mix languages in one sentence. Several multilingual scenarios were used. Losses on the new domain stayed minimal. Forgetting of the base model dropped sharply. The popular LoRA method was the main rival. This approach gained about fifty-four percent on retained old skills. It gave up only about four percent on the new domain. That is a favorable trade for real deployment.
arxiv-2510-19123:
Muhammad Ahsan Razaq and Claudio Altafini examine when a crowd stays wise under hostile interactions and correlated starting opinions. Opinion dynamics on signed networks, where some links are friendly and others antagonistic, can either sharpen a group's average judgment or wreck it, depending on the model and the network.

Conditions are given for several standard models, including DeGroot and Friedkin-Johnsen forms, showing when each improves or undermines collective wisdom. The extension to dependent initial opinions reveals how correlation changes the shape of the regions where wisdom improves. The results matter for platforms where disagreement and influence mix.
arxiv-2510-19223:
Paul Agbaje and five co-authors explore mutual learning among graph neural networks, replacing the usual teacher-student setup of knowledge distillation. Distillation normally needs a large pretrained teacher to train a small student for use on limited devices, but no such teacher may exist for a new graph task.

Working without any pretrained teacher, the authors show that simple, shallow graph networks can learn together and end up performing better at inference than they would alone. Sharing knowledge among peers squeezes more from modest architectures. That collaborative route suits settings where training one giant model first is not an option.
arxiv-2510-19323:
Levin Maier and Francesco Ruscelli extend two classic results of geometry. Their setting is magnetic systems on infinite-dimensional groups. A strong right-invariant metric pairs with a magnetic field. Half Lie groups supply the stage. Groups of smooth rearrangements are a key case. Particles there follow magnetic geodesics.

The authors define a magnetic form of Mañé's critical value. It lives on the universal cover. Above that value, the lifted flow matches a Finsler geodesic flow. A full Hopf-Rinow theorem also holds. Geometers get the completeness properties they rely on, now in a far larger setting.
arxiv-2510-19423:
Jia-Kai Dong and three co-authors introduce ETOM, a five-level benchmark for how well language model agents orchestrate tools inside the Model Context Protocol ecosystem. Older benchmarks test tools one at a time, missing the overlap between similar tools and the difficulty of planning across several servers, which makes agents look better than they are.

Ground truth is built from sets of tools with equal function, allowing objective scoring without relying on a model judge. The five levels climb from single-tool use to complex cross-server planning and handling requests outside the system's scope. Early results show rigid hierarchies can hurt without careful design.
arxiv-2510-19523:
Xiaoqi Feng, Bingzhe Hou, and Kui Ji extend the Cowen-Douglas class of operators from complex to quaternionic Hilbert spaces. Cowen and Douglas introduced these geometric operators in 1978, linking each one to a holomorphic vector bundle. Quaternion multiplication does not commute, so the extension is not a routine copy of the classical theory.

After setting out basic facts about the S-spectrum and right eigenvalues, the authors show each quaternionic Cowen-Douglas operator corresponds to a Hermitian right holomorphic quaternionic vector bundle. Two operators are unitarily equivalent exactly when their bundles match. For the simplest class they give canonical matrix forms, and they show curvature alone, a complete invariant in the classical case, no longer decides equivalence here.
arxiv-2510-19723:
Ashish Chouhan and Michael Gertz build resources for dialogue systems that guide citizens through European Union legal texts, instead of just answering single questions. EU laws and rules are open to all, but laypeople find them hard to work through. Their EUDial dataset comes from two hundred four blogs of the European Parliament's Citizens' Enquiries Unit.

The dataset holds eight hundred eighty multi-turn dialogues. Each runs a little over four turns on average, with an opening question, a structured answer, and follow-ups. Their LexGuide framework pairs retrieval-augmented generation with a layered topic map, to keep talks coherent and complete. The results suggest guided, active navigation can close much of the gap between legal texts being open and citizens truly grasping them.
arxiv-2510-20023:
Alexander G. Tartakovsky and three co-authors sum up the work of Tze Leung Lai in the field of sequential tests. Lai made key gains in tests that run as data come in. He set sharp best-possible bounds for the classic sequential test and its kin. He also gave a broad frame for tests of mixed claims about a system.

Lai also shaped change point work, where the task is to spot when a stream shifts. He set new best-possible rules and fast steps that still guide the field. He used these tools in health data work as well. The article sets his main results in the wider tale of sequential tests and change work.
arxiv-2510-20223:
Divyanshu Kumar and five co-authors systematically study how simple perceptual changes can jailbreak multimodal language models that accept images and audio as well as text. Their safety evaluation covers nineteen hundred adversarial prompts in three high-risk categories, tested against seven frontier models from vision-language and audio-language families.

Techniques such as visual keyword decomposition, semantic masking in images, and pitch, speed, or echo changes in audio bypass filters that look nearly perfect on plain text. Attack success rises above seventy-five percent under modified inputs in several settings, with one visual method reaching very high rates on some models. The authors conclude that safeguards trained mainly on text do not transfer across modalities, leaving a serious safety gap.
arxiv-2510-20523:
Jan Hajduček and eleven co-authors test how far a tool called EMCD can be trusted to gauge spin and orbit pull at the ten-nanometer scale. The tool works in a transmission electron scope and picks out one element at a time. Its truth at fine probes has been in doubt. Their test stuff is FeRh, a solid whose first-rank shift joins shape and pull in one step.

The ratio of orbit to spin pull stays in line with X-ray marks for probes down to near six nanometers. That sets a sound zone for firm counts. At fine probes with wide cone views, the ratio climbs. The team lays that climb on tool facts and on fine mix shifts in the probed mass.
arxiv-2510-21223:
Kexuan Shi, Yandong Wen, and Weiyang Liu study model merging, where several fine-tuned versions of one base model are combined into a single model. Older methods blend the models' internal numbers directly and can suffer when those numbers disagree across tasks or point in conflicting directions.

Their approach, called Functional Dual Anchors, works instead with synthetic inputs. Each anchor input is built so that the change it triggers in the model matches the change linked to one task. That view links merging done after training with training on all tasks at once. A careful starting scheme is added, and tests show the anchors help on their own and also add value when combined with standard merging methods.
arxiv-2510-21523:
Ramón Nartallo-Kaluarachchi and six co-authors measure how shaky reward estimates infect the choices of generative models used for scientific discovery. Such models, here generative flow networks, learn to build objects step by step in proportion to a reward, and errors in that reward become uncertainty in every downstream decision.

They thread that uncertainty through the model using polynomial chaos expansions fitted to small ensembles of trained copies. The expansion's coefficients convert directly into sensitivity indices that name which reward parts drive which decisions, a breakdown that deep ensembles and dropout methods cannot give. Four of five supporting guarantees were machine-checked in a proof assistant. On three real tasks, from catalyst choice to protein signaling, the method exposes fragile and sturdy decisions that ensembles alone would hide.
arxiv-2510-22023:
Yifan Liu leads a nine-author team improving recommendations from plain-language requests. A shopper describes what they want in words. Standard retrieval scores each item by comparing request and description. But a single request embedding is a weak stand-in for relevance. Relevance can peak in several separate places at once.

Their method, GPR-LLM, asks a language model to judge relevance for some candidate passages. It then fits a Gaussian process over those judgments. The scoring surface can bend and form multiple peaks. Tests covered four recommendation datasets and two model backbones. The flexible version beat simpler single-peak kernels. It also beat strong baselines, including dense retrieval and cross-encoders. The work treats relevance as a landscape to learn, not one distance to measure.
arxiv-2510-22723:
Brain scans, genetic markers, and memory tests each carry part of the story of Alzheimer's disease. Riddhik Basu and Arkaprava Roy combine those data types in a 2025 imaging genetics analysis, using records from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative to study disease progression.

Simpler regressions link cognitive scores, spinal fluid biomarkers, and demographics to states from normal cognition through mild impairment to Alzheimer's. A screening and penalized regression approach then searches high dimensional genetic data for markers tied to decline and white matter health. Genes including CLIC1, NAB2, and TGFBR1 emerge from that search, alongside strong roles for standard cognitive measures and tau protein levels.
arxiv-2510-22823:
Aid groups must pick language models they can afford and trust. Poli Nemkova leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they compare commercial and open weight models. The task is detecting human rights violations. Texts span seven languages, many low resource.

The team ran seventy eight thousand multilingual inferences. Six models were tested in total. New scores track calibration, bias, and language stability. Aligned models held accuracy steady across languages. Open weight models varied much more. Low resource tongues like Lingala and Burmese showed the gap. The study frames a cost versus reliability trade off.
arxiv-2510-23323:
Francesco Innocenti wrote a thesis on scaling deep neural networks with predictive coding, a brain-inspired alternative to backpropagation. That standard method trains modern AI but is energy hungry and unlikely to be how brains learn. Predictive coding networks instead settle neuron activity by repeated balancing before any weight update.

The thesis develops theory and practice for that repeated inference, which recent work suggests brings gains over the standard method. Scaling predictive coding could yield efficient learning machines closer to biology. He examines where the method stands and what it needs to reach large networks.
arxiv-2510-23423:
Diederik van Engelenburg and three co-authors measure how likely a starting point connects to the edge of a large box in models tied to the Ising model of magnetism. This one-arm probability is a basic probe of behavior at the critical point. The team studies three related percolation setups, including the Fortuin-Kasteleyn version of the Ising model and a double random current model.

Their proofs show the decay rate of this probability depends on the setup and on the number of dimensions in sharp ways. For the Fortuin-Kasteleyn model they pin down rates above four and six dimensions, with matching borderline cases. One outcome settles a conjecture by Chayes, Coniglio, Machta, and Shtengel. The upper critical dimension of the Fortuin-Kasteleyn model equals six, unlike the ordinary Ising model, where it is at most four.
arxiv-2510-23623: Alexey V. Gavrilov proves a formula for the Euler characteristic of a triangulated manifold whose dimension is even. That number is a classic one-number summary of a shape, often built by adding and subtracting counts of faces of every dimension. Gavrilov's formula uses only the counts of faces of even dimension. Its weights stay the same for every such manifold, no matter how large the even dimension is.
arxiv-2510-23823:
The H0DN Collaboration delivers a community consensus on the local value of the Hubble constant, the number that sets the universe's current expansion rate. Many distance methods feed into it — parallaxes, Cepheids, red giant tips, supernovae, and more — but combining them is tricky because calibrations correlate and methods differ. The collaboration built a Distance Network that reviews every dataset critically and combines them with covariance weighting.

The network's baseline value lands at about seventy-three and a half kilometers per second per megaparsec, with an uncertainty near one percent. Top indicators agree internally, and swapping parts of the network barely moves the answer. Dropping Cepheids or the red giant method changes little, and galaxy-based indicators shift the value by less than a tenth of a unit. The tension with early-universe estimates remains stark, at about seven sigma against one combination. All software and data products are public.
arxiv-2510-24023:
Saujas Vaduguru and three co-authors teach large multimodal models to form linguistic conventions, the shorthand that people naturally build with repeat partners. Humans exploit shared context to say less while meaning the same, coordinating on short utterances that only make sense inside the conversation. The team trains models to do the same, using simulated reference games between models and no new human data.

In repeated games over photographs and tangram images, the trained models then communicate with people more efficiently. Message length falls by up to forty-one percent across an interaction, while success rises by fifteen percent. Human listeners also answer faster when paired with a convention-forming model. A clean ablation carries the theoretical point: training on success alone, or on cost alone, does not produce conventions. Both pressures together are required, mirroring the trade-off that shapes human shorthand.
arxiv-2510-24123:
Nao Kominato and four co-authors report that part of the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A has grown brighter over about twenty years. They study a non thermal filament in the northeast of the remnant, at its forward shock. This filament has the fastest particle acceleration among the outer shells, so it is a prime place to study how shocks energize particles.

Since the year 2000, the filament's flux rose by several tens of percent and then leveled off, while its spectrum stayed much the same. The shape also changed and split into two parts. One part rose then steadied, while the other held a steady flux, a contrast the authors link to nonlinear processes at the shock.
arxiv-2510-24223:
Mahmut Kemal Ercan and four co-authors design a way to hide a signal's time of arrival in uplink OFDM communication while keeping the link working. A base station can estimate arrival time from pilot signals, and the authors deliberately distort those pilots per subcarrier. The distortion raises the sidelobes of the detection function relative to its main peak, confusing timing estimates.

The design follows two goals based on sidelobe levels, under limits on transmit power and on how far the pilot can stray from the best communication choice. They also bound the harm to communication using channel estimation error. The result is a principled trade off between privacy of timing and link quality.
arxiv-2510-24923:
Seth Benzell and Kyle Myers frame what lab tests of new work tech can and can not say on gaps between workers. Many such tests ask if a tool lifts high skill or low skill staff more, then use that to guess long run gaps. Their model has each worker do a task or hand it to the tech.

The gap effect turns on two things: how alike task skills are across staff, and how staff skill stacks up next to the tech. As the tech gets strong, the sign of the gap effect can flip more than once. So a test at one tech level may point the wrong way for the next. Their frame warns firms to read such tests with care.
arxiv-2510-25023:
Rahil Soroushmojdehi, Sina Javadzadeh, Mehrnaz Asadi, and Terence D Sanger split brain waves into shared and own parts with a new model, SPIRE. When more than one brain zone is logged at once, zone own acts blur the web level acts that link them. Their model uses more than one code arm to pull the two apart.

New loss terms keep the shared and own codes in line and apart at once. Trained just on calm data, the model held its split when shocks were applied. On fake sets with known hid codes, it beat classic odds tools when waves were bent or off in time. On deep brain shock logs, shared codes marked each shock type well.
arxiv-2510-25623:
Davide Romano, Jonathan Schwarz, and Daniele Giofre test verifiers for legal thinking. Their 2025 paper studies test-time scaling in law. Test-time scaling improves model results with extra computation. It has proven effective in math and programming. Formal domains show clear verification signals there. Argumentative domains like law remain underexplored for scaling.

They study verifier-based methods for legal multiple-choice questions. Five benchmarks supply the testing tasks here. A family of seven reward models serves as verifiers. Outcome-level Best-of-N verification is tested first. Process-level tree search verification is also tested. Realistic low-N budgets constrain both methods. Their study studies verifier utility systematically. Domain specialization affects utility in their tests. Model size and supervision type also matter greatly. Process-supervised models differ from outcome-only models. Roles of verifiers can swap across those traits. Legal thinking may need varied scaling strategies.
arxiv-2510-26123:
Jacopo Borga and Ewain Gwynne study directed distances in a random triangulation equipped with an orientation. Their model is the uniform infinite bipolar oriented triangulation, the local limit of finite bipolar oriented triangulations around a typical edge. A triangulation splits a surface into triangles, and the bipolar orientation gives each triangle a source and sink direction, so paths can be required to follow the arrows.

Borga and Gwynne build a Busemann function that measures directed distance to infinity along a natural interface. In the scaling limit it becomes a stable Levy process, with exponent two thirds for longest paths and four thirds for shortest paths. Bounds for finite maps imply typical longest paths grow like length to the three quarters power.
arxiv-2510-26223:
Soumya Satpathi, Suparna Sarkar, and Swapan K. Pati map the phases of a one dimensional chain where spins of size one half and one alternate. Such mixed spin chains are model magnets where quantum effects are strong. Frustration is added through next nearest neighbor couplings that compete with the nearest ones, and single ion anisotropy, a preference for spin direction at each site, is also included.

Satpathi and the team find that moderate frustration can drive the ground state from ferrimagnetic order, where unequal opposing moments leave a net moment, to antiferromagnetic order. Weak easy plane anisotropy also destabilizes the ferrimagnetic state. Under strong frustration and anisotropy, signs of a novel phase with spin density wave like modulation appear. Small systems, matrix methods, and finite temperature tools are combined.
arxiv-2510-26423:
Dong Huang, with six co-authors, tackles a quiet weak point in software testing: the oracle, the rule that says whether a program's output is right. Writing good oracles by hand is slow. Their system, Nexus, uses several AI agents to draft, debate, and fix oracles for a function under test.

Huang and the team give four agents distinct testing outlooks, let them critique a first draft, then run the oracles against a plausible version of the function in a safe sandbox. Any oracle that fails is repaired using the exact error it hit, then checked again. On seven benchmarks, Nexus beat prior methods by wide margins. Its oracles also caught more bugs and raised the success of automatic program repair from about thirty-five percent to about sixty-nine percent in one test.
arxiv-2510-26623:
Spencer Teetaert, Sven Lilge, Jessica Burgner-Kahrs, and Timothy D Barfoot track the shape of soft, bendy robots in real time. Continuum robots flex along their whole length, which makes their state hard to estimate. Past methods either used simplified step-by-step models with no account of uncertainty, or ran full stochastic filters no faster than the sensors feeding them.

Teetaert and his three co-authors present a sliding-window filter that works in continuous time. It keeps a moving window of recent data, which sharpens accuracy over a plain filter while still running online, faster than real time. The authors call it the first stochastic sliding-window filter built for continuum robots. They offer it as a promising base for future work on robot perception and control.
arxiv-2510-27023:
Rui Liu, Jan Hannig, and J. S. Marron strengthen a statistical tool that finds real features in noisy images. Smoothing can reveal signals, but the amount of smoothing is a free choice that affects conclusions. SiZer and its two-dimensional extension scan many scales for significant slopes and curvatures, yet the image version lacked a fully valid testing procedure until now.

Using a fresh probability approach, the team builds distribution theory that makes the image method a valid hypothesis test. On pure noise images it controls false alarms, where the older method flags spurious features. When signal is present, it keeps high power and finds true slopes and curvatures in real data such as gamma camera images. The advance makes multi-scale image claims more trustworthy.
arxiv-2510-27123:
Yihong Guo, Junjie Luo, Guodong Gao, Ritu Agarwal, and Anqi Liu add fairness across groups to offline bandit learning. Offline contextual bandits learn decision policies from stored history without live trials. Maximizing total reward alone can widen reward gaps between groups, a serious concern when resources are limited and some groups gain far more than others.

The team imposes group-sensitive constraints, either capping reward disparity at a chosen threshold or minimizing it during optimization. A doubly robust estimator, which combines two estimates so one can correct the other, sharpens disparity measurement during training, and convergence guarantees are provided. On synthetic and real datasets the method cuts group disparities while keeping overall performance competitive, offering a practical template for fairer policy learning.
arxiv-2510-27223:
Tonmoy Deka, Liton Majumdar, and five other co-authors built a new tool for reading the air of distant planets, reported in 2025. Their target is WASP-69b, a giant planet outside our solar system. Heat glow from such a planet carries hints of its gases and heat profile. The James Webb Space Telescope now records that glow in fine detail.

Their tool, NEXOTRANS, works backward from the glow to the gases that made it. It mixes physics-based light models with smart search methods and chemistry that allows out-of-balance gases. Applied to Webb data across a wide band of infrared light, it pinned down water, carbon dioxide, and other gases. One fit hints at sulfur dioxide, a sign of light-driven chemistry in the planet's air.
arxiv-2510-27323:
Xicheng Zhang and Yuanlong Zhao study faster ways to solve random equations in this 2025 paper. The equations are stochastic, driven by chance, and include Volterra equations, where the present state depends on the whole past. Their slopes can be rough in time, even spiking at points. The standard step-by-step solver struggles with such spikes.

Their trick swaps the clock: time advances in random jumps set by a Poisson process, a counter of random events. The solver then leaps with the jumps instead of marching on a fixed grid. They prove the leaping answer closes in on the true one, and they give exact rates. The rate reflects both the kernel's roughness and the clock's own jitter. Tests include equations driven by a long-memory noise.
arxiv-2510-27623:
Qiusi Zhan and nine co-authors show in 2025 how visual backdoors can be planted in agents that see, read, and act. A backdoor makes an agent act normally until a set trigger appears, then follow an attacker's multi-step plan. Here the trigger is a real object in the scene, not a word. Object looks shift with angle and light, which makes the trick hard to plant well.

Their framework, BEAT, trains on varied scenes, tasks, and trigger spots. A first pass copies good conduct, then a contrast step teaches the agent to split trigger from non-trigger views as a choice between paired options. The work maps a new risk for sight-driven agents in homes and work sites.
arxiv-2511-00223:
Hussein Nassar and Andrew Weber study thin patterned sheets, such as corrugated or creased shells, that like to bend without stretching. Because the sheets are thin, stretching costs far more energy than bending, so their natural moves keep lengths fixed. The authors report a recent result that pins down exactly which bending moves are possible for surfaces with a repeating pattern.

The result ties how the sheet seems to stretch, while keeping true lengths fixed, to how it bends and twists. The link echoes a classic theorem of Gauss on curved surfaces. Worked examples and use cases show how designers might use the rule for flexible shell mechanisms.
arxiv-2511-00923:
Khushi Banthia and Rickmoy Samanta study vortex dipoles, pairs of swirling flows that propel themselves, moving on a catenoid, the hourglass shaped surface formed by rotating a hanging chain curve. The catenoid has variable negative curvature, so geometry itself steers the motion.

They build the full dynamical system, including how the two vortices interact and how each interacts with the curved surface. The Hamiltonian dynamics make dipoles follow the surface's geodesics, matching recent results, and a conserved momentum comes from the surface's rotational symmetry. Direct and exchange scattering are showed, along with rotating motion for chiral pairs. A finite size dipole model then shows self propulsion emerging to leading order, directed across the dipole axis.
arxiv-2511-01223:
Zahra Mehraban and colleagues ask how a self driving steering model trained in one country adapts to driving on the other side of the road. They adapt PilotNet, an end to end driving model, from United States right hand traffic to Australian left hand highways using real road data.

Four training routes were compared. One was the raw United States baseline. Others used flipped United States data, fine tuning on Australian data, or pretraining on flipped data followed by Australian fine tuning. Flipped pretraining alone hurt stability, because the learned features were misaligned. Followed by fine tuning, though, it gave the lowest prediction error. It also gave the strongest attention to left side road cues. A saliency analysis tracked where the models look, and repeating the study on ResNet confirmed the same pattern.
arxiv-2511-01323:
Jiabao Ji and colleagues benchmark whether language models with search tools give complete answers to ambiguous, multi step questions. A question like which actor from the film Heat won an Academy Award hides traps: several films share the title. The full cast must be reasoned over to gather every qualifying name.

Their data generation pipeline builds questions from text corpora linked to a knowledge graph, embedding name ambiguity and multi hop reasoning in a natural, verifiable way. The resulting data set holds thirty six hundred questions, half with explicit ambiguity. Even the strongest current model answered poorly, with low exact match scores on both ambiguous and unambiguous questions. The authors argue answer completeness is an under measured weakness of search augmented systems.
arxiv-2511-01723:
Maxime Dherbécourt, Joël Bellessa, Clémentine Symonds, Guillaume Weick, and David Hagenmüller settle a dispute about light scattering from molecules in an optical cavity. When a molecular vibration couples strongly to a cavity mode, the two form polaritons. Early reports claimed big changes to spontaneous Raman scattering from such systems. Later experiments mostly disagreed.

The authors build a microscopic quantum model that keeps the spatial shape of the polariton modes. In a cavity filled evenly with molecules, overlap between polaritons and cavity resonances enforces selection rules. Those rules suppress the claimed Raman peaks, which matches most experiments. In a thin, quasi-two-dimensional layer, the rules lift. Peaks at the polariton energies then return. The key factor is the spatial overlap of cavity and vibration. The model now makes that factor calculable.
arxiv-2511-01823:
Thiago Dias, José Roberto Iglesias, and Sebastián Gonçalves test the fairness of consumption taxes with agent-based simulations. Consumption-based systems, which tax spending rather than income, are often defended as simple and neutral; the authors examine whether they actually redistribute wealth in a socially fair way.

Simulating wealth exchanges among agents under flat consumption taxes, they compare universal redistribution of the revenue with optimal targeted redistribution. The regressivity is stark: the poorest 40 percent of households contribute over half of the total tax revenue at most tax rates, because poorer households spend nearly all they have. Even the better redistribution schemes struggle against this built-in tilt. The authors present the numbers as quantitative input for designing fairer fiscal policy.
arxiv-2511-02023:
Helmut Eberl, Maximilian Fahrecker, and Josef Pradler examine whether a modest electron beam could create and reveal a hypothetical kind of light particle. The particles they consider carry a tiny fraction of an electron's charge, or interact through electric or magnetic dipole moments. Their plan places production underground and uses a CCD sensor as the detector.

Working through the production math first on paper and then by computer, the authors find the setup could explore a region of possibilities that direct detection experiments have not yet reached. They also argue that the dipole moment of a light fermion could be probed, given enough beam time or a higher beam energy.
arxiv-2511-02123:
Xuheng Li and Quanquan Gu improve Thompson sampling, a classic strategy for the contextual bandit problem, where an algorithm repeatedly picks an action, sees a reward, and must balance exploring against exploiting. Their version is designed for settings where reward noise varies, and the theory aims for regret bounds that depend on that variance rather than worst-case assumptions. Earlier variance-aware work leaned on confidence-bound algorithms, leaving sampling methods behind.

The algorithm, a variance-aware feel-good Thompson sampling method, handles general reward functions, not just linear ones. The analysis extends a tool called the decoupling coefficient to measure model complexity. The resulting regret bound matches what confidence-bound methods achieve for linear contextual bandits, and the authors show it is optimal with respect to model dimension.
arxiv-2511-02823:
Chloe Loughridge and five colleagues work on AI control, a framework for estimating the risk of advanced AI systems. Good control tests need strong attack policies, but complex agent settings offer little data to tune them. Their 2025 paper improves attacks inside SHADE-Arena, a set of realistic control test environments, despite that data shortage.

They split attack skill into five parts: modeling suspicion, choosing attacks, planning, execution, and subtlety. Each part is tuned on its own. To beat the data limit, they built a probabilistic model of attack dynamics, tuned settings inside that simulation, and showed the gains transfer to the real arena. Attack strength rose sharply: the safety score fell from 0.87 to 0.41 with their scaffold in place.
arxiv-2511-02923:
Ivan Zvonkov, Gabriel Tseng, Inbal Becker-Reshef, and Hannah Kerner test a shortcut for mapping farmland from space. Good land cover maps track land use change, a driver of climate change, but drawing them the usual way is slow. Their 2025 study uses geospatial embeddings, compact numeric summaries of satellite data, to classify cropland in Togo with far less hand work.

They built maps from embeddings by two systems, Presto and AlphaEarth. Both reached high accuracy in sorting cropland from other land. The authors conclude that embeddings can simplify mapping workflows while staying accurate. That matters most where ground data is scarce: cheaper, current cropland maps feed better estimates of land use change and its climate effects.
arxiv-2511-03023:
Sina Montazeri, Yunhe Feng, and Kewei Sha present PublicAgent, a team of language model agents that answers questions from public data. Open data could ground public decisions, yet non-experts struggle to find data sets, map their schemas, and run sound statistics. Single models falter on the full workflow: attention thins, reasoning styles clash, and errors slip through. Their 2025 framework splits the job among specialists.

Separate agents clarify intent, discover data, analyze it, and write the report, each checked at its own stage. Tests across five models and fifty queries yielded five design principles. Specialization helped even the strongest model. Some agents helped always, others only for certain models. Removing discovery or analysis caused mass failures, while removing reporting hurt quality. The principles guide when multi-agent designs pay off.
arxiv-2511-03123:
Aditi Chakrabarti, Divya Jaganathan, Robert Haussman, and L. Mahadevan watch what happens when a moving pressure spot skims across a very soft solid. Their 2025 experiments reveal a steady V-shaped wake on the surface, much like the wedge behind a fast boat or a supersonic jet. A simple geometric argument already explains the pattern in outline.

Their theory blends three effects: elastic waves in the solid, surface tension, and gravity. The resulting dispersion relation slides smoothly between Kelvin's theory of wakes on liquid surfaces and Rayleigh's theory of elastic surface waves. Between those classics sits a soft wake regime the team identifies for the first time. It offers new ways to probe how soft surfaces move and respond.
arxiv-2511-03223:
Yaohong Chen and colleagues blend two neural designs to predict air pressure over a wing cross-section. Slow fluid simulations and wind tunnels usually supply those numbers for aircraft design checks. Their hybrid model learns shape from many wing profiles, then maps flight settings and position to pressure at each point.

Tests covered several well-known profiles under varied speeds and angles. Errors stayed very small, and the model gave answers far faster than full simulation would allow. Because the shape code is compact, the system can size up new profiles quickly. The work points toward quicker design loops, where engineers screen many shapes early and save heavy testing for the most promising few.
arxiv-2511-03423:
Jiyoung Lee, Song Park, Sanghyuk Chun, and Soo-Whan Chung present VoxStudio, a system that paints pictures straight from spoken descriptions. Text-to-image tools lose tone, feeling, and other cues that speech carries beyond words. VoxStudio squeezes raw speech into compact tokens that keep both meaning and emotional shade, skipping a separate transcription step.

Alongside the model, the team releases VoxEmoset, a large paired set of emotional speech and images built with an advanced speech synthesizer. Tests on three benchmarks show direct speech-to-image generation works and reveal where it still strains. Keeping prosody in the loop lets a shaky or joyful voice steer the picture, not just the words it happens to carry.
arxiv-2511-03823:
Jan Kocon and Maciej Piasecki lead a large consortium presenting PLLuM, a family of open Polish large language models, the largest such family built for Polish. Most model development has centred on English, leaving other languages with weaker support, and PLLuM was built by major Polish research institutions to close that gap.

Training used a new corpus of one hundred forty billion Polish tokens, plus instruction and preference datasets. A responsible AI framework adds data governance and a hybrid module for output correction and safety filtering. Base and instruction-tuned variants are described, with a public administration task as a demonstration. Public release aims to support open research and sovereign AI capacity.
arxiv-2511-04123:
Tengjie Li, Shikui Tu, and Lei Xu propose a training-free diffusion framework that generates sketches in a chosen style, guided by text prompts and reference style sketches. Vision-language progress has advanced sketch generation, but most methods synthesize generically and cannot control style precisely, while style transfer often leaks reference content.

Reference features enter as auxiliary information with linear smoothing instead of overwriting attention keys and values, and a style-content guidance mechanism separates manner from subject. Content leakage falls and quality rises, even when reference and target differ structurally. Multiple references can be blended through a joint module for multi-style output. Experiments showed accurate style alignment with flexible control.
arxiv-2511-04223:
Junhui Cao, Denis Novokreschenov, and Alexey Kavokin revisit arrays of exciton-polariton condensates as simulators of classical XY models. Such arrays reach phase-locked states quickly, and those states are mapped to two-dimensional spin arrangements, but whether they truly minimize the XY energy, and how fast convergence scales, has stayed unclear.

An analytical model shows an array of N condensates holds N stable phase configurations. Pump power selects among them: low power favours the smallest energy eigenvalue, high power the largest, and middle power visits all eigenstates. Formation takes on the order of one hundred picoseconds regardless of array size, supporting exceptional speed and scalability for polariton simulators.
arxiv-2511-04323:
Jiayu Li and Xiangrong Zhu study interior estimates for solutions of a linear Poisson equation with a potential term on a Riemann surface. The coefficients sit in a Zygmund-type space of barely integrable functions, and the surface is taken to meet an isoperimetric bound, a borderline setting where standard estimates can fail.

Interior bounds are established under those weak assumptions. Matching Harnack inequalities, which bound how much a positive solution can vary across a region, follow as uses, along with a global estimate. Borderline coefficient smoothness appears across analysis, so pushing Poisson estimates into this space strengthens a tool many later arguments quietly depend on.
arxiv-2511-04623:
Yutong Wen leads ten authors with PromptSep, a generative system for separating sounds. Language-queried separation can pull a named sound from a mixed recording. Generative versions already beat older masking methods on audio quality.

Two limits remain: users often want a sound removed, not extracted, and text alone can feel clumsy. PromptSep uses a conditional diffusion model fed by carefully simulated training data. It handles both extraction and removal in one framework. Vocal imitation joins text as a second way to point at a sound, letting users hum or mimic what they mean.
arxiv-2511-04723:
Mohamadreza Akbari Pour and two colleagues forecast remaining useful life for industrial machines. Knowing how long equipment will last cuts downtime and guides maintenance timing. Many models miss fine time patterns or fail to stress the most telling features.

Their design joins temporal convolutional networks with a modified fusion transformer. A two-way LSTM encoder-decoder links short and long dependencies inside that transformer. A multi-time-window scheme feeds several look-back lengths at once. Together, the parts aim at steadier life predictions across operating conditions, helping plants schedule repairs before failures force shutdowns.
arxiv-2511-05023:
Yifan Deng and co-authors report odd transport in single crystals of the kagome metal ZrV6Sn6. Kagome lattices, with their corner-linked triangles, host rich magnetic and electronic states and draw wide study.

The team found that resistance in a magnetic field can grow as a square or as a straight line, based on field and current paths. Hall and quantum oscillation tests fit the straight-line part to the Abrikosov model, at first. That model fails on the direction gap, so they extend it to two-dimensional linear bands, which restores the match.
arxiv-2511-05123:
R. Brivio and co-authors report GRB 240419A, a gamma-ray burst whose afterglow is the most distant yet seen with measured optical polarization. Bursts are bright blasts powered by fast jets, but the shape of their jets and fields is still in doubt.

Early polarization can split rival models of the jet and its magnetic field. The team pins the burst redshift at a value above five, tracks its afterglow across many bands, and takes early optical polarization data. Past bursts gave mixed signs, so this far case adds a rare test at cosmic dawn.
arxiv-2511-05223:
Pietro Caputo and Mario Morellini set up a nonlinear spin-exchange dynamics for Ising systems and study how fast it settles. Spins swap through collisions set by a kernel, in a Boltzmann-style equation that keeps mean magnetization fixed.

The kernel is chosen so the long-run state is the Ising model with a set interaction and a mean profile from the start state. They prove a broad convergence result for any interaction and kernel. For weak interactions, they show the system relaxes at an exponential rate, tied to decay of relative entropy.
arxiv-2511-05323:
Kilian Lichtner and co-authors present REAL, a tool that removes Ramsey quantifiers from formulas in linear arithmetic over integers, reals, or a mix. Ramsey quantifiers can state traits, like infinite cliques, that first-order logic cannot, which makes them key for liveness checks.

Past removal methods were slow. REAL speeds the step up a lot and takes a friendly input form based on SMT-LIB. Uses span program checks and monadic decomposability. The tool turns a deep logic result into a step that verification software can run in practice at long last.
arxiv-2511-05423:
Maynard Koch and co-authors scan the IPv6 internet by probing subnet-router anycast addresses, a little-used route into a vast address space. Finding live IPv6 hosts is hard, since the space is far too large to sweep one by one.

They compare anycast probing with hitlists, AI-made target lists, and random probes. On average, one anycast probe found about a tenth more router addresses than a random probe, and it was far less skewed by rate limits on replies. The work gives network census teams a sharper tool for mapping the live IPv6 net.
arxiv-2511-05523:
Ciaran O'Connor, Mohamed Bahloul, Steven Prestwich, and Andrea Visentin review how forecasters predict electricity prices with uncertainty attached. As wind and solar power grow, prices swing more, and a single forecast number hides real risk. Probabilistic methods give a range of likely prices instead, which helps traders and grid planners judge exposure.

The review traces the field from Bayesian and distribution-based methods through quantile regression to conformal prediction. It covers day-ahead markets and also the harder intra-day and balancing markets, where timing is tight. The authors weigh scoring rules, model choice, and open problems such as forecast validity and the lack of shared standards.
arxiv-2511-06723:
Evelyn Chee, Wynne Hsu, and Mong Li Lee teach multimodal models new tasks in sequence without erasing old skills. Continual learning already struggles with forgetting in one data type; mixing images, text, and other senses adds the burden of fusing fresh information across modalities each round. Their framework starts from a pretrained model rather than from scratch.

A cross-modality adapter with a mixture-of-experts structure integrates information spread across senses as tasks arrive. An alignment loss builds sturdy shared representations, while regularizing the ties between old and new representations protects earlier knowledge. Across multimodal datasets, in both new-class and new-domain sequences, the approach beat baselines on accuracy and forgot less.
arxiv-2511-06823:
For restoring images corrupted by harsh noise, Ji Li and Chao Wang build a plug-and-play method around a diffusion-model denoiser. Most earlier methods of this kind were built for gentle Gaussian noise and use a least-squares measure of fit. Impulse noise, which randomly destroys single pixels, breaks those assumptions.

Working within a maximum a posteriori system, the authors adapt the fit term to the noise at hand using a generalized Gaussian scale mixture loss. That loss covers a broad family of noise distributions. An iteratively reweighted least squares scheme solves the resulting problem, calling the diffusion denoiser at each proximal step. On benchmark images the method removed non-Gaussian impulse noise better than previous methods.
arxiv-2511-07023:
Junjun Pan and five co-authors address a deployment problem for graph anomaly detectors: new but perfectly normal nodes appear after training, and the detector starts raising false alarms. They trace the degradation to two causes. Semantic confusion makes unseen normal patterns look anomalous, while aggregation contamination lets unseen neighbors distort the representations of familiar nodes through message passing.

Their system, TUNE, adapts a pre-trained detector at test time without retraining or new labels. A graph aligner maps shifted data back toward the original distribution at the attribute level. It is trained by minimizing representation-level shift, with estimated aggregation contamination serving as the signal of how far things have drifted. On ten real-world data sets, TUNE greatly improved the robustness of pre-trained detectors against both synthetic and genuine unseen normal patterns.
arxiv-2511-07923:
Bingyu Li, Tao Huo, and Da Zhang segment the underwater world without training on it. Marine monitoring needs fine species and habitat maps, yet underwater datasets lag far behind land imagery. AquaOV255 supplies the missing benchmark: two hundred fifty five categories across more than twenty thousand images.

A combined benchmark joins six underwater datasets for open-vocabulary evaluation. Earth2Ocean, a training-free framework, transfers land-trained segmentation to the sea. Models must name creatures they never trained on, from text alone. Success would let ecologists survey reefs and fisheries with models that adapt by vocabulary rather than by expensive new annotation campaigns.
arxiv-2511-08023:
Nicola Menadeo, Serena Giardino, and Miguel Zumalacarregui study how clumpy space-time changes gravitational waves as they travel. Massive bodies break smooth symmetry, letting different wave polarizations interact in ways that resemble lensing. In modified gravity theories, extra mass like terms can also make wave speed depend on frequency.

The authors compute this lens induced dispersion first in general relativity for a spherical matter distribution. They then treat symmetron gravity, a screened theory that hides changes near dense bodies. Dispersion grows across much of its parameter space, and Earth itself could block or strongly alter many events for some values.
arxiv-2511-08123:
Furio Surfaro and co-authors study when liquid liquid phase separation appears in a patchy particle model switched on by ions. The model describes globular proteins in solutions with multivalent ions, a setting tied to biological condensates. Patches on each particle can differ, and that unevenness turns out to steer the whole phase diagram.

Binding energy between ions and each patch type decides whether a coexistence region grows or vanishes. Ions can shift attraction from stronger patches to weaker ones, erasing the transition in the process. New experiments on bovine serum albumin with trivalent cations fit this picture, clarifying charge driven separation in biological systems.
arxiv-2511-08323: Abhirup Chatterjee and Sobhan Kumar Sounda analyze geometric phase for three level quantum systems described by SU(3) representations. They work with mixed states of open systems undergoing depolarization. Their picture uses an eight dimensional Poincare sphere tied to SU(2) polarization ideas and non unit vector rays. The work stays within a pure state approach limit. Their results are reported to agree with the established Pancharatnam, Berry, and Aharonov Anandan formulations of geometric phase.
arxiv-2511-08823:
Wonbong Jang, Jonathan Tremblay, and Lourdes Agapito teach a diffusion model to imagine a real room or street from new camera angles after seeing only one photograph. Earlier view-synthesis systems handled small camera moves or tidy object-centered scenes, not the messy everyday places people actually photograph.

Their model, DT-NVS, is a three-dimensional-aware diffusion system built on a transformer backbone, trained with image-only losses on a large collection of casually shot real-world videos. New self-attention designs translate images into spatial representations, and fresh camera conditioning lets training work on unaligned footage. A training trick swaps which frame plays the reference role. On generalized view synthesis from a single image, the system beats earlier diffusion and deterministic methods while still producing diverse plausible views.
arxiv-2511-08923:
Jingyu Liu and eight co-authors fuse the two rival ways language models write. One is diffusion, which drafts many tokens in parallel. The other is autoregression, which picks one token at a time and usually wins on quality. Their architecture, TiDAR, thinks in diffusion and talks in autoregression inside a single forward pass.

Structured attention masks let the model draft candidate tokens with diffusion while sampling final outputs autoregressively, soaking up idle GPU capacity in the process. Exact key-value cache support keeps serving overhead low. At one point five and eight billion parameter scales, TiDAR beats speculative decoding on measured throughput and beats diffusion models such as Dream and LLaDA on both speed and quality. The headline claim is a first: autoregressive-level quality at roughly five to six times the tokens per second.
arxiv-2511-09123:
Farzad Kianvash, Marco Barbieri, and Matteo Rosati design a way to measure a phase at a remote site without trusting the channel that carries the probes. Private remote quantum sensing must estimate accurately while leaking little to an adversary who can also disturb the estimation itself.

Earlier work bounded performance by observed noise alone, but with no channel model those bounds are too loose to be useful. The new protocol uses continuous-variable states in a single-user setting, a first for this problem, and assumes a typical class of lossy attacks that measurement data can validate. Tools from quantum communication then give the true estimation error and privacy, both for many channel uses and in the finite-size regime. The realistic channel assumption tightens the guarantees to practical levels.
arxiv-2511-09223:
Panya Trakoolgerntong and six co-authors build a tool that previews links inside GitHub pull requests for code reviewers. Reviewers often get links to issues and outside resources, but automated tools usually discard those links. That forces reviewers to switch contexts and lose information when summaries are generated.

The tool, AILinkPreviewer, uses large language models to summarize linked pages, drawing on pull request titles, descriptions, comments, and link content. Across 50 engineered repositories, contextual summaries scored best on automatic metrics such as BLEU and BERTScore. Yet in a small user study, most participants preferred the non-contextual summaries for actual use. The contrast highlights a trade-off between metric performance and perceived usability in review support tools.
arxiv-2511-09423:
Nicolas Escobar-Velasquez extends Matérn random fields, a staple of spatial statistics, to fields living on tori. Matérn covariances are popular because their parameters are interpretable and their path behavior is understood in flat space. Working through pseudo-differential calculus, he first shows torus Matérn fields have exactly the Euclidean smoothness behavior.

The main results allow the operator's order to vary from place to place across the torus. The field's local smoothness at each point is set by the order there. Only the order's local germ matters for nearby regularity. A canonical test field confirms both the existence threshold and the smoothness formula. Weighting the spectral density yields mixtures of smoother ordinary Matérn fields.
arxiv-2511-09623:
Kun-Feng Lyu, Rahul Muraleedharan, and Kuver Sinha study particle scattering through the quantum links it creates, using group theory as the lens. Viewing the scattering matrix as a map between representation spaces that respects the symmetry splits pure symmetry structure from dynamics. Which operators can appear is fixed by how the input states break down.

For basic particles, only identity and swap keep products apart; generic collisions entangle. In Yang-Mills theory, color-kinematics duality pins the color kernel to a fixed ray. That yields a universal maximum entanglement for right-angle collisions, for any kinematics. Higher-dimension operators break that universality in telling ways, making color entanglement a probe of effective interactions. Requiring entanglement to survive the process even forces the Yang-Mills coupling structure and the color Jacobi identity.
arxiv-2511-09723:
Balachandra Devarangadi Sunil, Rakshith Venkatesh, and Shantanu Todmal adapt a crowd density estimation method from still images to video monitoring. Counting crowds matters for public safety and event management, but video adds temporal complexity and heavy computation. Their system generates crowd density maps with a diffusion-based denoising model.

Narrow Gaussian kernels sharpen the maps. A regression branch plus a similarity-based consolidation step combine multiple map outputs into one robust result. An event-driven sampler driven by optical flow keeps only frames with significant crowd movement, cutting computation and storage. Evaluations with overlay plots and mean absolute error show the method capturing crowd dynamics. It works in dense and sparse settings alike, aiming at real-time monitoring.
arxiv-2511-10023:
Farzan Saeedi, Sanaz Keshvari, and Nasser Shoeibi work on automated diagnosis of retinopathy of prematurity, an eye disease of premature infants where timely screening matters. Their study applies deep learning, centering on custom convolutional neural networks built for this task rather than borrowed pre-trained models. They examine data set curation, preprocessing, and design together, weighing accuracy against computing cost and running time.

The tailored networks beat pre-trained counterparts on accuracy and F1 scores, and a voting system over models improved results further. The custom design also eased the computing burden that deep networks usually impose. The authors show deployment in dedicated software and hardware setups, arguing the system can serve as a practical diagnostic aid in clinical settings.
arxiv-2511-10223:
David F. Anderson, Aidan S. Howells, and Diego Rojas La Luz analyze stochastic reaction networks whose reactions happen inside compartments that can split apart. Cells and their internal units make real chemistry non-homogeneous, so models need units with their own dynamics. Here the split rate of a unit depends on how much of a chosen species it contains, following a general approach proposed in 2020.

Earlier work handled content-independent unit dynamics and characterized when the process explodes, meaning infinitely many events in finite time. The authors show that characterization fails once contents matter. Under the assumption that the reaction network admits a linear Lyapunov function, they prove fresh sufficient conditions for non-explosivity and positive recurrence, extending the theory toward cell division and intracellular transport models.
arxiv-2511-10323:
Dávid Kószó, Tamás Aladics, Rudolf Ferenc, and Péter Hegedűs attack alert fatigue in static code analysis by building the dataset the field is missing. Analysis tools flood developers with warnings, many not worth acting on, until real bugs get ignored. Training filters needs large labeled collections, which barely exist, especially for Java. The authors present a methodology that collects warnings and categorizes them as actionable or not.

Applying it produced NASCAR, a dataset of over one million Java static analysis reports, released publicly together with the generation tools. The scale and the actionable labels are the contribution: machine learning researchers can now train and benchmark warning filters on realistic data. The authors frame the release as infrastructure for making static analysis usable again.
arxiv-2511-10423:
Jiayang Meng and four co-authors show that a common privacy defense in federated learning leaks more than expected. In federated learning, devices share model gradients rather than raw data, yet those gradients can hide the training images inside them. Adding noise to gradients is a standard defense, and older attacks lose most of their power against it.

Their attack guides a conditional diffusion model with the leaked gradient itself, using the model's natural denoising strength to undo the added noise. It needs no prior knowledge of the target data distribution. They also prove error bounds and study how noise size and model shape affect reconstruction quality. Experiments confirm reconstructions stay strong under Gaussian noise, beating earlier attacks.
arxiv-2511-10523:
Egor Pakhomov, Erik Nijkamp, and Caiming Xiong introduce Convomem, a benchmark for judging how well artificial intelligence systems remember conversations. It holds 75,336 question-answer pairs covering user facts, recall of what the assistant said, preferences, changes over time, knowing when to abstain, and implicit connections between messages.

Their experiments compare simple full-context approaches, which feed the whole conversation history to the model, against retrieval-based memory systems such as Mem0. On histories shorter than 150 conversations, full context reached 70 to 82 percent accuracy while the retrieval systems managed only 30 to 45 percent. Long context works best for roughly the first 30 conversations and stays viable to about 150, beyond which hybrid or retrieval methods become necessary as cost and delay grow.
arxiv-2511-10723:
Katya Leidig and five co-authors ask how reliably the faint outer glow of a brightest cluster galaxy can weigh its dark matter halo. The diffuse stellar halo records the galaxy's assembly history, and deep Hyper Suprime-Cam imaging has shown the stellar mass in wide annuli tracks halo mass, but the best radial definition remained unclear.

The team built a mock observing pipeline that mimics the survey on IllustrisTNG simulations, reproducing observed profiles across six orders of magnitude in surface density. Simple circular apertures scatter much more than projected ellipsoidal annuli. They identify an optimal annulus range and present Sérsic-based fitting functions that predict the profiles from halo mass, with a median error that improves when the central galaxy's stellar mass is added. The functions are meant for future wide-field surveys.
arxiv-2511-10823:
Tim Randolph and Karol Węgrzycki break a classic algorithmic barrier for subset balancing problems, a family that generalizes subset sum, partition, and equal subset sum. Given an integer vector and a small fixed set of allowed coefficients, the task is to find a nonzero coefficient assignment whose weighted sum is exactly zero.

The textbook meet-in-the-middle method sets a running-time barrier that earlier work had beaten only on average inputs. Randolph and Węgrzycki beat it in the worst case for several coefficient sets. They improve the best exact algorithm for equal subset sum by an exponential margin, answering an open question. Their machinery carries the representation technique of Howgrave-Graham and Joux from average-case to worst-case inputs. It uses new ideas for mixing, flexible representations, and recovering genuine solutions from near misses.
arxiv-2511-11623:
Yushan Jiang and seven co-authors work on predicting graft-versus-host disease after liver transplantation, a rare complication that is often fatal. Catching it early could allow treatment in time, but the disease is so uncommon that ordinary prediction models drown in data from patients who never develop it.

Records from twenty-one hundred transplant patients treated at Mayo Clinic between 1992 and 2025 include only forty-two cases of the disease. A multi-modal deep learning framework combines demographics, lab tests, diagnoses, and medications from before surgery into one risk estimate. Handling four data types at once, under heavy imbalance, is the technical core of an effort aimed at earlier warning.
arxiv-2511-12023:
N. T. Dung and N. T. Hang study stochastic Volterra equations with small noise, a class of models where the present state depends on the whole past path. They focus on how the random solution moves around its deterministic limit when the noise is small. The work gives a precise picture of that fluctuation.

Using tools from Malliavin calculus, the authors show the fluctuation follows a central limit theorem, so its spread takes a normal form in the limit. They also give an optimal estimate for how fast that limit is reached. An example with a fractional Brownian motion kernel shows how the general theory applies.
arxiv-2511-12123:
Zejiao Liu and six co-authors aim to improve how teams of learning agents explore together. In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents often explore on their own, with no coordination. That limits both what the joint policy can express and how well the team searches for better behavior.

Their framework adds a conductor that shapes the joint policy and coordinates exploration. A hierarchical method, HCPO, updates the conductor and the agents in directions tied to better joint performance, with a proof that performance moves in a steady, improving way. Local conductors keep training gains without needing messages at run time. Tests on three hard benchmarks beat strong baselines in efficiency and stability.
arxiv-2511-12523:
Adam Dziwoki and Rostislav Horcik examine what happens when the oracle inside equilibrium-finding algorithms answers with slightly wrong utilities. Double Oracle and Fictitious Play are standard methods that build toward a Nash equilibrium in zero-sum games by repeatedly adding best responses. The authors assume the best response is computed after the payoffs are perturbed.

Counter to first intuition, they show such perturbations cut the number of iterations for both algorithms. In some cases a well-chosen perturbation makes the expected iteration count logarithmic. perturbing is costly if every pure strategy must be scanned, but when strategies carry inner structure the perturbation can be done efficiently, keeping the gain practical.
arxiv-2511-12623:
Antonin Barbe, Benjamin De Bruyne and Romain Allez study how the eigenvectors of a large random matrix change when the matrix grows by a few rows and columns. They compare a Wigner matrix with its principal minor, the smaller matrix inside it, in both real symmetric and complex Hermitian cases, while the added size stays fixed as the whole grows.

Two results emerge. In the bulk of the spectrum, an eigenvector of the larger matrix projects mainly onto eigenvectors of the smaller one at the same spectral level, a stability they call local projection. At the spectral edge, the change of basis between leading eigenspaces is governed by a small random antisymmetric perturbation. Both laws are expressed with classic Airy and sine kernels, and extended to sample covariance matrices.
arxiv-2511-12723:
Gennaro Vessio proposes LAYA, a new output head for neural networks that listens to every layer, not just the last one. Standard networks base their final answer on the deepest representation alone, discarding the low-level and mid-level patterns computed earlier. LAYA instead learns attention weights over the features from all layers, tuned to each input, and blends them into the prediction that the network finally reports.

Those same weights double as an explanation: they state how much each layer contributed to a given decision, with no extra explanation tool needed. On image classification tests, LAYA matched standard performance while its layer scores tracked the true contribution of each layer in follow-up checks. The patterns it found were structured and task-dependent, showing which depths a task actually uses. The design fits many architectures, offering interpretability that comes from inside the model rather than after it.
arxiv-2511-12823:
Sajed Jalil, Shuvo Saha, and Hossain Mohammad Seym aim to open up code generation help for Bengali speakers. Bengali has hundreds of millions of native speakers, yet language models are rarely trained or tested for it, and fine-tuning tools demand expertise and money that users in emerging markets may lack. Their approach needs no fine-tuning at all. It combines test-driven development, where tests are written before code, with a code interpreter that runs and checks the generated code, using open-weight models.

With Bengali prompts, the method lifted code generation accuracy to eighty-five percent overall. Even the smallest model in a family reached nearly the accuracy of the largest when wrapped in this loop. All results are shared publicly for checking and reuse. Careful prompting workflows, rather than bigger models, can carry coding tools into low-resource language communities.
arxiv-2511-12923:
Prashasti Tiwari, Dylan Lewis, and Sougato Bose find a fast way to prepare quantum ground states. Ground states of many-body systems are valuable starting points for sensing, hardware benchmarks, and simulations, but preparing them slowly, by adiabatic change, wastes time and invites decoherence. The authors instead evolve a simple starting state for a short, fixed time under a second Hamiltonian whose couplings they tune classically to minimize energy. The question is how to scale that trick from a few qubits to many.

In studies up to fourteen qubits, the winning strategy was a warm start: take the ground state already prepared for one fewer qubit, then add the new qubit's couplings step by step. That incremental route scaled best among those tried, and it offers a concrete recipe for near-term devices.
arxiv-2511-13023:
Jiacheng Wang and five co-authors benchmark whether the compression tricks built for large language models work on small ones. Small language models are meant for phones and edge devices, but how quantization, shrinking their numbers to fewer bits, behaves at that scale was largely unexamined. SLMQuant runs multi-track evaluations of state-of-the-art quantization methods across architectures and tasks, asking where the bottlenecks sit for small models specifically.

The headline finding is that small models are not just little large models. Their quantization sensitivity differs fundamentally, and methods optimized for large models transfer suboptimally because of small models' distinct architectures and training dynamics. The authors extract the factors that govern effective small-model quantization and turn them into design principles for compression tailored to this class. For engineers, the benchmark replaces guesswork with measurements.
arxiv-2511-13223:
Yuxiang Zhang and 7 co-authors present TokenSqueeze, a way to shorten the long reasoning traces of large language models. Models such as DeepSeek-R1 gain strength from long chains of thought, but those chains cost time and memory. Earlier shortening methods often lost accuracy, so balance is the central problem here.

TokenSqueeze trains only on text the model made itself, picking samples whose depth fits each problem's difficulty. A second step rewrites the wording to be clearer and shorter without changing the logic. In tests, a seven-billion-parameter model cut token use by about half on a math benchmark while keeping its score.
arxiv-2511-13323:
Marianne Bessemoulin-Chatard, Tino Laidin, and Thomas Rey prove long-time convergence for a finite volume scheme for a nonlinear kinetic model with two interacting species. Earlier results needed data close to equilibrium and used weighted estimates in a narrow setting. The new work widens the class of starting data that still settle down over time.

Their proof leans on Boltzmann entropy and on bounds that the scheme keeps from the start thanks to its monotone design. Those bounds let them control nonlinear terms without assuming closeness to equilibrium. They also show the scheme's own time-step dissipation helps stabilize the whole argument.
arxiv-2511-13423:
Jorge Lamas studies emergent geometry in the Coherence-Curvature Model, a system of linked graphs shaped by energy rules. The model's energy couples how well a graph stays connected, its Ollivier-Ricci curvature, and a penalty on edge density. Simulated annealing at low temperature then grows the low-energy shapes whose geometry he measures.
