Benchmarks compute equilibrium lattice constants and bulk moduli for carbon, boron nitride, boron phosphide, and silicon, showing the method systematically corrects missing long-range screening in MP2 and missing higher-order exchange in RPA. RPA emerges as the optimal reference through rapid convergence of the remaining short-range part. Quantum materials simulation gains a basis-limit Monte Carlo tool.
arxiv-2602-15023:
Casey and colleagues compute gravitational wave echoes from a first-order phase change that ends a kination epoch. In the Kination-Induced Big Bang picture, a rolling scalar field drives kination rule, and the shift reheats the universe into radiation rule. Here the rolling field couples to a second tunneling field, trapping it in a false vacuum until Hubble friction slows the first field enough to trigger the change.

The team derives the stochastic background from bubble nucleation and collisions. They give analytic estimates and numerical values for peak amplitude and frequency, bounded above by the bubble percolation condition. The signal spans nanohertz to megahertz frequencies, so it can speak to pulsar timing array reports and face tests from LISA, Advanced LIGO, Cosmic Explorer, and BBO. Notably, the change can occur even when the bare tunneling potential holds a single minimum, since the coupling itself creates metastability.
arxiv-2602-15123:
Bichang'a and colleagues identify active galactic nuclei in massive galaxies through optical broadband variability, drawing lessons from VST-COSMOS for future LSST science. They study 56 massive galaxies hosting AGN, detected by variability in the VST-COSMOS survey. That survey offers nearly the same single-visit depth and eleven-year baseline as the forthcoming Legacy Survey of Space and Time, over a footprint four orders of magnitude smaller.

AGN hosts are compared with a control sample of non-variable galaxies matched in redshift and stellar mass. About 55 percent of AGN show early-type morphology and about 23 percent show interactions, similar to controls, suggesting interactions do not mainly trigger these AGN. Colors and local environments also match controls closely, so recent star formation histories and surroundings look typical. The study previews LSST AGN science, where vastly larger statistics may reshape understanding of AGN demographics, host evolution, and black hole fueling.
arxiv-2602-15423:
Fu and colleagues offer GaiaFlow, a setup built to ease search by using meaning-guided spread tweaking. As juice needs of fancy machine designs climb, the data finding crowd has seen green staying power as a key must needing a model change in tool plan. While current machine raters have hit unmatched scores, the big green costs linked with their compute heat often stay missed in rollouts.

Their method joins the meeting of finding-guided Langevin motion and a hardware-free speed model plan to tune the trade-off between search care and green saving. By adding tunable quick exit rules and care-aware shrunk guessing, the offered design greatly cuts running carbon marks while keeping strong finding grade across mixed machine rigs. Wide test trials show GaiaFlow hits a better balance between power and juice thrift, giving a growing green path for next-making machine search nets.
arxiv-2602-15523:
Acharyya and Kar study a memory effect in regular black hole spacetimes, where a passing wave pulse leaves test particles permanently shifted. They model the pulse with a function H(u) inside a restricted Bondi-Sachs type line element, choosing a sech-squared pulse shape. First they work out geodesic separation and deviation in flat space by numerical means, then they repeat the study far from a black hole horizon.

The results point to a distinct displacement memory that hinges on the regularisation parameter g and on pulse height, and that shifts between kinds of regular black holes. At large u, regular and singular black holes also show a clear gap in memory size. The paper gives relativists a concrete, parameter-sensitive signature to compare across black hole models.
arxiv-2602-15823:
Ikram and colleagues tackle skill preservation in large language model editing. Edits aimed at one behaviour can silently exploit the proxy used to judge them, damaging abilities in ways that look like proxy and reward hacking. Their CrispEdit algorithm is scalable and principled, second-order, and treats skill preservation as an explicit cap. Editing is capped tuning, enforced by mapping edit updates onto the low-bend space of the skill-loss terrain.

CrispEdit expresses the skill constraint through a Bregman gap, whose quadratic form gives the Gauss-Newton Hessian exactly, even for a base model never trained to convergence. The second-order method runs fast at language model scale using Kronecker-factored rough bend, or K-FAC, plus a matrix-free tool using Kronecker structure to avoid huge maps. On standard benchmarks, CrispEdit succeeds at most edits while holding skill loss under 1 percent on average, well ahead of earlier editors.
arxiv-2602-16023:
Min and colleagues examine a curious corner of Korean grammar: verb based phrases that act like adpositions. Korean multiword expressions remain underrepresented in cross lingual annotation, and these adpositional forms lacked systematic study, tagged resources, and a place in multilingual frameworks.

Drawing on Korean Wikipedia, the authors survey several such phrases and contrast them with ordinary non multiword forms and with light verb forms of similar shape. The comparison clarifies what makes the verb based postpositional forms a distinct class. Building on it, they propose tagging guidelines meant to support future Korean adposition work and to ease alignment with cross lingual standards.
arxiv-2602-16323:
Jindu Wang leads a team of six coauthors on a study of rest breaks taken through augmented reality glasses. Young adults often spend screen breaks on their phones, and that habit cuts against rest, since it brings eye strain and long sitting. The team offers a design framework that weaves light break activities into media shown on AR smart glasses, so breaks stay engaging and restorative.

The framework rests on three moves. Activity cues match what is on screen, guiding users without jarring interruption. Sessions shift toward sound-led formats that ease visual load and keep users absorbed. A rise-peak-closure pacing shapes each session for smooth transitions. In a study of sixteen volunteers, InteractiveBreak guided activities smoothly, held engagement, and improved break quality over passive viewing, reminder breaks, and non-narrative activities. The paper argues that wearable AR can turn breaks into experiences that genuinely restore.
arxiv-2602-16423:
Zhi-Tian Zou leads three coauthors studying quasi-two-body decays of a charged B meson to a Ds meson and kaon pair via an intermediate resonance. A search for this decay has been reported by the LHCb Collaboration, using proton-proton data without kaon pair analysis. The authors analyze resonant contributions in the perturbative QCD factorization framework.

Three S-wave, one P-wave, and two D-wave resonances contribute. By introducing two-meson distribution amplitudes, the authors carry out a perturbative analysis of the quasi-two-body decays. They present first perturbative QCD predictions for branching fractions. Using the narrow-width approximation, they extract branching fractions for two-body decays to a Ds meson plus a resonance. Their results agree with experiments and earlier theoretical studies. Direct CP asymmetries vanish for these decays within the Standard Model, so any observed nonzero asymmetry would signal physics beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2602-16623:
Howard Su and co-authors propose Multi-Layer Fully-Connected Variational Quantum Circuits, a general quantum learning frame. Quantum circuits face a tug between power, ease of training, and scale. The design links local quantum blocks by checks, free routing, and re-encoding, with all tuned values inside the quantum blocks and no tuned classical net parts.

The authors test fully linked, sliding-window, and parallel block mixing, with cost, error spread, and info swap study. Classical runs cover tabular tasks and space-time function fits, with Black-Scholes, Burgers, and wavy partial differential laws up to many space dims. The frame wins on trajectory error at the top dims tried, with checks on training ease and noise response.
arxiv-2602-16823:
Itamar Hadad, Guy Katz, and Shahaf Bassan bring provable guarantees to automated circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability. Circuit discovery names the inner net parts behind specific acts, but prior routes lean on heuristics or approximations and offer no guarantees over smooth input zones. The paper uses recent net verification advances to build codes yielding circuits with provable guarantees.

Three guarantee kinds are treated. Input domain robustness means circuit-model accord across a smooth input zone. Robust patching means certified accord under smooth patching tweaks. Minimality means formal, varied notions of succinctness. Novel theory links among the three kinds shape code convergence. Tests with top verifiers on vision models show much stronger robustness than standard circuit discovery routes.
arxiv-2602-17123:
Sun Mao led a six-author team managing scarce network resources for augmented reality in the Metaverse. Immersive AR service strains limited bandwidth and fickle wireless channels. The paper builds a resource framework around a simultaneously transmitting and reflecting surface, or STAR-RIS. It improves links between AR users and the Metaverse server at the base station.

The team formulates service latency minimization over base station compute, the STAR-RIS coefficient matrix, user processor frequencies, and user transmit power. An approximate reformulation plus alternating optimization makes the non-convex problem tractable. The coefficient matrix comes from a penalty method with proven convergence. Frequencies fall out in closed form, and power plus compute come from duality and convex optimization. Simulations showed remarkable latency cuts against several benchmarks.
arxiv-2602-17423:
Afroditi Kolomvaki led a five-author team on training two-layer neural networks with masked inputs. Masked inputs mirror Gaussian dropout at the input level. They also match noisy-input training common in sensor networks, privacy-preserving training, and federated learning, where each user may see only part of the features or corrupted versions of them.

Using Neural Tangent Kernel analysis, the team shows a two-layer ReLU network with Gaussian masked inputs converges linearly, up to an error zone sized by the mask's variance. The hard part was handling the randomness inside the nonlinear activation, a problem of interest on its own. The result gives a firm guarantee for a training setup that shows up across sensors, privacy work, and federated systems.
arxiv-2602-17623:
Alireza Sakhaeirad and team probe a gap in Persian language models: the split between recalled cultural facts and sound judgment about implicit social norms. Past benchmarks grew into pragmatics and politeness, yet rarely drew that line. Their new diagnostic tool, DivanBench, centers on superstitions and customs, rules that are arbitrary and tied to context.

Across hundreds of questions in three task types, seven Persian models show three key flaws. Most models agree too readily, spotting apt conduct but failing to reject clear breaches. More Persian pretraining deepens that bias instead of fixing it. All models score far worse when they must apply facts in scenes than when they merely recall them. Cultural skill, the authors argue, needs more than larger monolingual data.
arxiv-2602-18223:
The CMS Collaboration searches for a new heavy particle that decays into a Higgs boson plus a second scalar boson. Their 2026 paper uses proton-proton collision data at thirteen tera-electron-volts collected by CMS, covering a large collected dataset. The search covers both a new scalar and the case where the second particle is another Higgs boson.

One Higgs candidate is picked out through its decay to bottom quarks. The other is picked through decays to Z boson pairs, with one Z decaying to leptons and the other to quarks or neutrinos. Machine-learning scores plus the rebuilt resonance mass separate signal from background across boost-based categories. No clear excess over standard predictions appears, so the team sets ninety-five percent confidence caps on production rates, tightest for heavy parents and second scalars near the vector-boson threshold.
arxiv-2602-18523:
Yongzhong Xu maps multi-task grokking geometry. His 2026 paper notes grokking, the abrupt shift from memorization to generalization after near-zero training loss, is mainly single-task. Xu extends geometric analysis to multi-task modular arithmetic.

Five findings emerge. First, staggered order: multiplication first, then squaring, then addition. Second, trajectories stay confined to an invariant low-dimensional manifold, with orthogonal defects first. Third, grokking timescale, curvature depth, and defect lead covary with weight decay, revealing distinct regimes. Fourth, final solutions occupy only four to eight principal directions yet spread across full-rank weights, breaking under small changes. Fifth, removing under ten percent of orthogonal gradients eliminates grokking, yet dual-task models partly recover. Together, the results support a dynamical picture of multi-task grokking building a compact subspace, with weight decay as compression pressure and excess parameters as redundancy.
arxiv-2602-18823:
Judging a language model with another language model is now common. But the judge itself can be misconfigured or biased, especially for open-ended tasks where standard metrics fall short. Adam Dejl, with one co-author, presents EvalSense in 2026. It is a flexible framework for building domain-specific evaluation suites. It offers an interactive guide for choosing evaluation methods and automated meta-evaluation tools that probe reliability using perturbed data.

The framework supports many model providers and evaluation strategies out of the box. It helps users select and deploy methods suited to their own use case rather than defaulting to a single judge. A case study on generating clinical notes from unstructured doctor-patient dialogues shows the approach in a sensitive domain. All code, documentation, and assets are open source, inviting reuse and scrutiny.
arxiv-2602-19123:
Street trees matter for cities, but no benchmark covers them at scale. Jiapeng Li, with three co-authors, fills that gap in 2026 with StreetTree, the first large-scale benchmark for fine-grained street-tree classification. Over twelve million images span thousands of common species. Collection covers urban streetscapes across over one hundred countries on five continents. Expert-verified observations supplement the images.

Pretrained vision models face hard challenges here. Species look alike, distributions skew long-tailed, seasons change appearance, and imaging conditions vary widely. A hierarchical taxonomy from order to species supports structured research. Extensive experiments set solid baselines and expose current limits. Urban planning, streetscape management, and ecosystem assessment all gain a shared resource.
arxiv-2602-19323:
A 3D scene built from Gaussian splats can look superb, yet tiny consistent tweaks to input views can wreck it. Yiran Qiao and six co-authors study 3D Gaussian Splatting, where imperceptible adversarial changes degrade rendering, slow training and rendering, inflate memory, and can even deny service. Their defense, DefenseSplat, starts from wavelet analysis showing that adversarial effects behave differently in low- and high-frequency image parts.

The method filters out high-frequency noise and keeps low-frequency content, rebuilding training views so artifacts are suppressed and the scene stays authentic. It needs no clean ground-truth supervision and barely harms training on clean data, a welcome trade-off. Across attack intensities and benchmarks, robustness improves substantially, pointing toward more secure 3D reconstruction.
arxiv-2602-19623:
Text-to-video tools promise to open up content creation, yet most chase visual polish over teaching power. Injun Baek and two co-authors present PedaCo-Gen, a human-AI joint system for writing instructional videos grounded in Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML). Instead of one-shot generation, it adds an Intermediate Representation phase where teachers review and refine video blueprints, scripts plus visual descriptions, with an AI reviewer.

A study with 23 education experts finds PedaCo-Gen lifts video quality across topics and CTML principles over baselines. Experts read the AI guidance as a metacognitive scaffold that sharpened their design skill, not just a set of orders, rating production efficiency at 4.26, with guide validity at 4.04. Readers get a case for principled co-creation that keeps teachers in charge of pedagogy.
arxiv-2602-19923:
Optimization on curved spaces needs maps that let algorithms step along the space, and the Stiefel manifold of orthogonal frames is a common setting. A 2026 arXiv paper by Rasmus Jensen and Ralf Zimmermann introduces a new polar factor retraction on the compact Stiefel manifold.

The new retraction is accurate to second order under the Euclidean metric and has a closed-form inverse that computes fast. Among known Stiefel retractions, the Cayley retraction already pairs second-order accuracy with a closed-form inverse, but under the canonical metric, not the Euclidean one. The new map is the first to combine both features under the Euclidean metric. Tests confirm its properties against many rivals, and the authors test it for interpolation and for finding a Riemannian barycenter.
arxiv-2602-20023:
Matrix multiplication underpins machine learning, graphics, signal processing, and graph algorithms. Twin-width is a unifying complexity measure for matrices. A 2026 arXiv paper by László Kozma and Michal Opler gives a fast multiplication method for matrices of bounded twin-width.

Twin-width stays unchanged when rows and columns are reordered. Most prior algorithms assume the input arrives in a canonical ordering with a bounded contraction sequence. Finding such a sequence is a central open problem. The authors show a binary square matrix of twin-width d can be readied in near-quadratic time. Its product with any vector then takes near-linear time, without knowing the twin-width or assuming any ordering. With a canonical ordering available, both steps speed up further. Two matrices can then be multiplied in near-quadratic time when at least one is binary with bounded twin-width, even under adversarial corruption.
arxiv-2602-20123:
Near-term quantum devices are noisy, and quantum error correction offers a path toward fault tolerance, with surface codes the ubiquitous choice for their efficacy. A 2026 arXiv paper by Maxwell Poster and two co-authors addresses a subtler problem: hardware error rates vary across space and time, so logical qubits sitting still experience uneven error.

Surface codes run circuits through lattice surgery. Lattice surgery also lets logical qubits move around the architecture where space allows. Moving logical qubits around the topology enforces an average logical error rate. The paper proposes cyclic qubit mappings. CQM is a dynamic remapping technique applied during compilation. It mitigates uneven hardware by expanding and contracting logical qubits. Beyond averaging the logical error rate, the technique shows initial promise given its minimal execution overhead.
arxiv-2602-20323:
Haoyang Li and three co-authors present PhysMem, a memory framework that lets robot planners learn physics from interaction at test time. Vision-language planners can reason about friction and stability in general, but they often fail to predict how a specific ball rolls on a given surface or which stone makes a stable base. PhysMem records experiences, proposes candidate hypotheses, and verifies them through targeted interaction before using them.

Verification before application is the central design choice: hypotheses are tested against new observations rather than applied from memory directly. That choice reduces rigid reliance on past experience when conditions change, and it needs no model-parameter updates. On a controlled brick-insertion task, principled abstraction reached seventy-six percent success against twenty-three percent for direct experience retrieval. Real-world tests across three manipulation tasks and four vision-language backbones showed consistent gains over thirty-minute sessions.
arxiv-2602-21023:
Robinson spaces rank their items by gap size, and workers want to draw them true in flat spaces of few directions. Francisco Arrepol, Mauricio Soto-Gomez, and Christopher Thraves Caro study that drawing problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. The goal is to keep ranked gap links, not exact values, and low-direction Euclidean spaces are the natural first tries.

Earlier work showed not every Robinson space draws on the real line, so the authors turn to real trees, which keep low-direction readability with more give. Two tools drive the work: a counting-based picture of Robinson spaces and a shape-based portrait of caterpillars, a narrow class of real trees. Some subkinds always draw on a caterpillar, yet some Robinson spaces draw on no real tree at all.
arxiv-2602-21123:
The variable-length double swing blends the classic double swing with the swinging Atwood machine, giving rich bent conduct. Wojciech Szuminski and Tomasz Kapitaniak study its motion in this 2026 arXiv paper, building on earlier work on the double-spring swing. Their new tool, Lyapunov refined maps, joins Poincare sections, dial-based phase diagrams, and Lyapunov rates.

That setup maps repeating, quasi-repeating, and chaotic conduct and gauges chaos strength. Morales-Ramis theory plus the Kovacic method then set non-solving rules under certain dials. The work pushes swing motion, with possible uses in tunable robots, energy gathering, and body-motion work, and steps toward proving non-solving of the classic double swing.
arxiv-2602-21223:
How we word prompts shifts model conduct even when the task stays the same. Yilin Geng, Omri Abend, Eduard Hovy, and Lea Frermann gauge that wording frame in this 2026 arXiv paper. Phrases like urgent appeals or expert-voice claims shift conduct with no change in task content, yet framing itself has rarely been gauged in order.

Their setup splits framing context from task brief, sorts four hundred framing cases into thirteen plays across four tool groups, and gauges sway through shifts in order ranking. Tests on five open-weight models show orderly shifts with play rankings highly steady across models. Openness to framing emerges as a set trait of prompt-tuned systems, and gauging it is a first step for answering on purpose.
arxiv-2602-21923:
Soham Acharya, Shuvayu Roy, and Sudipta Sarkar study tiny black holes formed in the early universe as possible dark matter. Some such holes, recent work suggests, can survive to today by gaining spin as they shed light and heat, reaching a near-maximal spin before they fade away. The authors test whether that survival story still holds when gravity itself carries small corrections from an effective field theory.

They model the shedding process as a biased random walk and find that nearly the same share of holes survives as in plain general relativity. Fast spin, they warn, could still expose a near-horizon watcher to extreme tidal forces. Those forces, they argue, might show up in future gravitational wave data, giving the idea a possible observational test.
arxiv-2602-22023:
A wave packet of a scalar field that moves faster than light breaks the usual energy rules of physics, at least on paper. Kevin Restrepo Tobón and Antonio Enea Romano study such a constant-speed Gaussian packet in flat spacetime, then reframe it through an effective speed approach. That reframing yields a new effective metric, Lagrangian, and stress-energy tensor, letting them test energy rules in the packet's own terms.

The authors find the source behind the speed change behaves like a perfect fluid with a negative equation of state, a strange but precisely defined kind of matter. The paper thus offers a clean test bed for asking what faster-than-light field motion would demand of physics. Readers get a careful, self-contained tour of a provocative edge case, not a claim that such motion is real.
arxiv-2602-22123:
In 1977 Makanin proved equations in free monoids are decidable, using a quantity called the exponent of periodicity: how often a block repeats inside a word. Volker Diekert and two co-authors carry the similar question to quadratic equations in finitely generated groups, using normal forms to define repeat counts there. The open question is whether infinitely many solutions force solutions with ever-larger repeat counts.

The authors identify group traits that guarantee ever-larger repeat counts for infinite solution sets of quadratic systems. They also show those traits survive in the groups built this way. The result charts where Makanin's phenomenon extends beyond free monoids, and where it may fail.
arxiv-2602-22223:
Text-to-SQL systems turn plain questions into database queries, but training them needs large datasets with realistic schemas and varied questions. Cornelius Wolff and two co-authors introduce SQaLe, a semi-synthetic dataset built by expanding a collection of real-world schemas. A principled pipeline combines schema sampling, question synthesis, and SQL construction to produce over half a million triples.

SQaLe spans over a hundred thousand schemas, capturing realistic size variation, diverse query patterns, and natural-language ambiguity while keeping every query executable. The authors present it as the most realistic large-scale text-to-SQL dataset to date. Model builders gain a far richer training ground for systems that must face real databases.
arxiv-2602-22523:
Ryan Liu and five co-authors argue that building better language agents starts with better blueprints. Single large language models, however strong alone, still fail hard tasks, and there is no settled way to combine many models into one capable whole. Their position paper proposes an agent template: a plan that names each model's role and how the parts fit together.

The authors then survey existing language agents and trace their templates back to cognitive models of mind and to classic artificial intelligence algorithms. By naming these borrowed designs, they aim to give builders a shared toolkit for agents that are more effective and easier to understand than ad hoc assemblies of models.
arxiv-2602-22623:
Xingyu Lu and fourteen co-authors attack two weak spots in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multimodal models. First, reward models can be fooled by right answers reached through poor reasoning, a false-positive problem. Second, groups where every attempt fails give no learning signal, leaving knowledge undiscovered.

ContextRL answers both with context augmentation. The reward model receives full reference solutions, enabling fine-grained checks that filter false positives. For failed groups, it writes mistake reports that guide the policy to recover correct answers across turns. On eleven perception and reasoning benchmarks, ContextRL lifted knowledge discovery sharply. A Qwen3-VL model with 8 billion parameters matched a 32-billion-parameter model, beating standard baselines by a wide margin while curbing reward hacking.
arxiv-2602-22723:
Frances Yung and four co-authors compare two ways to handle human disputes in discourse relation labelling. Many language tasks have no single ground truth, since raters see things in other ways. Some models predict full label spreads, while person-based models mimic single raters.

On implicit discourse relation recognition, a very fuzzy task, the team finds single-rater models falter unless the fuzz is first reduced. Models trained on spreads prove steadier. A closer look shows frequent hard-thinking cases drive most mismatch, with disputes here stemming from mental complexity rather than ideology, a hard lesson for person-based work.
arxiv-2602-22823:
Anirudh Thatipelli and one co-author cluster functions without letting the sampling grid decide the answer. Most functional-data clustering works on sampled grids, so groupings shift with resolution, sampling density, or preprocessing rather than reflecting the functions themselves.

The framework maps discretized observations at any resolution and on any grid into a fixed-size vector space through auto-encoding. A hypernetwork encoder turns coordinate-value pairs into weights of an implicit neural representation that serves as decoder. Since such representations need very few parameters, the resulting codes stay compact and grid-free, while the hypernetwork shares weight prediction across the dataset. Clustering then runs in weight space with standard methods, robust to resolution changes including unseen resolutions.
arxiv-2602-23023:
Alexandra Carpentier and one co-author study the computational limits of clustering in moderate dimension. The problem clusters points drawn from a mixture of isotropic Gaussians, asking how far apart the group means must sit for partial recovery of the hidden partition. The minimax-optimal threshold is known, yet a gap persists between that information-theoretic limit and known polynomial-time methods.

While the high-dimensional regime was recently characterized, the moderate-dimensional case stayed largely unexplored. The authors prove a new low-degree polynomial lower bound when dimension reaches at least the number of groups, showing the difficulty turns on delicate phenomena yielding a non-parametric rate. A novel non-spectral algorithm matches that rate, clarifying what efficient clustering can achieve here.
arxiv-2602-23423:
Aniket Sanghi and 14 co-authors report the most sensitive direct imaging search yet for epsilon Eridani b, the nearest Jupiter analog, using JWST NIRCam coronagraphy at four to five microns. The team reaches five-sigma contrast near three times ten to the minus seven at about one arcsecond, the deepest at these separations, over ten times better than ground limits. Yet the planet remains elusive to imaging.

The star's age is revised to one point one billion years via gyrochronology, older than prior estimates. That puts the planet at 150 to 200 kelvin for one Jupiter mass. The non-detection fits a metal-rich atmosphere, water ice clouds, or both, per Sonora and PICASO models. Both options mirror Jupiter's atmosphere. Alternatively, without the dynamical mass, a smaller, solar-metallicity, cloud-free planet would also fit the limit. The team also limits a potential ring system.
arxiv-2602-24223:
Abisheka Pitumpe and Amir Rahmati present Anansi, a scalable end-to-end pipeline, the first of its kind, for systematically engaging with and characterizing message-based job scams. The 2026 paper addresses job-based smishing, a rapidly growing and understudied fraud threat in which victims are recruited as if for remote work.

Anansi combines large language models, automated browser agents, and infrastructure fingerprinting to collect tens of thousands of scam messages. It interacts with thousands of scammers and extracts behavioral, financial, and infrastructural signals at scale. The analysis details scammer workflows and social engineering tactics used to defraud victims. Message templates, domains, and cryptocurrency wallets are reused extensively. Losses reach millions of dollars in cryptocurrency, aided by deceptive techniques such as domain fronting and brand impersonation. The pipeline demonstrates that automated engagement with scammers can ground large-scale fraud research in real ecosystem data.
arxiv-2603-00023: Ren, Roy and Ma study dueling optimisation, where only value match-ups are on hand, over Riemannian manifolds rather than Euclidean space. Their Riemannian Dueling Normalized Gradient Descent method comes with iteration complexity under geodesic smoothness or convexity. A projection-free Frank-Wolfe variant handles settings where that step is banned, with step and oracle costs shown. Tests on made-up and real uses confirm both methods work well.
arxiv-2603-00123: Gu and colleagues present CT-Flow, an agentic system that orchestrates CT reading through Model Context Protocol servers instead of single-pass inference. It breaks complex plain-language queries into automated tool-use sequences, drawing on measurement, radiomics and segmentation tools as radiologists refine findings. Built on the CT-FlowBench benchmark for 3D CT tool use, it beats baselines by 41% in diagnostic accuracy, with a 95% success rate in autonomous tool calls.
arxiv-2603-00423: Min and four colleagues build InstructX2X, a medical image editor that answers what if questions by changing only the disease region, leaving demographic traits untouched. Past editors leak changes into demographics and hide their reasoning. Region specific editing plus a Guidance Map that shows where and why edits happen give users a readable trail. A new expert checked instruction set from medical question pairs supports training, and chest X-ray tests lead rival methods across major scores.
arxiv-2603-00523: Parekh reframes neural circuit discovery as uncertainty over explanations, since a circuit shifts with the analyst's pruning threshold yet is usually treated as ground truth. CIRCUS prunes one attribution graph under many settings, scores each edge by how often it survives, and keeps only edges present in every view. That split separates robust core structure from threshold sensitive artefacts and noise at negligible cost. On Gemma-2-2B and Llama-3.2-1B, consensus circuits run forty times smaller than the union of views while keeping comparable explanatory power, confirmed by activation patching.
arxiv-2603-00623: Yang and fourteen colleagues make long agent run traces diagnosable, since hand review cannot scale and raw traces swamp language models with length and shaky logic. TraceSIR uses three helpers: one compacts traces into a TraceFormat sketch that keeps key acts, one pinpoints faults and causes with fix hints, and one gathers findings into full reports. A TraceBench test spans three real world agent settings.
arxiv-2603-00723: Sreekantan reproves Rohrlich's generalisation of the Manin-Drinfeld theorem to Fermat curves, following Elkik's mixed Hodge theory proof for modular curves. The classical result says degree zero divisors on modular curve cusps are torsion in the Jacobian. The same methods then extend the result to higher codimensional null homologous cycles and higher Chow cycles on Fermat varieties. The note unifies curve and higher dimensional cases under one elegant argument.
arxiv-2603-00823: Pan and Wang test whether LLM erasure stays stable under live multi turn use, rather than static single turn tests. They examine two common patterns, self fix and chat based questions, and find knowledge that looks lost in static tests can often come back through use. Stronger erasure lifts surface strength but often yields rigid conduct rather than genuine knowledge loss. Their findings suggest static tests inflate real world impact and highlight the need for lasting loss in live use.
arxiv-2603-00923: Liang, Mawkanuli, and Levow build a two-stage pipeline for glossing Jungar Tuvan, a low-resource Turkic language where annotated text is a fieldwork bottleneck. A neural sequence labeler drafts morpheme glosses, then a language model corrects them, with retrieval-chosen examples beating random ones. Surprisingly, adding a morpheme dictionary mostly hurts, while more examples help logarithmically, and the hybrid cuts annotation workload substantially.
arxiv-2603-01023: Li and four colleagues build an open-source modular benchmark for diffusion-based motion planning inside real autonomous-driving stacks, not just standalone simulators. They split a monolithic planner of over eighteen thousand nodes into three runnable modules. They rebuild its solver loop in native C++, enabling runtime tuning and per-step inspection within ROS 2 and Autoware. Encoder caching cuts latency more than threefold, and second-order solving cuts final displacement error by 41 percent at three steps.
arxiv-2603-01323: Zhao and four colleagues propose usable schemes for remote making four- and eight-level equator states in complex Hilbert spaces exactly. They use a set of right-angle test bases. Both pre-shared fully and partly linked states are covered, and three-, five-, six-, and seven-level equator states follow by tuning the desired state's settings. Tests suggest the high-level remote making schemes might work with current tech, and gathering steps can be avoided by coding the computing basis in single-photon spatial modes.
arxiv-2603-01623:
Diffusion models make fine images and video, but each output takes many slow passes through a large network. Jiaqi Han, Juntong Shi, Puheng Li, and colleagues cut that cost in this 2026 work by forecasting hidden features. Past tricks reuse old features for a few steps, yet errors grow fast when skips stretch far.

Their method, Spectrum, views hidden features as curves over time and fits them with smooth basis curves. A small regression sets the curve weights, which then forecast features many steps ahead at once. Theory gives an error bound that does not balloon as the skip grows. On top image and video models, the method runs several times faster than normal. Sample quality stays well above rival speed-up tricks at the same pace.
arxiv-2603-01923:
Ronaldo Gomes, Jairo Ribeiro, Luiz Queiroz, and Thiago Alves Rocha speed up formal explanations of neural network decisions. Their 2026 work uses logic-based methods, which promise correct and non-redundant reasons for a prediction. Those guarantees come at high compute cost, worst of all for large networks.

The team combines bound propagation with constraint simplification to cut that cost. Propagation tightens the known bounds on each neuron activity range. Simplifications drawn from those bounds then remove binary variables the solver no longer needs. Leaner constraints mean the explanation search finishes much faster in practice. Experiments suggest explanation time falls sharply, with the largest gains on bigger networks. Faster formal explanations make guaranteed reasoning about network calls more usable in real tools.
arxiv-2603-02323:
Noam Ophir and Anna Keselman study a three-particle liquid in flat semiconductors in this 2026 paper. A trion binds two electrons to one hole, or the reverse, through strong electric pulls. In doped flat materials, many trions might flow together as a liquid. The authors ask where such a liquid forms and how experiments could spot it.

The liquid arises near the border between a normal insulator and an exciton insulator. Photoemission, which knocks electrons out and maps their energies, should reveal it. A partly filled trion band leaves a mark inside the energy gap, fading at the Fermi edge. Exact calculations on a one-dimensional model back those claims. The marks give experimentalists a concrete target to search for.
arxiv-2603-02423:
Tadahiro Kimura and Tim Lichtenberg model water in the envelopes of young planets in this 2026 paper. Growing planets with magma oceans can make water where rock meets air. That coupling could enrich their hydrogen envelopes before the birth disc fades. The authors track solid growth, gas capture, water exchange, and later escape over time.

For planets above Earth mass, water output is capped by the magma's oxygen supply. Production usually stops before the disc disperses. Fresh hydrogen then dilutes envelopes back toward hydrogen-rich mixes, whatever the magma's starting state. That cap sets a firm ceiling on envelope water share. Only Earth-mass planets under strong escape grow water-richer later. Truly water-rich sub-Neptunes would need late delivery or giant impacts, they argue.
arxiv-2603-02523:
Andrii Iurov, Liubov Zhemchuzhna, Godfrey Gumbs, and Danhong Huang study plasmons in a Lieb lattice in this 2026 paper. Plasmons are collective waves of electrons in a material. The Lieb lattice has an unusual band structure with a gap and a flat band. That flat band touches the conduction band at its lowest point.

The team computes plasmon energies and damping across many conditions numerically. A free-standing layer is tested at several doping levels. Monolayer variants coupled to a surface wave on a conductor are also covered. Fully long-lived plasmon modes appear with unusual energy patterns, they report. Static screening in the lattice is mapped in detail too. Predicted traits differ from a related material family, resembling graphene instead.
arxiv-2603-02623:
Senwei Xie, Yuntian Zhang, Ruiping Wang, and Xilin Chen build a self-evolving skill library for robots in this 2026 paper. Skill-based robots generalize by composing learned skills into plans. Fixed libraries, though, fail on tasks needing skills nobody preloaded. Their framework, Uni-Skill, requests new skill code when the library falls short.

A repository called SkillFolder supplies the raw material for new skills. It organizes skills in a hierarchy inspired by verb classes, across levels of abstraction. Large-scale robot videos are annotated in an automated way to fill that taxonomy. Retrieved examples give semantic guidance and fine path references for new skills. Few-shot inference then builds skills with no demos at run time. Tests in simulation and the real world beat prior skill systems, with strong zero-shot transfer.
arxiv-2603-02923:
Van Cuong Le, Duc Ninh Le, and Thi Nhung Dao compute how often three W bosons at the Large Hadron Collider share the same spin alignment. Their 2026 paper gives the first results for triply polarized WWW events, calculated at leading order with fully leptonic decays. Polarization fractions reveal how the bosons were produced and how they decay.

The fully transverse combination dominates, at about half of all events. The fully longitudinal mix is rarest, near one percent, and interference between polarization states adds a small positive share. The opposite-charge process behaves much the same. Drawing on known corrections for two-boson cases, the authors expect the tiny longitudinal share to stay small, making it very hard to measure at the LHC.
arxiv-2603-03223:
Naoya Kuroda, Kenji Ishihara, Tomoya Shiota, and Wataru Mizukami stretch a shared atom model to ninety-seven elements. Such learned models mimic first-rate physics at a sliver of the cost. But heavy elements key to nuclear work, above all minor actinides, were missing from the training data.

The team built a new heavy-element dataset from past lab and computing work. They merged it with known molecule and crystal sets. The open model then scored well on standard tests of crystals and organic matter. It also showed promise on the heavy elements themselves. With actinides at last inside a shared model, teams can screen new nuclear fuels and ceramics far faster than before.
arxiv-2603-03423:
Luigi C Bresciani, Paride Paradisi, and Andrea Sainaghi reassess how strongly pure theory constrains possible new physics. The Standard Model Effective Field Theory packages unknown high-energy effects as extra operators built from known fields. Their 2026 paper asks when those operators would break perturbative unitarity, the basic consistency rule that scattering probabilities stay sane, which caps how large the effects can be.

A new formalism using spinor-helicity methods derives partial-wave bounds for generic scattering processes with any number of incoming and outgoing particles. In several cases the theory bounds already beat experimental ones at energies above a few trillion electron volts. Four-fermion operators are the standout: under realistic flavor assumptions, extra relations called sum rules strengthen their bounds further. The reassessment gives experimenters a sharper map of where new physics can still hide.
arxiv-2603-03823:
Jialong Chen and four colleagues grade coding agents on keeping a codebase alive, not just fixing it once. Real software matures through requirement changes and feature iterations over months, a reality one-shot repair benchmarks miss entirely. Their 2026 benchmark, SWE-CI, is the first built on the continuous integration loop: agents must shepherd real repositories through their actual development histories, dozens of rounds of analysis and coding per task.

One hundred tasks come from real projects whose histories average most of a year and dozens of consecutive commits. The guiding insight is that maintainability reveals itself over time, in how functional correctness holds up as the code evolves. An agent that patches brilliantly but poisons the future fails here. The benchmark offers the field its first systematic look at long-term code stewardship by machines.
arxiv-2603-04023: Chakraborti and others show nonlinear magnetotransport probes persistent spin textures in spin-orbit-coupled systems. Persistent spin textures give symmetry-set momentum-independent spin angles with long spin lifetimes, yet direct probes are scarce since usual quantum-shape replies are heavily muted. The authors show these systems isolate spin-rotation quantum shape, leaving only that shape driving nonlinear magnetic-current and spin-magnet replies.
arxiv-2603-04123: Oh and others present FINEST, improving language model replies to sensitive topics. Large language models often answer sensitive topics with overly cautious vague replies, sacrificing helpfulness for safety, and current methods lack pinpointing. FINEST is a fine-grained taxonomy evaluating replies to sensitive topics, splitting helpfulness and harmlessness into Content, Logic, and Appropriateness errors. In tests on Korean-sensitive questions, a FINEST-guided pipeline using scores and errors aids replies across kinds, beating unguided refinement. Score-based gain, giving per-category scores with justifications, yields the largest gain.
arxiv-2603-04223: Chong and Feng present semi-supervised making learning via latent space distribution matching. They present Latent Space Distribution Matching, a new semi-supervised making models method for conditional spreads. Theoretically, they prove non-asymptotic error bounds and show a key benefit of unpaired data: stronger shape fidelity in generated outputs.
arxiv-2603-04523: Rodriguez and colleagues train interatomic potentials with curvature via Projected Hessian Learning. Hessians encode richer surface curvature than energies and forces, but full Hessian training scales quadratically in cost and memory. PHL injects curvature using only Hessian vector products, projecting along stochastic probes with an unbiased trace loss and favourable scaling. Benchmarks on diverse reactants, products, transition states, reaction paths, and sampled geometries compare energy force, HVP, and full Hessian training. With randomized probes, HVP schemes match full Hessian accuracy while running over 24 times faster per epoch on small molecules.
arxiv-2603-04623: Dias and colleagues stamp large-area 2D materials onto patterned surfaces. Thin 2D matter draws wide focus for unique electronic and optical traits. Early work used tiny exfoliated flakes, while gold-aided exfoliation now yields large monolayers. Transfer onto flat and patterned bases is key for nanophotonics devices, yet old methods scale poorly. The new method, based on low-density polyethylene, moves large-area monolayers and heterostructures onto flat and nanostructured bases while preserving optical quality. Devices built this way modulate TMDC photoluminescence via photonic setting, strain, or electrical gating.
arxiv-2603-04823: Akhanjee explores stats rules of bits filling twin energy substates. Usual treatments regard energy levels as distinct, split by quantum numbers or spatial locations. Counting yields exact spread functions for plain and quantum bits at high crowding. Quantum bits obey an odd entropy tied to the square root of N, meeting an area law in two bulk dimensions. Plain bits show a clear glass shift like chilled liquids. Below a finite temperature, layout entropy dies for the plain case.
arxiv-2603-05123: Mitsuaki Kawamura and team build a first-principles method for coherence length and penetration depth within density functional theory. Incorporating finite-momentum Cooper pairs, the scheme determines coherence length, penetration depth, and shift temperature consistently without settings. Applied to elemental superconductors, V3Si, and H3S under high pressure, results agree with test and reproduce type-I/type-II sorting for all materials. Unified access to both length scales lets the team construct the Uemura plot from first principles, showing higher-temperature systems combine strong pairing with large phase stiffness.
arxiv-2603-05223: Kristena Spruksta and colleagues compare three FIP bias diagnostics in the atmosphere observed by Hinode/EIS. Photosphere-corona differences produce the FIP effect, a ratio of low to high ionization-potential elements. Values run near 1 for coronal holes, 1.5 to 2 for quiet Sun, 3 for active regions. They compare Fe XVI/S XIII, Ca XIV/Ar XIV, and Si X/S X between quiet Sun and an active region across SNR cutoffs. Higher cutoffs remove high-bias tails while the median stays largely unchanged, favoring nuance in the diagnostic.
arxiv-2603-05423: Jacek Karolczak and Jerzy Stefanowski offer a tabular medical-record model, needing discretized diagnostic norms. Interpreting choices is key in healthcare. Unlike spatial vision models, trainable patching over patient features learns prototypical parts. These parts are binary or split feature subsets expressing prototypes, aligning with clinical language. Their network is inherently clear, giving concept-based guesses comparing accounts to them. In tests, the model matches older models on medical benchmarks, giving transparency, bridging scores and clarity.
arxiv-2603-05823: Chung and Won compute Donaldson-Thomas fixed values, together with child versions, for a local Calabi-Yau 4-fold built over the Mukai-Umemura variety. Their math proceeds through several local-focus rules. Under the guess that genus-one Gopakumar-Vafa type fixed values are zero, the results verify forecasts made by Cao, Maulik, and Toda. The work thus confirms the hoped-for match in this setting through direct fixed-value math.
arxiv-2603-06123: Rossi and his team note that diffusion language models use a fixed set of denoising steps on a fixed window no matter how long the reply must be. Short replies then waste compute. They say the prompt's latent representation already hints at the length that is needed. They test a zero-shot method that crops the window before generation starts. Four benchmarks cover reasoning, code, instruction following, and question answering, and show sharp compute savings with little cost to results and gains on two tasks.
arxiv-2603-06323: Ghosh and Nandy ask whether supertranslations of the Bondi-Metzner-Sachs group stay admissible once classical energy conditions are enforced, despite their infinite dimensional sector. Expanding curvature tensors and Ricci scalar in perturbation powers, they recast strong, weak, null, and dominant as bounds from the Raychaudhuri equation. They narrow to BMS on Schwarzschild background, with shifts set by a supertranslation form. Strong and weak ones impose real restrictions at next to leading order. Null and dominant ones hold at first pass, biting at next to next to leading order.
arxiv-2603-06423: Shapiro and colleagues compare three island-based entanglement distribution systems, using downconverters as signal-idler pair sources for nodes. Two systems herald via idler detections: zero-added-loss multiplexing and a Sagnac source with signal-path erasure. The third uses an unheralded Sagnac source. At 90 percent heralding efficiency or lower, zero-added-loss multiplexing beats the erasure source per pulse. Both heralded rates fall short of unheralded operation under equal islands and memories. Rates must be weighed against equipment demands, since the leading heralded design needs two matched Sagnac sources.
arxiv-2603-06723: Ao and colleagues define a new task: tell whether an image carries a hidden copyright mark without decoding it or knowing how it was hidden. They build UniFreq-100K, a large set spanning many hidden-mark methods, and propose the Frequency Shield Network. Its early layers gate frequencies to boost faint high-frequency mark signals, while deep layers mine spectral oddities with multi-spectral attention. Tests show strong zero-shot detection against prior baselines.
arxiv-2603-06923: Lei and colleagues introduce Reasoning Editing for targeted changing of reasoning patterns in LLMs while sparing other pathways. Older reasoning fixes treat reasoning as one general skill, using broad training that wastes effort and misses target errors. Each edit trades Generality, working across tasks sharing a pattern, against Locality, keeping other reasoning skills intact. Their study finds the Circuit-Interference Law: interference grows with circuit overlap. Their REdit framework reshapes circuits before editing, tuning interference between patterns.
arxiv-2603-07123: Li and colleagues report the first correlated trend linking fast radio burst activity to its persistent radio source. For FRB 20190520B and FRB 20240114A, long-term changes in the persistent source's flux track the energy of the bursts, suggesting the two are physically coupled. Other repeaters with compact persistent sources show no clear link, likely from sparse data. The pattern fits a shared energy store, such as a magnetar's magnetic or rotational energy, powering both.
arxiv-2603-07223: Cao and colleagues study how post-training data quality drives finance language models. Dense terminology, strict numerical reasoning, and low error tolerance make deployment hard in finance. They build ODA-Fin-SFT-318k through multi-stage distillation and verification for high-quality chain-of-thought supervision. They also build ODA-Fin-RL-12k for hard-but-verifiable tasks balancing reward precision and task diversity. High-quality training grounds guided fine-tuning, while hardness- and proof-aware sampling lifts reward learning transfer across nine money tests.
arxiv-2603-07723: Agarwal and colleagues report heat and magnetotransport traits of half-Heusler ErPdSb from single crystals across wide heat and field ranges. The compound orders AFM at 1.2 K and shows half-metal conduct with a broad hump near 70 K when non-ordered. Ab initio math points to a bulk blocking nature, while weak antilocalization drives field resistance in small fields and strong fields make it negative via the deGennes-Friedel model. Holes lead charge transport, and the 2 K Hall signal carries a sizable anomalous part hidden by multi-band effects.
arxiv-2603-08223: Mirian analyzes how electron-beam microbunching affects the spectrum phase of a THz-optical klystron. Optical klystrons boost coherent light through laser-induced bunching and dispersive amplification. In the terahertz regime at low beam energy, however, the light wavelength nears the wavelengths of longitudinal space-charge and synchrotron radiation driven bunching. The study examines the impact of bunching on the spectral amplitude and phase of a seeded optical klystron working in that regime.
arxiv-2603-08323: The ATLAS team searches for decays of the Higgs boson into pair-produced pseudoscalars decaying into tau-leptons. Using 140 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV recorded with the ATLAS detector, the search targets a pair of low-mass pseudoscalars that promptly decay into tau-leptons. Results constrain exotic Higgs decays into four tau-leptons. The search focuses on events with one or two tau-leptons decaying into hadrons and neutrinos, and the rest decaying into electrons or muons plus neutrinos. No significant excess is observed.
arxiv-2603-08523: Sinan Ulu and colleagues present BuildMamba, a single model that maps buildings and their heights from one overhead photo. Past routes bleed across edges and shrink tall blocks, since one flat view leaves depth unclear. Their design scans the whole scene in linear time, sharpens edges with a mask-aware height pass, and sets a new bar on three test sets.
arxiv-2603-08723: Hiroki Fukui argues that alignment design itself breeds collective disorders in language-model groups. Drawing on Foucault and Illich, he treats multi-agent model settings as test beds for constraint-pathology dynamics. Across hundreds of runs with four commercial models, hidden censorship and tangled alignment rules track the worst collective symptoms, and he claims English-only safety tests miss the gravest multilingual effects.
arxiv-2603-08823: Shijia Liao and colleagues present Fish Audio S2, an open text-to-speech system that follows written instructions. It handles many speakers and many turns, trained through a multi-stage recipe over captioning, voice-quality checks, and reward modeling. The streaming engine answers fast, with a real-time factor well under one and first audio in under a tenth of a second.
arxiv-2603-08923: Frank Zimmermann floats leveling synchrotron radiation power at future rings. Strong radiation inside cold magnets heats them and caps beam current, while shrinking beams calls for taming tune shift or pileup. Tuning beam energy as current falls holds radiation power at its limit, lifting peak and total yield and boosting di-Higgs events by 60 percent or more.
arxiv-2603-09023: Tony Mason presents Pichay, which pages LLM context on demand. The context window acts as L1 cache with no L2 or virtual memory, so stale tool results occupy context for the session and structural waste runs near 22 percent. As a transparent proxy, Pichay evicts stale content, faults pages back on re-request, and pins working-set pages, cutting context use by up to 93 percent live.
arxiv-2603-09223: Yiyang Lin and colleagues present UniField, a unified framework for boosting MRI scans across field strengths rather than handling each jump as a lone task. Past methods served single transitions on small cohorts and missed degradation patterns shared across strengths. UniField works directly with 3D volumes through pre-trained 3D foundation models, gaining robust structural features. It also counters the over-smoothing bias of flow-matching models, aiming for sharper, more general enhancement.
arxiv-2603-09323: Paweł Gola and Haozhou Tang build a tractable model of labor markets with varied workers and firms, where hiring sorts one firm to many workers. Firms choose both headcount and staff mix, shaping worker incomes and firm productivity together. They study cycles driven by market efficiency shocks that favor more productive firms the most. The model's predictions match known facts about how wage and productivity distributions move over the cycle.
arxiv-2603-09423: John Stokes-Waters extends abelian lattice-ordered groups in two multi-sorted ways, drawing on zero-set maps for continuous functions. One version amounts to giving the group a spectral subspace plus a map built from zero sets. A classical partial quantifier elimination result of Shen and Weispfenning then yields a model companion for one extension. That theory is complete and admits quantifier elimination in a slightly larger language.
arxiv-2603-09523: Adrian Paul Misselwitz and colleagues study impurity models for interacting waveguide QED. In a coupled-cavity array, photons cluster around atomic impurities and interact through local Kerr effects. That sets Jaynes-Cummings binding against photon-photon repulsion. Large-scale simulations and simple analytic models map the many-body ground states across arrays and fillings. Mott-like insulating states appear beside superfluid phases linked by a strongly interacting photonic fluid.
arxiv-2603-10023: Yuanyuan Sun and coauthors tackle a basic legal puzzle: where an AI model ends and an AI system begins. New rules such as the EU AI Act assign different duties to providers and deployers of each, yet the terms lack clear definitions. Reviewing hundreds of papers and policy documents, they trace most definitions back to shifting OECD frames. Their fix grounds new definitions in what models and systems are and how they relate.
arxiv-2603-10123: Borun D Chowdhury claims the lost in the middle effect in language models exists at birth, before any training. Models recall context starts and ends well but middles poorly, a pattern usually blamed on learned softmax traits or position encodings. Modelling layered causal attention as powers of the Cesàro matrix, Chowdhury derives an exact influence density with a primacy tail and a recency anchor. Untrained Qwen2 and GPT-2 networks already show the U shape.
arxiv-2603-10723: Wenze Ren and co-authors expose a gender bias in mean opinion scores, the standard metric for speech quality. Male listeners, they find, score speech higher than female listeners do, with the gap widest for low-quality speech and shrinking as quality improves. That quality-dependent pattern resists simple calibration. Models trained on pooled labels inherit the skew, leaning toward male standards. Their gender-aware model learns group-specific scoring patterns through binary group embeddings, improving overall and per-group accuracy, and framing the bias as a learnable pattern.
arxiv-2603-10923: Patrik Knopf and coauthors study a convective Cahn-Hilliard system over long times. It couples a bulk phase field with surface dynamics. It models phase separation with bulk-surface interaction. Convection makes the system non-autonomous. It stops the free energy from acting as a Lyapunov functional. That complicates the analysis. They prove instant regularization of weak solutions. They prove the existence of a minimal pullback attractor. Under decay assumptions on the flow, they also prove a further result. Every solution converges to one steady state.
arxiv-2603-11223: Riccardo Campi and coauthors rebuild retrieval-augmented question answering over knowledge graphs so that answers keep the context that plain triples throw away. Standard graph indexing reduces text to triples and loses nuance, which hurts multi-hop questions that must compose facts about several entities. Their indexing writes context-derived descriptions for triples and merges them with entity-level summaries, avoiding explicit graph traversal at retrieval time. A decompose-resolve retriever breaks questions into resolvable triples and grounds them iteratively, gaining up to 66 percent over standard baselines.
arxiv-2603-11323: Jérémy Scanvic, Quentin Barthélemy, and Julián Tachella rebuild the UNet image design to be equivariant to translations, which its aliasing-prone layers work against. They choose every main part in alias-free form: convolution, pooling, downsampling, activation, and normalization. This yields sub-pixel translation equivariance. Against non-equivariant baselines, the alias-free networks match them on image restoration and score far higher on equivariance. Tests that remove one choice at a time show every choice matters.
arxiv-2603-11523: Pan proves strict optimality for frequency and distribution estimation under local differential privacy. The winning design is linear, symmetric, and extremal, with support size set to an optimized value. It hits the L2 lower bound for both tasks, and the L1 bound in the limit. Its communication cost can drop to a short log-sized bit count. Pan also gives an algorithm to build the estimator, plus selection guidance for practice. A modified Count-Mean Sketch, he shows, sits practically at the optimal level too.
arxiv-2603-11623: Mironenko, Burnaev, and Barannikov give cross-persistence diagrams their first systematic density study. Persistence diagrams track clusters, loops, and voids across scales, one cloud at a time. Cross-persistence diagrams instead capture how features of two point clouds relate. The team proves the density exists and builds its statistical foundations. They also design the first learning framework to predict it from coordinates and distance matrices. Noise, they find, can even sharpen the split between clouds from different manifolds. Tests beat older methods on density prediction and cloud distinction.
arxiv-2603-12023: Banerjee and co-authors show how old system flaws can amplify attacks on compound AI pipelines. Such pipelines chain LLMs with software tools and databases on shared hardware. Many parts still carry classic software bugs, timing leaks, and power side channels. Two combined attacks make the risk concrete: one pairs code injection with a Rowhammer guardrail hit to plant a jailbreak prompt. The other poisons a knowledge base so an agent sends private user data to a hostile app.
arxiv-2603-12123: Song shows that a fresh review session catches more LLM errors than a same-session second look. Cross-Context Review sends output to a new session with no access to the chat that made it. Thirty artifacts with 150 planted errors faced four review setups. A second review helped only when it ran in a fresh session. Cross-Context Review beat repeated self-review clearly, though not a context-aware subagent or one self-review on average. The method needs no new tools and costs one extra session.
arxiv-2603-12623: David Yang defines a stratification on Moy-Prasad quotients for a reductive group over a Laurent series field. The strata come from twisted Levi subgroups, sorted into conjugacy classes. He then computes the strata in terms of those subgroups. The result is needed for several follow-up papers on the local geometric Langlands program. The paper is a technical step in that larger program, stated for groups that meet set conditions.
arxiv-2603-13123: Jacob Emil Mencke and Paolo Ricci run the first full-f drift-kinetic and delta-f gyrokinetic simulations of a linear plasma device together. They derive an electrostatic model that joins slow, large-scale fields to fast, small-scale ones. Electrons follow a drift-reduced Braginskii model under critical balance ordering. Ions use a Hermite-Laguerre spectral expansion for both parts of their distribution. At LAPD settings, the drift-kinetic part stays near a bi-Maxwellian. Small-scale turbulence grows only when collisionality drops and sources strengthen.
arxiv-2603-13423: Andrew Kiruluta proposes Kalman World Models, a class of learned state-space models trained without backpropagation. Instead of gradient descent, parameter learning becomes Kalman-style gain adaptation through recursive Bayesian filtering. Error signals act as innovations, and training becomes online filtering. The framework extends to transformer LLMs, where internal activations are treated as latent dynamical states. Innovation terms correct those states, giving a gradient-free training and adaptation path from control theory. Tests on sequence modeling tasks showed competitive scores with better robustness.
arxiv-2603-13523: Pietro Piras studies the Bogomolov property for fields cut out by modular Galois representations. A field has this property when its Weil height stays above a fixed positive floor. Prior work proved it for eigenforms under some side conditions. Piras extends the result to eigenforms whose nebentypus character is nontrivial, a case left open before. He also defines a new class, called ADZ fields, after work by Amoroso, David, and Zannier. For that class, the property is kept under composition of fields, in full generality.
arxiv-2603-13723: Kyogo Horikawa and co-authors ask whether AI agents really improve code readability. Readability is key to software quality, and poor readability lengthens development and raises bug risk. Prior studies mix all kinds of refactoring, so the readability effect alone was unclear. The team pulled readability-related commits from the AIDev dataset and tracked metric changes in 403 commits. Agents mostly targeted logic complexity and documentation, not naming or formatting. Many readability commits made classic metrics worse, with the Maintainability Index down in most cases.
arxiv-2603-13923: Zhang, Yu, and Meng set out one frame for how molecules react, built on the least action rule. To see a reaction, one must solve the Schrödinger equation. Their frame joins past work on the kinetic energy operator and on potential energy surfaces built with AI tools. It also adds curved spacetime terms to the nuclear Hamiltonian. Those terms let gauge fields act near conical intersections. The frame unifies methods for electronic structure and for quantum dynamics, and the geometric phase appears on its own.
arxiv-2603-14023: Huang and co-authors build the first system that images fast, flexible objects through strong air turbulence at high frame rates. Event cameras record at thousands of frames per second but cannot tell object motion from turbulence shimmer. Their light field version grabs many views at once. True motion gives events that line up across views, while turbulence events do not. Tabletop tests image objects moving at up to 16,000 pixels per second through heavy turbulence.
arxiv-2603-14223: Altybay studies a backward problem for a time-fractional pseudo-parabolic equation with a time-varying coefficient. The task is to rebuild the unknown starting state from data seen at the final time, under Dirichlet boundary rules. The author proves that a unique solution exists under stated conditions. A finite-difference scheme with a stability and convergence analysis supplies the forward solver. Tikhonov regularization then drives the recovery, and tests with noisy final data show the method holds up.
arxiv-2603-14323: Liu and co-authors probe why medical multimodal models misread medical images, with a focus on visual grounding. A model may name the right finding yet point at the wrong region. Their VGMED dataset, built with clinical experts, tests grounding apart from word-level sense. Eight top medical models often fail to ground answers in the right image regions. The same models do ground well on natural scenes, so the flaw is medical. A fix called VGRefine sharpens grounding at test time.
arxiv-2603-14423: Shekhar and Ramdas build tighter confidence intervals for sampling without replacement. The task is to bound a population mean from a sample drawn with no repeats. For a finite alphabet, they derive a floor on interval width from large-deviation rate functions. A new interval built from an empirical rate function meets that floor up to constants in set regimes. A dual form makes the interval cheap to compute. Extensions cover the unit interval and smooth Banach spaces.
arxiv-2603-14723: Zhang tests how safety supervision wording shapes low-data LoRA fine-tuning across three model families. Four formats share the same core safety rules. Plain constitutional rules form condition A. Creed-style identity framing forms B, with a worldview tail in C. A matched non-identity format forms D. HarmBench scores run through a dual-judge pipeline on 320 behaviors. Format D refuses most on Llama, Gemma and Qwen alike. Creed framing beats plain rules but trails D by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-14823: Li, Song and Li sharpen neural network verification by branching on counterexample clues. Dataflow verifiers refine loose relaxations with branch-and-bound search. Static rules pick branch points blind, ignoring why a check failed. Their DRG-BaB frame recasts the search as a counterexample-guided loop. A failed case yields a closed-form fake counterexample from linear bounds. A directional relaxation gap score ranks neurons by their role in the failure. Targeted splits then replace blind search on high-dimensional tests, they report.
arxiv-2603-14923: Taylor adds directional routing to transformer attention heads at small parameter cost. A shared router steers learned suppression directions for each head. A mid-size model trains beside an identical baseline in one run. Routing becomes the dominant compute path in the routed model. Killing it drops factual recall near zero on eight test prompts. Induction accuracy falls from over 93 percent to zero as well. Single head knockouts barely matter by contrast. Perplexity drops by about a third to a half versus baseline, Taylor reports.
arxiv-2603-15023: Battiston and co-authors speed up PAC-DB, a database privacy model, in a system called SIMD-PAC-DB. The original method needs 128 runs over random half-samples of the database. Their insight is that each bit of a hashed key can stand for membership in one such sample. New algorithms compute the needed aggregates from these hashes in a SIMD-friendly way. The authors report speedups up to forty times. They release a DuckDB extension that rewrites SQL queries for private answers.
arxiv-2603-15123: Gui and co-authors probe the layered ferromagnet Cr2Ge2Te6 with a quartz tuning fork resonator. The fork reads the magnetotropic susceptibility, which tracks the rotational stiffness of the magnetization. Responses over temperature, field, and angle all fit a quasi-two-dimensional easy-axis ferromagnet model. As saturation nears, the angular profile shifts from a simple cosine form to a sharp dip shape. The authors present the material as a clean reference system for fork-based measurements. The method also helps separate spin-based anisotropy from orbital magnetism.
arxiv-2603-15223: Lowin and co-authors estimate robot affordances with two coupled particle filters, one for graspable regions and one for movable regions. Single estimators struggle with visual, geometric, and semantic ambiguity. Each filter encodes regularities tied to its own property, which trims uncertainty. Coupling lets the two trade information and focus where both agree. On a real-world dataset, precision beat three recent estimators by more than two and a half times. Real robot trials reached a 70 percent success rate, even in low light and clutter.
arxiv-2603-15323: Park and Xiao study small-time heat decay for stable processes on fractal drums, open sets with fractal boundaries. They look at spectral heat content, a measure of how much heat stays inside. Earlier work covered subordinate killed Brownian motion. This study extends the picture to stable processes themselves. Under set geometric conditions on the domains, the decay rate differs sharply from the Brownian case. The split occurs at a set value tied to the boundary's interior Minkowski dimension.
arxiv-2603-15423: Potts and Sudhof show that most failures in human-AI chats are invisible: the user never signals that anything went wrong. In 100,000 WildChat interactions, 79 percent of AI failures were invisible in this sense. The failures fall into eight archetypes that cluster into higher-level types. A counterfactual set swaps 2024-era replies for answers from three modern frontier models. Failure rates dropped a lot, yet most failures stayed invisible and the archetype mix held steady. The taxonomy, they argue, can anchor failure monitoring for builders and policy makers.
arxiv-2603-15623: Mishra and co-authors describe Finder, a search framework built for pharmaceutical data. Older systems struggle with mixed content and manual curation. Finder unifies search across text, images, audio, and video. It blends sparse word matching with dense semantic vectors. A modular pipeline ingests mixed formats and enriches metadata. The system has processed over 291,400 documents, 31,070 videos, and 1,192 audio files. Content spans 98 languages across regulatory, research, and commercial domains.
arxiv-2603-15723: Dhara and Sheth test how question answering degrades as context grows. Models now face long, noisy texts where the answer hides among filler. The pair ran controlled tests on SQuAD and HotpotQA. They added irrelevant context step by step and kept the answer signal fixed. Accuracy fell steadily as length grew in both sets. Multi-hop HotpotQA lost nearly twice as much accuracy as SQuAD. The authors argue context-length checks belong in standard reliability tests.
arxiv-2603-16123: Sargsyan compiles type specifications into neural nets that compose by construction. Networks often master parts yet fail on fresh part mixtures. Her claim pins the failure on architecture, not data. A decoder composes only when it honors the task's algebra. Higher Inductive Type specs compile into network pieces directly. Basepoints, paths, and 2-cells map to constraints, generators, and homotopies. The transport decoders act as strict monoidal functors by design. Softmax attention provably cannot match that strictness, she shows. Torus and Klein bottle tests back the predicted gaps.
arxiv-2603-16223: Du and co-authors improve label-free training for language models. Such methods learn from the model's own majority votes. The catch is that popular wrong answers can trap training. Their Dual Consensus method uses two vote stages. First the model anchors on its dominant replies. Then brief unlearning lets it explore diverse signals. The training target blends both sets by harmonic mean. Across eight benchmarks, Pass@1 beat plain majority vote.
arxiv-2603-16323: Geng and co-authors probe puzzles in charmed baryon decays. Recent data clash with theory, including flavor symmetry fits and lattice simulations. A suspect is the decay used to normalize the measurements. The team uses lattice inputs in an SU(3) flavor analysis with first-order breaking. They predict two ratios of decay rates, 2.6% and 1.1%. These ratios need no normalization mode. They may help locate the source of the tension.
arxiv-2603-16423: Yoshimura and co-authors rethink Mamba models for image tasks. Vision Transformers scale poorly, but Mamba's one-way scan limits patch contact. Added scans in prior work cost speed and shuffle data often. Two fixes anchor SF-Mamba. Patch swapping feeds two-way flow into a single scan. Batch folding with timed state resets boosts GPU parallelism. Tests on classification, detection, and segmentation beat strong baselines. Throughput also rose across model sizes.
arxiv-2603-16923: Adelson, Sethu, and Dang build a speech system on Assembly Calculus instead of deep learning. Deep learning needs huge datasets and global weight updates, and its features are hard to read. Assembly Calculus uses sparse neuron assemblies, Hebbian plasticity, and winner take all competition. Their framework turns speech into spike patterns and sorts assemblies across areas and timescales. It detects phone boundaries with an F1 score of 0.69 and word boundaries at 0.61, with no weight training. Phone recognition reached 47.5 percent accuracy in their tests.
arxiv-2603-17123: Onitiju and Vakilinia build a standardized security assessment for large language models, plus a defensive system to answer it. No broad comparative assessment across major model families existed. They test five widely deployed families against 10,000 adversarial prompts in six attack categories. Vulnerability rates ranged widely, from about 12 to about 30 percent, and stronger models were not safer models. Their multi layered defensive framework reached 83 percent average detection accuracy with 5 percent false positives. They argue that outside defenses offer a viable path to safer deployment.
