arxiv-2604-21223: Runheng Liu and three colleagues detect machine-written text without training, using implicit reward models derived from public instruction-tuned and base models. Their IRM method needs neither preference collection nor task-specific fine-tuning, unlike earlier reward-based detectors. On the DetectRL benchmark it tops both zero-shot and supervised rivals, offering a lightweight check against misuse of fluent generated text.
arxiv-2604-21523: Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan and three colleagues test evaluator models across image-to-text and text-to-image tasks. They use perturbations hurting quality along hallucinations, spatial reasoning, and visual fidelity, testing whether evaluators catch errors. On more than 4,000 instances spanning 40 dimensions, they test 4 models with single-answer, pairwise, and model-guided scoring. Evaluator models show blind spots: they miss perturbed outputs, at times over half, struggle with compositional and spatial errors, and miss hallucinations contradicting input images. Pairwise comparison is more reliable, though failures persist.
arxiv-2604-21623: Panopoulos and colleagues build A-THENA, a light early-warning intrusion detector for Internet of Things networks that reads packet timestamps to catch attacks sooner. Its transformer design uses a time-aware hybrid encoding plus a network-specific augmentation pipeline that hardens the model against varied traffic. Tested on three benchmark intrusion datasets, it beats traditional positional encoding, feature-based models, and rival time-aware systems on accuracy with near-zero false alarms. It also runs live on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W.
arxiv-2604-21723: Le Fur, Martín-Cano, and Sánchez show how two polar quantum emitters can stay entangled through a terahertz channel. Strong visible-light driving creates dressed states whose energy gap can be tuned into the terahertz range. The emitters' polar nature then lets them couple to a terahertz photonic mode, producing steady entanglement with concurrence above 0.9 under feasible settings. Both control and state readout happen optically, with no direct terahertz handling.
arxiv-2604-21823: Deffayet and four colleagues quantize a stable classical system. It pairs a harmonic oscillator with a ghost of negative energy, linked by a polynomial. A kept number with a positive discrete spectrum forces four results. The results are a pure point spectrum unbounded above and below, unitary evolution, a well-defined vacuum, and bounded average values for squared variables. Computer checks back the results. That discrete spectrum keeps the system stable when interactions grow.
arxiv-2604-22023: Spohn and three colleagues study the Habitable Worlds Observatory's field of regard and characterization with a scheduling algorithm. The authors introduce a scheduling algorithm in EXOSIMS that models orbital information and detection probabilities. Field of regard is a driver of mission yield, with yield falling when it is less than 90 degrees. Each additional characterization reduces yield by 22%, and requiring four instead of one lowers yield by 52%. Longer surveys mitigate this penalty: the loss from increasing characterizations from 1 to 2 is 38% for a 2.5 year survey and 14% for about an 8-year survey.
arxiv-2604-22523: Yoshida and six colleagues work out how magnetic dipolar forces couple sound-like waves to magnetic waves in thin ferromagnetic films under an in-plane field. Starting from Maxwell's equations with elastic deformation included, they derive coupled equations of motion predicting mixing between magnetostatic waves and Lamb waves, elastic waves traveling in plates. For a yttrium iron garnet film, the dispersion relations show anti-crossings, where the two wave branches repel instead of crossing. The mixing gaps run from a tenth of a megahertz to several megahertz.
arxiv-2604-22723: Mutisya and Mugane find word structure in Giriama, a Bantu tongue with only 91 labeled pattern sets, by joining transfer from Swahili with clustering done without labels. Their method gives noun classes to 2,455 words and finds two new, never-noted patterns: an a- form for Class 2 and a short k'- form. Checks on known verb sets confirm strong base-form accuracy.
arxiv-2604-23023: Kolokolov and Yu develop a penalised regression frame for varying coefficients and variable picks when response and covariates are Itô semimartingales with jumps. Coefficient curves are fit by spline fits and estimated by least squares from truncated high-frequency moves. In finite cases, they prove consistency and derive a usable limit distribution for the integrated estimate. Extending to high cases, a group-wise penalised estimate with truncated penalty attains the oracle trait. That delivers consistent picks, as shown on over two hundred high-frequency factors.
arxiv-2604-23123: Ma and six colleagues build mean spectral energy distributions for 56,969 Sloan quasars below redshift 0.75, using light from mid-infrared to ultraviolet. Sorting by iron strength, stronger iron lines go with redder ultraviolet, optical, and infrared light, a sign of more dust. Sorting by accretion rate, light reddens as the rate rises except in the optical, which turns bluer, showing a complex optical region. Sorting by hydrogen line width gives redder optical and near-infrared light but bluer ultraviolet and mid-infrared light, hinting that viewing angle shapes torus emission.
arxiv-2604-23323: Liu and ten colleagues build a robust audio-text retrieval method that refines audio and text embeddings with cross-modal attention. A refinement module combines transformer projection, linear mapping, and bidirectional attention, while a hybrid loss blends cosine similarity, L1, and contrastive objectives. Silence-aware chunking and attention pooling handle long, noisy audio from 5 to 15 SNR in small batches. Tests on benchmark datasets show gains over prior methods, which struggle with long, noisy, weakly labelled audio.
arxiv-2604-23423: Kinyon gives a short, elementary proof of a little-known fact about rings, the algebraic systems where addition and multiplication behave much like they do for ordinary numbers. A zero divisor is a nonzero element that multiplies another nonzero element to give zero, and Kinyon shows that a ring with only finitely many such elements must itself be finite. He also pins down a precise bound on how large the ring can be.
arxiv-2604-23523: Gaaloul and colleagues build a loop that updates safety rules for machines that sense and act in the real world. As conditions change, rules must change too, but edits must obey the rule grammar and must not merely fit past data. Their loop pairs what-if reasoning with strict grammar checks to keep edits sound. Tested on self-driving control, it fixes a flaw in a rule from a standard baseline.
arxiv-2604-23623: Fu and nine colleagues present Tandem, a reasoning framework that pairs a large language model with a small one to cut cost without losing quality. The large model acts as a strategist, drafting a compact set of key reasoning insights. The small model then carries out the full reasoning to the final answer. A cost-aware stopping rule halts the large model once enough guidance exists. It cuts compute by about two-fifths on maths and coding tests.
arxiv-2604-23823: Atek and colleagues present a deep JWST census of faint objects from the epoch of reionization. Lensing probes the UV brightness curve to record depth. The curve at redshift near seven keeps rising steeply. Its faint-end slope sits near minus two, with no clear bend at the faintest levels reached. Faint objects thus supply most of the photons that ionize, enough to sustain that era. This runs against models that predict an early plateau.
arxiv-2604-23923: Ye and colleagues build a vertical GaN alpha-particle detector with a 20-nanometre ultrathin dead layer plus a guard ring. It shows ultralow leakage current under high reverse bias, an energy resolution of about 2.7 percent, and charge capture near 96 percent. Geant4 simulations show for the first time that uneven depletion width drives partial energy leakage, producing the extended low-energy tail. Their uneven-width model matches experiment, guiding design of better GaN radiation detectors.
arxiv-2604-24023: Ji and seven colleagues introduce ServImage, a benchmark that ties image generation and editing to real commercial value. It gathers paid design tasks and designer deliverables, scores outputs on meeting briefs, visual quality, and commercial need, and adds a model that predicts whether a human would pay. That payment model reaches 82 percent accuracy on human-annotated candidates, grounding image evaluation in buying decisions.
arxiv-2604-24123: Wang and five colleagues propose FDIM, a video quality metric that works across traditional and neural codecs in SDR and HDR. Neural codec artifacts vary with content and look generative, so older metrics that assume classic artifacts miss them. FDIM mixes deep multi-scale features with stable hand-crafted cues to catch structural, textural, and semantic damage. Trained on over 16,000 sequences, it generalizes to unseen codecs across ten test sets and tracks human judgment closely.
arxiv-2604-24223: Locatelli and six colleagues map climate misinformation playbooks in the Global South from 226,775 climate-related YouTube videos from Brazil. As outright science rejection fades, subtler narratives that accept warming while attacking solutions gain ground. Two patterns dominate: traditional denial fighting evidence, and a new denial that attacks mitigation and adaptation policy. New denial comes from a wider cast, draws higher engagement, and uses slicker persuasion, hitting regions already facing deep inequities and testing moderation for older denial.
arxiv-2604-24323: Becchetti and five colleagues tour locality sensitive filtering on the sphere, bridging hashing and filtering. Filtering allows asymmetric regions to control queries and updates apart, gaining power. The tour treats angular distance on the sphere under symmetric Gaussian filters, same as cosine match. Using basic math, the authors derive sharp chance bounds and a proof of long-run optimality. Optimality holds among schemes with fixed filter spreads. They exploit Gaussian filter structure for a fast build, giving an easy entry point.
arxiv-2604-24823: Takeuchi develops a measure-based theory for galaxy evolution. Populations are probability laws on a state space. Evolution combines transport and jumps. Transport covers internal change; jumps cover mergers. With Wasserstein distance and curvature bounds, transport is a gradient flow. Jumps generate nonlinear shifts from many-body links. At low density, only two-body processes remain. The system is thus bound by variational rules and curvature bounds.
arxiv-2604-24923: Adebali and Pietrow test whether Doppler images of lambda And can yield activity parameters. They feed solar spectra from surface images into a toy model. They ask whether spots alone explain the activity modulation of this RS CVn star. With no public starspot models for its type, they use solar spectra as the only available stand-in for its spots. Even under simplified assumptions, lambda And's spectral behavior comes out qualitatively right. Spot activity seemingly drives the chromospheric signal, explaining most of its variation.
arxiv-2604-25023: Pearson proves the Mukai conjecture for locally factorial Fano varieties defined via their Cox rings, in a certain class. The conjecture characterises projective-space powers among smooth Fano varieties. Pearson proves the conjecture when the ambient toric variety is smooth, with a stronger lower bound matching the spherical-varieties case. He interprets key terms geometrically, one via the moment polytope of the ambient variety. Another term becomes an upper bound on a coefficient sum in an anticanonical divisor decomposition.
arxiv-2604-25123: Liao, Agarwal and Bourgey develop closed-form expansions for the implied volatility of VIX options in forward variance models. They build on weak-approximation techniques for VIX option prices. The formulas allow fast, accurate calibration with no numerical root-finding from option prices. They test the expansions in standard and rough Bergomi-type models, and numerical experiments confirm their accuracy.
arxiv-2604-25823: Tang and fourteen colleagues pin down plasma density profiles in a 10 GeV laser-plasma accelerator using two independent diagnostics. Beam data resolved along the accelerator join laser spectral measurements. Distinct shapes can otherwise yield similar final beam energies, hiding the physics. With plasma downramps included, their constraint matches simulation along the full length for two channel sizes. Validated simulations say a 65 cm accelerator would reach 15 GeV. They also point to about 20 GeV in about 70 cm at the same laser energy.
arxiv-2604-25923: Dhar and two colleagues survey four decades of work on evaluation methodology in natural language processing, organizing it into a taxonomy of 22 recurring concerns. Language-model advances have revived doubts about evaluation, yet many critiques predate current models in NLP's long methodological tradition. For each concern, the authors track its recent visibility and its presence in institutional checklists. Some concerns have faded from view, and many lack checklist coverage. The review points to targets for fresh investigation and field-level action.
arxiv-2604-26023: Garatti, Nenna, Rota Nodari, and Tamanini extend a dynamic formula for the Schrödinger problem, which links optimal transport with entropy-driven diffusion, to probability measures whose support is unbounded. Earlier proofs needed compact supports to control the regularity of the potentials involved. Using fine estimates on second derivatives and entropic interpolation, they build a nearly self-contained proof and obtain a velocity field with suitable polynomial growth. The result supports using the dynamic formulation for Gaussian and mixed Gaussian models.
arxiv-2604-26123: Lappi and Triantafyllopoulos test when the Gaussian approximation to high-energy scattering in the Color Glass Condensate framework fails. While that approximation describes multi-gluon correlators starting with two-gluon exchange well, they show in theory and in simulations that it breaks for correlators starting with four-gluon exchange. Incoherent diffraction in photon-nucleus collisions is the main example: the gap comes from weak scattering and persists as unitarity corrections grow. Full JIMWLK evolution gives larger cross sections in every kinematic regime studied.
arxiv-2604-26223: Cao, Michel, and Jamieson presented StreamGuard, a 5G design that protects video-call quality when radio resources run short. A monitor inside the radio network reads call quality, a controller picks priority actions balancing quality against fairness, and a marking module steers each subflow into the right queue. On a real testbed, call quality rose by up to 70 percent at similar background throughput.
arxiv-2604-26423: Montanez-Barrera and Michielsen tested Quantinuum's 98-qubit Helios-1 chip against clean simulations on JUPITER, Europe's first exascale machine. Circuits reaching 48 qubits with 3,384 two-qubit gates ran on 4,096 nodes holding 16,384 superchips, giving a yardstick at the edge of what classical machines can still do. To 48 qubits, Helios-1 samples could not be told apart from clean ones. Wider study put steady performance up to 93 qubits, with outputs turning random-looking at 95 qubits.
arxiv-2604-26623: Kikianty, Naude, Roelands, and Schwanke develop integration theory for locally band preserving functions on Dedekind complete f-algebras. They construct Darboux and Riemann integrals and show the two agree. The theory of integrable functions is then tied to order differentiable functions through a Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. A Mean Value Theorem for Integrals also holds, and integration by parts and substitution go through.
arxiv-2604-26723: Alba and Sánchez study binary relations defined with two generalized inverses, GD1 and 1GD, for maps on vector spaces of infinite dimension. They work with finite potent endomorphisms, maps whose powers eventually stabilize, and describe both inverses through the AST decomposition of such a map. That description yields algorithms for computing the inverses and shows the two relations form partial orders, a ranking-like structure, on finite potent endomorphisms. The result completes the theory of these inverses beyond the finite matrix case.
arxiv-2604-26823: Dong and three colleagues introduce MujicΛ, a framework for rebuilding the universe's starting conditions from galaxy redshift surveys. It strengthens the L-BFGS optimizer with a projection step and rank-order matching, forcing the rebuilt starting field to stay Gaussian and robust to survey gaps. Tested on a mock catalog from the Millennium simulation, it recovers the true density field down to the model's resolution and broadly recovers the cosmic web's structure. The method also speeds field-level inference for coming large surveys.
arxiv-2604-26923: Chen and six colleagues introduce ClassEval-Pro, a benchmark of 300 class-level coding tasks across 11 domains, built by an automated three-stage pipeline from real GitHub code. Each task passes test suites with over 90 percent line coverage and validation by a language-model judge panel. The best of five frontier models scores only 45.6 percent on first-try class completion, with about 18 points separating it from the weakest. Failures split mainly into logic errors and dependency errors, marking cross-method coordination as the core bottleneck.
arxiv-2604-27223: Graf introduces Graphify, a framework that lets coders model graph data shapes visually. It then builds a type-safe backend on its own. Graph databases flexibly handle linked data. Weak schema rules, however, bring doubt when code runs and painful query writing. Graphify maps GraphQL artifacts by a set rule onto the Gremlin query engine. It supports full CRUD tasks and layered queries of any depth. Its tool turns complex GraphQL requests into a single tuned Gremlin query, with layered filters, multi-key sorts, and paging.
arxiv-2604-27323: Gong and four colleagues propose RSCNet, a spectral correlation network for multi-source remote sensing image sorting. It fuses hyperspectral imagery with SAR and LiDAR data. Hyperspectral and SAR or LiDAR data offer matching spectral and structural information for land-cover sorting. Yet fusion faces spectral overlap in high-dimensional hyperspectral data and mixed traits across sources. RSCNet addresses those challenges through spectral selection. A Key Band Selection Module picks spectral bands on the fly from the hyperspectral data under cross-source guidance, easing overlap and cutting information loss.
arxiv-2604-27423: Huang and Zhang study closed manifolds that are almost Kähler and negatively curved in section. They prove a small Nijenhuis tensor forces each signed Hirzebruch genus component to be at least one. In particular, the signed Euler number is at least n plus one, confirming the Hopf conjecture in this setting. Their proof leans on fresh bounds for harmonic forms over the universal cover, a refined vanishing theorem, and Atiyah's index theorem. The result extends Gromov's Kähler result to the almost Kähler case under that condition.
arxiv-2604-27623: Croft, Kendrick, and Hutson explore near-threshold bound states in a Rb plus KRb model with coupled-channel calculations. They find states with strong long-range character close to threshold, likely lasting to depths of at least 100 GHz under each threshold. These states couple only weakly to short-range states and sit outside the chaotic manifold, spending little time at short range. As a result, they resist laser destruction, live long regardless of state density, and can cause narrow Feshbach resonances when shifted across thresholds by fields.
arxiv-2604-27823: Csáji and Sun take the flip view: rather than easing stable rules for spread goals, they tune school goals over stable matchings. They first study mix matching and propose a Diversity-Constrained Deferred Acceptance method finding stable matchings cutting violations under the one-to-all rule. They launch a fast-time framework for tuning any school goals over student sets. Their key gain is a general cut using stable matching structure to transform goals into easy problems. Tests on fake markets confirm strong spread scores while keeping stability.
arxiv-2605-00123:
Shubham Kumar and Narendra Ahuja introduce LOCA, a method that explains why a specific jailbreak prompt succeeded against a safety-trained language model. Earlier work explained jailbreaks globally, through shared directions in the model's internal representation space tied to harmfulness or refusal. But different attacks, and different harmful request types, may work through different internal changes, so a global story can miss the real cause.

LOCA instead finds a minimal set of interpretable changes in the intermediate representations that causally restore refusal on an otherwise successful jailbreak. On pairs from a large jailbreak benchmark, across Gemma, Llama, and Qwen chat models, it induces refusal with about six changes on average, where prior methods routinely fail even after twenty. The authors present it as a step toward mechanistic, case-by-case explanations of jailbreak success.
arxiv-2605-00223:
Á. Valenzuela Navarro and 12 co-authors measure how dust dims starlight toward the Milky Way's Nuclear Bulge, the dense star cluster at the galaxy's center. Heavy, patchy dust in that direction hides the true brightness of its stars and blocks accurate mass estimates. The team needed a clean sample of stars that truly belong to the region.

They select red clump stars by their motion and build a detailed reddening map, which shows thread-like dust structures and a gradient across a giant gas cloud nicknamed the Brick. Counting the selected stars, with corrections for missed ones, gives a stellar mass near 1.2 billion solar masses for the Nuclear Bulge. Their dust ratios agree with earlier measurements.
arxiv-2605-00323:
Minghui Chen and 5 co-authors attack hallucination in vision-language models, which often describe details that are not in the picture. A common fix trains the model on judgments distilled from a stronger model, but that can demand finer perception than the student has. The student then learns to guess rather than to see, a mismatch the authors name and study.

Their framework, OSCAR, instead lets the model supervise itself. Models, they note, are better at checking a description than at producing one, a gap they exploit. A tree search builds preference pairs, scored by a two-level reward, and direct preference training refines the model in rounds. OSCAR set new best scores on hallucination benchmarks while also improving broader multimodal skills.
arxiv-2605-00423:
Qincheng Lu, Sitao Luan, and Xiao-Wen Chang speed up signal recovery for MIMO wireless systems, where many antennas transmit and receive at once. Finding the best recovery is provably hard, and the hardest practical case is under-determined, with fewer receive than transmit antennas. Recent diffusion-based detectors show promise but need many sampling steps and degrade exactly in that hard case.

Their method, GD4, recasts a graph-based diffusion process that denoises directly in the discrete symbol space, rather than in a relaxed continuous one. That change allows good answers in one or a few evaluations. Under a similar computing budget, GD4 produced better solutions than rival diffusion detectors and respected classical methods, in both under-determined and over-determined systems. The result is a more favorable trade between solution quality and running cost for receiver design.
arxiv-2605-00523:
Lukas Zenger develops intuitionistic common knowledge logic, a reasoning system for groups of agents who know that they know, built on constructive logic. Classical common knowledge logic assumes every truth is decidable either way. The intuitionistic version interprets knowledge operators for several agents, plus a common knowledge operator, over two-layered Kripke models. An intuitionistic ordering there interacts with the agents' accessibility relations.

Zenger gives axiomatizations and analytic cyclic sequent calculi for the logic and for its restrictions to reflexive, S4, and S5 style models, proving all of them sound and complete. He establishes the finite model property and decidability, and shows proof search can be automated. A translation embeds classical common knowledge over S5 into the intuitionistic system. Finally, he proves the proof-search and validity problems for all these logics are solvable in exponential time.
arxiv-2605-00623:
Yanbiao Ji and 9 co-authors recover the hidden reward behind an expert's acts from a diffusion-based policy. Inverse reinforcement learning normally needs adversarial training to guess what an expert aims at. Their system, EnergyFlow, uses a single-number energy function whose slope is just the field the diffusion model learns, tying action models and reward finding into one object.

Under the max-entropy rule, they show the learned score function recovers the gradient of the expert's soft value function, so a reward can be read off with no foe. Forcing the field to be a true gradient shrinks the search space and tightens how well it holds up away from the training data. They also pin down when the reward can be recovered at all. On robot-arm tasks, EnergyFlow led the field at copying experts while yielding a reward signal beating rival approaches for later learning.
arxiv-2605-01323:
Wazir Ali, Adeeb Noor, and Saifullah Tumrani built SiNFluD, a first benchmark data set for spotting figurative language in Sindhi, a language with few digital tools. They gathered raw text from blogs, social media, and literary sources, then had two native speakers label it.

The two labelers agreed well, which gave the team a firm base for testing. They ran standard cross-checks and then tried three large multilingual models plus a few-shot method based on sentence embeddings. The largest model, XLM-RoBERTa-XL, did best. The data set gives future work on Sindhi a shared test bed, and it shows how far current multilingual models still have to go on this language.
arxiv-2605-01423:
Junkun Jiao and eight co-authors built HepScript, a small formal language for data analysis in high-energy physics, designed to be written by both people and AI agents. Analysis at this scale is slow because workflows demand deep field knowledge and code tied to one experiment's stack.

HepScript states analysis logic in a tight syntax that hides the stack below it and turns intent into production-ready code. First built for the Beijing Spectrometer III experiment, it cut the code humans must write by over nine tenths in case studies. Its narrow grammar also gives agents a small, safe action space: agents drafted working specs for core analysis stages straight from published papers, with a high success rate. The authors present the shared language as a translation layer among experts, agents, and the production system.
arxiv-2605-01723:
Aref Pahlevani, Morteza Rafiee, and Mehdi Ansari-rad study the Mpemba effect in a pair of coupled oscillators. The effect is the result that a hotter system can settle faster than a cooler twin. One oscillator is driven parametrically, its stiffness pumped in time, and each sits in its own thermal bath.

Using the covariance-matrix machinery, they track relaxation under plain white noise and under colored noise with a Lorentzian spectrum, fed through one channel or both. Two yardsticks, distance to the steady state and weight on the slowest mode, tell the same story. The drive is the master knob. As it nears the stability edge, the crossing time where hot beats cold shrinks steadily. Colored noise strengthens the effect and widens the region of settings where it appears, most when both oscillators hear it. It stays a secondary push on a structure set by the slow mode.
arxiv-2605-02223:
Tung Vu and colleagues tackle speech tampering where a few words inside a recording are replaced to change its meaning while keeping the speaker's voice. Voice cloning and speech synthesis make such partial edits realistic. Past benchmarks focus on whole-utterance fakes or a single tampered region, leaving multi-region localisation untested.

They introduce MIST, a large multilingual data set in six languages with one to three word-level inpainted segments per utterance, made by guided semantic replacement and neural cloning. Fake content is only a small share of each file. Their method, ISA, scans in a coarse-to-fine sliding window and works with varied backbones. A new metric scores fine-grained localisation across regions whose count is unknown in advance.
arxiv-2605-02623:
Yiming Ding and six co-authors widen a video search task: finding every moment in a video that matches a written query, not just one. Classic moment retrieval assumes exactly one match, but real queries may match several moments, or none. Their generalized setting requires the full set of matches, or an empty answer when nothing fits.

To study the task, the team builds Soccer-GMR, a large benchmark from soccer videos with realistic positive and negative queries, made by a semi-automated pipeline with human checks. A unified scoring protocol covers rejection of empty cases, location of true moments, and end-to-end performance. Baselines include a plug-in adapter for existing retrieval models and a tailored reinforcement reward for fine-tuning multimodal language models, giving the new task a starting point.
arxiv-2605-02723:
Members of the Euclid Collaboration present CosmoPostProcess, a simulation-based method that corrects a bias in how galaxy clusters are picked for cosmology with the Euclid space telescope. Clusters chosen by richness, a count of member galaxies, suffer selection effects: chance projections along the line of sight can inflate the count and distort stacked mass profiles.

The algorithm runs large simulations, paints galaxies onto halos with an occupation model, and mimics the survey's detection and richness steps, matching the Euclid definition without a color cut. A new method estimates cluster centers from projected galaxy density and is checked against Euclid pipelines. Baryon effects enter through a correction tuned on fluid simulations, and the corrected profiles agree closely with reference values. Bias patterns under changed cosmology are also assessed.
arxiv-2605-02923:
Isaac Pérez Castillo argues that a repeatable lab test can be read as a computation. That reading has consequences for what functions can be said to exist in the physical world. Lab procedures end after finitely many steps. They report numbers for a physical quantity.

Once the protocol, background conditions, and reporting rules are fixed, the procedure works like an algorithm. Grant an explicit bridge principle, in the spirit of the physical Church-Turing thesis. A repeatable test then computes a map from inputs to outputs. That function exists, in the sense fitted to its outputs. Finite precision is no barrier. What matters is a stepwise approach to a requested accuracy, not exact reals at once. Protocol choice and randomness do not defeat the claim. They specify which map a given protocol realizes.
arxiv-2605-03023:
Marten Folkertsma, Lorenzo Grevink, Jonas Helsen, and Alicja Dutkiewicz tackle how to build strong random unitary designs on grids with only local links. Such designs act like truly random operations and matter for quantum tests and secure random unitaries, but grid limits make them hard to build.

The authors give two constructions. One adapts a known all-to-all result through routing, while the other works directly on the grid with no extra systems and reaches the best possible depth for fixed grid dimension. Together, the methods also yield strong pseudorandom unitaries on grids at optimal depth.
arxiv-2605-03123:
Kevin J. Sung and sixteen co-authors introduce ffsim, an open-source library for fast simulation of fermionic quantum circuits. Fermion systems keep particle number and spin projection fixed, and general simulators waste effort by ignoring those symmetries.

By building those conservations in, ffsim cuts memory use and run time and beats a similar library on benchmark tests. Beyond basic gates, it offers variational forms, time evolution tools, Slater determinant sampling, and links to Qiskit and PySCF, with full documentation. Demo runs cover circuits up to sixty-four qubits, showing the library's reach for chemistry and physics work.
arxiv-2605-03323:
Guanda Huang, Xiaodian Chen, Shu Wang, Xiaobin Zhang, and Licai Deng search TESS Cycle 7 data for stars that oscillate at high frequencies. TESS short-cadence light curves offer sharp sensitivity to rapid pulsators, but a uniform search must weed out contamination and known objects carefully.

From tens of thousands of light curves, they selected strong high-frequency signals, vetted them at pixel and light curve level, and confirmed seventy-three rapid oscillators: white dwarfs, hot subdwarfs, and A-F stars. Detailed frequency analysis followed for each target. Two stars show clear multiplets matching rotational splitting, and the uniform catalog supports future seismic studies.
arxiv-2605-03423:
Xi Yu, Weicai Li, Lin Yin, and Tiejun Lv propose an adaptive dual-path framework for covert semantic communication, where hidden data rides inside task features rather than signal power. Conventional covert methods overlay messages on the waveform, while semantic coding offers a subtler hiding place tied to the task itself.

One path handles the public task openly; a second path jointly encodes public and covert content with contrastive alignment, and adaptive block selection switches paths by task need. Against a strong independently trained attacker on Cityscapes, detection fell to near guessing, while primary task performance beat the baselines.
arxiv-2605-03523:
Lorenzo Carlucci and Oriola Gjetaj generalize three classic Ramsey-style theorems to colorings of barriers. Barriers are a structured setting in combinatorics and logic. Friedman's free set and thin set theorems and the rainbow Ramsey theorem all govern what homogeneous structure a coloring must contain.

They formulate and prove the barrier versions. They then analyze strength through computability. Upper and lower bounds on solution complexity for computable instances are given, plus uniform reductions between problems. Corollaries give proof-theoretic results on logical strength, in the spirit of reverse mathematics. They locate how much reasoning power these combinatorial principles require.
arxiv-2605-03623:
Zhiqi Li, Duowen Chen, Yuchen Sun, and Bo Zhu propose a unified way to make diffusion and flow-based generative models produce results in only a few steps. Their framework rests on cumulative flow maps, which connect small local updates to finite-time transport across probability space, borrowing ideas from flow-map methods in physics.

A cumulative parameterization lets existing models support few-step and even one-step generation while preserving synthesis quality. Only minimal changes to time embeddings and training objectives are needed, and model capacity does not grow. The team demonstrates the approach on image generation, geometric distribution modeling, joint prediction, and signed distance function generation, each with reduced inference cost compared with standard many-step sampling.
arxiv-2605-03823:
Dan Tsir Cohen, Steve Hanneke, and Aryeh Kontorovich settle a question about when learning with general metric losses can be Bayes-consistent in the realizable setting. Bayes-consistency means a learning rule's risk converges to the best possible as data grow. Earlier work covered classification and real-valued regression. General metric losses stayed open since 2022.

The authors work with an instance space and a label space carrying possibly unbounded loss. They find necessary and sufficient conditions on the hypothesis class. Under them, a distribution-free rule's risk converges almost surely to zero on every realizable distribution. The characterization turns on a combinatorial obstruction: an infinite non-decreasing Littlestone tree with growing gap parameters. It extends earlier tree structures to the metric loss setting.
arxiv-2605-03923: Thais Gomes Ribeiro and five co-authors study Taylor varieties, algebraic varieties that arise from the Taylor expansion of rational functions in several variables. Among these varieties they look for non-defective hypersurfaces. They prove that one specific family of cases, with two variables and a parameter choice one step beyond the degree, gives new examples of hypersurfaces whose Hessian is identically null. They add to the known cases of hypersurfaces with a Hessian that is zero throughout.
arxiv-2605-04023:
Hamta Sedghani, Zahra Seyedi, Mauro Passacantando, and Danilo Ardagna model decentralized edge caching for mobile social networks as a game. Multiple content providers compete for the limited storage of edge devices. They face different budgets and operating costs. Low-latency content delivery depends on what gets cached where. The framework jointly accounts for provider budgets and device storage limits. It also accounts for how all parties interact.

The interaction is cast as a layered game. A Stackelberg model covers provider-device interactions. A non-cooperative game covers the competing providers. Under light storage constraints, provider competition forms an exact potential game. That guarantees a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium and convergence with no central control. When storage binds, that structure is lost, yet broad tests still show stable convergence driven mainly by provider competition.
arxiv-2605-04123:
Mahendra Goray and Bijan Saha test a cosmological model that tries to unify the dark sector while allowing an anisotropic early shape. The model couples a massless nonlinear spinor field to a Modified Chaplygin Gas inside Kantowski-Sachs spacetime, which permits different expansion rates in different directions. Their goal is to probe uneven expansion and unified dark matter-dark energy dynamics against current data.

Model settings were constrained with a Markov Chain Monte Carlo fit using supernova, cosmic chronometer, DESI, and cosmic microwave background distance data. The inferred expansion rate sits in the high sixties in standard units, and the shear value is consistent with zero. That indicates an effectively isotropic universe today. The model reproduces late-time acceleration. It fit the combined data better than the standard model by their chi-squared values. It was favored by the Akaike Information Criterion.
arxiv-2605-04323:
Leng and three colleagues assemble a vast soil dataset for machine learning. Soil underpins farming, carbon cycling, and environmental health, yet soil data sits fragmented across formats and protocols, keeping models stuck on small predictive tasks. LUCAS-MEGA fuses European soil observations around the LUCAS survey into one resource. It holds over seventy thousand samples and more than a thousand features spanning physical, chemical, biological, and visual traits, drawn from sixty-eight source datasets.

A multi-agent pipeline called SoilFuser, checked by humans, standardizes formats and fixes unit and codebook mismatches. It brings everything into a feature space ready for machine learning. The authors pretrain SoilFormer, a multimodal tabular transformer, on the fused data with a feature-masking objective. Training stays stable, predictions are strong, and outputs carry uncertainty estimates. Learned representations also recover relationships consistent with known soil processes, and the dataset ships with open access and query APIs.
arxiv-2605-04423:
Prabal Saxena and Thomas Fauchez model how high volcanic plumes rise on planets outside the solar system, using the TRAPPIST-1 system as a focus. Explosive eruptions inject gases that can change an atmosphere's chemistry and climate, and close-in planets may be strongly heated from inside, driving intense volcanism.

They adapt a classic one-dimensional plume model, first built for Venus and Mars, into an open Python framework. The model couples vent conditions, air entrainment, and atmospheric stability to predict rise height and overshoot. After checking it against the original code and scaling laws, they apply it across a suite of exoplanet conditions.
arxiv-2605-04523:
Ivan Bondarenko and five co-authors describe the winning system in a shared task on faithful multi-turn response generation, where answers must stay grounded in provided reference passages across a conversation. Their entry competed in the generation track of an international evaluation campaign.

The system is an ensemble of seven different language models, each run with two prompting styles, with a smaller model acting as judge to pick the best candidate answer for each case. It placed first among twenty-six teams by a wide margin over the strongest baseline. Ablations show the diversity of model families, sizes, and prompts is essential, and the team also releases a compact adapted model with a strong cost-performance balance.
arxiv-2605-04823:
Zoltán Bajnok, Dávid Fülepi, and Máté Lencsés study what happens when a quantum system's boundary rule is suddenly switched to another rule. Both rules are integrable, meaning the system keeps special structure that aids exact calculation. They ask how average values of local quantities then evolve over time.

The authors build a general method based on form factors for bulk and boundary-changing operators. They apply it first at the conformal point of the Lee-Yang model, then to its massive version. Their formulas for post-quench averages are checked against numerical calculations using a truncated conformal space method adapted to changing boundaries.
arxiv-2605-05123:
Alper Kamil Bozkurt and four co-authors address choosing and fine-tuning a pretrained policy for a new task when online interaction is tightly budgeted. Policies are usually trained offline from stored data, then one is picked for deployment. Offline estimates can be unreliable, while online evaluation spends the very interaction budget that fine-tuning needs.

Committing to one policy is also risky, since nobody knows beforehand whether it will improve with fine-tuning, especially when conditions change. Exhaustively fine-tuning every candidate would break the budget. The authors propose an adaptive approach that shares the budget between selection and fine-tuning as evidence arrives, aiming to deploy a policy that both starts well and keeps improving.
arxiv-2605-05223:
Yunpeng Zhou studies why switching on several learned features at once in a transformer can become unstable, a question at the heart of steering sparse autoencoder units. Such autoencoders pull apart stacked features, yet the theory of composing distinct meaning units together is thin. The usual linear picture of inner codes ignores nonlinear cross-talk inside too-large codebooks.

Zhou models the space as a large sparse cone and derives an asymptotic threshold for collapse when parts combine, under a round codebook model. In a high-bias regime, he shows the ReLU step turns small linked wobbles into a steady drift that grows under composition, a ratchet effect. Tests on structured units from the CLEVR dataset match the forecast scaling, with layered correlations speeding the shift.
arxiv-2605-05723:
Pufferfish privacy protects secrets defined by the data holder, beyond standard differential privacy's fixed template. Ni Ding, Wenjin Yang, and Zijian Zhang introduce a scheme calibrated through a generalized Wasserstein distance between data laws. Noise from Laplace or Gaussian laws is scaled using an upper bound on that distance.

They prove the scaling meets Rényi Pufferfish privacy for a range of the order parameter. At the limit, the scheme recovers the known mechanism for the standard pufferfish guarantee. Extensions cover the exponential mechanism as well, uniting several noise choices under one distance-based recipe.
arxiv-2605-05923:
Felix Boakye Oppong and three co-authors work on joint models that link repeated biomarker measures to survival outcomes. Such models often track only the average path of a marker over time. The authors note that how much a marker varies may also carry news about a patient's risk.

Their two step method first takes residuals from a mixed effects model to build personal measures of variation over time. Those measures then enter a standard joint model beside the average path. Simulations show sound performance across varied settings. In data from a large glioblastoma trial, both the level and the variation of white blood cell counts helped predict survival.
arxiv-2605-06223:
Junhyuk Kwon and four co-authors build a navigation agent that asks smart questions when a user's request is ambiguous. A request may match several similar objects, and demanding a full description up front burdens the user. Worse, agents often lock onto a distractor that fits the gathered details and decide too early, wasting the whole dialogue.

ProCompNav first builds a candidate pool, then narrows it through recursive comparative judgment. Each round picks an attribute that splits the pool, asks the user a binary question, and drops candidates that clash with the answer. No attribute needs to be unique to the target for the process to work. On two benchmarks the method led on success rate while sharply shortening user responses.
arxiv-2605-06323:
Berk Guler and three co-authors build assistive teleoperation for handling ropes and other deformable linear objects. Such objects have effectively endless configurations and tangled dynamics, and depth uncertainty makes them hard to perceive and react to during remote control. AssistDLO joins real time multi view state estimation, visual assistance, and a shared autonomy controller built on control barrier functions that respects the object's geometry while guiding the grasp.

A user study on bimanual knot untangling, with 22 participants and ropes of varied length and stiffness, tested the design. Gains depended strongly on operator skill and rope traits. The controller lifted novice success from 71 to 88 percent, acting as a skill equalizer, and suited stiffer ropes best. Experts preferred the visual assistance instead, a split the authors say demands adaptive shared autonomy.
arxiv-2605-06423:
Zeyuan Chen and four co-authors introduce Pop Quiz Attack, a black-box way to test whether a large language model memorized a given training example. Membership inference matters because models can reveal private training data. Their idea turns target data into quiz-style multiple-choice questions and reads membership from the model's answers.

Across six widely used models and four datasets, the attack reaches an average ROC-AUC score well above prior methods. The authors also study what drives success, including question complexity and data type. Tested defenses, from filters to differential privacy, reduce the attack but do not remove the privacy risk.
arxiv-2605-06523:
Hao Ye and nine co-authors study how reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards reshapes a model, focusing on low-rank parts of its weights. Earlier work found the new reasoning skill sits mainly in rank-1 components. Using periodic rank-1 substitution, the team spots implicit reward overfitting: test performance can look fine even while training rewards stay low.

They report three further patterns. The rank-1 component keeps little knowledge beyond math reasoning, training optimizes a specific singular spectrum with heavy-tailed values, and the linked singular vectors align more strongly over time. Together the findings suggest this training mainly improves sampling efficiency and may guide continual learning methods.
arxiv-2605-06623:
Zhexuan Wang and six co-authors introduce MASPO, a framework that optimizes the prompts of all agents in a multi-agent language model system together. Each agent's role prompt matters, but tuning prompts one by one misaligns local goals with whole-system success. Joint optimization across interacting agents is the hard, mostly unsolved problem they target.

MASPO judges each prompt by how much it helps successor agents succeed downstream, bridging local edits and global outcomes without ground-truth labels. An evolutionary beam search, guided by data, navigates the huge prompt space. Across six varied tasks MASPO consistently beats leading prompt optimization methods, with an average accuracy gain just under three points.
arxiv-2605-07123:
Zixuan Xie and three co-authors give the first theory of how chain-of-thought reasoning boosts in-context reinforcement learning. Agents that adapt to new tasks from context alone, without retraining, do better when they generate reasoning steps. Why that helps had not been explained mathematically.

Working with a linear transformer in a policy evaluation setting, the authors prove chain-of-thought steps act like repeated temporal-difference updates. Evaluation error falls geometrically as reasoning lengthens, then levels at a floor set by context length. They also prove the needed transformer settings are a global best fit for pretraining, explaining how such behavior can emerge.
arxiv-2605-07523:
Sarita de Berg and five co-authors study a geometry problem where point locations are known only roughly, as regions that each hide one true point. Fetching a point's exact position costs effort, so the goal is to compute the Pareto front, the set of points not beaten on both coordinates, while fetching as few as possible.

For possibly overlapping rectangles, their algorithm is instance-optimal in the number of fetches: no method can fetch asymptotically fewer on any fixed input. Its running time stays within a logarithmic factor of optimal, and for unit squares they achieve universal optimality in running time as well. The authors note this is the first universally optimal algorithm for overlapping planar input.
arxiv-2605-07823:
Mateusz Jacniacki and Maksymilian Bilski test whether language model agents can pick up the unwritten rules of a group chat. Online groups enforce implicit norms through social sanctioning, and an agent that cannot read those signals will keep offending. Their benchmark, SCENE, builds plausible multi-party chats where scripted personas follow a hidden norm and sanction breaches.

The benchmark measures two adaptation abilities: responding to negative sanctioning, and inferring the norm from peers' behavior alone. Six frontier and open-weight models were evaluated. Claude Opus 4.7 and Gemini 3.1 Pro adapted to implicit norms significantly more than the open-weight models tested. The authors offer SCENE as one step toward dynamic, interactional evaluation of social capability.
arxiv-2605-08023:
Junyu Cao studies what happens to the smallest eigenvalues of the Laplacian as a family of compact Kähler manifolds degenerates. Such families approach a singular limit, and the rate at which small eigenvalues shrink carries geometric information. Earlier work by Dai and Yoshikawa settled a lower-dimensional case.

Cao extends that result to higher dimensions and derives the exact asymptotic rates. The proof joins Li's uniform Skoda inequality with the method of auxiliary Monge-Ampère equations, a tool developed by Guo, Phong, Song, Sturm, and Tong and adapted by Guedj and Tô. As an application, the study gives estimates for degenerations whose singular fibers are reducible.
arxiv-2605-08123:
Dylan Forde studies how to train attention layers built on optimal transport, where a Sinkhorn solver balances attention weights across long contexts. Running the solver inside training is costly on TPU hardware, and gradients through many solver steps are awkward to compute exactly.

Forde splits the solve into a stopped base phase and a short refinement tail, then differentiates only the surrogate tail. For the reported two-step path, the backward pass collapses to one reference plan tile times an explicit modifier field, giving block-wise costs and small extra memory. A dustbin bridge extends the same schedule to the augmented support used in the TPU runs.
arxiv-2605-08423:
Omatharv Bharat Vaidya, Connor Jerzak, Nhat Ho, and Chandrajit Bajaj make low-rank fine-tuning adaptive. A standard LoRA adapter freezes one small update shape per layer. That is efficient but rigid. The right correction can depend on the input. It can also depend on what earlier layers have already computed.

Their queryable design keeps a shared memory of low-rank update atoms. Each block of layers builds a query from its current low-rank state. It adds a running summary of previous blocks. It then retrieves a content-dependent mix of atoms by attention. The mix is applied inside the bottleneck. The model keeps LoRA's efficiency while the update changes with context and depth.
arxiv-2605-08523:
Stanislaw Kowalski and four coauthors speed up a core quantum chemistry calculation by teaching it with machine learning. Their target is the density matrix at real temperatures, usually found through costly matrix splitting. A recursive expansion method maps neatly onto deep network structure, and learned coefficients replace formulas that do not exist in closed form for warm systems.

A rescaling trick means one trained model serves many temperatures and chemical settings without retraining. The method leans only on fast matrix multiplication, suiting modern graphics hardware well. On small and medium matrices it runs about ten times faster than standard splitting methods. Electronic structure work gains a faster path for warm, fractional electron systems.
arxiv-2605-08623:
Xindi Wang, Haining Li, Tao Ding, and Bolin Cai lead drone fleets in places with no fixed base. The drones must take photos of the ground. They must also keep up radio links for ground users. Two jobs at once, in fast change, is the hard part. Their plan learns task weights at two levels. One level sets broad taste for a whole run. One level shifts weights step by step as things change.

Mixing both levels keeps training steady. It also keeps the fleet quick to react. In tests, runs learn faster and stay more stable. More tasks get done than with past plans. Drone teams gain a way to shift their top jobs as a task unfolds.
arxiv-2605-08823:
Gabriel Franco and four coauthors map the magnetic field threading the nearby Riegel-Crutcher cloud, a cold atomic gas structure drawn into long thin filaments seen in self absorption. Whether magnetic fields actually shape such clouds remains open. Their survey gathers over ninety thousand starlight polarization readings, the largest for this region, combined with space mission distance data.

The cloud sits about one hundred fifty parsecs away, near the Pipe Nebula, and its sky plane field matches dust emission polarization from the Planck satellite independently. Filament directions align tightly with that field. Together the evidence makes a strong case that an ordered field sculpts this cloud and links it to a larger magnetized complex nearby.
arxiv-2605-09223:
Miraj and six colleagues solve frame selection for long videos, where a query must be answered from a few frames. Existing methods use efficient heuristics without modelling query conditioned structure, or multi stage pipelines with heavy preprocessing cost. Their method, CREST, is training free and grounded in how query frame relevance changes over time.

Relevance over time varies in structured ways: sharp curvature marks salient events, while flat regions mark redundant segments. Using local curvature to guide selection, CREST spends a fixed frame budget better across brief events and slowly evolving evidence. With the same backbone and frame budget, CREST beats AKS on LongVideoBench and VideoMME. It keeps 93 to 95 percent of MIRA accuracy, at only a small fraction of its preprocessing cost. On TempRel, a diagnostic benchmark for temporal selection, CREST gains over AKS, and judge based tests show its frames yield more coherent descriptions.
arxiv-2605-09323:
Prots keeps the local displacement description of phonons but names the global geometric object behind it: the configuration space of translational order on a fixed background. Fixing the orientational part of crystalline order by cutting the frame bundle down to a point group makes the translational order parameter a section of an associated torus bundle.

For symmorphic crystals the point group acts by linear maps on the torus; in nonsymmorphic crystals the action is affine and records the group's extension class. A discrete structure group yields a flat Ehresmann connection, whose covariant differential replaces the displacement gradient. That differential founds the phonon sector as a Lagrangian field theory. When torus holonomy fixes an equilibrium point, the constant section gives back the local displacement field. For quadratic elastic Lagrangians meeting objectivity, the theory reduces to linear elasticity and the sound spectrum.
arxiv-2605-09423:
Kang and three colleagues build SimWorld Studio, an open-source Unreal Engine 5 platform for making evolving embodied learning environments, tackling the shortage of auto-generated 3D worlds. Existing embodied simulators use hand-made scenes or templates, while recent LLM-based 3D generation mainly makes static scenes, not deployable worlds with tasks and interfaces.

At its core is SimCoder, a coding agent writing engine-level code for 3D worlds from language or image notes. SimCoder self-evolves through verifier feedback, build errors, physics checks, and VLM notes, revising worlds and adding tools. Generated worlds ship as Gym-style worlds. Agent feedback guides SimCoder to adaptive lessons near the learner's capability frontier, so worlds grow harder as it improves. Three navigation studies show self-evolution lifting reliability. Generated worlds lift agent performance a lot on unseen benchmarks, and co-evolution beats fixed-environment learning by 18 and untrained agents by 40.
arxiv-2605-09623:
Deng and three colleagues propose a framework that dynamically splits deep neural network layers across the edge cloud continuum. Existing partitioning methods are usually static, ignoring runtime changes, and are often tested only in simulation. Their framework profiles the model at startup, measures link quality between nodes, and revisits the split periodically as conditions shift. A real testbed links a Raspberry Pi at the edge, a laptop as fog, and a desktop as cloud.

Tested on three widely used convolutional networks, VGG16, AlexNet, and MobileNetV2, the adaptive framework cuts energy by about 27 to 36 percent. It cuts end to end latency by about 6 to 23 percent against a static baseline. Those gains confirm that adapting the split to live conditions beats fixing it in advance, a practical win for AI on resource constrained internet of things devices.
arxiv-2605-09723:
Bhat and three colleagues modeled how lone neutron stars cool when their cores hold hyperons mixed with kaon-condensed matter, exotic states of dense matter. Their equation of state, the pressure recipe for the star's interior, rests on a relativistic mean-field framework. It adds chiral dynamics for kaon condensation plus a three-body force that keeps massive stars stable. Proton superconductivity, the pairing of protons, plays the deciding role.

Without superfluid effects, fast neutrino cooling wipes out any visible trace of strangeness at fairly low masses. Strong proton superconductivity at high density shuts down the fast nucleon and hyperon cooling channels, leaving kaon-driven cooling dominant in massive stars. That pattern matches several recently found cold lone neutron stars, offering a possible observational fingerprint of strange matter inside them.
arxiv-2605-09823:
Zou and four colleagues built CalBench, a benchmark for multi-agent calendar scheduling under private information. AI helpers increasingly act for users with access to calendars and inboxes, yet must coordinate without exposing everything they know. In each CalBench task, several agents manage separate private calendars and schedule a stream of meetings while keeping disruption costs low.

No agent can see another's calendar, so success needs coordination by talking, not central planning. Scenarios come with exact oracle answers and simple non-LLM baselines for comparison. Across seven model families, mere completion hid real failures. Agents left avoidable cost on the table. More talk did not mean lower regret. And privacy-preserving silence starved teammates of cost facts needed for fair burden sharing.
arxiv-2605-10123:
Hioki, writing alone, introduces the Phase-Coherent Transformer, a complex-valued transformer replacing softmax attention with a gentler design. Complex-valued transformers mostly borrowed softmax from real-valued designs, but row-scaled token rivalry may clash with phase-keeping computation. The new design gates L2-normalised complex query-key similarities with a real-valued, element-independent, smooth function, swapping token competition for token-non-competing attention that keeps phase across layers.

Across mid-scale benchmarks covering long-range memory, layered reasoning, place recall, phase-based memory and overlap, and image sorting, the model extends strongly. Under size-fair match it steadily beats the usual softmax transformer and its direct complex-valued sibling. It stays competitive with Multiscreen, the strongest real-valued baseline, even on tasks like NIAH and LRA-Text. Cut-out tests confirm the design is not chance: gates dropping reverse-aligned phase parts collapse on long-range recall.
arxiv-2605-10223:
Kai Pan and Rong Hou argue that business AI agents fail less from too little freedom than from too little oversight. Their 2026 paper presents Dynamic Tiered AgentRunner, an execution protocol drawn from a live multi-tenant software platform. It aims to keep powerful language-model agents governable, auditable, and affordable in company settings.

Three mechanisms do the work. Risk-adaptive tiering matches review effort and computing budget to each task. Separation of powers splits proposing, reviewing, executing, and verifying across independent processes. A verifier-recovery loop treats failure as a normal state to learn from. On the live platform the system reached 88.9 percent task success with only 0.5 percent unreviewed risky errors. Latency fell by 46.8 percent and inference cost by 58.2 percent against an always-full pipeline.
arxiv-2605-10323:
Jiwon Jeong and four colleagues improve how language models recommend items by respecting how strongly a user likes something. Hybrid systems feed collaborative filtering signals, patterns from many users' behavior, into language models through prompting. Most collapse explicit ratings into positive-only feedback, throwing away the graded strength of preferences. Their 2026 paper proposes Ordinal Semantic Anchoring, or OSA, to keep that strength.

OSA turns each graded preference level into a numeric text token, and treats the token vectors as anchors that line up user-item patterns inside the model's hidden space. Strength-aware alignment across levels preserves preference meaning while merging collaborative signals with the language model. On multiple real-world datasets OSA consistently beat existing baselines, with the clearest edge in pairwise preference evaluation, where the model must judge which of two items a user prefers.
arxiv-2605-10623:
Cameron Ibrahim and six colleagues treat hypergraph splitting as a spread problem for quantum tuning. Quantum tuning algorithms are by nature random, yet usually used to find one high-quality solution. Their 2026 paper studies splitting problems where the output itself is a probability distribution over splits. It is driven by maximin and minimax goals such as Fair Cut Cover.

The authors show these goals align well with the readout distribution from QAOA. A scheduling toy problem, the Greatest Expected Imbalance problem, aims to cut the worst mean imbalance across hyperedges. QAOA solvers hold spread-based solutions in quantum states, with squared objectives for standard and multi-goal QAOA. Tests on real and synthetic hypergraphs show low-depth multi-angle QAOA beating classical baselines on the proposed goals.
arxiv-2605-11223:
Maximilian Triebel, Marco Menner, and Dominik Helfenstein introduce VLATIM, a benchmark testing whether vision-language models can solve point-and-click puzzle games the way people reason through them. Existing benchmarks often overlook the physical reasoning these games demand, and VLATIM targets the divide between abstract logical reasoning and continuous action spaces that need precise mouse control.

The benchmark uses the classic physics puzzle game TIM and runs in five progressive parts, from basic visual grounding and domain understanding through multi-step manipulation to full puzzle solving. Results show a clear split between reasoning and execution: large proprietary models plan well but struggle with precise visual grounding. They still lack human-like problem-solving capability. Benchmark designers get a test that separates planning skill from execution skill.
arxiv-2605-11523: Song and colleagues present NAVIS, an on-SSD graph search system that cuts position-seeking overhead for search. On-disk graph search dominates databases, but updates must traverse the graph to find neighbours before linking. That cost grows through packed layouts coupling edge fetches to full vector loads, and through static entrance graphs drifting from inserted regions. NAVIS answers with vector reads and an entrance graph updated from concurrent traversals. It adds an edge-list cache. Insertion throughput rises up to 2 point 74 times and search throughput up to 1 point 37 times.
arxiv-2605-11623: Chokyi, Tawfik and Chattopadhyay test one geometric model for early and late cosmic acceleration in f(Q,L_m) gravity with holographic dark energy. They adopt a minimal polynomial, reconstructing late-time dynamics with it as a fluid. The result shows smooth acceleration and stable Hubble behaviour and a near-de Sitter equation of state. Bayesian analysis of Pantheon, chronometer and DESI BAO data leaves coupling weakly constrained and LambdaCDM-consistent. Early on, the quadratic term drives Starobinsky-like inflation matching Planck. Quantum-gravity corrections shift higher-order observables.
arxiv-2605-11723: Wang and thirteen colleagues present CaC, advancing video reward models via spatiotemporal concentrating. CaC first scans time to anchor anomalous windows, then grounds spatially, finally judging via chain-of-thought reasoning. The authors build the first large-scale video anomaly dataset with per-frame boxes and temporal windows. A three-stage paradigm first learns spatial and temporal anchoring, then optimizes via two-turn GRPO with IoU rewards. CaC improves anomaly accuracy by 25 point 7 percent and cuts video anomalies by 11 point 7 percent as a reward signal.
arxiv-2605-12423: Matousek reports COMPASS measurements that map quark motion in the nucleon. Hadrons made in deep inelastic scattering reveal how quarks move sideways and how their spins line up. That framework turns those patterns into maps of quark motion and spin, plus rules for how hadrons form. Hydrogen data from 2016 and 2017 should soon yield new momentum facts and may first reveal the Boer-Mulders effect in an unpolarised nucleon. Polarised deuteron data have already cut d-quark transversity errors by two and a half times at large momentum share.
arxiv-2605-12723: Roohi and Mahdavi show that the tangle in rarefied micro-nozzle flows is largely a lining-up effect. A density slope test identifies the squeeze layer station. A jump thickness defines a shock frame. In physical axes, the leading breakdown mode of centre line curves holds only eighty-three percent of swing energy. The jump frame lifts that figure to ninety-eight percent. A 2D shock window breakdown confirms the tightness is not a centre line fluke. In the lined-up frame, the first mode holds about ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2605-12823: Murdeshwar and four colleagues add curvature to coarse-grained potentials. Coarse-grained simulations reach timescales all-atom methods cannot, but force-matched potentials capture the gradient, leaving curvature out. Their framework adds Hessian-vector matching to force matching, adding curvature without building the full Hessian. They split the Hessian into a precomputed all-atom Hessian and a covariance correction. Hessian-vector matching lifts slow-mode accuracy above force matching for eight of nine proteins, and cuts bond error.
arxiv-2605-13023: Krznarić and López define a new notion of translations in the hyperbolic plane and solve the curve shortening flow equation there explicitly. They then treat ancient convex solutions, solving the flow when the curvature function separates by variables. Finally, they prove area estimates for closed ancient solutions of the flow, completing the trio of results.
arxiv-2605-13223: Eldesokey and colleagues argue that judging text to image models needs annotation matched to each skill. Uniform rating scales ignore how skills differ, so scores can mislead even as models converge. Skill aligned annotation gives steadier signals, higher agreement between raters, and more stable rankings across models. They also build an automated pipeline that applies the protocol at scale with spatially grounded feedback.
arxiv-2605-13523: M. Murabito and M. Stangalini explore how waves in the solar chromosphere shape coronal plasma composition, using high-detail spectropolarimetry. All models so far highlight wave action, notably the ponderomotive force linked to Alfvenic perturbations, as a key factor. Recent solar readings have tied wave signals to coronal regions with raised FIP bias, an excess of elements with low first ionisation potential. The present work tests Stokes V asymmetries as a diagnostic for wave action linked to fractionation, the process sorting them by ionisation traits.
arxiv-2605-13723: Ben Wilson and three colleagues argue the phrase human in the loop falsely implies safety for AI choice systems. Human oversight is a popular plan for concerns about bias, misinformation, manipulation and transparency, yet what watch means is rarely asked. The authors ask whether the loop image helps grasp of what is needed and done in a given choice context. Loose use of the image hides steps and results, feeding humanwashing, where writers use words mainly to present systems in the best light.
arxiv-2605-14323: Yu, Su and Abdullah study chaining sub-policies over time in Markov decision processes with changing rewards. Their General Dijkstra Search is proved to recover globally optimal goal-reaching policies by composing intermediate optimal sub-policies in time order. From its search-select-update principle they derive Dynamic Latent Routing, a post-training method claimed to match or beat supervised fine-tuning in low-data settings across four datasets and six models.
arxiv-2605-14423: Wang, Yang and Su study federated actor-critic training where agents share a common linear subspace representation but keep personalised local policy parts. Agents iteratively estimate the shared subspace, local critic heads, and local policies. Under single-timescale updates with Markovian sampling, finite-time convergence is proved via a joint linear approximation framework. Critic error and policy gradient norms are shown to converge to zero, with linear speedup in the number of agents despite heterogeneous trajectories.
arxiv-2605-14523: Mohtashim, Innan and Shafique pair quantum circuits with ordinary neural layers to read feelings from spoken voice. Their HQTN-SER design links speech features through a tensor network modelled on matrix product states, then blends quantum measurements with a learned classical embedding. Tested on three public emotion datasets, the system reached roughly 80 percent on RAVDESS, 78 on SAVEE and 74 on MDER, using few qubits.
arxiv-2605-14623: Sun, Khangulyan, Liu and Liu analyse seventeen years of Fermi-LAT data on the microquasar SS 433. They detect four gamma-ray sources in the region, including a newly identified source outside the W50 nebula and east and west excesses tied to the X-ray lobes. No significant periodicity is found for the previously reported source, and the two excesses show distinct spectra suggesting different physical origins.
arxiv-2605-14723: Wu and team introduce SepsisAgent, a world-model-augmented language-model agent for sepsis treatment in intensive care. Sepsis care needs step-by-step choices as patients change fast. A learned Clinical World Model simulates responses to trial fluid and vasopressor plans. The agent follows a propose-simulate-refine loop before prescribing. World-model access alone gives uneven results. Three-stage training covers dynamics, workflow cloning, and agentic reinforcement learning. On MIMIC-IV trajectories, it is claimed to beat older rivals with the best safety profile.
arxiv-2605-15023: The CMS Collaboration searches for new physics in events producing three massive gauge bosons, W or Z particles, in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Selection targets the boosted regime where all three bosons carry transverse momentum above 200 GeV and standard model backgrounds are sparse. Hadronic decays appear as large-radius jets with two-quark substructure, tagged as V-jets. No excess over standard model expectations appears, so the team sets bounds on effective-field-theory Wilson coefficients.
arxiv-2605-15223: Nenad Petrovic and three others build a language-model workflow for mapping RISC-V supply chains. Heterogeneous, messy data is handled by language models for text and vision-language models for diagrams, tables, and scans. Extracted items and ties form a knowledge graph of parts and links. Model-driven engineering and constraint modeling then validate dependencies, spot chokes, and assess risk, with a human in the loop for querying and validation. RISC-V cases show usable, clear insights.
arxiv-2605-15323: Vincent Macri, Michael Jacobson, and Renate Scheidler improve Jacobian arithmetic in global function fields along the approach of Hess. One improvement cuts costly reduction steps by tuning for typical inputs rather than worst cases, given a degree-one place exists. The second trades memory for time by caching often used intermediates. Large-scale analysis and experiments show the methods run a lot faster than open rivals, and their public implementation is said to be the first aiding unique divisor-class representatives.
arxiv-2605-15523: Hongxi Li and eight colleagues propose a scene-text editing method that builds style and glyph prompts from the original image itself, without extra style or glyph encoders. A diffusion transformer first trains on large self-supervised data, then refines on a small set of paired images, using in-context learning to edit text in any vocabulary while preserving background style. Tests across languages show leading results on both text accuracy and style consistency.
arxiv-2605-15923: Chun-Peng Chang and four colleagues present Invaria, a point cloud encoder with scale-density invariance via next-resolution prediction and receptive fields. 3D encoders prove sensitive to sampling resolution and scale changes, since models overfit densities and scales rather than learning invariants. Next-resolution prediction teaches invariants, and the encoder gains during resolution shifts while staying efficient through size and fewer tokens. On ScanNet, Invaria scores 56.0 percent higher mIoU at 3 times lower resolution and 20 percent higher at 3 times smaller scale, with a 45 percent smaller model and 40 percent fewer tokens.
arxiv-2605-16023: Feldhus and twelve colleagues ask why the same language model grades answers differently when only the answer format changes. A one-to-five score and a true-or-false label can yield systematically different marks. Tracing five open models with edge attribution patching, they find a shared evaluator circuit in the middle-to-late layers. They argue a stable judgment signal is later bent by fragile format-specific branches.
arxiv-2605-16223: Deganutti and four colleagues provide a fully automated test framework for design animation video generation, a field with no standard benchmark. Design animation sets strict rules: set parts must move with set motion, direction, speed, and timing, while other regions stay stable and layout holds. Their framework spans four facets: layout fidelity, motion correctness, temporal quality, and content fidelity. It removes reliance on subjective human judgment and sets a common basis for tracking progress.
arxiv-2605-16423: Sun and Wu propose Nonlinear Bipolar Compensation, a post-training quantization approach that adds nonlinear fixes to reduce the effect of outliers. Current quantization methods suffer a speed-accuracy tradeoff and limited general use, while recent compensation methods add lightweight linear layers yet fail on outliers. They further design Bipolar Logarithmic Transformation, which maps the quantized input and its error into a new space where a simple linear layer applies compensation. Experiments across tasks, models, and quantization methods confirm its effectiveness, robustness, and generality.
arxiv-2605-16523: Ehatamm and three colleagues present Lean-QEC, a first-of-its-kind Lean 4 formalization of stabilizer codes. It delivers machine-checked distance certificates end to end. Certifying a code's distance bound is hard in general, so published distances often rest on unscalable hand proofs. Others rest on unverified solvers that leave a trust gap. A verified satisfiability encoding of the distance condition breaks that barrier. The pipeline produces Lean-checked proofs for industrially viable quantum low-density parity-check codes, reaching 144 qubits outside the Lean kernel.
arxiv-2605-16723: Cunha's team studies colloidal rods under shear, where flow is often assumed to screen hydrodynamic interactions between rods. Using particle simulations and scaling analysis, they find that assumption breaks down at shear rates and concentrations common in experiments. That coupling among neighbors drives a cascade of tumbling events. The collective motion disrupts flow alignment and sharply raises viscosity and normal stress differences, matching recent lab work. Current models for colloidal rods, they argue, need revision.
arxiv-2605-17923: Yucheng Guo and eight colleagues propose AdaptiveLoad, a framework for training large video diffusion models faster. Mixed-mode datasets vary wildly in sequence length, and equal-token batching ignores the quadratic cost of self-attention, causing load imbalance and idle GPUs. AdaptiveLoad pairs a dual-constraint load balancer, capping memory and compute together, with a fused LayerNorm-Modulate CUDA kernel. On the Wan 2.1 world model, imbalance falls from 39% to 18.9%, peak VRAM use rises 22.7%, and throughput grows 27.2%.
arxiv-2605-18423: Jonathan Diller and sixteen co-authors present REBAR, a 2026 quantitative benchmark for the ethical and legal compliance of autonomous systems.
