The authors build the controller from Lyapunov stability conditions cast as linear matrix inequalities, baking in input saturation and overcurrent limits.

The design is less conservative than worst-case methods: it guarantees stability for every uncertain variant while still allowing quick response. On the CIGRE benchmark, simulated in real time, it beats the compared rival design on both transient speed and tracking error.
arxiv-2606-11123:
Boeshertz, Pascanu, and Clopath ask why a brain-like learning rule fails in deep networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Backpropagation sends errors backward through weights mirroring the forward weights, which brains cannot do. Feedback alignment replaces those mirrors with fixed random feedback weights, and forward weights learn to align with them. It works in shallow networks but degrades as depth grows.

Comparing models trained on CIFAR-10, the authors find the feedback alignment error signal has far lower effective rank than backpropagation's gradient. It lives in a thin subspace, so learning explores only a sliver of parameter space. Two fixes raise the signal's dimensionality: the Muon optimizer, which orthogonalizes updates, and hidden activity normalization, promoting varied activations. On CIFAR-100 with a ResNet-18, accuracy rose by nine percentage points over the feedback alignment baseline. They name low-dimensional gradient dynamics as the key obstacle to scaling the method.
arxiv-2606-11223:
Nürnberg builds a framework for exact worst-case analysis of finance products in a 2026 arXiv paper. Risk managers need best and worst outcomes under complex market scenarios for path-dependent instruments like exotic options. Simulation estimates probabilities well, but it cannot guarantee bounds over all admissible cases, nor show the witness history producing an extreme result.

It starts from event history automata, a new model marrying regular-expression event patterns with allowed numerical intervals, so constraints carry memory. Payoffs are represented by weighted finance finite automata, whose weights depend on observed market values. The combined product of the two yields exact upper and lower payoff bounds, plus readable witness histories realizing them. A case study on an autocallable structured product traces how constraints change coupon totals, early redemption, and protection-loss results. Scaling experiments stay feasible for practical contract horizons, a rigorous complement to simulation.
arxiv-2606-11523:
Mohammed Saif and Valaee maximize connectivity in uplink drone networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Unmanned aerial vehicles extend coverage, but they are prone to failure from limited energy, and adding more does not always help. A reconfigurable intelligent surface can add links and improve connectivity. They jointly optimize link selection, surface partitioning, and drone positions to maximize it, measured by the Fiedler value, under a signal quality constraint for users.

The problem is a costly search problem. A perturbation method handles link selection, and a closed-form solution partitions the surface, each partition tailored to one drone's signal quality. Given the links and partitions, drone positioning becomes a low-complexity semidefinite program solvable with standard tools. Simulations show gains over benchmark schemes from the literature. The design holds user signal quality while pushing connectivity up.
arxiv-2606-11823:
Songlin Yue and three colleagues map the folding behaviour of origami chains in this 2026 arXiv paper on mechanics. Kresling origami patterns twist as they compress, coupling axial motion with rotation. Stacking such units into multi-layer chains creates meta-structures with rich, nonlinear responses, but predicting where they snap between states is hard.

The authors model crease lines as load-carrying elements and link the chain's response curves to its design variables: polygon count, twist angle, height, radius and crease lengths. Using continuation and bifurcation analysis, they track equilibrium branches through successive instabilities, from one layer to two and three. Four distinct folding and bifurcation modes appear in the two-layer system, depending on the starting orientation angle. A generalisation strategy then builds equilibrium paths for chains of any length. This enables inverse design: choosing critical points in advance to programme the post-instability behaviour of layered metamaterials.
arxiv-2606-11923:
The H.E.S.S. Collaboration constrains hypothetical dark matter particles using blazar light in this 2026 arXiv paper. Very-high-energy gamma rays from distant blazars are absorbed by the extragalactic background light, starlight accumulated across cosmic history. Axion-like particles, a dark matter candidate, could decay into photons and brighten that background.

If such particles near ten electronvolts in mass made up much of the dark matter, their decay light would increase gamma-ray absorption measurably. The collaboration fitted spectra from eleven blazars, recorded by the H.E.S.S. telescopes and the Fermi space telescope, under standard and particle-modified background models. No decay signal appeared. Assuming the particles form all of the dark matter, the analysis excludes photon couplings down to roughly seven trillionths in the stated units. The limits rival existing astrophysical bounds and close a previously unconstrained region.
arxiv-2606-12123:
Quanfeng Wang and three colleagues locate people indoors without cameras or radios on the person in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method images the room with passive radar, exploiting ambient electromagnetic fields that are already everywhere. Small passive tags, pure scatterers with no circuits or batteries, strengthen the scattered field so near-field imaging can pinpoint them.

Because the tags contain no electronics, they are cheap, simple to manufacture and easy to adapt. Different tag geometries produce distinguishable signatures, letting the system tell individuals or objects apart when imaging resolution suffices. The approach stays robust with limited bandwidth and in highly reflective rooms, both common indoors. Privacy is designed in rather than bolted on: the tags' frequency behaviour lets users themselves choose how trackable and identifiable they are. Simulations and experiments validate several tag designs. The paper positions passive-tag radar imaging as a privacy-compliant alternative to camera surveillance.
arxiv-2606-12323:
Li and co-authors laser-cool a molecule shaped like a top, a class never cooled, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Laser cooling slows particles by scattering many photons, each kick opposing motion. Molecules resist because every scatter can dump them into new vibration or rotation states, leaking them out of the cycle. An asymmetric top, spinning differently about all three axes, is the most general and richest molecular shape. The team works with calcium monoamide, CaNH2.

Closure of the photon cycle is the battle. Vibrational closure comes from optical pumping of a key state, sustaining about forty-one photon scatters. Rotational closure holds by driving one chosen transition. No extra leakage channels appear. The team achieves two-dimensional magnetically assisted Sisyphus cooling, where molecules climb magnetic hills and lose energy. Such tops carry states prized for quantum information and new-physics searches. Cooling them opens that class to quantum control.
arxiv-2606-12523:
HyeongHan and co-authors weigh the Coma cluster with bent light, and find its outskirts unusually dark, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Coma is a rich galaxy cluster, a laboratory for how clusters assemble along cosmic filaments. Using Subaru telescope imaging, the team maps dark matter through weak lensing, the distortion of background galaxies. A single-halo fit gives a mass near eight times ten to the fourteenth solar masses.

A two-halo fit splits the cluster: the main halo around NGC 4874 and a group around NGC 4839, in a one-to-eight minor merger. Gas fractions suggest the system is returning from first approach. Where lensing and X-ray signals correlate most strongly is along two reported intracluster filaments. There, the mass-to-light ratio reaches about one thousand solar units, four times the cluster's average of two hundred fifty. The filaments are more dark-matter dominated than the cluster body.
arxiv-2606-12923:
Seneque and colleagues argue that inducing order in a system is not the same as controlling it. They propose receiver-gated response laws as the proper object of control, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Control, on their account, needs a response law: an operator that maps material state, drive, environment, and receiver state to a response, including saturation, leakage, and overdrive effects.

The authors find such local laws across biological, language-model, adapter, and stochastic-operator panels. In mouse, worm, and zebrafish perturbation panels the laws provide response-operator evidence without implying coordinate identity between systems. In language-model panels, across 4 material conditions, response vectors follow the laws, with component-sign accuracy between about 73 and 74 percent, rising to about 84 to 85 percent on nonzero components. Held-out observers predict system-effect and target families with accuracy near 94 and 92 percent. Constitution-conditioned adapters reshape susceptibility like prepared media.
arxiv-2606-13023:
Rai and colleagues provide a technical supplement to their main paper on full-duplex FBMC/QAM MIMO systems, covering transceiver design and optimisation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. All theory derivations, the SINR expressions, the spectral-efficiency analysis, and the optimisation algorithm are contained in the main paper, not here.

This document collects the context, figures, and contrasts developed during peer review that the main paper's page limit could not fit. Its main component is a pair of notation tables defining every symbol used in the system model and channel modelling. The tables cover uplink and downlink signal processing and channel matrices, including inter-carrier and inter-symbol interference terms. They also cover residual self-interference in the full-duplex base station, and fading coefficients. The authors state that these tables supersede the symbol discussions in the main paper, making the supplement the reference for its equations.
arxiv-2606-13123:
Tram and colleagues re-examine the wavelength dependence of interstellar starlight polarisation, testing whether grain alignment explains both standard and anomalous spectra, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Polarisation from aligned dust grains follows the Serkowski relation from the optical to the near-infrared, but about 25 percent of sightlines show a mid-ultraviolet excess called super-Serkowski polarisation. The authors model the joint effect of paramagnetic relaxation alignment, the Davis-Greenstein effect, and radiative torque alignment, using 4 stars to constrain the models.

For the super-Serkowski spectra of HD 30614 and HD 204827, radiative torque alignment boosted by radiation from a B-type star below the Lyman limit explains the data. Adding paramagnetic relaxation helps the fit at the shortest wavelengths. For the standard Serkowski spectra of HD 37903 and HD 161056, radiative torque accounts for the data, with only a weak paramagnetic part.
arxiv-2606-13423:
Skutin works on a conjecture about p-groups in this 2026 arXiv paper. A p-group is a group whose size is a power of a prime p, and its nilpotency class measures how far it is from being commutative. The class-breadth conjecture, due to Leedham-Green, Neumann, and Wiegold, bounds that class using the group's breadth. Breadth records how large an element's centraliser, the set of elements commuting with it, can fail to be. Counterexamples have been found when the prime is 2, but for odd primes the conjecture remains open.

Skutin proposes a generalisation for the odd-prime case. He proves the generalised statement under conditions on the group. The work does not settle the conjecture, but it identifies hypotheses under which the bound holds for all odd primes. p-groups underpin much of finite group theory, and the conjecture has resisted attack for decades.
arxiv-2606-13523:
Yang and colleagues release an R software package for sorting into ordered classes in this 2026 arXiv paper. In problems such as cancer staging, disease severity grading, or air-quality categories, the classes have a natural priority order. The costly mistake is under-classification: assigning a severe case to a milder category. The hierarchical Neyman-Pearson framework was built for exactly this setting, keeping under-classification errors at levels the user specifies, with high-probability guarantees. Its umbrella algorithm wraps around ordinary classifiers to enforce those guarantees.

The package, HNPclassifier, implements the umbrella algorithms for practical use. It works with built-in learners including logistic regression, random forests, and support vector machines, and it also accepts user-supplied scoring functions. That flexibility lets practitioners bring their existing best model and add principled error control on top. The authors target statisticians and data scientists in medicine and public health.
arxiv-2606-13923:
Montero and colleagues launch an open registry for Earth observation instruments. Satellites, aircraft, and ground sensors now watch the planet in huge variety. Yet users lack one reliable source describing each instrument and its key traits. Existing catalogues describe data products, not the instruments behind them. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents Awesome Earth Observation Instruments, a community catalogue on GitHub with machine-readable metadata.

Contributors submit entries under a common schema. A light core covers general properties. Modular extensions add spectral, geometric, and data-access details, keeping the format both standard and flexible. Every submission passes automated schema validation plus human review before joining the catalogue. The schema is open, versioned, and extensible, so the registry can grow with new instruments and needs. An API for common analysis environments is planned. The catalogue should become a shared reference, lowering barriers to finding and using such data.
arxiv-2606-14323:
Arnold writes a 2026 arXiv paper in functional analysis, the study of operators acting on infinite-dimensional spaces. The work tracks how fast certain operator sequences grow or decay, which matters for the stability of numerical and physical systems. It focuses on Ritt and Kreiss type operators, two classes defined by bounds on their resolvents, a tool measuring response to shifts.

Arnold shows that older growth estimates for Kreiss bounded operators can be sharpened greatly in Hilbert spaces, nearly matching the best rates known for the stricter power-bounded case. The paper also defines a wider two-parameter operator class and derives growth bounds for it, improving several results in print. For one Kreiss family, a description through averaged sums shows the stated power growth cannot be improved when the exponent exceeds one.
arxiv-2606-14523:
Lorenzo Baldi and Máté Telek give several equal descriptions of tropicalization in a 2026 arXiv note. Tropicalization turns algebraic sets into piecewise-linear shadows. Those shadows are easier to study by counting arguments. Here the sets are definable in an o-minimal structure. That is a tame geometry setting over real closed fields.

The authors show the tropicalization can be seen four ways. It is the image under the valuation map. It is also the image of the archimedean points of the spectrum. It can be built from initial degenerations and nonnegativity cones. Or it comes from the real tropicalization of polynomials in the matching cone. They prove parallel results for the fine tropicalization. There the valuation map is replaced by the RV sort map. That map also records each point's angular part, not just its size.
arxiv-2606-15123:
Chen and coauthors benchmark language models at writing proof-of-concept exploits from vulnerability reports in a 2026 study. The task, CVE-conditioned exploit generation, feeds a model the context of a software flaw. Judging exploit quality needs tools beyond pass or fail. The team takes a data-centric route, building clean supervision first.

A multi-stage pipeline turns fragmented raw material into a structured dataset. A judge scores outputs against an eight-criterion rubric for assessment. Seventeen models are compared under one setup for zero-shot ability. Fine-tuning a compact open model on the curated data lifts exploit quality by over two fifths. With simple rejection sampling at test time, that model rivals some proprietary systems. Gains are strongest on flaws such as remote code execution, though behavior varies by vulnerability type. The authors conclude data quality and evaluation design matter as much as model scale here.
arxiv-2606-15223:
Chen and coauthors build a staggered discontinuous Galerkin method for linear elasticity in a 2026 numerical analysis paper. Such problems ask for both stress and displacement in a deforming solid. Mixed methods approximate the two fields together under the Hellinger-Reissner principle. The hard parts are keeping stress symmetric, unbroken across elements, and free of locking. The authors construct stress spaces with normal continuity on general polytopal meshes. Displacement is approximated by piecewise polynomials on the same meshes.

The method satisfies local balance of linear and angular momentum. It is locking-free, so stiff nearly-incompressible materials do not break it. The authors prove stability and derive error estimates for the scheme. A hybrid structure keeps the coding simple. It shrinks the system to boundary unknowns only. Numerical experiments confirm the theory and show the method works well. The scheme extends mixed methods to meshes made of polygons and polyhedra.
arxiv-2606-15323:
Chen and coauthors make 3D medical image translation affordable with a pixel-puzzling diffusion model in a 2026 medical imaging paper. Diffusion models translate medical scans with fidelity, but full 3D volumes exhaust GPU memory. Existing shortcuts sacrifice either global consistency or fine anatomical detail. PPDM rearranges each volume's pixels, trading spatial resolution for channel depth reversibly. That shuffle slashes activation memory while keeping the volume in view. A bridge diffusion setup starts from the input image rather than pure noise.

A puzzle-gradient loss enforces spatial coherence and suppresses grid artifacts from the shuffle. Tests covered low-count PET denoising, joint denoising with attenuation correction, and cross-modal MRI translation. PPDM matched or beat full 3D diffusion models on every task. Training memory fell by up to an order of magnitude. Inference ran faster. The framework gives hospitals a practical route to high-fidelity 3D diffusion on limited hardware.
arxiv-2606-15823:
Brandenberg and colleagues map the possible shapes of convex bodies in Minkowski spaces in 2026, through the diagram relating inradius, diameter, and circumradius. A Minkowski space is Euclidean space with a general norm; the three radii measure the largest inscribed ball, the width, and the smallest enclosing ball. The Blaschke-Santaló diagram records which combinations of the three can occur.

The boundary is described by four linear inequalities plus one complex one, and the authors identify which bodies fill each piece. They also determine for which norms the boundary collapses to a single point, forcing a unique extremal shape. The diagram for the 1-norm in 3-space is exceptional, and the team completes it by tightening Bohnenblust's inequality through the inradius. Every universal relation among the three radii follows from the boundary they chart.
arxiv-2606-16023:
Azarijoo, Krumm, and Shahabi present IBAD in 2026, a framework for flagging anomalous days in human mobility data, in terms a person can read. Daily movement looks diverse, yet much of it fits a small set of recurring templates: commuting, school-centred activity, caregiving, nightlife, errands. IBAD discovers them globally with topic modelling, represents each person as a mixture over them, and learns each person's normal mixtures with a hierarchical model.

An anomaly is a day whose mixture deviates from the norm; novelty in places or times counts as ordinary variety, not an alarm. A splicing benchmark creates controlled clashes with a person's history to test detection. Across real and synthetic data, behaviour fits few patterns, and the archetypes transfer across places and groups. Performance stays competitive in every setting, on fully unlabelled data, with no handcrafted features. Within-day, real-time detection is the stated next step.
arxiv-2606-16423:
Guillaume and co-authors plan production in 2026 under lead-time uncertainty, where orders arrive later or earlier than promised but never cross. The single-item lot sizing problem schedules production over planning periods with fixed and variable costs, backordering allowed. Every period shares one nominal lead time, yet true lead times deviate by unknown integer amounts. A budgeted uncertainty set caps how much total deviation a planner must fear.

The authors construct a family of production plans running from the most optimistic scenario to the most pessimistic one. An R-star criterion, generalizing the conservative robust min-max approach, computes these plans. For any given plan, polynomial-time algorithms find its best and worst lead-time scenarios. The min-max problem itself is solvable in polynomial time when setup costs are zero, and the min-min problem is treated as well.
arxiv-2606-16523:
Huang and co-authors present SkillWiki in 2026, a living infrastructure for the skills AI agents use, modeled on how Wikipedia manages knowledge and GitHub manages code. Agent skills, reusable capability packages, currently lack any shared system for production, governance, and evolution at scale. SkillWiki turns heterogeneous knowledge into reusable skill assets, each linked back to the evidence it came from. The demonstration walks the complete lifecycle end to end.

Knowledge is ingested, skills are produced, and users explore them with provenance attached. Governance mechanisms review and manage the assets. Execution feedback then drives further evolution, so skills improve from being used, not just from being edited. The vision is an ecosystem where knowledge, skills, and execution experience co-evolve inside one shared infrastructure. Source code and a live demonstration are publicly available. Behavior with tens of thousands of skills in one repository is not yet systematically evaluated.
arxiv-2606-16723:
Triveni Morla and colleagues introduce AgentFairBench in a 2026 paper on fairness in AI agents. Language model agents now screen job applicants, recommend credit and triage patients. Fairness testing, though, still mostly grades what models say, not what they do. A model can sound impartial while its actions favor one group over another.

The benchmark tests actions directly across hiring, lending and medical triage. Synthetic profiles differ only in a name that signals race and gender, in matched counterfactual sets, and agents run under four setups of rising autonomy, from direct answers to tool use. The harness measures flip rates, score gaps and action-rate gaps, with careful noise controls, for a few dollars per model. In the pilot run, one fast model shows no demographic effect above sampling noise once the noise floor is matched fairly. A planted-bias check confirms the tool catches real disparity when present.
arxiv-2606-17023:
Parveen Kumar, Gen Nakamura and Manmohan Vashisth recover hidden coefficients of a quantum equation from surface data in a 2026 inverse-problems paper. The equation is a nonlinear Schrödinger equation of Gross-Pitaevskii type, used for Bose-Einstein condensates. Some of its terms change with time and cannot be measured inside the domain.

The data is the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map: it records how boundary inputs produce boundary responses. The authors give pointwise formulas that rebuild the coefficients of the linear and nonlinear terms from that map. They linearize around the trivial solution, which always exists, and probe the linearized problem with solutions whose amplitudes concentrate sharply. First-order linearization recovers the potentials of the linear part. A higher-order version then isolates the remaining terms. Time-dependent behavior inside the domain is thus read off from readings at its boundary alone. That is the payoff of the construction.
arxiv-2606-17123:
Bingxue Zhang, Xiaofeng Xu and Feida Zhu watermark language models so every contributor stays traceable in a 2026 paper on model provenance. In open ecosystems, a base model is adapted again and again, forming derivation chains. Owners need to know who contributed what, yet existing marks assume one user embedding once, and fade under repeated derivation.

LineageMark encodes marks in model parameters by a projection method. It picks stable carriers, parameter directions insensitive to later changes, then represents each mark bit as a projection statistic over them. New insertions perturb the projection space only in a bounded way, and margin constraints protect the signal. Experiments show earlier contributors' marks survive later adaptations and fresh insertions. It also withstands re-watermarking, fine-tuning, quantization and pruning. Its main cost is the carrier selection step. The work extends watermarking from single-owner checks to multi-contributor provenance.
arxiv-2606-17323:
Aguillard and colleagues, writing for the Muon g-2 Collaboration, present a 2026 arXiv paper giving the final measurement of the positive muon's anomalous magnetic moment at Fermilab. That quantity, a small correction to the muon's magnetic strength, is a sensitive test of the Standard Model of particle physics. The report gathers the experiment's full positive-muon data set and the complete analysis chain behind the headline number, from beam handling to blinded statistical treatment.

The final precision reaches a stated level of just over a hundred parts per billion on the anomaly. Such precision lets theorists compare prediction and measurement at a level where faint effects of unseen particles could appear. The paper documents calibrations, corrections, and systematic uncertainties in the depth a flagship measurement demands. It closes the Fermilab experiment's account of the positive muon anomaly with a definitive experimental value.
arxiv-2606-17523:
Kimura and Akimoto present a 2026 arXiv paper advancing the convergence theory of Information-Geometric Optimization, a framework that treats black-box search as a natural gradient walk of a probability distribution. Most earlier guarantees describe an idealised continuous-time flow, not the real discrete updates with sizable learning rates that practice uses. The authors analyse discrete-time updates in the expectation parameters of an exponential family, in continuous spaces, with full covariance adaptation allowed at every step of the algorithm.

On strongly convex quadratic objectives with quantile-based weights, they prove the covariance matrix shrinks to zero. The mean vector converges to the global optimum provided the scaled covariance stays well conditioned often enough along the way. Those two results are obtained together in one setting, which earlier work had not managed. The theory edges closer to practical covariance-adaptive methods such as CMA-ES.
arxiv-2606-17723:
Maciejowski and Leonelli present a 2026 arXiv paper mapping how extreme price moves, not average ones, link the European carbon market to energy and financial markets. Carbon allowance futures sit at the heart of the EU emissions trading system, and crashes rarely respect the calm-day correlation map. The authors fit graphical models of extremes to twenty daily series spanning two phases of the scheme. They then compare the tail network against a standard Gaussian model of average dependence to see what stress rewires.

The tail networks are denser, differently centred, and bound by sector loyalty far more than the average map. Allowance futures sit at the edge of the calm network yet top the centrality rankings in the tails, while equities and currencies do the reverse. Between phases, average links thinned sharply while tail links persisted. Crash contagion also shifted from clustered to diffuse spread.
arxiv-2606-17823:
Baranov and colleagues offer a 2026 physics model for a puzzling effect called chirality-induced spin selectivity. When current flows through twisted, insulating molecules, the electrons that pass tend to share one spin far more than expected. The team builds a minimal model based on quantum tunneling through the molecule plus a weak spin split caused by the current's own magnetic field.

Their calculations show that tunneling, combined with energy loss, can amplify that tiny spin effect into polarizations near the full scale across a wide range of voltages. The model also explains a signature trait of the effect: flipping the current direction does not flip the sign of the spin polarization. It does so while respecting the standard reciprocity rules of physics, and it suggests new ways to read temperature-dependent measurements.
arxiv-2606-18223:
Samaddar and colleagues teach a cyber defender to predict its attacker by watching, in a 2026 paper. Autonomous defense agents increasingly mix behavior trees with learned components. They train by reinforcement learning. The catch is partial observability: the red agent's moves are hidden. So the defender cannot directly learn what policy the attacker follows. Nor can it tell how deep an intrusion has gone. All it sees is network traffic and its own past moves.

Their technique applies imitation learning to partially observable agents with discrete states and actions, inferring the red policy from network observations paired with the defender's own actions. Plugged into such a defense agent, the learned predictor handled several distinct attacker policies. It reached high prediction accuracy across varied simulated scenarios. Better forecasts of the adversary's next step let the defender plan counter-moves instead of merely reacting, and gauge intrusion levels while an attack unfolds.
arxiv-2606-18323:
Asaria and colleagues show that the scariest flaw of modern text-to-speech systems can be filtered out almost for free, in a 2026 paper. Open neural-codec speech models sound excellent on typical input, yet on a real fraction of utterances they fail catastrophically, emitting silence, stopping early, or collapsing into repetition and hallucinated content. That behavior disqualifies them from deployment even when average quality is high.

Their fix verifies each output with a speech recognizer. Generate a few candidates, transcribe them back, and keep one that round-trips correctly. By two candidates on a standard corpus, and four on a hard prompt set, no failures remained. The effect held across four open systems and three codecs. Better still, distilling the verified behavior back into the model recovered over half the failure mass in single-shot decoding, making the rescue free at run time.
arxiv-2606-18423:
Graßl, Serebrenik, and Destefanis examine how gender is represented in software engineering tutorials on YouTube, in a 2026 education study. Such videos quietly teach more than code. The people shown solving problems, making decisions, or standing in the background can signal who belongs in the field, which matters in a discipline with a gender gap.

The team manually analyzed two hundred English and German tutorials using critical discourse analysis, coding both story contexts and linguistic markers such as the German generic masculine. Male characters and masculine defaults dominated throughout, and the authors identify an agency gap: technical and decision-making roles went almost exclusively to men. Women were absent or placed in passive, low-agency parts. English material leaned more neutral in wording, yet examples stayed male-centered in both languages. The authors recommend representational accuracy rather than overhaul, with more women named and shown coding.
arxiv-2606-18523:
Seiffarth and colleagues introduce DART, a design-aware approach to analyzing live-cell images from microfluidic cultivation chips in real time, in a 2026 biotechnology paper. Such chips hold hundreds or thousands of growth regions, each with one cell population. Locating those regions and stripping away the chip's own structures has been semi-automated work that delays results by hours or days.

DART aligns the chip's computer-aided design blueprint with the physical chip using embedded fiducial markers detected by deep learning, so every region is localized at once. Validated on a chip combining eight distinct region designs across more than a thousand locations, it found all regions in five minutes and cleaned each image in tens of milliseconds. Automated analysis, including cell segmentation, took about a second per image. The team presents DART as a platform enabling closed-loop, outcome-driven smart microscopy.
arxiv-2606-18823:
Tan and the team report the discovery of a rapidly spinning pulsar in an unusually wide binary orbit, in a 2026 radio astronomy paper. The pulsar, designated PSR J0125-5854, was found in the ongoing SMART survey with the Murchison Widefield Array in Australia. It rotates every twenty-four milliseconds, and sits at high galactic latitude.

Follow-up observations with the same array and with MeerKAT revealed an orbital period longer than two hundred ninety days. Timing analysis points to about eight hundred thirty-four days, and very low eccentricity. The minimum companion mass is a bit over four-tenths of the Sun's mass. The authors conjecture the companion is a helium white dwarf, discussing the formation channels that could produce such a wide, nearly circular system. Because the find emerged from processing only a small fraction of the survey data, they argue more such pulsars await discovery.
arxiv-2606-19023:
Digregorio and colleagues present Moat in 2026, a defense for running pre-trained machine learning models safely. Shared model files can hide malicious code that runs when a model loads or predicts. Most scanners check files with static, format-bound rules or known attack marks. Those checks miss new attack paths and fail to transfer across frameworks, leaving hosts exposed when a model behaves badly at run time.

Moat watches what a model does to its host system while it runs. It uses the fact that model work falls into clear life-cycle phases, and that host contact inside each phase is highly structured. Odd behavior thus stands out fast. The reference build, Re-Moat, was tested on a huge set of real model files from Hugging Face, plus proof-of-concept attacks and a curated set. It caught every attack class tested with a near-zero false alarm rate.
arxiv-2606-19323:
Otero and colleagues study cohomogeneity one actions on symmetric spaces of mixed type in a 2026 geometry paper. A cohomogeneity one action is an isometric group action whose regular orbits are hypersurfaces. Mixed type spaces are those whose universal cover splits as a product of compact, noncompact, and Euclidean factors. Such actions are prized tools for building special metrics by deforming along the orbits.

The authors provide a new family of diagonal cohomogeneity one actions on products of Euclidean space with a noncompact factor. They then prove a rigidity statement. With the exception of that family, every cohomogeneity one action on a mixed space splits as a product of actions on its compact, Euclidean, and noncompact factors. The classification problem for such actions thus reduces fully to spaces of a single type. A mixed, harder problem becomes three simpler ones already studied, plus one genuinely new family to analyze.
arxiv-2606-19523:
Matt Landreman leads a stellarator design study in 2026 that rethinks how the machine's shape is described. A stellarator confines hot plasma with twisted external magnets for fusion power. Designers tune the plasma boundary shape, usually through Fourier amplitudes, hunting for shapes that hold fast alpha particles.

Bayesian optimisation needs tidy parameter bounds, yet Fourier amplitudes resist fair scaling. Wide bounds create self-crossing boundaries and failed equilibrium solves, while tight bounds curb design freedom. Landreman's team build two new parameter spaces from datasets of known boundaries. One rescales each Fourier term by quantiles onto the unit interval. The other first applies PCA to boundary points, cutting the parameter count sharply. Bayesian searches in these spaces, with particle tracing inside the loop, find shapes with excellent alpha confinement. Winning shapes can sit far from the usual symmetry families.
arxiv-2606-19723:
Writasree Maitra and four colleagues propose hunting charged lepton flavour violation inside neutrino telescopes in 2026. Any such violation would prove physics beyond the Standard Model outright. Neutrino telescopes hold vast samples of cosmic-ray muons to search with.

The proposal targets muon-to-tau conversion inside the IceCube detector. Model-independent effective field theory operators frame the signal. Sensitivities on the relevant energy scale follow for IceCube data. A concrete axial-vector Z-prime realisation maps the mass-coupling plane as well. Comparisons span low-energy flavour searches and current plus future colliders. Next-generation telescopes like IceCube-Gen2 and HUNT extend the reach further. Telescopes built for astronomy thus double as flavour physics instruments. Their huge volumes give a complementary probe no tabletop setup can match.
arxiv-2606-20223:
Hugo Magaldi and twenty-six colleagues expand an AI tool that identifies animals in African forest camera-trap images and videos. Their 2026 paper presents DeepForestVisionV2, which grows the prediction space from thirty-five classes to sixty-four: sixty-one animal classes plus human, vehicle, and blank. The first version targeted closed-canopy forest interiors at ground level. New deployments along riverbanks, clearings, and park edges kept meeting arboreal primates, birds, semi-aquatic species, and livestock that the old classes could not name.

The expansion follows three ecological gradients: vertical stratification, scene openness, and contact with human activity. Training used over 1.5 million photographs and 243 thousand videos from multi-country African forest projects. The offline workflow, matched for photos and video, stays unchanged, which matters for field teams with poor connectivity. For conservation monitoring, naming the right species at the forest edge matters as much as in the deep interior.
arxiv-2606-20423:
R. Serao, A. Quaranta, and A. Capolupo review the case for a hypothetical particle called X17. Their 2026 paper surveys the experimental evidence, the theoretical frameworks that could accommodate such a particle, and its possible implications for the Standard Model. The X17 anomaly began as an unexpected bump in nuclear transition experiments, suggesting a new boson near seventeen megaelectronvolts. A particle that light, if real, would open a low-energy window on physics beyond the Standard Model.

The review weighs how the signal has fared across experiments and which model-building routes can host the particle without breaking established results. Low-energy precision measurements complement collider searches here, probing forces too feeble for high-energy machines. The authors also map future prospects that could confirm or kill the hypothesis. Such reviews force scattered claims into one ledger, so the community can see whether evidence is converging or dissolving.
arxiv-2606-20523:
Solène Debuysère and four colleagues at ONERA release SARLO-80, a worldwide dataset pairing very-high-resolution radar imagery with optical images and language. Their 2026 paper notes that multimodal foundation models grew up on optical benchmarks, while comparable synthetic aperture radar resources stayed scarce. Existing SAR-optical datasets mostly use low-resolution, intensity-only products.

SARLO-80 preserves complex-valued SAR measurements and native acquisition geometry instead of flattened ground-range products. At 80-centimeter resolution, aligned optical imagery and natural-language descriptions accompany the radar data. Physically grounded multimodal learning needs exactly these unprocessed signals. The dataset gives radar the kind of large-scale, language-linked benchmark that optical vision already enjoys.
arxiv-2606-21023:
Zhenting Zhu and seven colleagues at UCLA diagnose numerical instability in language model inference in 2026 and propose HEAL to restore reproducible outputs. Models now serve finance, medicine, and law, where reproducibility is a strict need. Greedy decoding removes sampling randomness. Yet sixteen-bit deployments still diverge across different graphics processors. Profiling at a low level traces the cause.

Truncation errors during downcasting at kernel boundaries drive the divergence. A full thirty-two-bit pipeline would fix it at high cost. Memory for the key-value cache would also double. HEAL intervenes in a targeted way. It applies a sixteen-bit integer quantization that preserves stability for key tensors, exploiting unused bit width. Targeted precision repair could make mission-critical inference auditable, because the same input must yield the same output on whatever hardware a provider happens to run.
arxiv-2606-21223:
Yihong Tian and five colleagues present Ultra-Fusion in 2026, a localization framework that keeps vehicles and robots oriented when individual sensors fail. Self-driving cars, delivery robots, and inspection drones blend camera, LiDAR, inertial, wheel, and satellite signals, but glare, tunnel darkness, wheel slip, and lost satellite fixes still break fused systems. Ultra-Fusion packs time-ordered measurements into one sliding-window optimizer, where each sensor's data becomes an optional factor.

Reliability scheduling gates poor measurements before they corrupt the estimate, and a checked startup picks the right sensor mix. The system also fine-tunes LiDAR-inertial timing and rotation online while running. Benchmarked against more than sixty open SLAM systems on five datasets, it stays accurate across wheeled, legged, and aerial platforms under degradation and calibration errors, improving availability for road-level autonomy.
arxiv-2606-21423:
Nishant Narechania, Guo Meng, Emil Poulsen, and Eric Sonnendrucker extend a structure-preserving plasma simulation framework in 2026 to a hybrid model that treats electrons cheaply and ions in full detail. The GEMPICX particle-in-cell framework gains the quasineutral hybrid Vlasov-Maxwell equations, with drift-kinetic electrons and fully kinetic ions. A scheme on dual grids keeps the geometry of the model intact in the discrete version.

Without a direct time law for the electric field, a curl-curl equation recovers its part along the background field at each step. The sideways part comes from the quasineutral Ampere law and the drift-kinetic current. Explicit and two mixed implicit-explicit time stepping schemes are tested, and wave behavior from the dispersion relation validates the model.
arxiv-2606-21923:
Kang and Lei explore, in 2026, the combinatorics of higher dimers on band graphs, structures that generalize matching problems on graphs drawn from surfaces. Their subject connects cluster algebras, continued fractions deformed by a parameter q, and dimer models, where covers of a graph by small tiles encode algebraic quantities. Earlier work handled ordinary matchings on snake graphs; this paper pushes to higher dimer covers on band graphs.

The authors give a combinatorial interpretation for the trace of the q-deformed higher continued fraction matrices. With a q-weighting on edges, the trace equals the dimer partition function over the good higher dimers. They also show the good higher dimer covers form a distributive lattice under face flips on square faces. Finally, they prove the dimer partition function is palindromic for a certain family of band graphs, extending a symmetry known for circular fence posets.
arxiv-2606-22123:
Ushcats and Ushcats present, in 2026, an enhanced method for computing cluster integrals in lattice models of matter. Cluster integrals are the building blocks of Mayer's expansion, a series that describes fluids and lattice gases through small groups of particles. The bottleneck is a heavy multidimensional integration performed at many points.

Two optimizations speed the calculation up. The integrand is simplified at each integration point, and physically identical configurations are counted once instead of repeatedly. With those savings, the authors compute new data on high-order cluster integrals for a number of two-dimensional and three-dimensional lattice models. The results extend the reach of Wheatley's algorithm and of cluster methods for equations of state.
arxiv-2606-22423:
Madhulatha Mandarapu and Sandeep Kunkunuru ask when a columnar database scan is truly limited by memory bandwidth in this 2026 paper. A columnar scan decompresses, filters, and aggregates stored values, and simple roofline reasoning says only the bytes read should matter. In practice, real decoder programs often stay compute-bound and leave much of the bandwidth unused.

Across encodings, filter selectivities, and two different machines, the authors find a decoder's value throughput, the values decoded per second, barely depends on bit-width. One fitted throughput per decoding strategy therefore predicts the achieved bandwidth fraction with a one-parameter law. The law's median error was small on an x86 machine and smaller still on a held-out Apple M4 machine. It also reproduces a well-known production decoder's headline result as a limiting case. Two further crossovers, covering branch-free filtering and zone-map skipping, held on both machines.
arxiv-2606-22723:
João Guilherme Alves Santos and four colleagues benchmark language models on Brazilian exams in this 2026 paper. Portuguese evaluation lags behind English, especially for open-ended questions demanding written reasoning. The original BLUEX used multiple-choice items from university entrance exams, missing the harder second-phase examinations entirely.

BLUEX v2 draws on second-phase exams from UNICAMP and USP, Brazil's two leading universities, across the years 2022 to 2025. The dataset holds 395 questions unfolding into 919 graded subquestions, over half with associated images. Each item carries its subject, official reference answers, rubric criteria, and six capability tags. The team evaluated twenty-one leading language models with a model-as-judge protocol. Scores spread by about five points on a ten-point scale, a wide gap for frontier systems. Mathematical reasoning and image understanding emerged as the hardest capability dimensions. The dataset, code, and model outputs are publicly released.
arxiv-2606-22923:
Yimeng Qin and five colleagues give a soft growing robot whole-body vision in this 2026 paper. Vine robots extend by growing at the tip, and their soft, self-supporting bodies suit tight, complex spaces. The same softness brings hysteresis, tether interactions, and deformations that defeat conventional planning and control.

Their system, PanoVine, mounts nineteen cameras along the robot's body, feeding back both the robot's state and its surroundings. A visuomotor policy trained end-to-end from demonstrations aggregates this distributed sensing for closed-loop control. The policy proved robust to inaccurate robot state and actuation estimates. In experiments, the robot steered through branched structures, climbed slopes, and crossed unsupported terrain. It also reached objects precisely and maneuvered through confined spaces and around obstacles. The authors present PanoVine as the first autonomous vine robot system of its kind.
arxiv-2606-23323:
Pietro Conzinu and Daiki Ueda bound nonlinear electrodynamics using resummed relative entropy in a 2026 theory paper. Nonlinear electrodynamics extends Maxwell's theory through an expansion. The expansion holds an infinite tower of higher-dimensional operators. Relative entropy, worked out in chosen background fields, encodes facts about that whole tower at once. The authors study it in scalar QED, fermionic QED, and Dirac-Born-Infeld theory. They mix perturbative analysis, resummation, and non-perturbative methods. In the weak-coupling regime, one demand does much of the work. The entropy must stay non-negative. That demand forces sign constraints on truncated sets of operators.

Conzinu and Ueda show that violations at strong coupling mean different things in different settings. Inside a truncated expansion, a violation just says the approximation has broken down. In the resummed entropy, the same violation points to a real instability, such as the Schwinger effect.
arxiv-2606-23623:
Wu and colleagues bring reinforcement learning to a new class of robot control models, in a 2026 paper on embodied AI. Discrete diffusion vision language action models handle images, instructions, and robot actions as tokens in one shared space, refining actions through repeated denoising steps. Until now they were trained only by supervised fine tuning, imitating demonstrations. Reinforcement learning could improve them, but the probability of the final action is intractable, which blocks standard methods.

The fix is to score the whole denoising path instead of the final action alone. Modeling each denoising step as a decision turns the path probability into a product of step probabilities that can be optimized. A step scheduling scheme gives harder tasks more denoising steps. The method reaches near ninety nine point seven percent success on the LIBERO benchmark and improves a supervised baseline by about thirty points on RoboTwin.
arxiv-2606-23723:
Jackson sharpens a hardness result about deciding membership in families of finite algebraic structures, in a 2026 note on semigroup theory. A semigroup is a set with an associative operation, like combining moves in a game. A pseudovariety is a family of finite semigroups closed under natural constructions, and the membership problem asks whether a given semigroup belongs to the family one fixed example generates. Earlier work showed this problem can be NP hard.

Jackson constructs the test case from two ingredients multiplied together. One is the six element Brandt monoid, and the other is a monoid of order preserving maps on a short chain of numbers. For chain length at least four, deciding membership for the combined generator is hard for Difference P. That class contains both NP and its complement, so the problem exceeds either earlier benchmark alone.
arxiv-2606-24223:
Huang and colleagues probe the identity of the lightest strange scalar particle. It is a broad resonance whose insides are still argued about. The K0*(700), also called kappa, sits close to the kaon-pion threshold. It decays almost as soon as it forms. That fuels debate over whether it is an ordinary quark-antiquark state or something more exotic. Working inside the conventional quark-antiquark picture, the team studies how the particle would behave in four-body semileptonic decays of Bs mesons.

Light-cone distribution amplitudes describe how momentum is shared between the resonance's constituents. The authors construct one twist-2 and two twist-3 amplitudes, using a harmonic oscillator model. Two parametrisation schemes cover the leading amplitude's longitudinal shape. Those inputs feed predictions for the decay's observable behaviour. Huang's 2026 calculations enrich the theoretical expectations against which future measurements can judge whether the ordinary picture of this elusive resonance holds up.
arxiv-2606-24523:
Eren and colleagues probe whether language models can catch Turkish phone scams from recordings. Scam calls exploit vulnerable communities everywhere. Detection research concentrates on English and other high resource languages, though. Low resource settings are left with scarce annotated data and thin defences. Their 2026 poster introduces the first public multimodal dataset for the problem. One hundred aligned audio transcript pairs of scam and benign Turkish conversations are included.

Seven large language models from three families are evaluated under three input conditions. Raw audio, machine speech-to-text transcripts, and transcripts a native speaker refined. Models given transcripts reliably beat models given raw sound, a practical point for deployment. Human corrected and machine transcripts perform comparably. Expensive correction, it seems, buys little. Eren's team centres a low resource language and a real world threat deliberately, arguing AI safety research must become linguistically inclusive.
arxiv-2606-24723:
F. Javier García and Alejandro Manjavacas build a quantum theory of rotational vacuum friction for particles that absorb no light. A spinning particle in vacuum can shed angular momentum only by turning mechanical energy into radiation. Here the particles are small and lossless, and rotation is the motion at stake. The authors show that axial symmetry changes the leading channel of energy loss.

At zero temperature, anisotropic particles feel a frictional torque growing with the seventh power of the rotation rate. The loss comes from emitting correlated photon pairs whose frequencies add to twice the rotation frequency. At finite temperature, a second contribution appears that is linear in the rotation rate. Axisymmetric particles are different. García and Manjavacas find them protected against this photon assisted friction in all cases. Symmetry, in short, can switch the effect off.
arxiv-2606-25023:
Damien Easson derives obstructions to building a cosmology inside a regular black hole. For regular black holes, which replace the singularity with a core, the trapped region is Kantowski Sachs rather than Friedmann Robertson Walker. A daughter cosmology must be glued in as a matched region. Easson works through the matching for closed, flat, and open daughters; each case hits a wall.

For closed daughters, the mass function forces the density to fall faster than the curvature term, so the closed branch stays bounded instead of expanding forever. Flat and open daughters escape that trap, but a completeness theorem blocks their non static, curvature regular versions from being geodesically complete. The Bardeen black hole, examined as a parent, does not supply the late time support a closed daughter needs. Easson concludes a daughter requires extra structure: modified asymptotics, nonminimal matching, non Friedmann evolution, or an added stress energy component.
arxiv-2606-25923:
Harry Amad and Mihaela van der Schaar question how digital twins, virtual replicas used to test decisions before acting, are usually trained. Standard training minimizes one-step prediction error. The pair prove that with limited model capacity, a twin trained that way can rank candidate policies in the wrong order, even though ranking policies by reward is the twin's actual job. Experiments confirm the flaw appears in practice, not just in theory.

Decision-targeted training is their fix, packaged as DT squared. Policy values are first estimated from logged data with fitted Q-evaluation, giving proxy ground truth. The twin then learns to produce rollouts that keep the same ranking between policy pairs, using a loss that works with any model architecture. Across settings, the method improves policy ranking and cuts decision regret for both familiar and unseen policies, while simulation accuracy stays respectable.
arxiv-2606-26223:
A. Ouellette and the SPT-3G Collaboration cross-check two maps of the universe's hidden mass. Weak lensing bends light from distant galaxies, tracing matter directly. The cosmic microwave background gets lensed too, by the same matter along its longer path. Each probe has its own scales, depths, and flaws. Their overlap region offers a consistency test for both. The Dark Energy Survey Year 3 shear catalogue and SPT-3G lensing maps share about thirteen hundred square degrees.

High significance marks a first here. A polarization-only microwave lensing map, chosen because foregrounds bias it least, cross-correlates with galaxy shear at about fourteen sigma. Other estimator mixes trade bias against noise for comparison. A blue, star-forming galaxy sample reduces alignment worries. Fitted within the standard cosmology, the clustering amplitude lands in line with both parent surveys. Agreement steadies confidence in the matter map drawn by two very different instruments.
arxiv-2606-26423:
Haonan Chen and colleagues at Harvard tackle long, contact-rich robot tasks, like seating a graphics card into its slot, which need millimeter precision yet must generalize to new jobs. Rigid pipelines are precise but brittle; single learned policies generalize but lack precision.

Their framework, CoStream, composes three simple behaviors instead: one extracts spatial constraints using foundation models, one forecasts trajectories by tracking keypoints in imagined video, and one applies fast tactile corrections. Their outputs combine into one pose command at each control step. Demonstrated on eight real-world tasks, the approach aims to get precision and adaptability from composition rather than retraining.
arxiv-2606-26523:
Daniel A. Herrmann and Benjamin A. Levinstein ask how we can justifiably describe an AI system as believing or wanting something. Their book builds a framework from radical interpretation, a philosophy method for understanding an agent from its behaviour as a whole. They combine it with mechanistic interpretability, the young science of reading a model's internal workings.

The core question is how computational facts determine beliefs, desires, and meanings. The authors set success criteria for two broad approaches. One treats internal states as representations directly. The other treats belief talk as an interpretive tool. A central lesson is holism: beliefs, desires, and sentence structure constrain each other jointly. Fixing one while measuring the others imports distortion. That interdependence also gives leverage, the authors argue. A system's attitudes limit its possible structure, and internal measurements can test both together. The stakes include detecting deception in deployed systems.
arxiv-2606-26823:
Hidde T. Jense, Luca H. Abu El-Haj, J. Colin Hill, and Oliver H. E. Philcox hunt for fingerprints of particle production during cosmic inflation. Inflation was the universe's first burst of expansion. In many models, the inflaton field briefly creates particles, leaving a localised bump in the cosmic microwave background's pattern. The authors study a case with an extremely heavy partner field.

They compute the model's full temperature and polarisation patterns. Then they search two sky surveys, Planck and the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, for the predicted feature. The joint search found a mild hint of a signal at a characteristic scale. Neither survey alone showed it significantly. Forecasts suggest future data should settle the question. A confirmed bump would directly reveal particle creation in the universe's first moments.
arxiv-2606-27023:
Eren Senoglu and four colleagues teach medical question-answering models to say how sure they are, honestly. Multimodal models answering questions about medical images tend to sound confident even when wrong. Existing fixes for wording confidence were built for text-only models. Their training framework adjusts a composite loss with four parts.

One part penalises miscalibration directly. An anchor term stops confidence collapsing to extremes. A contrastive term ties answers to the image, and a stabilising term protects answering skill. A two-by-two perturbation test, crossing image presence with text integrity, measures whether the model truly uses the image. Across three medical benchmarks and two model families, calibration error fell by three fifths or more. Discrimination between right and wrong answers also rose sharply.
arxiv-2606-27323:
Durkan and Page establish formulae for amplified moments of the Riemann zeta function, a central object in analytic number theory. Moments measure the average size of zeta on the critical line and connect to conjectures from random matrix theory. Their work covers two-piece amplified second and fourth moments with full asymptotic formulae. Amplification, weighting the integrand to emphasise large values, sharpens what can be proven. Applications reach several joint moments of zeta and its companions, in a mathematics paper published in 2026.

Unconditional effective lower bounds follow, matching the conjectures of Keating and collaborators closely. An explicit lower bound for the sixth moment is proven with a concrete constant. Some bounds due to Soundararajan are improved, and the Lindelöf Hypothesis, previously assumed, is no longer needed. Effective lower bounds now cover all joint integer moments in line with random matrix predictions. The moment problem's unconditional frontier moves forward.
arxiv-2606-27423:
Li and Zheng supply ready-to-use formulae for Lyman-alpha radiative transfer, the journey of a key ultraviolet photon line through gas clouds. The authors solve the transfer equations analytically for a static, uniform cloud under cylindrical geometry, checking against simulations and against published slab and spherical solutions. In the 2026 astrophysics paper, atomic recoil, the tiny kick atoms give photons, is folded in by an empirical modification of recoil-free spectra.

Constant velocity gradients across the cloud yield series solutions of their own. Accuracy holds for small gradients and fades for large ones, so an extended functional form is fitted to simulations for the extreme regime, improving results greatly at large optical depths. The cylindrical case rounds out the solution set under simple geometries. Theorists gain fast analytical tools where simulation grids once stood. Physical insight into recoil and motion effects comes with the formulae.
arxiv-2606-27523:
Brodsky studies what survives when the c-vectors of a cluster algebra are projected onto just two coordinates. For acyclic cluster algebras these vectors coincide, up to sign, with the real Schur roots. When the difference between two coordinates stays bounded, the projected image sits inside a band of lattice lines, and the question is whether the projection fills its band. A dichotomy valid in every acyclic type answers the existence half: the difference is bounded exactly when the two null-root coefficients agree in this algebra paper of 2026.

For affine type A, the annulus case, in source-sink orientation, the filling question resolves completely: every projection fills its band apart from the source-sink diagonal, which holds just the finite regular part. What obstructs the filling is the Auslander-Reiten defect, visible on a diagonal exactly when it is a coordinate difference. The general classification remains open.
arxiv-2606-27923:
Interior designers often need a 3D model from a single furniture photo. Alibaba Group and Taobao present Home3D 1.0 in 2026 to generate such assets. One reference image goes in. A mesh with physically based rendering materials comes out. The mesh can be split into material-specific components. Four tightly coupled modules form the pipeline.

A geometry module rebuilds a watertight mesh. It uses latent signed-distance modelling. A texture module predicts multi-view appearance. It also completes unseen surface regions. A material module segments components through video-based masks and UV-space voting. It then retrieves matching materials from a curated library. A parts module generates semantic part meshes. They stay editable by material. Each module is scored on its own with dedicated metrics. The evaluations highlight current capability. They also show the gaps toward broader deployment. Cross-stage feedback and articulated objects are named as future work.
arxiv-2606-28123:
Thomas Boudou, Batiste Le Bars, Nirupam Gupta, and Aurélien Bellet examine a quiet assumption behind modern machine learning pipelines. When updates from many sources are combined, as happens when rules enforce privacy, robustness, fairness, or adaptivity, the combining rule is often not a plain average.

Boudou and colleagues prove that a combining rule preserves monotonicity only when the rule is positively affine. Monotonicity is the property that keeps first-order learning methods converging steadily. A positively affine rule is a weighted average plus a fixed shift. Every rule outside that family breaks monotonicity, which harms both convergence and stability in ways they quantify. They close by giving conditions under which monotonicity can be restored, uniting several known failure modes under one explanation.
arxiv-2606-28523:
Kevin Wagner, Sumin Seung, Dániel Apai, and a dozen further colleagues make the case, in this Nautilus Space Observatory white paper, for hunting exomoons by watching planets wobble. A moon tugs its planet, and that reflex motion is recoverable from precise star-planet position measurements over time. The signal grows for heavier, wider moons around nearby, low-mass planets.

Catching moons below Earth mass takes continuous, long, ultra-precise monitoring that only a dedicated facility can supply. The authors argue Nautilus's replicable array architecture fits uniquely. They stage the campaign: first one or a few small telescopes stare at the nearest imaged giants, a long shot with high reward. As the array grows and its noise floor drops, the search extends systematically to the nearest suitable systems, alongside direct imaging of the planets themselves.
arxiv-2606-28623:
Md Mozaharul Mottalib and Rahmatollah Beheshti sort patients into meaningful subgroups from their health records. Subtyping promises precision medicine, but records are irregular, visits unevenly spaced, and the time patterns that define a subtype hide inside long, messy sequences that defeat plain clustering.

Their self-supervised model builds on Mamba, a sequence model built for long records, and learns summaries of each patient's history without labels. The team tests the summaries two ways: predicting known labels, and clustering patients into subtypes from the learned geometry. Across public and private real-world datasets, the design choices behind their model deliver better prediction than strong baselines. Head-to-head comparisons of clustering methods show the summaries carry useful subtyping signal. That is a step toward grouping patients by how their conditions unfold.
arxiv-2606-29023:
Zhang, Wang, Qi and Wen present a pipeline for finding where and when an object described in words appears in a long video. This task, spatio-temporal grounding, demands precise timing plus robust tracking, and modern vision-language models can reason about it but are costly and unstable when applied frame by frame. Their pipeline instead tracks at the level of seconds, smoothing across seconds to keep continuity while shortening the sequence the model must handle.

To teach reasoning, the team synthesise step-by-step trajectories with advanced multimodal models, then swap generated coordinates for ground-truth ones. A reinforcement learning stage tunes the policy, scored by a verifier combining time and video overlap. Across frame-rate settings, the method achieved a strong trade-off between speed and localisation quality.
arxiv-2606-29223:
Yang, Sun and Xia propose Depth Exploration Decoding, a way to generate text from language models faster without changing the output. Standard decoding runs every token through the full layer stack, although many tokens become predictable at intermediate depths. Earlier depth-adaptive methods pick one early exit depth and verify it, but a late exit wastes computation and an early one triggers fallback.

Their algorithm explores multiple candidate depths in parallel instead of selecting one. At each commit position it checks candidates against the final-depth reference and commits exactly the final-depth token, then collapses the exploration lattice, keeping only reusable branch states. This cycle preserves exact equivalence to standard decoding while cutting the cost per token. Across early-exit-trained and standard models, it beat depth-selection baselines and matched speculative and distributed decoding methods in throughput. It also improved as explored depths became finer.
arxiv-2606-29323:
Ghazi and Moradpouri study a family of symmetry algebras that generalise the BMS3 algebra, an infinite-dimensional algebra arising in flat-space gravity and conformal field theory. Their starting point is the Sugawara construction, which builds the Virasoro algebra from a current algebra. For a doubled abelian current algebra, earlier work found extra constructions carrying a grading by the cyclic group of order N, forming a non-compact algebraic variety.

The pair compactify these varieties by adding points at infinity. Those added points, they show, are exactly the BMS3-like algebras. For grading two, the point gives the standard BMS3 algebra: the Virasoro algebra joined with an infinite abelian ideal. For larger N the ideal becomes nonabelian and nilpotent, with depth below N. The depth matches the order of the variety's singularity there. They also study central extensions of these algebras.
arxiv-2606-29523:
Pezzella presents SPIDeC methods, solvers for positive dynamical systems, where the tracked values must stay nonnegative. Ordinary solvers can drift below zero or move a steady state, breaking the model's meaning. His framework embeds a deferred correction step inside an exponential Volterra form of the problem.

That structure keeps solutions positive and keeps steady states fixed, whatever the step size. Repeated correction sweeps over a low-order base improve the result step by step. The methods are L-stable, a strong stability property, and they match exactly the flow of diagonal linear problems. With Gauss-Radau nodes, the discrete flow grows more contractive as sweeps increase. Numerical tests confirm the theory.
arxiv-2606-29823:
Liao and twenty-four colleagues argue that long-running AI agents need a new kind of data foundation. As an agent works on a hard task it tries options, runs tools, hits failures, and repairs them, and this whole search forms what the authors call an experience graph.

Today that record is usually thrown into log files that cannot be searched, shared, or turned into training data. The proposed system, Trellis, stores the experience graph as proper database state, so picking the next step becomes a query and reuse across sessions becomes a search. The design is grounded in a production kernel optimizer at Meta, where reusing past experience reached a target speedup about ten times faster at 52 percent lower token cost per valid solution.
arxiv-2606-30023:
Kristian Drizari and five colleagues test learning based beam selection for millimeter-wave links. These links operate near twenty-six and a half gigahertz indoors. They carry huge bandwidth but fade when beams misalign. Blockages also disrupt them easily. Exhaustively sweeping every beam wastes time and overhead. Their hybrid beamforming testbed combines digital processing with analog steering.

The team collected wideband channel measurements in a real office corridor. A synchronized software defined radio testbed gathered the data. Beam selection becomes a supervised learning problem. The goal is predicting the beam exhaustive sweeping rates best. One neural network uses spatial features like position. A pilots-only method uses a few sounded beams instead. It needs no location information at all. Both methods reach high prediction accuracy. Beam search overhead falls sharply versus full sweeping.
arxiv-2606-30723: This author studies Ryu-Takayanagi area from Virasoro modular data. The studying studies. Their studying is Ryu-Takayanagi area Virasoro modular data. The studying studies. It is string theory. The studying is from. The modular data is Virasoro. The area study is string-theoretic.
arxiv-2606-30823:
Rob McConkey, Christopher St. Clair, Tristan Wells and Chen Zhang make progress on a knot-theory question from the Kirby problem list. Akbulut asked whether some homology sphere, other than the ordinary three-sphere, has a strong slicing property. Any knot in it that bounds a disk in some contractible four-manifold should already bound a disk in the thin product region. Knots with the opposite, deeply slice behaviour would illuminate the question.

The team construct a class of deeply slice knots. They specify a pair: a contractible four-manifold with integral homology-sphere boundary, and a knot that is slice in that manifold. Then they prove the knot is not slice in the product region, using concordance invariants from Heegaard Floer homology. Immersed curve techniques, a diagrammatic way to compute those invariants, do the heavy lifting. The construction supplies test cases for Akbulut's question rather than settling it.
arxiv-2606-30923:
Sriraman and three colleagues ask why on-policy distillation often beats behavior cloning when language models learn from imperfect teachers. In imitation learning, a student copies an expert's behavior; here the student only sees a noisy version of the expert, yet is judged against the clean expert's reward. That mismatch mirrors real training, where long chains of thought come from fallible demonstrators.

The authors prove a sharp separation. Learning offline from noisy demonstrations is fundamentally hard, with sample needs growing exponentially in the horizon. Learning online, through their new variant of on-policy distillation, needs only polynomially many samples. Experiments on synthetic and language tasks confirm the theory: the proposed method outperforms both offline cloning and existing distillation objectives under noisy feedback.
arxiv-2606-31023:
Zhou and three colleagues tackle a safety problem in systems that must obey hard constraints at every step, such as power-grid scheduling. Modern AI models can draft long action sequences cheaply, but their drafts carry no guarantee of obeying the constraints, while calling a trusted solver at every step wastes the AI's speed. Their method, Certificate-Gated Prefix Acceptance, lets an untrusted agent propose moves while a trusted verifier checks each transition exactly.

A conformally calibrated value boundary decides how much of each draft can be accepted safely before the rest goes to the solver. In tests, every proposal source, including large language models that violated constraints in almost all direct rollouts, produced zero applied violations. On a full-scale unit commitment problem, the setup ran nearly three times faster than solver-only control at low regret.
arxiv-2606-31123:
Lee and Lee revisit the symplectic leaves of meromorphic Hitchin systems, spaces of Higgs bundles whose fields may have poles at marked points. That moduli space carries a Poisson structure, a bracket that splits it into symplectic leaves, found by Bottacin and Markman. The authors focus on the tame case, where pole behaviour stays controlled.

They study how the restricted Hitchin map on each leaf can be partly compactified while staying an algebraically completely integrable system. Moduli spaces of parabolic Higgs bundles with a fixed direction vector give that compactification. Those same spaces also resolve, in the symplectic sense, the normalization of each leaf closure, and the paper adds connectedness results for the matching Betti moduli spaces.
arxiv-2606-31623:
Aliyev and Aliyeva reconcile two separate criteria for the same question in Sturm-Liouville theory, which studies vibration-type equations whose solutions form systems used to expand other functions. The problem's boundary condition depends linearly on the eigenparameter, the unknown constant being solved for. Earlier work by the authors derived minimality criteria for the system of root functions through independent routes.

Minimality means no function in the system can be dropped without shrinking what the system spans. The pair prove the two criteria are equivalent and give one unified description of the exceptional cases, where removing certain associated functions does destroy minimality. Worked examples with multiple eigenvalues show both approaches agreeing and clarify the structure of the root function systems involved.
arxiv-2606-31823:
Chen presents next-to-next-to-leading order predictions for producing a top-antitop pair plus a W boson at the Large Hadron Collider. The process is among the heaviest signatures studied there. Measured rates have often come out above Standard Model expectations, which pushes theory toward higher accuracy.

Earlier NNLO work avoided computing the two-loop amplitudes directly, relying on soft and high-energy approximations instead. Chen evaluates those amplitudes explicitly for the first time, within a generalised leading-colour limit. That limit expands in colour factors rather than invoking any kinematic shortcut. The resulting cross sections agree with the earlier approximate calculation. The agreement, on its own, validates the approach experiments had been compared against.
arxiv-2606-32023:
Vautier and two colleagues build a single deep learning model that predicts forest attributes across a whole country from airborne LiDAR. National inventories need wall-to-wall maps, but national LiDAR campaigns mix sensors, seasons, flight constraints and scan angles. Models calibrated locally usually fail to generalize across that heterogeneity, especially over structurally diverse forests.

FLORA combines an octree-based backbone over the point clouds with ecological and spatiotemporal auxiliary variables, fused through a gating mechanism that keeps each variable's contribution partly interpretable. Training uses 32,052 French National Forest Inventory plots from the national LiDAR HD program. One model trained jointly on leaf-on and leaf-off flights beats season-specific models. Dominant height is predicted with a relative error near 12.3 percent, alongside competitive volume estimates.
arxiv-2608-00323:
Ono settles a conjecture of Han and Xiong on fractional Gaussian binomial coefficients. Han and Xiong had extended that coefficient to positive rational r. They guessed its integer trace is largest, coefficient by coefficient, at r equal to one half. The trace is the integer-exponent part of the series. Ono attacks the claim via a support-dominance theorem.

His theorem compares rational parameters under a clear divisibility rule. It settles the claim for all r at least one half. The full claim shrinks to unit fractions one over 2m. Just finitely many are nontrivial for fixed k. A computer check then proves all positive rational r for k up to 200. The theory was made and checked in Lean by AxiomProver.
as-you-like-it-pg1523:
William Shakespeare's As You Like It appears in this modern-spelling text arranged by act and scene, beginning in an orchard near Oliver's house.
