Its bacterial complex first appeared as a human disease in Africa. It then traveled the world with the first modern human migrations.

Newer bacterial lineages later expanded with population growth and rode waves of exploration, trade, and conquest. Evidence suggests lineages adapted to particular human populations, and the globally successful modern ones provoke less inflammation in immune cells, possibly reflecting greater virulence and shorter latency. Human gene variants are in turn associated with particular lineages. Gagneux argues the disease's biology and spread were shaped by this long association.
europmc-pmc3270023:
Julia Salzman and colleagues reported that circular RNAs are common products of human genes, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Textbook splicing joins a gene's exons in their genomic order to make a straight molecule. Deep sequencing of RNA from normal and cancerous human cells kept turning up transcripts whose exons appeared shuffled.

Statistical estimates and biochemical tests gave strong evidence that a substantial share of the spliced output from hundreds of genes is circular, with the RNA's ends joined into a loop. In many cases the circular form was the predominant version of the transcript. The authors conclude this unusual splicing is not an oddity. It is a general feature of how human genes are expressed. That opens questions about what these stable circles do in the cell.
europmc-pmc3326523:
Filippakopoulos and a large team mapped the human family of bromodomains, proteins that read one kind of chemical mark on chromosomes, reporting in 2012. These modules latch onto acetyl tags placed on lysine building blocks, a key step in interpreting the cell's epigenetic code. Humans carry sixty one of them, sorted into eight families by shape and sequence.

The team solved twenty nine detailed crystal structures, covering every family, and compared them to find shared and family specific features. Testing representative bromodomains against arrays of chromosome protein pieces revealed new binding partners and showed that nearby marks, such as phosphate tags, strongly sway binding. One family member could grip two acetyl tags at once through a newly revealed mechanism. The maps lay groundwork for designing drugs against this rising target family.
europmc-pmc3347323:
Heald-Sargent and Gallagher reviewed how coronavirus spike proteins get armed to fuse into human cells, in a 2012 article. The spike, studding the virus surface, must grab a cell receptor and then fold dramatically to merge the viral and cell membranes. That folding is not automatic; the spike has to be primed first, like a trap being set.

Three triggers do the priming: docking onto a receptor, being snipped by host cutting enzymes, and the acidity inside the cell compartments the virus passes through. The review gives special attention to a family of surface cutting enzymes known to activate several viral fusion proteins, likely sitting beside receptors ready to split spikes as viruses arrive. The authors close by showing how this entry choreography points to places where antiviral drugs could jam the process.
europmc-pmc3415623:
Sjögren and colleagues showed in 2012 that gut bacteria help set bone mass in mice. Germ-free mice, raised with no microbes at all, grew denser bones than ordinary mice. Their bones held fewer osteoclasts, the cells that dissolve bone, per unit of surface.

Giving germ-free mice a normal gut community brought bone mass back to normal. The sterile mice also had fewer helper T cells and fewer osteoclast precursors in their marrow, plus quieter inflammatory signals in bone. Colonization corrected those immune features too. The chain, the authors argue, runs from gut microbes through immune tone to bone-eating cells. They float the gut as a fresh target for osteoporosis treatment.
europmc-pmc3471323:
Masella and colleagues presented PANDAseq, a program that joins paired DNA reads into single sequences, in BMC Bioinformatics in 2012. Studies of microbe communities rely on reading a marker gene from both ends, then stitching the two reads where they overlap. Simple stitching throws away many reads over small errors, wasting hard-won data.

PANDAseq uses the quality scores attached to each base to fix mismatches and blanks in the overlap. In tests on simulated and real samples, it joined reads faster than rival tools and kept more of them, with few added errors. Gains in usable sequences ranged widely across test libraries. Masella's team notes the program scales to billions of read pairs on ordinary hardware.

The GBD 2015 Tobacco Collaborators track smoking and its death toll across the world. Their systematic analysis appeared in The Lancet. It covers 195 countries and territories. The span runs from 1990 to 2015. Tobacco control has spread in that period. Smoking still ranks among the top risks for early death. The team pooled 2,818 data sources. Models filled gaps by place, age, sex, and year.

Daily smoking fell to 25 percent of men worldwide. For women it fell to 5.4 percent. Those are drops of about 28 and 34 percent since 1990. Progress slowed after 2005 in many places. Four countries saw rates rise. Smoking still caused 6.4 million deaths in 2015. That was 11.5 percent of all deaths. Over half fell in China, India, the United States, and Russia. Population growth and aging push the total toll up. The authors urge faster prevention and quitting support.
europmc-pmc5444023:
Schmaal and co-authors run the largest brain scan study yet of major depression. Their meta-analysis appeared in Molecular Psychiatry. It comes from the ENIGMA Major Depressive Disorder Working Group. Past scan studies were small and clashed. This team pooled scans from 20 cohorts worldwide. All sites used harmonized methods. The sample held 2,148 patients and 7,957 healthy controls.

Adults with depression had thinner cortex in several zones. The orbitofrontal cortex, cingulate, insula, and temporal lobes all showed thinning. Effect sizes were small, near a tenth of a standard unit. First-episode and adult-onset cases showed the clearest gaps. Teens told a different story. They had lower total surface area, not thinner cortex. Frontal and sensory zones shrank most. Recurrent teen cases showed the strongest effects. The authors read this as a moving target. Depression seems to mark the brain in stage-specific ways.
europmc-pmc5445723:
Andersson and co-authors fix a hidden flaw in brain scan correction: movement during a single volume. Their methods article appeared in NeuroImage. Diffusion MRI builds each volume from stacked slices. Standard tools assume the head stays still during those seconds. Movement is treated as jumps between volumes. Real heads drift slice by slice.

The new method models movement as a smooth function over time. It works inside their existing eddy framework. That framework already handles distortion and signal dropout together. Tests on lifelike simulated data came first. The method recovered true movement with high accuracy. Measures such as fractional anisotropy came out cleaner. Gaps between still and moving scans shrank. A volunteer who moved on purpose confirmed the gain. Scans of elderly subjects lost their telltale movement signs. The work should sharpen studies of groups who move most.
europmc-pmc5460023:
Ponnuswamy and co-authors shield tiny DNA structures with a simple coat so they can survive in the body. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. DNA can be folded into precise shapes for drugs and tests. But body fluids break those shapes down. The salt level in blood is too low to hold them. Enzymes that chew DNA attack them as well.

The coat is made of short lysine chains. At the best mix, the shapes stayed stable in low salt. One key enzyme digested them ten times more slowly. Too much coat made the shapes clump. Adding a PEG partner chain solved that flaw. Coated shapes then resisted blood enzymes up to a thousand times better. They survived being taken into cells. In mice, more of them stayed in the blood. The method is cheap and works for any shape.
europmc-pmc5510723:
Yavorska and Burgess present a software paper in the International Journal of Epidemiology. It introduces an R package for Mendelian randomization studies. Such studies use gene variants as stand-ins to test cause and effect. They often run on published summary numbers rather than raw data. Code for the main methods was scattered across paper appendices.

The package gathers those methods in one place. It covers the inverse-variance weighted, MR-Egger, and weighted median approaches. Options include robust fits and penalties for odd variants. Interactive plots help users compare the methods side by side. Data can also flow in from the PhenoScanner database. The authors stress that sound biology must back any causal claim.
europmc-pmc5554123:
Elshaghabee and co-authors present a review in Frontiers in Microbiology. Their subject is Bacillus bacteria as possible probiotics. These spore-forming microbes survive harsh gut conditions well. They also stay stable during food processing and storage.

Bacillus strains make enzymes, vitamins, and compounds that fight other microbes. Such traits suit them for functional foods and health products. Yet the genus also includes harmful strains, which confuses buyers. The authors argue that safety must be judged strain by strain. Only strains that match well-tested safe ones should be used. Readers get a clear view of both the promise and the caution this field needs.
europmc-pmc5618223:
Tasoulis and Isbister gather a decade of snake venom composition studies in Toxins. New gene and protein tools made venom recipes fast to read. Over 100 studies had piled up without a shared view. Their review collates them into one database.

Studies covered 132 snake species across the front-fanged families. About 90 percent of each venom came from few protein families. Four families dominate overall, led by phospholipase A2s. Three-finger toxins and phospholipase A2s rule elapid venoms. Vipers lean on metalloproteases and serine proteases as well. Sixty-three families appeared in total. More than half turned up in under five percent of species, always in small amounts. Their roles stay unknown. Readers get evolutionary and medical bearings from one chart.
europmc-pmc5651823:
Aran and co-authors study tissue that looks normal but sits next to a tumor. This tissue is called normal adjacent to tumor, or NAT. Cancer studies often use it as a healthy control. The team combined data from two large projects to test that practice. They compared healthy, NAT, and tumor samples across eight tissue types.

The analysis covered 6,506 samples in total. NAT proved to be a distinct state between healthy tissue and tumor. The team found 18 genes switched on only in NATs. Shared changes pointed to inflammation signals from the tumor. Those signals seem to stir a response in nearby blood vessel tissue.
europmc-pmc5663723:
Sheth and co-authors review how the cancer drug cisplatin damages hearing. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Hearing loss appeared early in cisplatin use. Excess reactive oxygen species harm cochlear cells. Later work added inflammation to the picture. The review traces each mechanism.

Several protection strategies follow from the biology. Antioxidants can scavenge the harmful species. Certain receptors reduce inflammation in animal tests. Blocking the TRPV1 channel also protected hearing. Transporter inhibitors can keep cisplatin out. DNA damage and cell death pathways offer targets too. The authors gather recent drug approaches. Each approach grows from a known mechanism.
europmc-pmc5670723:
Leeman and co-authors present a framework paper in Implementation Science. It argues against lumping all strategies under one term. Implementation research studies how proven interventions enter real settings. Scholars now label every tactic an implementation strategy. The authors say that habit breeds confusion. It also blocks clean synthesis across studies.

Their system classifies strategies by actor and target. Actors sit in delivery, support, or synthesis systems. Targets span five levels, from intervention to process. Sorting by these traits yields five distinct classes. They are dissemination, implementation process, and integration. Capacity-building and scale-up complete the set. A colorectal screening case shows each class at work. The scheme should sharpen reporting and expose listing gaps.
europmc-pmc5679623:
Wu and co-authors present a systematic review in PLoS ONE. It links activity habits with quality of life in young people. Prior reviews focused on children with chronic disease. This one covers the general healthy population instead. Ages ranged from three to eighteen years. The team searched four databases plus reference lists. Work spanned 1946 to January 2017.

In total, 31 studies met the entry criteria. Most used a cross-sectional design, with six longitudinal studies. Three were school-based activity interventions. Higher activity levels tracked with better quality of life. More sedentary time tracked with lower quality of life. Several studies showed a dose-response pattern. The authors back school programs that promote active lifestyles.
europmc-pmc5763123:
Sanchez-Trincado, Gomez-Perosanz, and Reche review methods for predicting epitopes, the parts of antigens that immune cells spot. T and B cells build memory by knowing these small targets. Finding epitopes in the lab is slow and costly. Computer prediction can shrink the list worth testing.

The review first covers how T and B cells know their targets. That base shapes what good prediction needs. It then surveys the main tools for B cell and T cell epitopes. Each method's roots and workings get close review. The guide serves vaccine and diagnosis design work.
europmc-pmc5771023:
Hartman and co-authors test how farm practice shapes microbes in soil and wheat roots. Their field experiment crossed two management styles, conventional and organic. Each style ran at different tillage levels. The team read bacterial and fungal communities in both settings.

Richness barely moved, but community makeup shifted in clear patterns, they report. Tillage structured soil bacteria most, while management shaped soil fungi and root bacteria. Root fungi answered mainly to tillage. About a tenth of the variation traced to the tested practices. Sensitive microbes included common, well connected members. The authors frame the work as a base for smart microbiota farming.
europmc-pmc5789323:
Ježek, Cooper, and Strich review the two way link between reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial shape. Mitochondria constantly split and merge, keeping a fine balance. Their energy chain also leaks reactive oxygen as a side product. Too much of it injures cells, while small amounts carry signals.

Fresh work shows shape and reactive oxygen feed each other, the authors note. Warped shapes can raise output, which then harms the organelles further. That loop can spiral into lasting oxidative stress. The review focuses on what this cycle means for cancer growth and spread.
europmc-pmc5821623:
Steiner and co-authors argue that migraine is a neglected public emergency. Their editorial draws on the Eurolight survey of over 8,000 Europeans. It also cites a world survey run with the WHO. Both show headache care failing on a grand scale.

Migraine now ranks as the top cause of disability in under 50s. Tension and medication-overuse headaches add to the toll. Yet services stay thin in rich and poor nations alike. The authors call this neglect a forgotten epidemic. They press health politicians to fund real headache care. Readers get a blunt brief on a vast, under-treated burden.
europmc-pmc5828423:
Louca and co-authors test whether 16S gene copy counts can be fixed by prediction. Surveys count a marker gene to size up microbe groups. Species carry one to many copies of that gene. Raw counts thus flatter the copy-rich groups.

Tools claim to predict copy numbers from family trees. Checked against 6,800 genomes, the tools often failed. Good guesses held only for close kin of sequenced species. Some tools explained under 10 percent of the variance. Tools also disagreed with each other on real communities. The authors advise against default correction. Readers get a warning label for a common microbiome shortcut.
europmc-pmc5860123:
Matsumoto and co-authors present SCODE, an algorithm for gene network inference. Their article appeared in Bioinformatics. SCODE works on single-cell RNA data from cells that are differentiating. Such data can be ordered in pseudo-time, a scale of progress. That order turns the data into a fine-grained time course. Older network methods slow down badly on datasets this large.

SCODE uses ordinary differential equations to infer gene regulation. The team tested it on three single-cell datasets. It rebuilt the observed expression patterns well. Its networks matched a reference network as well as rival tools. Its run times were much shorter than the alternatives. The R code is shared freely on GitHub. The tool suits studies of how cells change type.
europmc-pmc5870823:
Tsai and co-authors build organoid models of human pancreatic cancer. Their article appeared in BMC Cancer. Organoids are small tumour copies grown from patient tissue. They are now a standard for drug testing before trials. The team grew organoids from surgery samples, fluid, and autopsy tissue. They also derived tumour cell lines and fibroblasts from them. Tests used flow sorting, staining, and microscopy methods.

Primary organoids kept tumour-like shape and structure, they report. Cell line spheres, by contrast, looked uniform and plain. The team then built mixed models with stromal and immune cells. Fibroblasts switched to an active, muscle-like state inside. Lymphocytes moved into the tumour parts of the model. Such models could help test immune therapies.
europmc-pmc5877023:
Sonenshine reviews the range expansion of tick disease vectors in North America. The article appeared in an environmental and public health journal. Ticks spread more kinds of pathogens than any other blood feeder. Their ranges have grown in recent decades, largely with climate change. Populations have also thickened in many long-settled areas. Four species anchor the review. They are the American dog tick, the lone star tick, the Gulf Coast tick, and the black-legged tick.

Each species is tracked against public health concerns. Living and non-living drivers of further spread get close attention. Habitat, hosts, humidity, and temperature all shape success. New colonies raise threats for people, livestock, and pets.
europmc-pmc6050223:
Rheaume and co-authors profile single retinal ganglion cells to find subtypes. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. These cells carry visual signals from eye to brain. About thirty subtypes were known before this work. Molecular differences between most subtypes stayed unknown.

The team sequenced 6,225 purified cells in total. Each cell yielded about 5,000 detected genes. Clustering sorted the cells into 40 subtypes. New markers and candidate control factors emerged. Several markers were checked with tissue staining. One subtype proved enriched in the right eye. The study also maps how subtypes branch from one population. A website lets readers compare subtype gene patterns. The work deepens the map of visual system wiring.
europmc-pmc6054923:
Embgenbroich and Burgdorf review current concepts of antigen cross-presentation. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Dendritic cells can display swallowed antigens on MHC I molecules. That display alerts killer T cells to threats. The process matters for viruses, tumors, and vaccines.

How the machinery works is still debated. Slow antigen breakdown seems to help the process. Antigens must escape storage compartments into the cytosol. Cut pieces then travel back for loading onto MHC I. Parts of the loading machinery move from inner compartments to endosomes. The review maps the main proposed pathways. It flags conflicting data and open questions too. Readers get a guided tour of a contested immune mechanism.
europmc-pmc6092123:
Guell and co-authors map the functional gradients of the cerebellum. Their research article appeared in eLife. The cortex stacks processing from basic to abstract. Whether the cerebellum follows a similar axis stayed unknown. The team used resting scans from 1,003 Human Connectome Project adults.

A diffusion map method revealed two main gradients. The first runs from motor zones to the default mode network. The second runs from unfocused to focused task processing. The known double motor map split along these lines. The triple nonmotor map did too. The second motor zone resembled a nonmotor zone. Readers get a hierarchy for cerebellar roles in thought and feeling.
europmc-pmc6107323:
Walker and co-authors report a study in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on teen vaccine coverage in the United States. The report uses data from the 2017 National Immunization Survey-Teen. It covers teens aged 13 to 17 years. Advisers urge routine shots at age 11 to 12 years.

The survey reached about 21,000 teens. Coverage rose for the HPV vaccine and for meningitis shots. The Tdap rate held steady at near 89 percent. About half of teens were up to date on HPV shots. Rates were lower in rural areas than in big cities. The authors say missed chances still need to be cut.
europmc-pmc6108423:
Remmerie and Scott wrote a review in Cellular Immunology on macrophages and fat handling in the body. Macrophages are immune cells found in most tissues. They eat debris and help start and calm inflammation. Many also take in and process lipids, or fats.

The review looks at how fat handling shapes what these cells do. Liver and lung macrophages carry many genes for lipid work. The authors argue that this work can steer cell behavior. When it goes wrong, it can add to disease. Readers get a clear tour of a side of immune cells that is often missed.
europmc-pmc6125623:
Machado and co-authors present a methods article in Nucleic Acids Research on CarveMe, a tool that builds metabolic models fast. Genome-scale models show how a microbe's chemistry works. They help design strains and study gut communities. Building them by hand is slow and needs much expert care.

CarveMe starts from one curated universal model. It trims that model to fit each new genome. The built models matched hand-made ones on growth and gene tests. The team built models for 74 gut bacteria. They also built a database of 5,587 bacterial models. Community models can be made from them in short order.
europmc-pmc6202423:
Clouaire and co-authors mapped chemical marks on histones at DNA breaks. A double-strand break can cause mutations and cancer. Cells fix breaks by two main paths. One path joins the ends. The other uses a clean copy as a guide. The study appeared in Molecular Cell.

The team used gene chip scans at many breaks in human cells. They tracked 20 chromatin traits at each break. They report marks that are unique to each repair path. One key find is a switch on histone H2B. A ubiquitin mark gives way to an acetyl mark. At guide-based repairs, histone H1 is lost. Ubiquitin and 53BP1 spread over wide zones.
europmc-pmc6243123:
Falzone, Salomone, and Libra trace how drug treatment for cancer has changed over time. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Cancer care began with surgery and cautery in ancient times. X-rays brought the first modern drug free approach near the end of the 1800s. After the Second World War, cell killing drugs opened the chemotherapy era. Those drugs improved survival for many blood and solid cancers.

In the 1980s, cell and molecular biology led to drugs aimed at single targets. Genetic engineering then brought lab made antibodies into care. Drugs that free the immune system followed, helping some advanced cancers that had no good options. The authors close with cell therapies and cancer vaccines now in early tests. Each era built on the limits of the one before it.
europmc-pmc6245623:
Munn and co-authors give guidance on choosing between two kinds of evidence review. Their guidance paper appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology. Systematic reviews answer a tight question by weighing study results. Scoping reviews map a field more broadly. They can chart what research exists, clear up concepts, or find gaps. Confusion between the two approaches has grown as scoping reviews spread.

Clear signs point to each approach. A scoping review fits when the aim is to scope a literature or study how research is done. It can also prepare the ground for a later systematic review. The authors warn that both kinds still need careful, open methods. Poorly matched reviews waste effort and can mislead readers. The guidance helps authors pick the right tool before they start.
europmc-pmc6266123:
Sassi, Tamone, and D'Amelio review the immune roles of vitamin D. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Vitamin D is best known for guarding bones and calcium balance. Lack of it also shows up in many chronic diseases with inflammation. Asthma, diabetes, and rheumatoid arthritis are on that list. Lab work points to a direct role in immune control.

Most immune cells carry the vitamin D receptor. Many can also switch the vitamin into its active form on site. Active vitamin D tends to calm autoimmune attack. It helps grow regulatory T cells and cuts some inflammatory signals. The review joins lab proof with patient observations. It asks whether disease changes vitamin D handling itself. The picture supports vitamin D as part of a healthy immune system.
europmc-pmc6275223:
Millar and co-authors reviewed all human data on how the body handles cannabidiol. Their systematic review appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Cannabidiol, or CBD, is a cannabis compound pursued for many conditions. It is usually taken by mouth. Animal work suggests that little of a swallowed dose reaches the blood. Human data were scattered before this review.

The search found twenty-four studies with usable measures. Half-life ranged widely by route, from hours after sprays to days after steady oral use. Smoking gave about thirty-one percent uptake. Peak levels rose with dose and came faster by inhaled routes. Food and fat based formulas raised peak levels. The authors stress how thin the data still are. Solid uptake data are vital before CBD dosing can be trusted. More formula types need testing.
europmc-pmc6304123:
Menyhárt and co-authors cross-check claimed survival markers for liver cancer. Their study appeared in Royal Society Open Science. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the main form of liver cancer. Past papers proposed hundreds of gene markers for it. Few are ever tested in fresh data sets. The team gathered 318 survival-linked genes from the literature. They tested them in three patient data sets.

About half the markers kept value in Asian patients. Far fewer held up in Caucasian patients. Three genes stood out in Asian data after strict correction. No marker beat simple cancer stage at predicting survival. One gene, KIF18A, predicted spread into blood vessels. The work prunes weak claims from the field.
europmc-pmc6323923:
Bult and co-authors report updates to the Mouse Genome Database for 2019. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The database is the reference source for laboratory mouse genetics. It sets official names for genes, alleles, and strains. It links genes to functions, traits, and disease models.

Two new interfaces headline this update. A Multi Genome Viewer compares genomes across mouse strains. A matrix tool pairs gene expression with phenotype data. That tool was built with the Gene Expression Database. Literature curation now runs more efficiently. Gene start site notes came from the FANTOM 5 project. The resource helps scientists use mice to study human disease.
europmc-pmc6342523:
Giovannucci and co-authors present CaImAn, software for calcium imaging analysis. Their paper appeared in eLife. Calcium imaging films neurons as they fire. New microscopes capture larger areas at finer time steps. The data flood demands automated, repeatable analysis. CaImAn is an open-source library built for that job.

It corrects motion in the movies first. It then finds active neurons in the signal. It can also align recordings across many sessions. Little user input is needed along the way. It scales from laptops to computing clusters. Both one-photon and two-photon imaging are supported. It can even analyze data as it streams in. Benchmark tests used hand-checked reference data.
europmc-pmc6420023:
Mounir and co-authors present new features in the TCGAbiolinks package, in PLoS Computational Biology. Cancer genome data now come in huge volumes from portals like the Genomic Data Commons. That portal holds studies from tens of thousands of patients across dozens of tumor types.

The package helps researchers fetch and join those data with healthy tissue data. New features cover the Genomic Data Commons and the GTEx healthy tissue project. The authors show how joined data reveal cancer patterns. Their tool aims to make big cancer data usable without heavy coding.
europmc-pmc6430823:
Sachs and co-authors name the protein SMARCAD1 as a guard that keeps retroviruses built into our DNA silent in stem cells of the early embryo. These viral leftovers came from infections long ago. Most stay quiet, but if they wake they can harm the genome. The study asks what holds them down.

SMARCAD1 gathers at two retrovirus groups, most of all at the active IAP group, and keeps their shut-off marks in place. When the team removed it, IAP elements and genes near them switched back on. Getting there depends on KAP1, a known shut-off factor, and KAP1 in turn needs SMARCAD1 to burn fuel and do its work. The result adds fuel-driven DNA repacking to the known steps that lock these regions down.
europmc-pmc6505623:
Kawai, Kawabata and Oda review enzymes that can break down PET plastic, in Applied Microbiology and Biotechnology. PET, short for polyethylene terephthalate, fills bottles, fibers and films, and most of it ends as waste. The authors sort the enzyme research into two camps with quite different needs.

Surface-modifying enzymes nick the outer chains of PET fibers without weakening them, and many hydrolases can do that job. True breakdown of the plastic itself is rarer. Only a few cutinases count as real PET hydrolases. The review sets out what such an enzyme must do, what X-ray crystal structures show about its shape, and how its cutting reaction works, then weighs uses in waste stream management.
europmc-pmc6518823:
Mansell and co-authors give guidance for DNA methylation studies on the Illumina EPIC array. Their paper appeared in BMC Genomics. It tackles three questions of study design and analysis. How strict should significance thresholds be? Is linear regression sound for this data? And how large must samples be?

The team measured methylation in the Understanding Society cohort. That cohort held 1,175 people. Null simulations set a 5% family-wise error threshold of 9 × 10⁻⁸. Most sites broke the normal-residual assumption of linear regression. Yet the team found no sign that this raised false positives. Power checks showed about 1,000 samples can detect small differences at most sites.
europmc-pmc6593623:
Coupland and co-authors study whether anticholinergic drugs raise the risk of dementia. Their nested case-control study appears in JAMA Internal Medicine. The data come from a large English primary care database. Cases were 58,769 patients with dementia. Matched controls numbered 225,574 people. Prescriptions were tracked up to twenty years back. The year before diagnosis was excluded to limit bias. Total exposure was summed by drug class.

Links with raised risk appeared for several classes. Anticholinergic antidepressants were one such class. Drugs for Parkinson's disease and psychosis drugs did too. Bladder drugs and epilepsy drugs also showed links. The links held after adjusting for other factors. The authors urge care when prescribing these drugs to older adults.
europmc-pmc6651423:
Kelley and co-authors map out how the NLRP3 inflammasome switches on and is controlled. Their review appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. NLRP3 is a core sensor of the innate immune system. It turns on caspase-1 when it detects infection or damage. That frees the cytokines IL-1 beta and IL-18. Faulty switch-on drives several disorders. Fever syndromes, Alzheimer's disease, and diabetes are among them. Atherosclerosis is also on the list.

Many unlike triggers can set the complex off. Ion shifts, mitochondrial trouble, and lysosome damage all feature. How NLRP3 senses them stays unsettled. Control by chemical changes and partner proteins is clearer. The review sums up both fronts for researchers.
europmc-pmc6769923:
Pinzi and Rastelli trace how molecular docking has shifted drug discovery. Docking predicts how a small molecule binds a target, at atomic detail. It can flag promising compounds, map binding patterns, and chart structure-activity links without prior knowledge of other binders. The method began as a way to understand molecular recognition.

Newer uses go much further. Docking now predicts side effects, hunts drugs that hit several targets, and finds new uses for old drugs. It also fishes for unknown targets of known compounds. Scoring functions remain a weak point, with rough energy estimates. Pairing docking with molecular dynamics is improving realism. Artificial intelligence may push it further still.
europmc-pmc6821723:
Wallet and co-authors review HIV hiding places in the brain, in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. Modern drug combinations control HIV well and have cut deaths sharply. They do not cure the infection. The virus sleeps in long-lived cells where drugs and immune attack reach poorly. In the brain, those cells are microglia, its resident defenders.

The review explains how microglia hold latent virus for years. That store may fuel drug resistance and reseed the rest of the body. It is also tied to thinking and memory problems seen in some patients. The authors weigh ways to clear or silence the virus there, and the hurdles each approach still faces.
europmc-pmc6827023:
Domínguez and co-authors review lipid oxidation in meat, in the journal Antioxidants. Meat supplies protein, vitamins, and key fatty acids. Its fats, though, react with oxygen over time. That process spoils flavour and colour, so shoppers reject the product. It also destroys nutrients and can form toxic compounds.

The review explains the chemistry step by step, from the first radicals to the compounds that cause off flavours. It covers how oxidation also harms pigments and proteins. Natural defences in meat, such as vitamin E and certain peptides, slow the damage. The authors survey added antioxidants and handling methods the meat industry uses to keep products sound.
europmc-pmc6874823:
Ma and co-authors review a two-way relationship in cancer biology, in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. The chemical mark m6A is among the most common decorations on RNA. It shapes how messages are cut, moved, and destroyed. Noncoding RNAs, which never build proteins, carry the mark too. Each side of the pair regulates the other.

Marking changes the behaviour of microRNAs, long noncoding RNAs, and circular RNAs. Through them it steers cancer cell growth, spread, and stem cell balance. In reverse, some noncoding RNAs guide or block the marking machinery itself. The authors argue this interplay may yield clinical tools for diagnosis and treatment.
europmc-pmc6899323:
Scheau and co-authors review matrix metalloproteinases in liver cancer spread, in Analytical Cellular Pathology. Hepatocellular carcinoma advances by the epithelial-mesenchymal transition, in which settled cells turn mobile. Matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes that cut through the tissue scaffold, are central players in that change. They also serve normal tissue renewal and blood vessel growth.

The gelatinases MMP-2 and MMP-9 are the pair most often cited in this cancer's transition. Others contribute too: MMP-7 is raised in tumours and frees cells to migrate when a small RNA that restrains it runs low. Natural inhibitors, the TIMPs, modulate the whole system. The review weighs the balance between enzymes and their brakes.
europmc-pmc6945523:
Larsson and co-authors use genetics to test whether body fat truly causes heart and vessel disease. Their study appeared in the European Heart Journal. Links between body mass index and cardiovascular disease are clear, but cause and effect are harder to prove. The team applied Mendelian randomization, which uses gene variants as natural experiments.

Data came from 367,703 participants in UK Biobank, covering 14 cardiovascular conditions. Genetically predicted higher BMI raised risk for eight outcomes. The list includes aortic valve stenosis, heart failure, deep vein thrombosis, and high blood pressure. Coronary disease and atrial fibrillation also featured. Fat mass drove much of the risk, with the strongest effect on the aortic valve. Fat-free mass, by contrast, hinted at protection against a few conditions.
europmc-pmc6964823:
Wilson and co-authors trace the history of vector control, the main weapon against insect-borne disease. Their article appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. Diseases such as malaria, dengue, and leishmaniasis burden the world's poorest people most. Controlling the insects and other carriers that spread them has shrunk many disease maps, more than drugs or vaccines have.

Before 1940, control rested on deep knowledge of local carrier ecology, with environmental fixes tailored to each species. Later decades leaned heavily on a few insecticides, with weak monitoring. Resistant insects, climate change, and elimination goals now demand a broader toolbox. The authors call for renewed investment in evidence-based control: local knowledge, mixed insecticide and non-insecticide methods, and proper evaluation. History, they warn, shows that complacency lets these diseases surge back.
europmc-pmc7010823:
Bent and co-authors test where wearable heart-rate sensors go wrong. Their study appeared in NPJ Digital Medicine. Wrist devices read pulse optically, sensing blood volume changes under the skin. Makers grade their own products, and their methods are rarely public. Suspected error sources include skin tone, movement, and signal mixing.

The team ran consumer and research devices through rest and activity across the full range of skin tones. Skin tone showed no significant effect on accuracy. Devices differed from each other, and activity mattered a lot: average error ran about a third higher during activity than at rest. All devices handled resting and steady raised heart rates reasonably well. They diverged when activity changed, and delays between device and reference signals ranged up to 43 seconds. For researchers and clinicians, the message is to pick devices carefully and distrust readings taken mid-transition.
europmc-pmc7053123:
Qin and co-authors review the metabolism of pancreatic cancer in Molecular Cancer. Pancreatic cancer ranks among the most lethal diseases. Growing evidence shows its cells rewire how they process fuel, and that rewiring helps the cancer form, progress, and resist treatment. Understanding it may open better strategies against a disease with a poor prognosis.

Pancreatic cancer cells reshape their handling of glucose, amino acids, and lipids to feed unlimited growth. They also trade metabolites with surrounding tissue in the tumour microenvironment. The same reprogramming underlies resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy. The review maps these changes and the crosstalk behind them. It then surveys the growing number of preclinical and clinical trials testing metabolism-targeted therapies. The authors argue that regulating tumour metabolism could lift outcomes that have barely moved for decades.
europmc-pmc7062823:
Park and Kim guide readers through histone deacetylases in Experimental and Molecular Medicine. DNA wraps around histone proteins, and chemical tags on those histones loosen or tighten the wrapping. Acetylation neutralises a positive charge and opens chromatin so genes can be read. Histone deacetylases remove those tags, packing chromatin down and cutting gene expression. The balance between adding and removing enzymes has long been a central topic in gene regulation.

The review briefly assembles current knowledge of these enzymes across their classes. It gives special weight to recent progress on class IIa deacetylases, whose behaviour differs from the better-studied class I group. The yeast enzymes that founded the field also feature, as do the complexes the enzymes join to repress transcription. For readers entering the area, the guide connects basic chemistry to the drug development that targets these enzymes in cancer and other diseases.
europmc-pmc7071223:
Cena and Calder define the healthy diet in the journal Nutrients. What counts as healthy eating keeps shifting as evidence grows about foods, nutrients, and disease. Some patterns are traditional, like the Mediterranean diet. Others were designed against specific risks, such as the DASH diet for blood pressure and the MIND diet for brain ageing. Both kinds stand against the typical Western diet.

The healthier patterns share a shape: more plant foods, including fresh fruit and vegetables, whole grains, legumes, seeds, and nuts, and fewer animal foods, especially fatty and processed meats. Epidemiological studies and clinical trials together indicate that such patterns lower the risk of common non-communicable diseases. In the DASH trials, the full diet cut blood pressure significantly more than a typical American control diet. The review assembles the features and the supporting data pattern by pattern, giving readers a grounded answer to a deceptively simple question.
europmc-pmc7083923:
Thompson and co-authors review ten years of work by the ENIGMA Consortium, published in Translational Psychiatry. ENIGMA links more than 1,400 scientists in 43 countries. Its teams pool brain scans and genetic data to study the brain in health and disease.

The review covers more than 50 working groups. Many focus on single disorders, from schizophrenia and bipolar disorder to epilepsy and autism. Others study aging, sex differences, or new analysis tools. The groups have run the largest brain imaging studies yet for many conditions. Readers get a map of how shared data and shared methods can make small, hard to repeat findings more solid.
europmc-pmc7104723:
Xia and co-authors report a powerful fusion inhibitor that blocks SARS-CoV-2 and other coronaviruses, in Cell Research. The team first measured how the new virus's spike protein fuses cell membranes, finding it fuses more strongly than the SARS spike. They then solved the crystal structure of the fusion machinery's core.

A fat-modified peptide called EK1C4, built from their earlier inhibitor EK1, stopped spike-driven fusion and pseudovirus infection at very low doses. It also blocked other human coronaviruses, including SARS and MERS, and slowed five live coronaviruses in the lab. Sprayed into the nose of mice, it protected them against a common-cold coronavirus, suggesting a possible preventive route.
europmc-pmc7111523:
Chen and co-authors explain how to curate genomes assembled from mixed microbial communities into accurate, complete sequences, in Genome Research. Sequencing a whole community at once avoids growing each microbe alone, which most microbes resist. But the resulting genomes often carry gaps, errors, chimeras, and stray fragments from other organisms.

Careful curation can fix many of these flaws and sometimes close a genome completely, with no gaps. The authors checked about 7,000 published complete bacterial genomes to test quality measures, and found that cumulative GC skew, a pattern in the DNA letters, helps verify accuracy. Their checks even exposed likely assembly mistakes in some reference genomes of cultured bacteria.
europmc-pmc7133023:
Raghupathi and Raghupathi examine how education relates to health across 26 OECD countries from 1995 to 2015, in Archives of Public Health. They used OECD and World Bank data with visual analytics to find country-level patterns. Education can widen opportunity, but it can also widen inequality, and the study tracks both sides.

Adults with more schooling had better health and longer lives than less-educated peers. University-level education stood out: higher attainment tracked lower infant mortality, longer life expectancy, and higher child vaccination rates. The authors also highlight years of life lost to early death as a health measure, and rates of young people outside work or training. They urge governments to aim education policy at shrinking health gaps.
europmc-pmc7177323:
Parimon and co-authors explain how alveolar type II cells help drive lung fibrosis. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. These cells line the air sacs of the lung. They make surfactant and repair the lining after injury. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, that repair role turns harmful.

Damaged type II cells take on a pro-fibrotic character, the authors argue. Air pollution and other stresses at the lung surface wear them down. Genetic risks can weaken them from birth. Aging adds further strain. The result is scar tissue that stiffens the lung and blocks breathing. Understanding these cells may point to treatments that protect them early. The review gathers the evidence linking their failure to the disease.
europmc-pmc7231123:
Grant and co-authors review evidence that vitamin D supplements could cut the risk of influenza and COVID-19. Their article appeared in Nutrients. The pandemic created urgent demand for added protection beyond quarantine. Vitamin D is known to support immune defense in several ways. It prompts the body to make antimicrobial peptides that slow viruses.

It also lowers levels of inflammatory cytokines that damage lung lining. That injury is what turns infection into pneumonia. The authors connect these mechanisms to patterns in flu and COVID-19 data. Winter outbreaks and latitude gradients enter their argument. They propose supplementation as a low-cost extra measure. The review is careful to rest on prior respiratory infection trials. It frames vitamin D as support, not a substitute for other measures.
europmc-pmc7246723:
Yun and co-authors review the roles of autophagy in oxidative stress. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Autophagy is the cell's recycling system, breaking down worn parts in lysosomes. It also answers stress, removes damaged organelles, and shapes development. Reactive oxygen species, byproducts of metabolism, sit at the center of the story.

At low levels, these molecules act as useful signals inside the cell. In excess, they damage tissue and drive disease. Autophagy serves as a major sensor of that redox balance. The review traces how the recycling system rises or falls with oxidative load. Mitochondria, the main source of the reactive molecules, get special attention. Understanding the two-way link may guide drugs for stress-related diseases.
europmc-pmc7259823:
Gonzalez-Reiche and co-authors trace how SARS-CoV-2 first entered and spread in New York City. Their study appeared in Science. Samples came from patients at the Mount Sinai Health System. The patients were seen between February 29 and March 18, 2020. Deaths in the city that spring soon passed counts seen in many other places.

The team sequenced 90 virus genomes from 84 patients. Family tree analysis showed many separate introductions. Most came from Europe or from elsewhere in the United States. Two tight clusters pointed to local community spread. Cases mapped across four boroughs. The authors argue travel limits came too late to stop seeding that had already happened.
europmc-pmc7275323:
Crisafulli and co-authors pool world data on how common Duchenne muscular dystrophy is. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in the Orphanet Journal of Rare Diseases. The disorder is a rare inherited condition caused by faults in the dystrophin gene. It weakens muscles progressively, mainly in boys.

The team searched two databases for studies published up to October 1, 2019. Forty-four studies entered the review and 40 the pooled analysis. The pooled prevalence was 7.1 cases per 100,000 males, and 2.8 per 100,000 in the general population. Birth prevalence was 19.8 per 100,000 live male births. Results varied greatly between studies, which the authors note when interpreting the global figures.
europmc-pmc7329523:
Berg and co-authors revisit the meaning of the word microbiome in the journal Microbiome. The field grew fast, yet researchers lacked one shared definition of its central term. About 40 experts met under the European MicrobiomeSupport project, and more than a hundred others answered an online survey.

The group proposes a definition built on a clear 1988 description by Whipps and colleagues, updated for modern methods. They also offer shared recommendations for how studies should be run and reported. A short history of the term frames the debate. Readers get a reference point for what counts as a microbiome and how the science around it should agree on terms.
europmc-pmc7332423:
Ackerman and co-authors describe a new virus-testing platform in Nature called CARMEN, built on the CRISPR protein Cas13. Most pathogens in circulation go undetected, partly because tests usually check one target at a time. Their system pairs tiny droplets of sample with droplets of test reagents in a microwell array.

A single array can run more than 4,500 test pairings at once. The team built an assay that tells apart all 169 known human-associated viruses with enough published genome data, then quickly added a test for the COVID-19 virus. The platform also subtypes flu strains and spots HIV drug-resistance changes. Shrinking the reactions cuts reagent cost per test by more than 300-fold.
europmc-pmc7360023:
Percie du Sert and co-authors present ARRIVE 2.0 in PLoS Biology, updated guidelines for reporting animal research. The original ARRIVE checklist appeared in 2010 to help readers judge and repeat animal experiments. Journals and funders endorsed it, yet reporting quality barely improved.

The update reorganizes the items to make them easier to use in practice. A Delphi exercise, a structured expert consensus method, split them into two sets. The Essential 10 form the minimum every paper should report, while the Recommended Set adds research context. The authors hope the clearer structure finally lifts adherence. Anyone who designs, reviews, or reads animal studies gets the new standard in full.
europmc-pmc7365923:
Tang and co-authors review the evidence on cytokine storm in COVID-19 in Frontiers in Immunology. By 25 May 2020 the disease had caused 347,192 deaths worldwide. Severely ill patients carried far higher levels of pro-inflammatory signals, such as IL-6, than milder cases, and high levels spelled a poor prognosis.

Autopsies found lungs crowded with inflammatory cells, mainly macrophages and T-helper 17 cells. The virus appears to drive IL-6 especially high while exhausting lymphocytes. Among treatments, the IL-6 blocker tocilizumab looked relatively effective and safe in early evidence. Steroids, checkpoint drugs, and blood-filtering devices also get review. Readers see how a runaway immune response became a central treatment target.
europmc-pmc7392423:
Lu and co-authors describe the United States CDC test panel for SARS-CoV-2 in Emerging Infectious Diseases. When the virus emerged in late 2019, no routine diagnostic existed. The panel they built uses three real-time PCR assays, all aimed at the virus's nucleocapsid gene, to detect infection from patient samples.

The assays could sense as few as 5 copies of viral RNA per reaction and showed a clean linear range across 8 orders of magnitude. They worked in nose and throat secretions, serum, and stool samples spiked with virus. No false positives appeared with other human coronaviruses or common respiratory germs. On 4 February 2020 the FDA granted emergency authorization, putting the panel into public health labs nationwide.
europmc-pmc7402623:
Le and co-authors explain a pollution paradox from China's COVID-19 lockdown in Science. Traffic vanished and factories paused, cutting some emissions by up to 90 percent. Yet northern China suffered extreme particle pollution at the same time, a natural experiment gone strange.

Satellite and ground data, combined with model simulations, untangle the chemistry. Unusually humid, stagnant air sped up particle-forming reactions on existing aerosols. Power plants and petrochemical sites kept emitting throughout. Falling nitrogen oxides also raised urban ozone, which strengthened the air's oxidizing power and made still more particles. The lesson is sharp: cutting traffic emissions alone cannot guarantee clean air when weather and chemistry conspire.
europmc-pmc7452723:
Jarmoskaite and co-authors set out how to measure binding affinities well. Such measures are core to biology and to building sound models. With high-throughput tools set to flood the field with data, standards matter more than ever.

The authors reviewed 100 studies of biomolecule binding. Most lacked records of key controls, such as the right incubation time or dose range. Without those, no reader can judge if a value is sound. Some reported values could be shown to be wrong, which warps later work. The authors give a framework to plan, run, and report clean equilibrium binding tests. Worked examples use the RNA-binding protein Puf4. The guide serves labs and teachers alike.
europmc-pmc7503223:
Białkowska and co-authors review spheroids as a form of three-dimensional cell culture. Flat monolayer cultures are the common lab model. They miss the cell-to-cell and cell-to-matrix contact of real tissue, though.

Many cell lines self-assemble into ball-like spheroids when grown in the right setup. Methods include hanging drops, scaffolds, and hydrogels. Each gives cells a more natural 3D home. Spheroid cultures serve drug and nanoparticle testing well. They also model diseases in ways flat layers cannot. The review sets out how to prepare spheroids step by step. It then stresses their most valued uses in research and testing. The authors argue 3D culture should stand beside the classic flat dish.
europmc-pmc7509623:
Fuller and co-authors run a systematic review of how well consumer wearables measure steps, heart rate, and energy use. Such trackers are small devices that record fitness and health measures. Their true accuracy was in doubt.

The team included 158 publications covering nine commercial brands. Fitbit was by far the most studied brand. In lab settings, Fitbit, Apple Watch, and Samsung measured steps with care. Heart rate readings varied more by brand. Apple Watch and Garmin were the most accurate there, while Fitbit tended to read low. For energy expenditure, no brand was accurate at all. The authors note that models change fast, so fresh reviews stay needed. Lab accuracy, they add, may not hold in daily life.
europmc-pmc7535623:
RECOVERY Collaborative Group reports a randomized trial of lopinavir-ritonavir for patients in hospital with COVID-19. The drug pair had been proposed from lab work and early study data at the time. The platform trial ran at 176 hospitals across the United Kingdom.

Patients got usual care alone or usual care plus the drug pair for ten days. Doses were 400 mg and 100 mg by mouth each day of treatment. A total of 1616 patients got the drug pair, and 3424 patients got usual care alone. Death within twenty-eight days was twenty-three percent with the drug pair and twenty-two percent with usual care. The authors found no benefit in survival time or in time to leave hospital alive.
europmc-pmc7571423:
Travaglio and co-authors link air pollution to COVID-19 cases and deaths in England. Over 300,000 cases had been reported there at study time. Factors beyond age that shape severity were unclear.

The team compared case and death data with pollution measures. Regional and local pollution data came from many sites. Nitrogen oxides showed positive links to mortality and infectivity. Those links held after controls for density, age and income. UK Biobank data pointed to fine particles as well. A rise in long-term PM2.5 linked to 12% more cases. Links held across time scales and added controls. The work offers a frame for health and emissions policy.
europmc-pmc7588823:
Daly and Robinson track psychological distress in the United States during the COVID-19 crisis. Concern grew that mental harm could last long term. People with prior mental illness were seen as at risk.

The study used eight waves of a national panel. Data ran from March 10 to July 20 in that year. The sample held 7319 people and 46,145 observations. Distress rose by 0.27 standard deviations as the crisis emerged. That rise ran from mid-March to mid-April. Levels then fell back to mid-March values by June. The pattern held across demographic groups studied. It also held for those with prior diagnoses. The authors read this as population resilience.
europmc-pmc7773323:
Dias and co-authors show that fat droplets inside cells help SARS-CoV-2 copy itself. Lipid droplets store fat and also play roles in infection and inflammation. Blood cells from COVID-19 patients held more droplets than cells from negative donors. Lab infection raised droplet forming in several human cell types.

Droplets sat close to viral proteins and viral RNA in infected cells. Virus particles were seen beside droplets under the microscope. The virus rewired fat making and uptake in host cells. Blocking a key droplet enzyme cut viral copying sharply. It also cut the output of inflammatory mediators. The authors propose this fat path as a drug target.
europmc-pmc7818423:
Homma and co-authors give an updated view of the Rab family of small GTPases. Rab proteins run the traffic of membranes inside cells. They guide the birth, movement, docking, and fusion of vesicles. Each Rab switches between an on state and an off state. Helper proteins flip those switches.

An active Rab sits on a set organelle or vesicle. It calls in partner proteins to move cargo through each step. New switch helpers and partners keep turning up. Chemical edits on Rabs add another control layer. CRISPR tools sped up gene knockout studies in animals and cells. Those studies revealed fresh body roles for many Rabs. The authors compile the newest lists of regulators and partners.
europmc-pmc7845223:
Novitzky writes on the care of devitalized, or dead, teeth. The article is an extract from a 1918 journal paper. It appeared in The Dental Register with tables of treated cases. Dental students of the day were keen on such methods. Teaching held that dead teeth should stay in the jaw.

Kept teeth still work as chewing tools. Students were taught that tooth dentin could be sterilized. Clean dentin would block rot and pus in and around the tooth. Novitzky lays out the case work behind these claims. The tables show outcomes case by case. The piece captures period practice in root-focused dentistry. It also shows the faith then placed in sterilizing the tooth. Novitzky favored removing dead teeth.
europmc-pmc7853123:
Raskov and co-authors review cytotoxic CD8+ T cells in cancer and its treatment. These killer T cells are the strongest arm of anti-cancer immunity. They back most winning immunotherapies today. Checkpoint drugs free them from brakes. Cell therapies fit them with new targeting receptors.

New cell generations use built or synthetic receptors. Trials are testing them across cancers. Combo plans may lift effects and cut side harms. The authors sum up how innate and learned immunity work together here. They track gains in cell design and drug pairing. Future treatment paths are weighed at the end. The piece centers the killer T cell as the core weapon.
europmc-pmc7902023:
Jiang and co-authors present a review of exhausted CD8+ T cells in tumours. T cells that face a tumour for a long time can wear down into a state called exhaustion. In that state they fail to control tumour growth. The review explains how the decline unfolds and what it means for therapy.

Exhaustion is not a single step. Cells pass from an early progenitor stage to a terminal stage. Each stage has distinct traits and markers. Checkpoint drugs work in part by expanding the progenitor pool. When that pool runs out, the drugs lose their effect. The authors argue that pairing checkpoint drugs with steps that shrink the tumour could help. So could steps that rebuild the progenitor pool. The review gives a clear frame for such combination plans.
europmc-pmc7906923:
Zafar and co-authors present a review of targeted therapies for neuroblastoma. This tumour is the most common solid cancer of childhood. It accounts for about 15% of childhood cancer deaths. Its mix of genetic and clinical forms limits how well standard treatment works. New therapies aimed at its molecular faults are badly needed.

High-throughput studies have revealed many genetic changes that drive the disease. The review summarises faults in genes such as MYCN, BIRC5, PHOX2B, and LIN28B. It then surveys targeted drugs in lab and clinical testing. Key routes include ALK signalling, MDM2, the PI3K/Akt/mTOR path, and the RAS-MAPK path. Epigenetic drugs also get cover. The authors favour drug combinations that strike several paths at once. They close with the gaps that must close before these options reach more children.
europmc-pmc7909923:
Murphy and co-authors report a mixed-methods study of remote consulting in UK primary care during the COVID-19 pandemic. In March 2020, general practices shifted most visits to phone, video, or online routes to cut contagion. The team tracked how that rapid change played out over the first months.

The study covered 21 general practices in the Bristol area. Remote visits reached 90% of GP consulting by April 2020. Total visit rates fell compared with the year before. Staff kept a focus on older patients, shielding patients, and people with poor mental health. Phone calls handled most problems. Video was used rarely, and text messaging rose more than three-fold. Interviews with staff traced the strain and the fixes they found. The authors say the model worked but needs care over clinical risk.
europmc-pmc7917723:
Lim and co-authors present a review of uremic toxins in chronic kidney disease. As kidneys fail, toxins they should clear build up in the blood. Those toxins sort into three classes by size and protein binding. Their build-up drives both further kidney damage and heart disease, a common companion of kidney failure.

Many toxins are known, but few have been studied in depth. The review focuses on seven of them, including indoxyl sulfate, p-cresyl sulfate, and TMAO. For each, it explains how the toxin harms kidney and heart tissue. Inflammatory signals such as TNF-α and IL-6 get their own treatment. The authors then survey ways to lower toxin levels or block their effects. The review aims to point therapy research at the most harmful actors.
europmc-pmc7937623:
Schinocca and co-authors present an overview of the IL-23/IL-17 pathway in rheumatic diseases. IL-23 is a signal protein made by macrophages and dendritic cells. It drives a class of T cells to release IL-17 and other inflammatory signals. That axis protects against bacteria and fungi when it works well. When it runs too hot, it feeds chronic inflammation instead.

The overview links the axis to a string of diseases. Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis lead the list. Ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, and rheumatoid arthritis follow. Blocking the axis has become a prized goal in drug research. Trials of blockers are reviewed across these conditions. The authors say the core idea is well supported, but the full contribution of the pathway still needs study. The paper gathers the latest evidence in one place.
europmc-pmc8091623:
Shinde and co-authors test the Novavax COVID-19 vaccine in South Africa as a new variant spread. The phase 2a/b trial randomized 4,387 adults to vaccine or placebo. Two doses came 21 days apart. About 30% of participants already carried antibodies at the start. The main test group held 2,684 people who began the trial uninfected.

Cases in that group numbered 15 on vaccine and 29 on placebo. Overall efficacy came to 49.4% among the baseline seronegative participants in the trial. Among HIV-negative participants, efficacy reached 60.1% in the same analysis window. Nearly all sequenced cases, 92.7%, were the B.1.351 variant then sweeping the country. A post-hoc cut put efficacy against that variant at 51.0% in HIV-negative participants. Side effects stayed mostly mild to moderate and brief.
europmc-pmc8127823:
Lien and co-authors present the Atlantic salmon genome and what it reveals about genome doubling. Salmon ancestors doubled their whole genome about 80 million years ago. Some 70 salmonid lineages descend from that event. Their genomes have been slowly returning to single-copy form since. This rediploidization is young enough to read in detail. The new assembly gives that story a reference text.

Big chromosome reshuffles marked the return to normal copy number. Bursts of jumping-element expansion lined up with those changes. Duplicate gene pairs sorted their fates across tissues. Far more pairs invented new jobs than split the old one. That finding defied the field's usual expectation. Older duplicates from a still earlier doubling gained no special protection. Protein interaction patterns barely predicted which copies survived. The genome now serves every other salmonid study. A fish of farms and rivers becomes an evolution lab.
europmc-pmc8139423:
Faria and co-authors combine genomics and epidemiology to trace the P.1 lineage of SARS-CoV-2 in Manaus, Brazil. The Amazonian city had already suffered a brutal first epidemic. Spread there ran largely unmitigated through the population. Then cases resurged despite the immunity that wave should have left. A new lineage stood at the center of the puzzle.

Virus genomes and case records were woven into one account. The work follows P.1 from first detection to dominance in the city during the resurgence months. Its spread pattern is the epidemiology half of the title. The genome half tracks the mutations the lineage carries. Manaus became a warning the whole world read. A place that paid heavily once was hit again. Whether prior immunity failed, waned, or was evaded mattered everywhere. The paper frames that question with hard sequence data. Unmitigated spread, the editors' summary notes, is the backdrop.
europmc-pmc8154323:
Zhou and co-authors survey robots at micro and nano scale that magnetic fields drive. Magnetic drive offers remote control without fuel. It also allows precise timing, reprogramming, and reuse.

The review sets out magnetic field basics and the materials these robots use. It describes rigs for steering them and ways to break symmetry for motion. Flagella-like designs that swim with a corkscrew motion get detailed treatment. Other designs and uses are covered as well. Readers gain a full picture of how small robots can be built, moved, and aimed. It also describes the test setups used for magnetic control.
europmc-pmc8168323:
Liu, Zhou, and Lee present a method to rebuild patient-level data from survival curves. Published Kaplan-Meier curves often stand in for raw trial data. Patient-level data remain the gold standard for fresh analysis.

Their two-stage approach first reads data points off the curve. It then rebuilds records for each patient. The team built the R package IPDfromKM and a web platform for the task. They aimed for a method that is simple and robust. Tests against known data check its accuracy. The tool lets researchers reuse survival results that would else stay locked in figures.
europmc-pmc8326123:
Wei and co-authors show that tagitinin C triggers ferroptosis in colorectal cancer cells. Bowel cancer is common, and surgery plus chemotherapy have limits. Ferroptosis offers a fresh way to kill resistant cells.

Tagitinin C is a natural product from plants. The team tested treated cells for growth, movement, and cycle changes. Death followed the ferroptosis pattern of iron and reactive oxygen build-up. The route ran through PERK, Nrf2, and HO-1 signalling. Blocking that path blunted the effect. The study names a new ferroptosis trigger. It may suit therapy-resistant tumours in time.
europmc-pmc8539723:
Kondo and co-authors review cytokine networks in rheumatoid arthritis. This autoimmune disease drives chronic inflammation that eats joints over time. It can leave people with lifelong disability. A web of cytokines and cells runs the joint damage.

Two signals, TNF-alpha and IL-6, sit at the center of that web. Many more have joined the list, among them IL-17, IL-21, and IL-23. Mapping this network led to biologic drugs and JAK inhibitors. Those drugs already changed care for many patients. The review covers each cytokine's role and its immune partners. The authors see room for safer, stronger treatments as the map sharpens.
europmc-pmc8599023:
Zhang and co-authors identify GABA made by B cells as a signal that limits anti-tumor immunity. GABA is best known as a signal in the brain. The team found that active B cells and plasma cells make and release it. They asked what this release does to nearby immune cells.

B cell GABA pushed monocytes to become macrophages that calm inflammation. Those cells made interleukin-10 and weakened killer T cell action. In mice, loss of B cells raised anti-tumor responses. Blocking the enzyme that makes GABA in B cells did the same. The work adds small molecules to the list of tools immune cells use to tune responses.
europmc-pmc8652023:
Speir and co-authors present the UCSC Cell Browser, a tool to explore single-cell data in a web view. Single-cell methods have grown fast, and their datasets are large and complex. Researchers need ways to look at gene activity and cell labels before deep analysis. Sharing results with others is also a hurdle.

The browser shows gene expression and sample details across a dataset. It can show several datasets at once. A free website hosts a growing set of public datasets. A free Python package lets teams build their own stable views. The tool is aimed at both first looks and shared display of finished work.
europmc-pmc8740823:
Olsen, Boyles, and Deane describe an update to the Observed Antibody Space, a database of antibody sequences. Antibody profiles can reveal disease states and vaccine responses. Most public data sit as raw files that are hard to use. This database cleans, annotates, and translates those sequences for easy access.

The update adds a new web server with standard search options. A sequence-based search is now offered as well. Each record gives both DNA and protein forms of the sequence. Notes flag possible problems in the data. The update adds 25 new studies, including SARS-CoV-2 and paired sequence data. All data are free to download.
europmc-pmc8888523:
Wang and co-authors chart prostate cancer incidence and death across the globe. The cancer is the second most diagnosed in men. It is also the fifth leading cause of male cancer death. The team used GLOBOCAN data for 174 countries in 2020. Trend data came from 89 countries over two decades. Rates were age-standardized for fair comparison. Development levels were tested as a correlate.

The world saw 1,414,259 new cases and 375,304 deaths in 2020. Richer countries showed higher incidence but lower death rates. Incidence rose in 65 countries over twenty years. Death rates fell in 45 countries. In the most recent years, both trends softened. The authors probe screening and treatment as causes. PSA testing likely explains part of the pattern. The study gives planners a worldwide baseline.
europmc-pmc8919523:
Pouwels and co-authors review non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, its mechanisms, and its care. NAFLD is the most common chronic liver disease in the Western world. It travels with obesity and diabetes. The spectrum runs from simple fat buildup to inflamed, scarred liver. Advanced fibrosis predicts the worst outcomes. Liver biopsy remains the gold standard for diagnosis. The review explains what the biopsy must show.

Care rests on weight loss and lifestyle change. Treating the wider metabolic syndrome matters as much. These measures work but are hard to sustain. Guidelines back pioglitazone and vitamin E for selected patients. Surgery for weight loss enters the discussion as well. The authors weigh each option's evidence. They stress accurate staging before choosing therapy. The piece is a practical overview for clinicians.
europmc-pmc9021023:
Cagan and co-authors compared somatic mutation rates across mammals to test links with lifespan and ageing. They sequenced 208 intestinal crypts from 56 animals spanning 16 species. Endogenous processes, such as damage from cell chemistry, dominated in every species. Mutation signatures resembled those known from humans, though their mix varied.

The yearly mutation rate fell as species lifespan rose, a link no other trait matched. By the end of life, total burden differed only about threefold despite huge gaps in lifespan and body size. The authors argue that mutation rates are under tight evolutionary control and may help drive ageing.
europmc-pmc9070423:
Qu and co-authors review biomaterials used to build scaffolds for bone tissue engineering. Scaffolds imitate natural bone matrix, giving cells a frame to attach, grow, and mature on. The review opens with the structure and strength of natural bone and the logic of engineering replacements. It then surveys scaffold materials, their history, types, properties, and uses.

Added signals, stem cells, and functional extras can raise a scaffold's performance. Large bone defects still defeat the body's own repair, so better frames matter. The authors map what an ideal scaffold should be: safe, active, and able to break down as bone regrows.
europmc-pmc9101823:
Yue and co-authors build machine learning models that predict acute kidney injury in patients with sepsis. Kidney injury is the most common grave problem of sepsis and raises the risk of death. Early warning would let doctors act in time to help. The team drew patient data from the MIMIC-III intensive care database.

In all, 3,176 patients were studied, and 2,397 of them developed kidney injury in hospital. The team selected 36 variables and trained seven types of model. The XGBoost model scored best, with an area under the curve of 0.821. It beat standard severity scores on the same data. The authors say such models can help flag high-risk patients for early care.
europmc-pmc9130923:
Lai and co-authors compare ways to process and characterize exosomes for research and product development. Exosomes are tiny vesicles shed by cells, carrying parts of their parent cells. They hold promise as disease markers and as therapies. Yet the field lacks standard good manufacturing practice and reference materials.

The review introduces exosome traits, roles in health and disease, and current clinical trials. It then compares isolation and purification methods by yield and purity for each sample type. A workflow follows field guidelines for studies of extracellular vesicles. Analysis methods are mapped to the traits they measure. Readers get practical help to choose sound methods and build reliable exosome work.
europmc-pmc9177423:
Fabre and co-authors track the lifelong dynamics of clonal haematopoiesis, the spread of mutant blood stem cell clones with age. Such clones become common across tissues as people grow older. When they carry certain mutations, cancer risk rises. How clones behave over time was poorly known.

The team tracked 697 clones from 385 people aged 55 or older over a median of 13 years. Most clones, 92.4%, grew at a steady exponential rate. Growth ranged from 5% a year for some mutations to over 50% for others. Family-tree analysis of 1,731 genomes added a lifelong view. Some mutations expanded early in life, others only late. Faster growth also meant higher risk of malignant change.
europmc-pmc9247923:
Mukherjee and co-authors review the role of animal models in biomedical research. Animal models imitate human disease progress, diagnosis, and treatment in other species. They are vital for drug discovery, toxicity tests, and device development. Such work in humans would often be barred by ethics.

The review covers small and large animal models across many fields. Uses include drug development, transgenic models, tissue engineering, and wound healing. Surgical models for vessels and spinal discs are also covered. Disease areas range from Alzheimer's disease to diabetes and arthritis. Each model has strengths and limits that need weighing. Ethical issues for each model type are kept in view throughout.
europmc-pmc9556323:
Bachy and co-authors compare two CAR T cell products in real-world care for diffuse large B cell lymphoma. Both axi-cel and tisa-cel had shown strong trial results in relapsed disease. No head-to-head trial had weighed them against each other. The French DESCAR-T registry offered a real-world test bed.

The study covered 809 patients who had orders for either product. Propensity matching paired the groups down to 418 patients. Best overall response rates were 80% for axi-cel and 66% for tisa-cel. Complete response rates were 60% and 42% in that order. Progression-free survival at one year favored axi-cel by a wide mark. Overall survival at one year also favored axi-cel. Toxicity ran higher with axi-cel, the authors found. Cytokine release and neurotoxicity events were both more frequent.
flammarion-death-and-its-mystery-after-d:
Book three of Flammarion's Death and Its Mystery came out in 1923. Latrobe Carroll gave After Death its English dress. Camille Flammarion had spent a life on stars and on the soul. Book two of the set was not found for this store, so the run jumps here.

Ghosts of the dead, signs at the hour of death, and homes that keep a shade fill the text. Flammarion weighs each tale with the care of a man of science. He ends in faith that the soul lives on past the grave. The book caps his great set on death and its riddle.
fort-new-lands-1923:
Fort turned his guns on the heavens in New Lands, his second book of 1923. The certainties of astronomy take the fire he had trained on the wonders of earth. New stars, odd moons, and lights where no lights should be crowd his files.

He holds that the sky is as full of the unexplained as the sea and the land below. The learned, he says, hide the gaps in their maps with smooth talk. The book is Fort's war on the official cosmos, fought with clips and wit. It extends the damned data method to the whole vault of heaven.
franklin-journey-polar-sea-1823:
John Franklin led an overland expedition from Hudson Bay to the Arctic coast of Canada between 1819 and 1822. His Narrative of a Journey to the Shores of the Polar Sea appeared in 1823. The journey made his name for endurance, at terrible cost.
