Franklin's party mapped the Coppermine River and hundreds of miles of coast, then turned back short of food. Starvation, cold, and murder stalked the return; eleven of twenty men died. Franklin himself ate his boots, the story said, rather than quit. The book's plain honesty about disaster gripped Britain and fixed the heroic image of Arctic travel.
fraser-edwards-life-and-teachings-of-tuk:
J. Nelson Fraser and J. F. Edwards wrote The Life and Teaching of Tukaram in 1923, the standard English life of the Marathi poet-saint. The text here is the 1932 reprint of the same work. Tukaram, a grain trader of Dehu in the seventeenth century, sang his faith in thousands of short abhangs to the god Vithoba.

The book tells of his poverty, his lost first wife and child, his visions, and his feud with the Brahmins who threw his poems in the river. It then sets out his teaching through translations of the abhangs: devotion, humility, and the name of God above all rite. Tukaram is Maharashtra's best loved saint. Fraser and Edwards made him known to the English world.
frost-new-hampshire-1923:
Robert Frost published New Hampshire in 1923, and it won the first Pulitzer Prize ever given for poetry. The long title poem is a loose, talkative tour of his adopted state. Frost had settled in New Hampshire and Vermont after his years in England, and the state became his poetic ground.

Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening, the book's most famous short poem, watches a man pause between a frozen lake and his promises. Fire and Ice weighs how the world might end in nine lines. Two Witches of Cousin County, Paul Bunyan tales in verse, and sharp lyrics fill out the volume. New Hampshire confirmed Frost as America's best-loved living poet, a reputation he kept for forty years.
frus-1861-d123:
William Dayton, the American minister to France, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 May 1861. The dispatch is document 123 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Dayton's first reports from Paris set the base line for the whole French file. He found a court that spoke fair words and kept its options open. His May letter told Washington just how firm, or soft, that ground felt under his feet. A base line, once set, let each later report be read for its change alone. Change alone, read week by week, was the truest fruit of his reporting.
frus-1861-d223:
From abroad on 18 May 1861, Mr. Fay sent Seward his latest account. It stands as Document 223 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d23:
On 22 June 1861, Henry Sanford sent a dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 23 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Sanford wrote often, and his letters brim with the energy of a man who liked the game. Brussels gave him a front row seat near France, whose emperor watched the war with care. The dispatch adds one more dated piece to the record of that close watch. His stream of letters from Brussels is one of the liveliest runs in the 1861 file. Few posts in the file match Brussels for sheer volume of lively paper.
frus-1862-d123:
On 8 August 1862, the State Department wrote to all its officers posted in foreign lands. It stands as Document 123 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

A note sent to all posts at once set one shared line for envoys and consuls alike. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d223:
Dated 12 July 1862, Document 223 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William Stuart, the acting head of the British legation in Washington. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-July found Lincoln drafting what became the Emancipation Proclamation, though the public did not yet know. Abroad, the question was whether Britain and France would press the North to stop fighting. Seward's letters to the legation that month, this one included, held a steady line. The war was an internal matter, and outside pressure would be resisted. Washington was a small town in 1862, and the envoys met socially as often as officially.
frus-1862-d23:
On 19 February 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 23 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d323:
On 9 September 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 323 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Dayton was the American minister in Paris.

Dayton wrote a week into Lee's Maryland invasion, which Paris followed as a test of whether the South deserved support. French officials who favored action watched for a big Southern win. His report that week belongs to the tense interval before Antietam answered the question, when every envoy in Europe was pricing the same uncertainty. The Paris mail sailed from Le Havre and took about two weeks to reach Washington.
frus-1862-d423:
Writing on 11 July 1862, Horace J. Perry sent this dispatch from Madrid to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 423 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Perry's July report came days after the Seven Days battles ended in Virginia, when European papers were full of Union retreat. His task in Madrid was to keep Spain from drawing the worst conclusions. Reports home also described Spanish policy in Mexico and the state of feeling at court. Seward read such letters from every post before framing his replies, so each one shaped, in a small way, the Union's voice abroad.
frus-1862-d523:
On 13 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The instruction is Document 523 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Five days after his last Dutch order, Seward was back at the same desk, a measure of how much detail the Hague file carried. The standing business included Dutch colonial ports in the West Indies, where the rules for belligerent ships had daily consequences. Pike's blunt reporting had made The Hague one of the Department's trusted smaller posts. The instruction shows the relationship in its mature form: frequent, factual, and free of ceremony, between two men who wrote as plainly as they thought.
frus-1862-d623:
On 18 September 1862 Jacob S. Haldeman sent this report from Stockholm to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 623 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Swedish file's last paper of the year.

Haldeman wrote the day after Antietam, in complete ignorance of it, as every minister in Europe did that week. His letter reported the north as he found it: friendly, neutral, and watching. When the battle news and the emancipation order reached Stockholm soon after, they fell on prepared ground. The dispatch closes a small, serene file, and its very calm is data. In the war's most dangerous month, the Union's northernmost European post had nothing to fear. It had little to ask.
frus-1863p1-d123:
From the London legation on 19 March 1863 came this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward. A second Adams letter in the volume shares the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 123 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Late-March reports from London charted a tense season. The ship question neared a head, and the South's friends in Britain pressed their case in the open. Adams's mail weighed each sign for Washington. This dispatch is one of a pair sent that day, part of the flow that made his legation's file the fullest in the volume.
frus-1863p1-d223:
From Washington on 29 June 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 223 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d23:
On 1 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams held the American legation in London. The letter is document 23 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, twin to the one before it.

Two sheets in one day split a post's business by topic, a habit on both sides of this exchange. Adams had much to sort: British feeling on the war, the South's agents, and the first word of the new year at home. This letter is the second half of his New Year's Day work, and it keeps the file's pace into 1863.
frus-1863p1-d323: On 14 November 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 323 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d423:
In Washington on 24 March 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 423 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d523:
21 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d623:
Dated 24 September 1863, document 623 is a letter from William Stuart, Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the autumn of 1863.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d123: Alexander Kirk, now styled Minister in Egypt, wrote to the Secretary of State on November 12, 1943. His dispatch is Document 123 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Kirk's Cairo post made him the host government's closest American watcher, and his messages in the summit fortnight carried the local scene. The record names the parties and the date. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d223:
Ambassador Laurence Steinhardt cabled Washington late on 16 November 1943, in telegram 1884, about a talk with Soviet ambassador Sergey Vinogradov in Ankara. The two men had met the day before and traded pleasure at the outcome of the Moscow conference.

Vinogradov said he had kept away from Foreign Minister Numan so the British ambassador could test whether Turkey cared more about the military or the political side of joining the war. He stressed that early entry would count as a real gift to Allied victory, while late entry would count for little. Steinhardt concludes that Vinogradov had orders to stand back from the Anglo-Turkish talks, ready only if Numan asked him about Soviet aims in the Balkans.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d23: A second Churchill message to Roosevelt bears the same date, August 11, 1943, and follows as Document 23 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two notes in one day was nothing unusual for the prime minister, who ran much of his war by letter and telegram. Why this one was needed, the catalog does not say. It is kept in the Foreign Relations series, on the eve of the Quebec Conference.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d323:
The Combined Chiefs of Staff issued paper C.C.S. 411/2 at Cairo on 26 November 1943, listing the points on which Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek's agreement should be obtained before he left for China. Lord Mountbatten drafted the list, and the chiefs amended and approved it that day.

Since the 535 extra transport aircraft for the Mandalay plan cannot be found, Mountbatten's plan from the first plenary session stands. Chiang's demand for a seaborne operation in March is noted for the world review of amphibious operations a week later. A strong fleet will gather in the Bay of Bengal by March. Mountbatten may divert no more than an average of 1,100 tons a month from Hump tonnage to the Burma campaign. Meanwhile the airlift strives for the full 10,000 tons into China by late winter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d423:
Louis Dreyfus, the American minister in Iran, telegraphed Secretary of State Hull from Tehran on 8 December 1943. His telegram, number 1096, reports the Soviet explanation for an early publication. The Declaration on Iran had appeared ahead of time in the Soviet Embassy's Persian newspaper.

The Soviet chargé told Dreyfus he had heard the Iranians meant to release the text on the morning of 5 December. His embassy therefore rushed its own publication to avoid being left behind. In a separate talk, the Soviet press attaché denied all knowledge of any release-date agreement and hinted he had not understood the declaration to form part of the general release. Dreyfus calls the two statements conflicting and both implausible: the chargé could simply have warned his colleagues, and the attaché had sat in the 4 December meeting where the release was arranged. He has not pressed the point.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d523:
Ambassador Averell Harriman cabled President Roosevelt directly from Moscow on December 20, 1943. Harriman, a businessman turned envoy, had Roosevelt's ear and used a direct channel to the President for his most important reports. The State Department printed the cable in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Three weeks after Tehran, Harriman's task was to judge how the new partnership looked from inside the Soviet capital: what Moscow expected, and where its patience might run short. His reports shaped Roosevelt's handling of Stalin more than almost any other source. For readers, this cable is front-line evidence from the embassy that watched the alliance's most difficult partner.
frus-1944-quebec-d123:
A second State Department briefing paper for Quebec, titled "U.S. Relations With the Soviet Union," takes a cooler look at the alliance. It states the American goal plainly: the closest, most cooperative relationship possible with Moscow. But it says wartime needs had put cooperation itself ahead of agreeing the principles cooperation must rest on.

The paper calls recent Soviet policy on Poland and the Baltic States far from encouraging. It warns that Moscow might mistake friendliness for weakness. Washington should show more firmness and speak more frankly, the authors argue, without risking military cooperation against Germany. Enduring cooperation, they conclude, cannot be bought by swallowing policies America judged destructive.
frus-1944-quebec-d223: An editors' note points forward in the volume. For the memorandum of agreement on lend-lease to the United Kingdom, initialed by Roosevelt and Churchill at Quebec on September 15, 1944, readers are directed to page 468. The note itself records no discussion; it simply keeps the conference's paper trail connected, linking the lend-lease debates printed earlier to the signed text printed later.
frus-1944-quebec-d23:
On August 10, 1944, Churchill sent a further message to Roosevelt. He kept up the near-daily rhythm of that month. The letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

By August 10, the German army in France faced encirclement. The alliance's arguments were shifting from survival to settlement. Churchill's letters pursued British interests through that shift. He wrote with his usual energy. For readers, the message forms part of a written bridge. It links the Normandy campaign to the Quebec Conference. There the two leaders would settle the war's remaining course. They would try to do so face to face.
frus-1945-50-intel-d123:
Tamm wrote to Hoover on 10 August 1946, two days after the authority's letter to Clark. The FBI's inside papers kept pace with the fight's public moves. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Tamm's memorandum gave Hoover the bureau's private reading of the ruling and its costs. Inside papers at such moments often plan the next step: acceptance, appeal, or quiet resistance. Readers following the FBI thread should read this beside the letters of 8 August. The public record shows what the bureau was told; Tamm's paper shows what the bureau told itself, and the difference is where institutional history lives.
frus-1945-50-intel-d223:
On 19 September 1947, the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter) sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 223 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Lawmakers were close to passing the National Security Act, which would put central intelligence on a firm legal footing.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d23:
Alfred McCormack, the secretary of state's special assistant for research and intelligence, wrote to General Magruder of the Strategic Services Unit on 4 October 1945. McCormack had just inherited the OSS's analysts at State. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The two men now held the two halves of the dead OSS between them, one at State and one at War. Their letters had to settle how the halves would still work together. This early exchange shows the heirs feeling their way, polite on paper and jealous in fact. Readers can follow the McCormack and Magruder thread as the volume's clearest view of the divided inheritance. Of the men who knew it could not stay divided for long.
frus-1945-50-intel-d323:
Minutes record the 15th Meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Board on 31 July 1947. It is document 323 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act was moving through Congress that year, and it would soon replace the wartime setup with the CIA.

No speeches fill these pages; the form is a tight note of points made and ground covered, kept for later use. Staff in other offices then worked from this record, treating its lines as the settled word. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d423:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 5, dated 12 December 1947, is document 423 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

The Council issued the early directives in a group, in the first winter of the CIA's life. Each one fixed a piece of the shared system, so that no agency could claim the whole field. Readers can watch a government invent a new kind of office and then fence it round with written rules. Read in order, the December directives show a full system being sketched in a single week.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d123:
Churchill reported his Moscow talks with Stalin in this top secret message of 22 October 1944. The excerpts printed in the Malta and Yalta volume cover the future partition of Germany. Churchill had just come from sitting with the Soviet leader, whom the cables call “U. J.”

Stalin, he writes, wants Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary to form a belt of free, anti-Nazi, pro-Russian states. Against his earlier view, Stalin would gladly see Vienna head a federation of south German states, taking in Austria, Bavaria, Württemberg, and Baden. Churchill likes the Danubian idea, which has always drawn him, but he would add Hungary. To that, Stalin is strongly opposed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d223:
War-significant equipment and true rebuilding credits must travel apart, Grew cabled Harriman on 26 January 1945. His secret instruction, number 173, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. State, Treasury, and the Foreign Economic Administration all agree on the separation, he reports.

Separate cables will carry the reply on the Fourth Protocol and the answer to Molotov's aide-mémoire, with its bearing on the 3-C agreement. This message gives background on postwar credits. A departmental study puts Russia's war loss at sixteen billion dollars of fixed capital. That is about a quarter of the prewar total, with stocks down perhaps four billion more. Even without foreign loans, the study reckons, Moscow could regain the prewar level of capital by 1948.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d23: Churchill kept the exchange moving with a message to Roosevelt on 19 November 1944, the third letter in three days. It is document 23 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering Malta and Yalta. Read in sequence, these November messages show the Anglo-American partnership working at full speed while arrangements for the winter conferences slowly came into focus.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d323:
America's Joint Chiefs gathered at Yalta on the morning of February 4, 1945, to set their agenda for the three-power talks. Admiral Cooke summed up the staff work done with the United States Military Mission from Moscow. Two large items stood out: linking operations in the field with the Soviet armies, and dealings with Moscow on the Far East.

The first item, Cooke noted, involved British, American, and Soviet talks together. Papers before the chiefs pulled months of exchanges with Moscow into one place. The session shows the American military team clearing its decks hours before the first full meeting with Stalin that afternoon.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d423:
Stettinius reported no Polish deal yet when the plenary met on February 9, 1945, in Bohlen's minutes. The President called on him as the day's chairman of the foreign ministers. Stettinius described the long debate on the Polish governmental question, held on the basis of an American paper. The presidential committee idea had been dropped, following Molotov's proposal.

On the formula itself, Molotov wanted time. He would put the new American considerations before Stalin before speaking finally. The ministers agreed to continue the discussion later and to report no agreement so far. Bohlen's record shows the conference's centerpiece still stuck, two days from the end.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d123:
Secretary of State James Byrnes cabled Ambassador Winant in London on July 5, 1945, with the senior names of the American delegation. The telegram is document 123 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering the Foreign Office's request after it shared its own roster on June 29.

Winant may tell the Foreign Office that the State Department delegation will include Byrnes himself, Assistant Secretaries Dunn and Clayton, and Ambassadors Murphy and Harriman. H. F. Matthews, who directs the Office of European Affairs, will also come, along with several specialists on European and Far Eastern political and economic matters. The exchange let the two Western delegations line up their experts before the meeting opened.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d223:
A briefing book paper warned Truman about Churchill's Commonwealth role, in a paper dated July 4, 1945. The paper is document 223 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It belongs to the set of studies prepared to ready the President for his first meeting with the other two leaders.

The summary makes a legal point with practical weight. At Big Three meetings Churchill may give the impression that he speaks for the whole British Commonwealth. In fact he represents only the United Kingdom. He has no authority to commit Canada, Australia, South Africa, or New Zealand, and Ireland has stayed neutral and is not in the United Nations. The Dominions are kept informed and consulted when time permits, but their consent is not his to give. The paper taught a new president the limits of his partner's signature.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d23:
Announce after departure, not before: Truman's message to Stalin of May 22, 1945, explains the publicity plan for the Hopkins trip. He was most pleased with Stalin's wire about the visit. He judged it wiser to announce the mission only after Hopkins left the United States. Announcing earlier risked a leak becoming press speculation.

Hopkins planned to leave the next morning, May 23. Later that day, Truman proposed to tell the press the mission's purpose. Hopkins was proceeding to Moscow with Harriman, to talk over matters then in discussion between the Soviet and American governments. The White House statement followed as planned. The cable shows secrecy being managed, not merely kept.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d323:
An airgram from Washington to Ambassador Harriman, dated June 29, 1945, reports a new fight over Rumanian oil. Soviet military authorities in Rumania, the Department had learned, had advised taking oilfield equipment from British-owned companies, calling it war booty. British officials in Bucharest had already protested to the Control Commission.

London meant to carry the protest to Moscow itself. Its case rested on three points: the removals broke Soviet pledges given in January, they harmed a clear British interest, and they would cut Rumanian oil output and so world supply. The airgram kept Harriman ready to support the British stand.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d423:
Churchill's answer to Truman's coal message arrives in Winant's cable from London of July 3, 1945. The Prime Minister's reply is quoted in full: personal and top secret. Churchill writes that he is in full agreement in principle with the President's proposal. A similar directive to Field Marshal Montgomery is being prepared.

One reservation follows. Certain points, Churchill notes, are being taken up by the Foreign Office with the State Department. London would like those points considered before its own telegram is despatched. The short cable thus records British assent to the coal drive, with details still to be squared between the two foreign offices.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d523:
Agreed points on aid to Poland are cabled to Ambassador-designate Lane on July 12, 1945, after Department discussions in which Lane took part. First, the United States will give full support to UNRRA in fulfilling the contemplated Polish program. That tentative program is substantial: almost half a million tons of supplies for the third quarter of this year, and a similar quantity for the fourth.

Even if more aid were available, the cable warns, shipping and port facilities probably could not move a larger program. Real difficulties may even be met in delivering the supplies UNRRA will have ready to send with American support. The cable closes with UNRRA's plans for a permanent mission chief for Poland.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d623:
Robert Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, reported oil needs from Hoechst on June 30, 1945. His secret wire is document 623 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It answers Edwin Pauley's query about supplies for U.S. forces in Germany.

Murphy cites figures given in confidence by a SHAEF supply officer, Colonel Vissering. Strict military needs in the U.S. zone would run near 200,000 tons of gasoline and like goods a month by December 1945. With 400,000 troops in a quiet zone, the need would drop to about 50,000 tons a month. Austrian crude, refined on the Danube, could serve where no combat was expected. Murphy stresses that these figures cover military needs only, not the least German civil needs. SHAEF, he adds, is keen to get any oil Austria, Hungary, or Rumania can spare.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1023:
Philip Mosely drafted this memorandum for the Secretary of State on July 16, 1945. It weighs plans to create a separate Rhineland-Ruhr unit. All such plans assume that western control of the area's resources would guard Allied security. Mosely lists the hard questions the other governments are bound to ask.

If Ruhr steel and coal still feed factories across Germany, what does controlling raw materials gain? If the area turns west, what trade shifts must western lands accept? If millions of Germans are crowded into a rump state, how will it live? And can France, Belgium, and the Netherlands, even together, really run so large a region? Britain joining in, he adds, would build a western bloc against Russia.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1123:
Carmel Offie, deputy political adviser at Allied Force Headquarters, reported to the Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. His post sat where the army's rule met civilian policy. The headquarters ran Allied operations in its theater and dealt daily with the lands the armies had freed.

Offie's message linked the officers who governed freed Europe with the envoys planning its future at Potsdam. What the summit decided on paper, men in his position had to carry out in towns and ports. His voice is the field command's part in the record. It grounds the high talks in the facts of rule on the ground.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1223:
Foreign Minister Togo of Japan cabled Ambassador Sato in Moscow on 17 July 1945, the day Potsdam opened. The pair's exchange forms one of the most telling threads in the volume. Japan, beaten but not surrendered, was seeking a way out of the war through Soviet doors.

Tokyo hoped Moscow would mediate, or at least hear an envoy, before the Allies closed in. Sato's task was to open that door. American codebreakers read this traffic as it passed, a fact Tokyo never knew. The cable opens the exchange that Potsdam's leaders watched in secret while they set Japan's terms.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1323:
Ickes, the Petroleum Administrator for War, wrote to Pauley, the reparations envoy, on 25 July 1945. Harold Ickes ran America's wartime oil policy from Washington. His letter joined the oil desk to the man valuing Germany's wealth for the peace.

Oil touched reparations at several points: German fuel plants, stocks, and the claims of nations whose fields the war had wrecked. Ickes's word gave Pauley the oil side of that ledger. This message shows the home agencies feeding the summit's money fight with their own facts. It is the energy desk speaking in the reparations record.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1423:
A third Soviet text dated 14 July 1945 completes the set Moscow tabled before the Potsdam Conference opened. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Read together, the three texts of 14 July show the breadth of the Soviet program: land, money, and power were all on its pages. The other delegations spent the next two weeks answering them. This closing piece of the set lets readers finish the opening picture before turning to the bargaining itself. The editors placed the run at the volume's end, where the conference's raw materials sit beside its results.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-123:
The United States delegation at Potsdam issued this memorandum on July 27, 1945. It belongs to the dense staff traffic of the conference's last week. Memoranda at that stage often carried near-final positions. Teams used them to align before the closing sessions. The paper was preserved and printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Late-conference memos have a special edge. The time for open options was shrinking. Writers knew their words might feed straight into agreed texts. Readers see the American machine tightening its lines. The memo helps explain the firmness the delegation showed as the end approached.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-23:
A rapporteur's report by Eden covers the foreign secretaries' meeting of July 19, 1945, at Potsdam. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Eden reported the morning's work to the plenary session of the heads of government.

Two items lead the report. First, the United States wished to amend the redraft of paragraph 3 of its Council of Foreign Ministers proposal. The meeting agreed to send that point to a drafting committee. Second came Germany's political questions. The secretaries had given further study to the political section of the draft agreement on principles for treating Germany. A revised draft, marked Flag A, was now submitted to the heads of government. Beyond clarifying the draftsmanship, the report signals steady, detailed progress on the German settlement's core text.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d723:
Joseph Grew, the Acting Secretary of State in Washington, wrote to Byrnes at Potsdam on July 16, 1945. Document 723 shows the home office at work while the leaders traveled. Grew, a veteran diplomat, kept the Department running. His letter reached the Secretary as the conference opened in Germany.

The Acting Secretary's letters form the spine of the Washington-Potsdam link. Grew passed news, flagged problems, and held lines at home. Readers see the Department as a two-front operation in July 1945. The document honors a quiet truth: summits rest on the staff who stay behind and keep the machine turning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d823:
A second Barnes letter from Bulgaria bears the date July 27, 1945, as document 823. Two reports in one day from Sofia mark pressing business. The representative wrote to the Acting Secretary of State in both. This one was printed in the second Potsdam volume beside the first.

Paired letters let a post divide its load. One may press a case while the other reports a fact. Barnes's pair shows a mission working at full stretch in the last week. Readers gain two dated points on Bulgaria's line. Together they sharpen the picture of a country whose fate the conference was sealing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d923:
The Economic Sub-Committee sent this second report to the foreign ministers at Potsdam on July 24, 1945. The printed text is an extract. It regrets that long talks on German, Austrian, and Italian reparations ended without agreement. The questions go back to the ministers for decision.

The members did accept that all three countries owed reparations. For Germany, they agreed the sum should be substantial. They split only on the method for carrying out such a program. The report thus marks the point where staff-level talks gave up and the dispute rose to the heads of government.
frus-1961-63v23:
Southeast Asia fills Volume XXIII of the 1961–1963 set. A regional block leads. Burma and Cambodia follow, each pulled between the blocs in these files. Indonesia takes the longest run, through West Irian's settlement.

Malaysia's birth fills the next block, with its neighbors' claims. The Philippines and Thailand close the volume, the firm allies of the set. The papers show a region sorted by pressure. Neutral, leaning, and aligned capitals each drew a different kind of aid, and the cables say why in plain terms. Cambodia's break with aid pressure threads the middle files.
frus-1964-1968-congo-vol-23:
Volume twenty-three of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1964 to 1968 in fact covers the Congo from 1960 to 1968. The Office of the Historian compiled it from declassified records. The Congo's independence in 1960 set off a crisis that drew in the United Nations, Belgium, and both Cold War camps.

The documents follow Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba's fall and murder, the Katanga secession, and the UN intervention. Later files cover the Simba rebellion, the hostage rescues of 1964, and the rise of Mobutu to lasting power. Washington's fear of a communist Congo drives page after page. The volume is the official record of a new nation's violent birth.
frus-1969-76v23:
Volume XXIII of the 1969-1976 series covers the Arab-Israeli dispute from 1969 to 1972. The first chapter treats the Rogers Plan. The next covers the cease-fire agreement of 1970 along the Suez Canal. A third takes up the interim settlement proposal for the canal zone. The final chapter follows proximity talks and a White House backchannel. It shows the State Department and the White House running rival tracks.

Cables and memos trace Egypt's and Israel's replies to each U.S. plan. The cease-fire chapters deal with missile moves and charges of breaches. By the close, both tracks have stalled. The volume sets the stage for the 1973 war.
frus-1977-80v23:
Mexico, Cuba, and the Caribbean fill Volume XXIII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1977-1980. Cuba opens the volume, with the largest section. Mexico follows. Sections then cover Jamaica, the Dominican Republic, Haiti and the Bahamas, and Guyana. Shorter sections treat the small states of the eastern Caribbean, Suriname and Trinidad and Tobago, and the region as a whole. The Cuba papers follow the Carter opening: interests sections, fishing talks, and the first easing of travel.

The Jamaica papers record U.S. business fears of seizure under the Manley government. Investors, one report says, doubted the country's stability and its leaders' aims. The volume shows a mixed hemisphere policy.
gao-gaoreports-b-297323:
L-3 Systems Wescam protested a Navy award for sensor systems in GAO decision B-297323, dated December 3, 2005. The winner was FLIR Systems. The goods were electro-optic sensor systems. The deal could run for 5 years. Counts ran from one unit to 94 units. The case turned on time, not on marks.

GAO dismissed the protest as late. A letter from the agency gave the firm fresh grounds to protest. The firm raised those grounds in briefs more than 10 days later. That gap broke the time rule. Fresh grounds must be filed in 10 days from when they are known. Late grounds in briefs cannot save a protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298123:
Capitol Supply protested the terms of a General Services call for furniture in GAO decision B-298123, dated June 28, 2006. The goods serve the Packaged Home Program. That plan sets homes for State staff abroad. Bid boards had to show photos of most goods. Photos had to cover 90 percent of goods bid. Line art was not enough.

GAO denied the protest. The photo rule had a sound base. Past rounds with line art were hard to score. Goods were trade goods with lists and test items due as well. Photo boards help the buyer see true goods. A firm rule that aids a fair score can stand, even if it adds work.
gao-gaoreports-b-299523:
Head Inc. protested an Army Corps of Engineers award to Hi-Way Paving. The contract covered airfield runway upgrades at Johnstown-Cambria Airport in Pennsylvania. The work ran as a design-build job. GAO ruled in B-299523 on June 8, 2007.

The dispute turned on a bold side offer. The firm pitched a build span of 11 months, down from 38 months. It sent that pitch in two sentences, with no proof. The terms sought upgrades past set minimums, not a new span. The agency read the pitch as off-path. It did not raise the point in talks. GAO found that path fair. A bare claim need not drive talks. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299723:
Forensic Quality Services-International protested a planned Federal Bureau of Investigation sole-source award. The work covers re-accreditation of the FBI Laboratory. The named source is a crime lab accreditation board. GAO acted in B-299723 on May 23, 2007.

The firm had sent a timely note of interest in the work. Such a note put it in line for review. But the agency had not yet ruled on that note. Nor had it fixed a plan to go sole-source in the end. A protest filed before those steps is too early. GAO cannot weigh a path not yet chosen. The plea came before its time. GAO dismissed the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299923:
K9 Operations protested a Homeland Security award for kennel services. The contract went to Britt's Bow Wow Bed N Biscuit. The work backs the Customs and Border Protection canine program. GAO decided B-299923 on August 6, 2007.

The award rested on the lowest-priced, fit bid. Drive distance and travel time shaped the fit test. The firm claimed the winner's site lacked city approval for overnight parking. GAO read the terms with care. They set no such approval as a must-meet bar. An agency need not enforce a bar its terms never state. Bias claims against the contracting staff lacked proof. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310023:
Snacks for a trails fete may not be bought with public funds in this GAO decision, B-310023, dated April 17, 2008. The Seward Ranger District of the Chugach National Forest hosts National Trails Day events. It asked if its funds could buy light snacks for guests from the public. Food buys face a strict rule in funds law.

GAO held the funds are not open for the snacks. Funds pay for food only with clear leave in law. Or the food must be a core part of a task the agency may do. Neither path fits here. Snacks add no real aid to the work of the day. Guest comfort is not a funded aim.
gao-gaoreports-b-310823:
Global Computer Enterprises, Inc. saw its protest thrown out (GAO decision B-310823, dated January 31, 2008). The Coast Guard got tech help for its money systems from QSS Group, Inc. The help came through tweaks to a task order. The firm called the tweaks out of scope for the order. It also called them a banned bundle of small-firm work.

GAO dismissed the protest. It lacks the power to judge if a tweak strays past a task order's scope. A law bar blocks most fights on task orders as well. The bundle claim fell with the same bar. Some buy fights sit past GAO's reach by law.
gao-gaoreports-b-311423:
Five health firms saw their protests thrown out — GAO decision B-311423, dated May 1, 2008. Eastern Medical Equipment, Inc. and Omnicare, Inc. led the group. Three more firms joined the fight. The awards at stake came from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. That shop runs the Medicare health plan for the old and the sick.

GAO dismissed the protests. Title 18 of the Social Security Act bars GAO from this field. Awards by that shop sit past GAO's reach by law. Some buy fights have a home in a court of law, not at GAO. This is one of those fields.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-123:
Department of Energy, GAO-05-123 of March 18, 2005, faults weak contract control on the department's biggest builds. The department pays firms billions of dollars a year for major projects. Each one costs more than $400 million. Many have run well over cost and past their dates. Poor contract handling sits at the root of most slips.

GAO checks three weak points. It checks how bonus pay is used to hold cost and time. It checks the trust in the data used to grade firms. It checks the trust in the tracking system top chiefs watch. More steps are needed, the title states, and the text names them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-223:
Credit Reporting Literacy, GAO-05-223 of March 16, 2005, tests what buyers know about the files that shape their credit lives. A 2003 law gave each person one free credit report a year. It set up a board to boost money smarts. It told GAO to gauge how well the public grasps credit reports and scores.

GAO asked how folks use their reports and scores. It asked how they fight errors in a file. It asked what shapes how much they know. Folks grasp the basics, the title finds. Aimed lessons could lift the weak spots, such as how scores get built and how disputes work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-323:
U.S. Public Diplomacy, GAO-05-323 of April 4, 2005, asks why the nation's tale lands so poorly abroad. The war on terror put a fresh stress on how the United States speaks to foreign crowds. Polls show ill will toward the land spread and deepen in those years. Each agency runs its own outreach: talks, shows, swaps, and news.

GAO asks how far those strands are tied into one plan. It asks how far firms and groups have been drawn in to help. No one national talk plan binds the work, the title finds. With no shared script, each arm pulls its own way and the tale blurs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-823:
Two power plants just south of the border are studied in GAO-05-823, a report from August 12, 2005. The plants opened in 2003 near Mexicali, Mexico. They sit 3 miles from Imperial County, California. Most of their power goes to the United States. Yet they face no U.S. or California emission rules. The county already fails some air standards. GAO compared their emissions and asked what harm they may do.

GAO found the plants' estimated emissions are low next to county sources like dust and vehicles. They match like plants lately approved in California. But health impacts are unknown. An energy study counted less than one added asthma hospital stay a year. It left out ER visits, drug use, and other harms. GAO also doubted the ozone figures, and said current laws may not protect county health well.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-23:
Costly financial products sold to troops are exposed in GAO-06-23, a report issued on November 2, 2005. Press reports in 2004 alleged that firms pushed pricey, needless insurance and funds on service members. GAO studied the insurance deals and the fund plans sold on and near bases. It also checked how regulators and the Defense Department police such sales.

Thousands of junior troops bought an insurance product tied to a savings fund. It costs far more than the $400,000 in cover the government already gives. Most troops leave service in a few years, so few built real savings. Thousands more bought fund plans that take 50 percent of first-year payments as a sales charge. Only about 10 to 40 percent kept paying, so many lost out. Regulators rarely heard complaints, since base staff seldom passed them on. Insurance sales also lacked fitness standards.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-423:
Chip making and software work moved toward China and India. GAO's September 7, 2006 report, GAO-06-423, studies offshoring in two industries. Offshoring means buying services from other countries that were once made at home. Making semiconductors abroad has a longer history. Software services drew more recent focus. GAO acted on its own authority for this study.

GAO traced how offshoring grew over time in each industry. It named the factors that let the growth happen. It then tracked trends in U.S.-based work as the industries went global. Readers get a dated snapshot of a shift in production. The study keeps to two industries in depth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-623:
A new Coast Guard radio system called Rescue 21 is reviewed in GAO-06-623, a GAO report dated May 31, 2006. Search and rescue is one of the Coast Guard's oldest and most vital missions. In September 2002, the service signed a contract to replace its 1970s radio system with Rescue 21. The new system was meant to help crews find and aid people and boats in distress.

GAO found that the project had run into major cost growth and long delays. Weak handling of requirements, poor project tracking, and shaky risk planning all played a part. The contractor's cost and schedule estimates also missed the mark. GAO said tighter management and stronger oversight at the top were needed to get the program back on track.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-723:
Cleanup of tainted uranium is the subject of GAO-06-723, a GAO report dated June 16, 2006. Before the 1998 privatization of the United States Enrichment Corporation, the Energy Department transferred about 45,000 metric tons of natural uranium to the firm. The uranium was meant to be enriched for nuclear fuel contracts. Later, about 9,550 metric tons proved to be contaminated with technetium, a radioactive metal. The corporation agreed to decontaminate it under federal oversight.

GAO reported that about 10 percent of the contaminated uranium remained to be cleaned. Oversight by the Energy Department had been hindered by delays in getting key data from the corporation. Without timely data, the department could not judge progress well. GAO urged steps to secure the data and finish the cleanup.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-823:
A border agency's technology rebuild is reviewed in GAO-06-823, released on July 27, 2006. Immigration and Customs Enforcement won $39.6 million in fiscal year 2005 funds to modernize its computer infrastructure. The program, called Atlas, bundles seven projects. Its goals include better information sharing for agents and officers. GAO judged the agency's spending plan against conditions Congress set in law.

GAO found that the agency was beginning to address weaknesses in the program. Its expenditure plan, with related documents, satisfied or partly satisfied the legal conditions. That judgment, though, rested on plans and promises rather than finished actions. Key improvements were still needed in how the program is managed. GAO warned that Atlas must prove itself in delivery, not only on paper.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-523:
U.S. aid for basic schooling abroad lacks a shared scoreboard, and GAO-07-523, dated March 30, 2007, makes the case for one. A section of Public Law 109-102 told GAO to analyze U.S. basic education work overseas. Several agencies run such programs, from the aid agency to the State Department. GAO described what each one does and how it plans its work.

Coordination is the weak joint. No government-wide system lines the efforts up at headquarters level. A new State Department push to plan aid country by country may help, but it is young. Proof of results is thin too: agencies lack steady methods to tell whether children learn more. GAO made three recommendations. Two target teamwork; the third pushes sound ways to judge outcomes. Staff met officials at home and in aid-receiving nations for the study.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-923:
A new shelter for the Chernobyl reactor is assessed in GAO-07-923, dated July 19, 2007. The 1986 blast wrecked the reactor and spread contamination. A quick-built shelter covers the ruins but is falling apart. Donor nations fund a giant replacement shelter. Two of three work parts are nearly done. The new shelter itself runs about seven years late. Its finish slipped from 2004 to no sooner than 2011. America is a major donor to the fund.

A contract fight drives much of the delay, GAO found. Ukraine disputed the likely choice of a French builder. The managing bank held to its procurement rules. Relations soured enough to chill new pledges. Shifting Ukrainian leadership added to the drift. Technical unknowns in the design remain as well. GAO urged benchmarks before future pledges are made. The State Department broadly agreed. It warned that benchmarks might add delay or cost. GAO held that firm marks aid both.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1123:
Rural aid programs run by two agencies are compared in GAO report GAO-08-1123, issued September 18, 2008. The Small Business Administration and the Agriculture Department's Rural Development offices both foster rural growth. Each backs new businesses and community projects. Some of their programs overlap in aim.

GAO weighed how far that overlap gives the two a reason to work together. It traced past and current joint efforts, in the field and with other agencies. Site visits showed places where staff already team up. GAO found room for the pair to improve how they collaborate. The report shows where shared work could stretch rural aid further.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-223:
Public worker retiree debts are sized up in GAO report GAO-08-223, dated January 29, 2008. State and local pensions promise income to retired public staff. New accounting rules also force governments to report health care owed to retirees. Some forecasts put those health debts above a trillion dollars in today's terms. The true national sum is not yet known.

GAO explains three yardsticks for judging how well these promises are funded. Yearly payments show whether governments keep pace with new debts. The funded ratio compares assets with what is owed. The unfunded balance states the gap in dollars. The report then reads the current standing of the plans.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-23:
Embassy evacuation readiness is probed in GAO report GAO-08-23, issued October 19, 2007. Since 1988, the State Department has ordered over 270 evacuations from overseas posts. War, unrest, disasters, and disease have all forced them. One recent case moved nearly 15,000 Americans from Lebanon. On average, a post has been evacuated every 3 weeks over the past 5 years.

Posts plan with emergency action plans and a central handbook. Staff at many posts called the handbook too broad and bulky to use well. GAO surveyed 243 posts for this review. It urged one office to own the lessons of each evacuation and spread them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-623:
Citizens of 27 countries can visit the United States with no visa under the Visa Waiver Program. Plans to end, grow, or tighten that program could flood visa offices with new work. GAO-08-623, dated May 22, 2008, works out how much staff and space the State Department would need in each case.

Ending the program could lift visa demand from about 500,000 people a year to as much as 12.6 million. That could call for about 45 new sites and hundreds of new staff, at a cost of billions. Fee income would cover much of the yearly cost. GAO found little backup planning and urged the department to get ready.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-723:
Health centers give basic care to people with few other options. A federal grant program run by the Health Resources and Services Administration funds those centers. GAO-08-723, dated August 8, 2008, asks how many needy areas still lack a center and how well the agency runs the program.

New grants cut the share of needy areas with no center from 47 percent in 2006 to 43 percent in 2007. The Midwest lagged most, at 60 percent in 2007. The agency also lacks data on what each site offers. Feedback to failed grant seekers is murky, GAO found, and help groups for applicants need closer watch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-823:
Charity groups feed and shelter disaster victims, with the Red Cross holding a federal support role. Hurricane Katrina strained that system. GAO-08-823, dated September 18, 2008, studies five large groups, their gains since Katrina, and what they can handle now.

The five groups differ widely in focus and shape. All are woven into the 2008 National Response Framework. The Red Cross role in a huge disaster is agreed in words but not clearly written down. A 2006 disaster supplement still needs updating to match. GAO tells the emergency agency to gauge group strength more fully and fix the paperwork.
garland-book-american-indian-1923:
Harper issued The Book of the American Indian in 1923, written by Garland and pictured by Frederic Remington. A scout image from Remington's A Bunch of Buckskins fronts the volume. Garland had spent years visiting reservations and hearing Native leaders at length.

Accounts of Plains Indian life and history fill the book, told with care and respect. Garland also records the harm that white settlement brought to Native peoples. Part report and part plea for justice, the work defends its subjects with rare sympathy for its time. It remains a window on how one famed prairie writer tried to set the record straight.
goldman-my-disillusionment-russia-1923:
Emma Goldman published My Disillusionment in Russia in 1923. Goldman had sailed to Soviet Russia in 1919, deported from the United States as a dangerous radical. She went as a friend of the revolution and left, two years later, as its critic.

Goldman described the crushing of free unions, the jailing of anarchists, and the Kronstadt sailors' revolt and its bloody end. She told how Bolshevik power, in her account, replaced one tyranny with another. The book was among the first breaks with Bolshevism from within the revolutionary left. Her firsthand scenes and names gave the account weight that later histories have confirmed in large part.
goldsack-selections-muhammadan-tradition:
William Goldsack was a missionary scholar in Bengal who translated Islamic texts for Christian and general readers. His Selections from Muhammadan Traditions, published in 1923, offers classified English selections from the six canonical hadith collections. Hadith are the recorded sayings and deeds of the Prophet Muhammad.

Goldsack arranges traditions from Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, and others by subject, from prayer to trade to family life. A reader can see what the tradition teaches on a topic without searching the vast Arabic collections. The book served missionaries and students as a handy, ordered gateway to Islam's second source.
gregory-hellman-hesperopithecus-1923:
William K. Gregory and Milo Hellman, two New York men of dental science, restudied the famed Nebraska tooth in 1923. The tooth had been named Hesperopithecus, a first ape man for America, the year past. Their notes deal with the type tooth and its true kind.

With fine care they set out the tooth's crown, roots, and wear, point by point. Bit by bit, the ape man marks fade, and a more lowly beast takes their place. The paper is the start of the slow walk back from the Nebraska man claim.
gregory-hellman-molars-hesperopithecus-p:
William K. Gregory and Milo Hellman, with a note by Gerrit S. Miller Jr., took the Nebraska tooth row a step more in 1923. Their theme is the back teeth, the molars, of two claimed ape men. One is Hesperopithecus of Nebraska, the other Pithecanthropus of Java.

Tooth by tooth, the team sets the worn Nebraska molar by the Java man's teeth. The match fails, and with it the claim of an ape man in America fades fast. The dry notes close the case that a year of press noise had blown so large.
hamlet-a-study-with-the-text-of-the-foli:
George MacDonald, the Scots novelist and poet, wrote this study of Hamlet at Bordighera at Christmas 1884, and printed with it the text of the play from the Folio of 1623. He dedicates the book to a relative, Alexander Stewart MacColl, to whom he says he owes the true understanding of the great soliloquy. His son Greville later called the commentary the most important interpretation of the play ever written, splendid for its intuitive grasp.

MacDonald reads Hamlet as a noble mind in a corrupt court, and defends both the prince and his maker. The Folio text follows his essay, in the spelling of 1623. The study is not cool scholarship; it is a poet's act of faith in another poet. Readers who love the play will find a warm, forceful companion, sure that Hamlet's delay has a moral root.
hemingway-three-stories-1923:
Ernest Hemingway was a twenty-four-year-old newspaper correspondent in Paris when Three Stories and Ten Poems appeared in 1923. A tiny press printed only three hundred copies. It was his first book, and almost everything he later became is visible in it.

The lead story, Up in Michigan, tells of a young woman's rough sexual awakening in a lumber town. Two more stories introduce Nick Adams, the hero of his later fiction, fishing and soldiering. The ten poems, snapshots of bullfights, executions, and war, are frankly apprentice work. The plain style that would change American prose is already forming. This slim Paris debut is where Hemingway began.
isaac-the-syrian-wensinck-1923:
Isaac of Nineveh, a seventh-century bishop who gave up his see for the desert, wrote the mystic treatises translated here by A. J. Wensinck in 1923. Isaac wrote in Syriac, and his works traveled across the Christian East in many tongues. Wensinck's was the first complete English rendering of this contemplative classic.

Isaac writes on prayer, tears, humility, and the stillness of the mind before God. His pages prize mercy above all: a merciful heart, he says, burns for every creature, even snakes. Monks of Mount Athos and the Russian tradition kept his words close for centuries. The translation made the desert father's voice plain to English readers at last.
jersey-devil-evening-journal-1909-01-23:
Panic grips two states in the Evening Journal pieces of January 23, 1909, from Wilmington. For a week, folk from New Jersey to Delaware swore a winged beast flew by night: hoof prints in snow, hens slain, and a shape like a crane with a horse's head. The Journal prints fresh tales: a church meet broke up in dread, and a crop of new tales from each town in its reach.

The tone veers from fear to wry doubt, day by day. These scraps are the wave as it broke, raw and live. They are prime sources on the famed scare.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-23:
Volume 23, from 1898, finds the Hurons in 1643 facing a bleak war. Iroquois wins multiply with each new season of fighting in the woods. Thwaites prints letters that read like reports from a doomed fort under siege.

Faith and hard realism fight for space on nearly every page. The priests see the danger in full, name it plainly, and stay. They tend the sick, teach the young, and guard the chapels at night. Supplies fail, allies waver, and still the daily work goes on. Few volumes show plain duty under hopeless odds with such force.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-of-carden:
Aaron of Cardena was a cabalist about whose life little is known. His book "Ḳarnayim" holds what the entry calls profound secrets. The work was wrongly ascribed to Isaac ben Abraham ben David, called the Blind. That error shows both the esteem it won and the age it came from.

Aaron names two more works of his, "Kitro Yeshu'ah" and "Peraḥ Ẓiẓ." Both titles point to his own name and priestly role. "Ḳarnayim" was first printed at Zolkiev in 1709, with a commentary by Simon ben Pesaḥ of Astropol. It was printed again at Jitomir in 1805 and at Leghorn in 1835, each time with fresh commentary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-123:
Abba, brother of Rabban Gamaliel, probably Gamaliel II, heads the first of two short lives under this name. He died without children, and Gamaliel married his widow under the law of levirate marriage. His having two wives at once is the only case of its kind known among the Talmudic authorities.

The second Abba was a Palestinian amora, born in Babylonia, who flourished in the third and fourth centuries. A pupil of Huna and Judah, he settled in Palestine and won a high name there. The entry calls him wealthy, famed for secret charity, strong as a halakist, and drawn to psalm verses as a preacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abel-shittim-ac: Abel-shittim stands by that full name only in Numbers, chapter 33, verse 49. As Ha-Shittim, the Acacias, it is the same place in Numbers, Joshua, and Micah. It was a town, or perhaps a district, of Moab, and the last camp of Joshua before he crossed the Jordan. Josephus knew a town Abila there, full of palm trees, sixty stadia from the Jordan. An acacia grove still stands near the likely site, though the palms are gone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abinu-malkenu-o:
Abinu Malkenu, meaning Our Father, Our King, names a set part of the prayer service. It is said with weight on the Penitential Days, from New Year to the Day of Atonement. The two calls stand apart in the Bible, in Isaiah and in Tobit. In the old service they were set side by side, in the Eighteen Benedictions and in feast prayers. In prayers of sorrow the joined form became the standing call.

A tale in Ta'anit ties the prayer to a drought and to Akiba. Eliezer ben Hyrcanus had said the full fast-day set of blessings, with no result. Akiba then stepped forward and said the Abinu Malkenu, and rain fell at once. The entry warns that this does not make Akiba its first user. At first it had no fixed count of verses. One later account gives nineteen, matched to the Nineteen Benedictions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-dob-bae: Abraham Dob Baer ben Solomon was rabbi in Orsha in the latter half of the eighteenth century. He wrote a work called Abraham's Well. It contains glosses on the first part of the code Shulhan Aruk, the Yoreh De'ah section. The book came out at Shklov in 1783. The entry is three lines long and gives nothing else about his life, family, or other writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abrahamson-abra:
Meyer Abrahamson was a German physician and medical writer born at Hamburg in 1764. He died there on October 21, 1817. He took his degree at Göttingen in 1783 and began practice in his home city, where his father had also practised medicine.

Soon he became physician to Hamburg's Jewish Hospital and to the city's poor. From 1784 he wrote widely and well on medical topics in leading journals. His books treat diseases of the eyes, the value of cowpox vaccination, hemorrhoids, and gout. A more scientific work, from 1806, studies the high death rate among pregnant women, new mothers, and newborn children. He belonged to learned societies in Germany and Sweden.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-karl-frie: Karl Friedrich Adler was an Austrian jurist born at Prague on March 31, 1865. His father Moritz wrote a book on war and peace plans in 1868. Karl studied at Prague and Vienna. From 1893 to 1898 he taught trade law at Vienna. In 1900 he took a chair in civil law at Czernowitz. In 1898 he took the Catholic faith. His books treat storehouse law, contracts, and the growth of social law. Dates run from 1892 to 1895. He also wrote for law journals of his day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aguilar-grace-9:
Grace Aguilar was an English novelist. She also wrote on Jewish history and religion. She was born at Hackney, London, on June 2, 1816. She died at Frankfort-on-the-Main on September 16, 1847. Her parents descended from Portuguese Maranos. She was the oldest child. Her schooling came mainly from her parents. She began a diary at the age of seven. She kept it almost until her death.

Her tales deal chiefly with Jewish subjects. One, "The Vale of Cedars," tells of Spain in the fifteenth century. "Home Influence" is a domestic tale. "The Women of Israel" gives portraits from Scripture and Josephus. In "The Spirit of Judaism" she defended her faith. "The Jewish Faith" did the same in letter form. She urged Jewish women to study Scripture. She also pressed them to learn Jewish history and Hebrew. Yet she herself kept ritual rules with care.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akabia-ben-maha:
'Akabia ben Mahalalel was a religious teacher, probably of the second tannaitic generation. Few of his sayings survive, and his teachers are nowhere named. The Mishnah shows him holding his own views with rare firmness. Where his colleagues followed other traditions, he kept the ones he had received.

The court once offered him its presidency if he would yield. He refused, saying he would rather be called a fool for life than a sinner for one moment. A sharp word of his in a legal debate brought a sentence of isolation on him. He bore it to the end of his days. On his deathbed he told his son to follow the majority, not him. His own motto was to remember whence one came, whither one goes, and before whom one must give account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-son-o:
Alexander, son of Herod, was born about 35 B.C. and died about 7 B.C. His mother was Mariamne, a Hasmonean princess. As heir through her line, he was sent to Rome in 23 B.C. He was educated in the household of Asinius Pollio. Herod brought him home about 17 B.C., with his brother Aristobulus. Alexander then married Glaphyra, a Cappadocian king's daughter.

His good looks and open manner made him a favorite with the people. Salome warned Herod against him without rest. Antipater's plots widened the breach. In 12 B.C. Herod charged his sons before Augustus, and a brief peace followed. About 10 B.C. Alexander was jailed on a tortured witness's word. Seized letters showed his bitterness. Jailed again about 8 B.C., he was tried for treason by a packed court. About 7 B.C. he was strangled at Sebaste, where his mother had wed thirty years before.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alguadez-meir-b:
Meir ben Solomon Alguadez was a court physician and chief rabbi in Castile. He lived in the fifteenth century. His birth and death dates are not known. He studied Talmud at Toledo under Judah ben Asher. He also trained in medicine and won fame for his cures. King Henry III made him his own physician.

The king also made him chief rabbi of Castile. The entry tells of a sharp verse exchange with a baptized rival. Alguadez turned the Ethics of Aristotle into Hebrew. He wrote cures for many ills about the year 1400. Old tales that he poisoned the king are called fables.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-altaras-1323: Altaras is a family name spelled in more than one way. The entry is not sure it is one name at all. A Spanish Karaite bore a like name long ago. He wrote a book of views by an older teacher. Two medieval writers name an Altaras in their books. One is Abraham ibn Daud in his book of tradition. The other is Joseph ben Zaddik. The entry is short and rests on those few traces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amos-1423:
Amos was a Jewish prophet of the eighth century B.C. His birth and death dates are not known. His home was Tekoa in Judah. That town lay five miles south of Bethlehem. He worked as a herdsman and a tender of fig trees. He told the priest of Bethel that plain fact. He was no prophet by trade or by birth, he said.

God called him from behind his flock, he held. That claim marks a turn in the tale of prophecy. Amos is the first prophet to write his words down. The entry weighs the date of his work with care. It sets his work in the reign of Jeroboam II. That reign must have ended between 750 and 740 B.C.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anger-1523:
Anger, as the entry defines it, is a violent passion roused by a wrong one has suffered. It seeks vengeance on the wrongdoer. The entry grades it from mere displeasure at unworthy acts up to wrath and fury, and lists the Hebrew words for each shade.

Much of the entry concerns the anger of God. The Bible's God is holy and no mere idea, the entry argues, so he resents evil in the moral world with force. That anger counts as part of his justice, not a flaw. The entry also treats human anger, its dangers, and how Jewish teaching judged and curbed it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arbib-eduardo-1:
Eduardo Arbib was an Italian deputy and author born at Florence on July 27, 1840. When his father died, he had to leave his studies and earn his bread as a compositor and press corrector. In 1859 he volunteered with the Alpine chasseurs of Piedmont for the war of independence.

He followed Garibaldi to Sicily in 1860 and was made lieutenant on the field of Milazzo. After service against Austria in 1866 he left the army for newspapers, rising to edit a Florence daily. In 1870 he founded La Liberta in Rome. Voters of Viterbo sent him to the Chamber of Deputies in 1880, and Perugia later did the same. His books include a history of the 1866 campaign and military tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-art-attitude-of:
Art in the Bible is treated as wisdom given by God, not as mere hand labor. Exodus chapters 31 and 35 credit it to divine filling, and the Talmud calls it hokmah, wisdom. Yet the entry warns against speaking of a purely Jewish art. Solomon's Temple used Phenician building, Zerubbabel's used it too, and Herod's Temple used Roman building. Jewish work was always shaped, often guided, by the art around it.

Fear of idols set the sharpest limit. The ban on images in Exodus chapter 20 was once read to cover all images, worshiped or not, and the pious avoided even the pictures stamped on Roman coins. Rabbinic reading narrowed the ban. It forbade set forms such as the four figures of Ezekiel and, above all, human figures that might draw worship.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-david-192:
David Asher, a German teacher and writer on deep questions, was born at Dresden on December 8, 1818. He died at Leipsic on December 2, 1890. He was one of the first Jews let into the Dresden gymnasium, but his widowed mother could not keep him there. He learned carving and gilding and worked his way across Germany and Austria as a journeyman.

A rich relative called him to London, where he learned English, taught, and studied language and thought. He tutored the chief rabbi's children and took a doctor's degree at Berlin. Settled at Leipsic, he taught English for seven years at the Commercial School. He also examined students and served as court interpreter. He wrote on Schopenhauer, fought attacks on Jews, and turned many books between German and English.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aspalathus-2023: Aspalathus is a word found only in the Apocrypha, in Ecclesiastes, called Sirach, chapter 24. From its context it appears to be the name of a fragrant wood, listed among sweet-smelling things. The plant behind the word cannot be identified, the entry says plainly. It gives the one passage, the likely sense, and the honest limit of knowledge, and nothing more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-arabi-al-mag:
Israel ben Samuel ha-Dayyan, called Ma'arabi, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia as a Karaite scholar of Cairo. He lived in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Among his pupils was the Karaite physician and writer Japhet ibn Zaghir. His own main work, written in Arabic, dealt with the precepts of Karaite law.

The article explains how little of that work survives. Only the sections on slaughtering animals and on the calendar remain, in manuscripts held from London to St. Petersburg. The slaughter laws were printed in Hebrew at Vienna in 1830. Ma'arabi also wrote on the six articles of belief and gave a commentary on the Ten Commandments. In his legal work he attacked rival views on marriage law and backed reform. The entry traces a scholar known mostly through fragments in distant libraries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malachi-b-jacob:
Malachi ben Jacob ha-Kohen, an Italian Talmudist, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as a judge at Leghorn in the eighteenth century. The entry calls him the last of Italy's great rabbinical authorities. A decision of his from 1732 survives inside another rabbi's responsa. He died before 1790.

The article centers on his famous handbook, Yad Mal'aki. Printed at Leghorn in 1767, it teaches the method of Talmud study in three parts. The first lists the Talmud's rules and technical terms in alphabetical order. The second covers rules for the codifiers. The third explains principles behind legal decisions and responsa. The book was reprinted at Berlin and Przemysl, a sign of lasting use. Malachi also wrote prayers for a Leghorn fast day. In the Eybeschutz-Emden dispute he sided with Eybeschutz. The entry preserves the methodologist Italian rabbis trusted last.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marks-b-s-10423:
B. S. Marks, an English portrait painter, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Cardiff in 1827, he trained there and painted portraits in Wales. As a Welshman he became a Royal Cambrian Academician. In 1867 he removed to London, where he worked for more than thirty years.

The article lists sitters worthy of a court painter. They include the Prince of Wales, Lord Rothschild, and Chief Rabbi N. M. Adler. Lord Shaftesbury, Lord Aberdare, and Field-Marshal Sir John Burgoyne also sat for him. Marks gave time to Jewish schools, serving on the Jews' Free School committee. For a long period he taught art without pay to pupils and teachers alike. He also backed the free-library movement and helped found libraries at Cardiff and Ealing. The entry closes with his children: an architect son, a mathematical editor daughter, and two daughters who paint.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-eliezer:
Menahem Eliezer ben Levi, a Lithuanian Talmudist who headed the yeshivah at Minsk, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn. Born at Wilna and trained under Solomon of Vilkomir, he won his reputation young with the "Ya'ir Kinno," a commentary on Kinnim, the most intractable of the Mishnah's tractates. Elijah of Wilna, the Gaon himself, praised it in words the entry quotes: heaven had aided him to find the meaning of a treatise in which so many commentators had failed.

After the Gaon's death his pupils commissioned Menahem Eliezer to comment on their master's notes to the Shulhan Aruk, a work he began but did not finish. His own writings on the Pentateuch and Mishnah, his novellae, and his responsa all remained unpublished when he died at Minsk on December 23, 1816.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshwi-al-ukbar:
Meshwi al-'Ukbari was the founder of the Jewish sect called Al-'Ukbariyyah, or the Okbarites, named for the city of 'Ukbara near Bagdad where he is said to have lived. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Karaite writer Ḳirḳisani is a main source for what is known of him.

His real name was Moses, the article says, until opponents twisted it into Meshwi, meaning one whose ideas are confused. He broke with both Karaites and Rabbinites, ruling that the Day of Atonement must always fall on a Sabbath and that prayer should face west, not toward the Temple. He also barred Sabbath sacrifices in the Temple and reportedly allowed his followers to eat fat.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mihaileni-10823:
Mihaileni, a small town in the Rumanian district of Dorogoi, was founded by Jews in 1792 under a written bargain with the land's proprietor. Richard Gottheil and E.
