A single marker that forecasts outlook and hints at treatment resistance could help sort patients for closer watch or new drug trials.
plos-pone-0348023:
Joanna Jadwiga Ilska, Fern McDonnell, and Jane Frances Ladlow ran the numbers on whether flat-faced dogs can simply be bred back to breathing properly. Bulldogs, French bulldogs, and pugs suffer a airway syndrome tied to their skull shape. Using a standard exercise-based breathing grade recorded for more than four thousand British dogs, plus pedigrees, the team estimated how much of the variation is inherited.

Breathing grade proved moderately heritable in every breed, and the related trait of pinched nostrils was heritable too, with the two genetically linked. Moderate heritability means selection can work: choosing parents with better grades should shift puppies toward easier breathing within breeds, without crossbreeding. The authors urge wider participation in the grading scheme so breeders have the data to act on.
plos-pone-0348123:
Tabea Thies, Philipp Buech, and Anne Hermes tested whether a speech-tracking technology can double as a breathing monitor, sparing speakers the chest bands normally used to record speech breathing. Electromagnetic articulography tracks tiny sensors on the body to follow speech movements. Their 2026 study recorded eighteen speakers producing sentences of varied length and complexity, comparing many sensor arrangements against the standard chest band signal.

The tracking method reliably captured inhales, exhales, and full breathing cycles. Horizontal distance measures worked best, especially pairing a sternum or rib sensor with one at the neck. Vertical measures wobbled more but never lost the breathing pattern. The authors propose the two-sensor setup as an easy add-on that folds breathing into speech research without extra gear.
plos-pone-0348523:
Paweł Chorab and Dorota Łozowicka examine a quiet source of error in ship design math: skipping middle slices when computing a hull's shape. Naval architects estimate underwater volume and the center of buoyancy by adding up cross-sections along the hull. Their 2026 study shows how leaving out intermediate sections distorts those numbers and compares classic calculation schemes.

Adding intermediate sections cut the numerical error in the worked examples. Sloppy geometry can mislead the stability checks that keep ships upright, so the fix matters beyond neatness. The authors propose a future search tool that picks section counts and placements automatically, weighing accuracy against computing cost. Better hull math means safer stability calls at the design stage.
plos-pone-0348623:
Wafaa A Mahmoud and colleagues surveyed medical students at a science and technology university in Jordan about how they study. Five hundred and fifty six students rated how often they use ten study habits, from rereading to self testing. Habits were grouped into proven active methods and common passive ones, then set beside self reported grades.

Just over half of students reported top grades. Use of proven methods rose step by step with grade level and raised the odds of top marks even after other factors were counted. Passive habits showed no such link. Because the survey is a snapshot, cause stays unproved, but teaching active methods early looks like a fair bet for schools.
plos-pone-0348823:
Emmanuel Nasinghe and co-authors set out a data science project in 2026 on tuberculosis in Kampala households, Uganda. The disease overlaps heavily with HIV there, many cases hide without symptoms, and it is hard to separate risks from the home, the germ, and the surroundings.

The team will use Makerere University computing power and records on patients and their household contacts to train learning models. Goals include spotting what drives spread inside homes and why treatment fails for some. The project is a plan rather than a result, aiming to turn routine health data into sharper targeting of testing and support.
plos-pone-0349023:
Ji-Young Son and Seung-Ho Han mapped the small arteries that pierce outward through the face, knowledge that surgeons need when they move living tissue flaps during reconstruction. Seven donated cadavers, fourteen half-faces, were examined with fine X-ray scanning and dissection. Every vessel branch at least half a millimetre wide was counted, measured at its origin, and plotted against fixed landmarks of the skull.

One hundred and thirty-four such vessels emerged from seven parent arteries. The facial artery's main trunk supplied the most and the thickest, appearing in every specimen. Maps showed distinct territories, and one branch spread widest while another packed vessels most densely near the nose. The authors offer their coordinate maps as a planning aid so flap surgeons can design around vessels they can actually expect to find.
plos-pone-0349223:
Xiao Liao and colleagues present STGAD, a system for spotting anomalies in streams of sensor data where many measurements move together, such as in servers or spacecraft. Nobody labels the failures in advance, so the system must learn what normal looks like and flag departures. Their design pits a generator against a critic in a training contest, with a transformer reading the time patterns.

At test time, each data window is compared with freshly generated normal versions, and the closest match leaves a residual that signals trouble. Two scores, from generation and from the critic, are fused with a threshold that adapts to each dataset. Tests spanned five benchmark sets, from server monitoring to aerospace telemetry, where the system also points to which variables went wrong.
plos-pone-0349423:
Kannika Damrongplasit and Kadir Atalay evaluated Thailand's unconditional cash grant for young children, using national survey data from 2019 and 2022 covering thousands of households. Their 2026 study matched grant-receiving families with similar non-recipients and compared early childhood development, learning materials, and children's screen habits, looking for both benefits and side effects of no-strings money.

Children in grant households developed modestly but measurably better. Yet those homes owned fewer children's books, even as children played more with homemade toys, and the children had more access to electronic devices with longer daily screen time. The authors conclude the grant works, but pairing it with nudges toward books and balanced screen habits would protect its gains.
plos-pone-0350023:
Robert Badgett, Sudha Xirasagar, and Hayrettin Okut ask whether strict copyright on widely used health questionnaires helps or harms science. Two famous tools, a burnout inventory and a mental status exam, charge royalties and forbid changes to their questions. The authors compared their citation patterns over time against four similar tools that are free to use and adapt.

If licensing fees and modification bans slow other researchers down, the restricted tools should gradually be cited less, relative to their topics, than the open ones. The comparison uses annual citation ratios drawn from the medical literature. The question matters for every field that measures people with standard scales: who owns a measuring stick shapes how much it gets used.
plos-pone-0350123:
Job Agba Opue led a team that turned a branch of pure math on supply chains. The math is semigroup theory, which studies one-way changes to a system. In their 2026 model, each shock or fix is one such change. Stack the changes up, and the math shows where the chain can break. It also shows which states are stable.

The team derived clear tests for total collapse. They found ways to spot spare capacity that can save a chain. Step-by-step methods prune the model down to those key parts. Test cases span factories, farm goods, and online sales. The authors say the tools turn vague talk of toughness into numbers planners can use.
plos-pone-0350223:
Peng Liu and co-authors charted acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in children and teenagers across poorer countries from 1990 to 2023 in work published in 2026, with projections to 2050. The cancer is the most common in childhood and often curable, yet outcomes split sharply by income.

Using global burden data, they counted new cases, deaths, and lost healthy years by income group. In 2023 the poorer countries saw tens of thousands of new cases and deaths, with boys hit harder. Rates per child fell while total cases rose with population. Workplace benzene and formaldehyde were the only modelled risks, a narrow slice of the story.
plos-pone-0350323:
Western Sweden's emergency departments swapped their triage system for a new one called WEST, and Samah Habbouche and colleagues studied how the change landed at the first two hospitals to adopt it. Their 2026 PLOS One study interviewed thirty-six triage nurses.

Nurses described the rollout stage by stage, comparing the new system's sorting rules with the old one's habits. Speed of adoption surprised even its supporters, and reports hinted at friction during the switch. The analysis used an innovation-spread framework, treating each department as its own social world. Lessons on training, timing, and nurse involvement should help the remaining departments adopt the system more smoothly.
plos-pone-0350623:
Decorative digital patterns are bulky to send and store, so Binmei Liu and colleagues built a compression method tuned for them. Their 2026 PLOS One paper mixes color grouping with a technique that flattens image data while keeping its local shape.

Colors are first grouped using the image's own color spread, then color and texture guide how the image is cut into pieces, and the flattening step adapts to each neighborhood. The method shrank files to about a sixth of their size while keeping measured quality high, with no clear visible loss. Large batches were handled quickly and with modest memory, suggesting use in design libraries and media sharing.
plos-pone-0350823:
Camilla Bjelland and colleagues reviewed a phone-based referral system for mothers in Ghana and Liberia in 2026. The system links rural clinics with district hospitals so women in labour emergencies reach care faster, a link that often decides survival.

The team combined interviews with dozens of rural and hospital staff in Liberia and a group discussion with midwives in Ghana. Workers said the system fit their daily routines and sped referrals, but shortages of phones, credit, and staff limited its use, and rollout stayed partial. The cross-country view shows what helps a simple mobile tool take hold in busy, low-resource maternity care.
plos-pone-0350923:
Andualem Addisu Birlie and colleagues mapped open defecation across Zambia and trained models to predict where it persists. Going outdoors instead of using a toilet spreads gut disease and pollutes water. A 2024 national survey covered close to thirteen thousand households. Map tools found clusters, while seven learning models raced to predict household practice from survey traits.

About twelve percent of households still practised open defecation. Hot spots clustered in southern, western, and eastern regions. A light boosting model predicted best among the seven. Maps plus prediction, the team argues, let sanitation programmes spend first where need and risk run highest, rather than spreading thin funds evenly.
plos-pone-0351023:
Chittaphone Vanhnollat and colleagues trapped mosquitoes across six provinces of Laos from 2021 to 2024 and screened them for flaviviruses, the family that includes dengue and Japanese encephalitis. Over twenty five hundred female mosquitoes from one hundred species were sorted into small pools and tested, with full gene reading for positive pools.

Gene reading recovered thirteen full virus genomes. One was Tembusu virus from a common mosquito type, closely matching a strain that harmed dolphins in Thailand. Twelve others were insect only viruses that do not infect people. Finding a mammal linked strain in Laos argues for wider virus watching beyond the two famous threats.
plos-pone-0351123:
The Antarctic scallop anchors food webs in the Southern Ocean, yet its genetic toolkit was nearly empty. Hye Jin Park and colleagues read the species' complete mitochondrial genome and built DNA markers for population studies, reported in this 2026 PLOS One paper.

The circular genome runs about fifteen thousand letters and holds the usual gene set minus one gene commonly missing in clams and scallops. Family tree analysis placed the scallop on its own well-supported branch, closest to a North Atlantic species. From the full DNA the team mined hundreds of thousands of short repeating markers and validated seven variable ones, giving future researchers tools to track scallop populations around Antarctica.
plos-pone-0351223:
Terahertz waves could carry the huge data loads of future 6G networks, but walls and human bodies block them easily. Tahniyat Aslam, Irfan Ahmed, and Sundus Ali modeled indoor terahertz uplinks with realistic three-dimensional antennas, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Most earlier work flattened antennas into two dimensions, ignoring how signals spread upward and downward. The new framework derives formulas for interference, coverage chances, and data capacity per area while people and walls block paths. Comparing the two antenna views shows where simplified models mislead designers. Indoor terahertz links, the authors argue, must be planned with the full geometry of rooms and bodies in mind.
plos-pone-0351323:
Some long stretches of RNA do not build proteins but still steer cancer, and Lu Pu and colleagues hunted for such molecules tied to survival in cancer of the womb lining. Their 2026 PLOS One study combined two large public cohorts holding hundreds of tumors.

Hundreds of these RNAs ran higher or lower in tumors than in healthy tissue. Thirty tracked with how long patients lived. Two stood out as critical: tumors behaved differently depending on their levels, and the pair connected to pathways known in cancer growth. The authors propose them as candidate warning markers, while noting lab work must confirm what the molecules actually do.
plos-pone-0351423:
A lichen called Usnea cornuta has a long folk medicine history, and Deepa Karki and colleagues gave it a modern laboratory workup. Their 2026 PLOS One study measured the extract's chemistry and tested it against oxidation, bacteria, and a diabetes-linked enzyme.

The extract proved rich in phenolic compounds and strongly quenched harmful free radicals. One fraction blocked the starch-digesting enzyme at very low doses. Chemical profiling named eleven compounds; computer docking suggested one, menegazziaic acid, binds the enzyme best, with favorable simulated behavior. The extract also halted staph bacteria in dish tests. The authors present the lichen as a candidate source for antioxidant and blood-sugar research.
plos-pone-0351523:
Chidiebele Petronilla Ojukwu led a team of six authors asking parents about children's physical activity, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Parents largely decide whether children join sports and active play. The team explored parents' satisfaction with current activity, their view of school-based options, the barriers they face, and the fixes they prefer.

Ojukwu's findings show what keeps children on the couch from the parent's seat: cost, time, safety, and access all feature in such accounts. Schools planning activity programs gain a parent-tested list of what would actually raise uptake. Children's activity is falling in many countries, with lifelong health effects. Listening to parents is a cheap, often skipped step toward reversing that trend.
plos-pone-0351623:
Gianna Vivaldo and co-authors modelled spring flow in a limestone karst aquifer in northwestern Tuscany, Italy. Karst systems react fast to weather yet hide complex plumbing, which makes them hard to manage under climate change. Their 2026 framework blends regression models with frequency analysis over eighteen years of flow, rain, and temperature records.

Weather alone could not explain the spring's long-term swings. Adding the system's short memory, about five days of carry-over, improved the models sharply. Frequency analysis pulled out yearly and half-yearly cycles whose strength waxes and wanes. Vivaldo and colleagues package the approach as decision support for groundwater managers who must plan around a reactive, partly hidden resource.
plos-pone-0351723:
McCulloch and colleagues modeled a fruit fly pest of blueberries in southern Georgia in a 2026 study. The spotted-wing fly lays eggs in ripe soft fruit, so growers need to know when numbers will rise or fall. Their computer model combined heat patterns with the timing of farmed berries and wild host plants nearby.

The standard run matched the early summer drop seen in trap counts from three seasons. Later parts of the season were harder to match, which showed the limits of using heat and host timing alone. Wild hosts that fruit in fall and winter helped keep flies going between berry seasons. The work gives growers a starting tool, while making clear where better local data are needed.
plos-pone-0351923:
Xiao Chen and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One climate paper. It forecasts Pacific Ocean surface heat weeks to months ahead. That window ties to the El Niño cycle, which shapes weather worldwide. Their model first splits daily heat records into two parts. One part is a smooth, slow trend. The other is a fast-changing remainder. Each part gets a branch suited to it. A learned gate then blends the outputs.

Tested on daily data from five watch regions, the model beat several deep learning rivals. It won at most one-to-three-month ranges. It also won under every El Niño phase, from onset to decay. Simple baselines still won at very short ranges, which the authors admit. They propose the approach as a base for richer ocean forecasts.
plos-pone-0352023:
Xiaodong Zhu and four colleagues test simple blood ratios as crystal balls for the sickest liver patients. Their 2026 study mines a large American intensive care database. Over eighteen hundred adults with cirrhosis at their first intensive care admission were included. Four measures built from red cell distribution width were examined. That width reflects how uneven a patient's red blood cells are, and it rises with inflammation. Outcomes were death within thirty days, ninety days, and a year.

Mortality was grim. Nearly a third died within a month, and almost half within a year. The red cell measures were tested for association with those outcomes after adjustment. Their predictive accuracy was graded with standard curves. Cheap, routine blood values that genuinely forecast survival would help intensive care teams enormously. Cirrhosis crises force fast triage decisions; a marker already sitting in every admission blood panel costs nothing extra to read.
plos-pone-0352323:
Croft and colleagues studied traffic pollution and hospital stays for lung infections in a 2026 paper. Doctors carefully confirmed whether each of more than four hundred patients had a viral infection, a bacterial one, or both. Pollution from traffic, including fine particles and gases, was tracked for the three weeks before each stay.

Links between pollution and admission were checked week by week before illness. The design let the team ask whether germ types respond to dirty air in the same way or on different schedules. Clearer answers could sharpen air quality warnings for people prone to chest infections. The careful case review by four doctors makes the infection labels unusually trustworthy for this kind of study.
plos-pone-0352423:
Suzuki and colleagues, in a 2026 study, hunt for blood signals that warn a COVID-19 patient is about to get worse. Samples were taken from infected patients before any downturn, then read with several deep molecular methods at once, covering proteins, fats, and other small molecules. Known warning signs, including an inflammation marker and white cell counts, held up in the data.

Beyond those, the team found a fresh panel of molecules that shifted before symptoms of decline appeared, and the panel tracked closely with established clinical and immune measures. One pattern stood out: several inflammation markers moved opposite to certain interferon types, the body's early virus alarms. The authors read that as a fingerprint of how this coronavirus muffles the alarm while inflammation builds. They present the panel as groundwork for early-warning tests and for research on the next pandemic virus.
plos-pone-0353123:
Ravneet Kaur and seven colleagues describe this 2026 PLOS One protocol for a pilot trial of a diet app for people with inflammatory bowel disease. The app, built together with patients, guides an anti-inflammatory diet and tracks eating. Forty patients at one center will be randomly assigned to use the app or receive usual care for sixty days, with the usual-care group crossing over halfway.

Because this is a protocol, it sets out measures rather than results. The main question is whether patients find the app usable and acceptable, judged by questionnaires and interviews. Secondary measures cover diet quality, urine markers of processed food intake, disease activity, quality of life, and stool and blood chemistry. The pilot will shape a larger trial and a template for judging diet apps in this disease.
plos-pone-0353423:
Salley and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a pilot study of a program called Talk With Me Baby, built into routine baby checkups. The words and back-and-forth talk a baby hears at home shape later school, health, and earning outcomes. The program coaches caregivers to talk more richly with their babies, but it had not been tested closely in rural or under-served clinics.

At least sixty-six caregiver and baby pairs will be recruited from two primary care clinics, starting when babies are two to six months old. Every family gets the coaching during regular checkups across a year. Before and after, the team will measure the home language setting with a recording tool that counts adult words and the turns of talk between adult and child. The pilot will show whether the program shifts caregiver talk in these clinics and will guide a larger trial.
plos-pone-0353523:
Lun Shen and seven colleagues published this 2026 study of artery plaque growth in the neck, a major stroke risk. Working from public gene data on plaque tissue, they hunted for genes tied to natural killer immune cells that track with worsening plaque, then checked the lead gene in single-cell data.

One gene, IGHG1, came out as the sole independent risk marker, and its levels ran higher in advanced plaques. It sat in pathways for immune attack and T cell signaling. Shen cautions that the gene usually belongs to antibody-making cells, so pinning down its true source needs more lab work.
plos-pone-0353723:
Gaurav Prakash, a single author, published this 2026 modeling paper proposing an earlier way to catch disease. Standard diagnostics wait for a measurement to cross a fixed line, yet illness often starts drifting earlier. Prakash models two meaningful measurements as a plane, then tracks whether a patient's values drift in the direction of disease, using synthetic data built from published trends.

His drift score flagged the pre-threshold group with patterns resembling early disease, even while single values still looked normal. Prakash presents the readable, unit-free metric as an idea needing real patient data before clinical claims.
plos-pone-0354123:
Hao Liu led a team of seven authors on this 2026 remote sensing study of benggang, a dramatic gully erosion form eating hillsides in southern China. Surface maps alone cannot show sinking or swelling ground. The team paired deep learning on sharp satellite photos with radar interferometry from ninety satellite passes over Wuhua County.

The photo model outlined eroded areas accurately, and the radar work resolved vertical movement of mere millimeters of movement per year into a smooth and continuous deformation map. Liu offers the combined watch as an early warning tool for geohazards.
plos-pone-0354423:
Kim and Cho, in a 2026 survey study, link poor sleep satisfaction to problem smartphone use among teenagers in South Korea. Heavy, hard-to-control phone use affects a sizable share of teens worldwide, and poor sleep is a suspected driver. The team asked whether anxiety and loneliness carry part of that effect.

Data came from nearly fifty thousand adolescents, sorted into general, at-risk, and high-risk users. High-risk teens used phones far longer each day and reported more anxiety and loneliness, as well as worse perceived health. Being female, long daily use, and low physical activity also tracked with risk. Tracing the pathways, the authors estimate anxiety carried about three tenths of the link between poor sleep and problem use, and loneliness about a sixth. They suggest that better sleep and support for anxious or lonely teens may cut problem use more than phone rules alone.
plos-pone-0354523:
Mehmet Emin Aksoy led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of how people learn basic life support, the emergency skills behind CPR. Trainees learned through lectures, a tablet game, or a virtual reality game, while a wearable head sensor tracked activity at the front of the brain during practice and testing.

Game-based practice engaged learners differently from lectures, and the virtual reality group showed brain patterns suggesting thriftier use of mental effort during the hands-on test. Aksoy argues training should be judged by brain measures as well as test scores when schools pick a format.
plos-pone-0354723:
Iris Pit and co-authors audited Europe's monitoring records for freshwater invertebrates, the small animals that signal river health. Rivers and lakes hold a rich share of species but face pollution, water extraction, and habitat loss. Their 2026 study gathered millions of records from twenty-eight countries for the early twenty-tens.

Records clustered in central Europe and England, leaving other regions and river types thin. Countries differed in sampling methods, reporting units, and how finely species were named. Those differences block clean Europe-wide trend estimates. Pit and colleagues argue that shared standards for naming and methods, plus better data exchange, are needed before biodiversity trends can be judged fairly across the continent.
plos-pone-0354823:
Xinyu Tian and co-authors developed a structured support programme for family caregivers of autistic children in China. Caregivers carry heavy, many-sided strain that can harm their health and the child's progress. Earlier structured programmes for this exact burden were scarce. Their 2026 development study blended family stress theory with evidence review and the team's own prior findings.

Expert panels refined the draft over two consultation rounds. The finished programme has three core modules covering stressors, how caregivers appraise them, and coping. Inside sit seven themes and twenty-two components, including teaching and mindfulness elements. Tian and colleagues present the programme as ready for formal outcome testing with caregiver groups.
plos-pone-0355223:
Deborah Kilday and colleagues compared delivery outcomes for mothers with and without COVID-19 across successive virus variant periods in the United States. Earlier work tied infection in pregnancy to serious harm, but whether risk changed as variants shifted was unclear. Their 2026 study drew on a national hospital database covering more than two and a half million deliveries.

About two percent of mothers had a COVID-19 diagnosis. Infection came with sharply higher odds of dying in hospital in every variant period studied. The Delta period showed the starkest elevation, while the first Omicron phase showed the smallest, though still raised. Severe maternal illness, early birth, and intensive care use were also tracked. Kilday and colleagues say variant era belongs in obstetric risk planning.
plos-pone-0355623:
Amy K Johnson and colleagues present the protocol for EUPHORIA, a trial aiming to raise use of HIV prevention medication among Black women in Cook County, Illinois, published in 2026. Black women face high HIV rates yet are rarely first in line for pre-exposure prophylaxis, the daily or on-demand medicine that blocks infection. The study works through eight family planning centers.

Clinics will adopt a bundle of support strategies at staggered times, so each center serves as its own comparison. The team will measure prescriptions, continued use, and what helps or blocks progress at patient, provider, and system levels. Because family planning visits are a trusted, routine contact point, success here could offer a model for closing a stubborn prevention gap.
plos-pone-0355723:
Matthew Johnson and colleagues extended an electrical method for reading the resting voltage across a cell membrane. That voltage guides muscle and nerve cells, but it is usually measured with fine electrodes. Their 2026 study adapted dielectrophoresis, which moves cells in an electric field, so it could estimate the voltage in excitable cells too.

The adapted model treats part of the voltage as sitting in the charged layer just outside the membrane. With that fix, estimates for nerve-like and heart-like cells matched values reported in earlier work. The method also tracked how estimates shift when the fluid around cells grows very dilute. Johnson and colleagues say it could help study ion channels without piercing cells.
plos-pone-0356623:
Marcus White and a mixed team of designers, clinicians, and stroke survivors tackle a long hospital design argument in their 2026 paper. Wards must choose between single rooms, which offer privacy and rest, and shared rooms, which offer company and watchful eyes. For stroke recovery, each option fails in its own way, so the team designed mixed rooms that borrow from both.

Working in a shared design lab, the group built four mixed layouts and showed them in virtual reality. Twenty experts and people with lived experience scored the designs against values such as activity, safety, control, and access to green space. Two mixed layouts won clear support. White and colleagues argue that flexible rooms can fit recovery needs better than either extreme.
plos-pone-0356723:
Yuchuan Yang, Qiang Hao, Jun Wen, Wei Zhao, and Chi Zhang reconstructed how phosphorus, life's limiting nutrient, flooded the oceans around 540 million years ago when complex animals were emerging. Their 2026 geochemistry study analyzed rock layers from phosphate mining country on the edge of China's Yangtze Plate, dating to the boundary between the Ediacaran and Cambrian periods.

Their reading: rising atmospheric oxygen supercharged chemical weathering on land, while tectonic grinding set how much rock was exposed to erode, together sending phosphorus seaward. Ocean upwelling then carried it into shallow water, where physical sorting, microbes, and possibly hot vents concentrated it into rich phosphate rock. The work ties the era's biological explosion's fuel supply to mountain building and air itself.
plos-pone-0356823:
Eman Salamah Albtoush, Keng Hoon Gan, and Saif Addeen A Alrababah studied whether deceptive Arabic news headlines betray themselves through style alone. Their 2026 cross-corpus study assembled five headline collections. It added translated English sets, prepared to preserve stylistic flavor. It measured wording and number patterns that differ between fake and genuine headlines.

Modern Arabic language models beat classical text classifiers consistently. They read sub-word patterns that capture both meaning and style. Adding hand-built features on top helped only where fakes leaned on flashy numbers or dates. It added nothing on the combined corpus. Still, the authors value the visible features for explaining a verdict. Pure neural scores cannot do that for editors deciding what to flag.
plos-pone-0357023:
Ramesh Shrestha and colleagues test a simple idea for preventing diabetes-related blindness in Nepal: teach schoolchildren, and let them teach their families. Eye damage from diabetes can be prevented when adults act early, but awareness is low. In one municipality, a school nurse ran a short education program for early secondary students, who then held sessions at home for a co-resident older family member; matched schools served as controls.

Student knowledge jumped after the program with a large measured effect, and family members also gained knowledge and better habits. Shrestha and colleagues gathered discussion evidence alongside the scores to judge how the child-to-family route felt in practice. They present nurse-supported school teaching as a cheap channel into homes that clinics rarely reach.
plos-pone-0357123:
Mai Tuyet Do and five colleagues surveyed 384 LGBTQ+ people aged eighteen to twenty-four across Vietnam in early 2025. They asked about suicidal thoughts, plans, and attempts. The questions covered their lifetimes and the past year. Their 2026 cross-sectional study also measured depression, anxiety, and stress with a standard questionnaire. It tested which background and mental health factors tracked with each outcome.

More than half reported suicidal thoughts at some point. About a third had made a plan, and roughly one in six had attempted. Stress and anxiety were the strongest companions of thoughts and plans. Anxiety alone predicted attempts. Higher income and living outside cities linked to lower risk. The authors call for routine anxiety and stress screening and affirming care for this group.
plos-pone-0357923:
Can Colakoglu and Sefa Levent Ozsahin published a 2026 clinical study in PLOS ONE on inflammation in advanced chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Doctors often read a simple blood ratio, neutrophils divided by lymphocytes, as a sign of body-wide inflammation. They compared stable patients on long-term oxygen therapy with those not on it, checking that ratio against standard markers such as C-reactive protein and white cell counts.

Patients on oxygen had markedly higher ratios, driven by lower lymphocyte and eosinophil counts, yet their standard inflammation markers were no higher than the other group's. Statistical modeling confirmed the ratio moved with blood cell counts rather than with oxygen levels or lung function. This discordant pattern, they argue, means a high ratio may mark a distinct immune state, not simply more inflammation, so clinicians should read it in context.
plos-pone-0358323:
Mieko Tsuruoka and Kenji Inoue published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on people applying for visual disability certification at a large eye hospital in Japan. Officials rate impairment using scores computed from eye-chart results, but those scores say little about whether a person can actually read. The authors compared three official scores against real reading tests in a small group, most of whom had glaucoma or other non-macular eye disease.

One score, based on visual sharpness, tracked reading performance closely: it lined up with the smallest print size people could read and with a standard index of reading accessibility. Scores based on visual field, by contrast, showed weak or inconsistent links to reading. The sharpness-based score, they suggest, can stand in for reading ability when direct tests are unavailable. They caution that very few participants had macular disease, so the finding may not extend there.
plos-pone-0358423:
Tapon Kumar Roy and four colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on rice farming in Bangladesh. For six years the team ran a light trap in Gazipur, catching insects to count them. They study how weather shapes the numbers of rice insect pests, and of the natural enemies that prey on them.

Light trap records over six seasons show pest numbers rising and falling with weather patterns. Knowing which weather favors pests, and which favors their enemies, helps farmers time control measures. Agricultural extension services in Bangladesh can turn these long-run patterns into warnings that protect the country's staple crop.
plos-pone-0359323:
Mateusz Kukla and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on wheelchair performance. It offers a preliminary model for estimating how much oxygen, per unit of body mass, a person uses while pushing a manual wheelchair. The estimate is built from two signals: mechanical power, the work the arms produce, and heart rate.

Oxygen uptake is the standard measure of aerobic effort, but measuring it directly needs laboratory gas equipment. A model that infers it from power and pulse could work courtside during training or testing. Sports scientists and rehabilitation clinicians who train wheelchair athletes are the audience for a lighter-weight estimate of effort.
plos-pone-0359423: Ouyang and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a steroid-like compound called dioscin and eye aging. In their tests, a sugar-based aging trigger made pigment cells at the back of the eye grow old and change type. The title reports that dioscin softened both effects, acting through a named chain of signals. Slowing such cell aging could one day help protect sight in older eyes.
pmc-13196923:
Shu-Xian Lin and Kuang-Sheng Yeh published a 2026 study of a drug-resistant germ strain in pets. The strain is a type of E. coli, a common gut germ that can infect the bladder. They checked samples from dogs and cats treated for bladder infections in Taiwan.

The team studied 400 germ samples from a teaching animal hospital, gathered over nine years. Gene tests confirmed 26 samples as the ST131 strain, known for resisting many drugs. Those samples carried many harm-linked genes. All resisted two common drugs, but all still responded to one strong reserve drug. Some resistance genes could pass between germs. The spread in pets matters for both animal and human health.
pmc-13197423:
Rym Baccouch and colleagues ran a 2026 trial on music paired with exercise for teens with poor vision. Teens born with visual impairment often have lower fitness and less daily independence. Music has boosted drive in other groups, so the team tested it within strength and body-sense training.

Fifty-nine teens split into three groups: training alone, training with music, and no training. After eight weeks, both training groups improved on all fitness tests. The music group scored higher than the plain group on sit-to-stand counts, a wall-sit hold, and one-leg balance. Reach distance did not differ. The control group showed no real change. Music may add gains for daily autonomy.
pmc-13201323:
Wolves shift where they roam as the seasons change, and a 2026 study led by Nathaniel H Wehr tests whether those shifts track the movements of their prey. The research article follows gray wolves, moose, and white-tailed deer in Minnesota, plus wolves and moose on Isle Royale in Michigan.

The team analyzed GPS collar records gathered from 2008 through 2021 and used cluster analysis to define seasonal patterns of space use. Mainland wolves changed their ranges in step with deer migration, while island wolves and moose kept steadier patterns. The results link predator movement to prey movement and argue for managing several species together.
pmc-13202823:
Research on blood and tissue markers for lung cancer screening is expanding fast, and a 2026 bibliometric analysis led by Huange Zhu maps the field's shape. The study retrieves publications from the Web of Science Core Collection and visualizes trends, collaboration networks, and emerging topics with several analysis tools.

The analysis covered 3,636 publications and found output growing exponentially since 2014 across the field. Collaboration formed a dual core around China and the United States, with Chinese volume high and American work more cited. Topic modeling grouped the literature into five directions, and burst analysis pointed to DNA methylation, liquid biopsy, and artificial intelligence platforms as future priorities.
pmc-13202923: A short correction notice from Tao Liu and co-authors, published in 2026, amends their 2025 BMC Plant Biology article on cotton PLATZ transcription factors and drought resistance in tomato. The notice states that a paragraph was duplicated by mistake in the introduction and must be removed, and it confirms the error does not affect the article's conclusions. Only the correction notice itself survives here, so the underlying experiments and results are not described.
pmc-13203023:
The gut talks to the skeleton, and a 2026 review by Alba Rodriguez-Bryant surveys that talk for ways to protect bone. The article studies the gut-bone axis in osteoporosis, on how gut microbes and their products influence nutrient uptake, gut leakiness, acidity, and immune control.

Rodriguez-Bryant and co-authors review diet plans meant to steer the microbiome toward bone protection. Options include butyrate and other postbiotics, chosen probiotic strains, prebiotic fibers, synbiotic mixes, and dietary patterns such as Mediterranean and vegetarian diets. The review also maps microbe product pathways and flags gaps that must close before these plans become standard osteoporosis care.
pmc-13203423:
Making art may measurably lift mental health, and a 2026 meta-analysis led by Xu Song pools the randomized evidence for painting-based interventions. The study gathers trials of painting activities for outcomes such as depression and anxiety, across age groups and types of art practice.

Forty-five randomized controlled trials met the inclusion criteria and passed a formal risk-of-bias assessment. The pooled effect was significant and large, indicating better scale-measured mental health after painting interventions in the combined data. Effects looked similar across intervention lengths, art forms, and gender mixes, while older adults appeared to benefit the most from taking part.
pmc-13207923:
Glowing carbon specks are too small to reach tumors well alone, and a 2026 review led by Xiaowen Xu examines hiding them inside membrane vesicles. The article surveys carbon dots and their hybrid carriers, which range from natural extracellular vesicles to laboratory-made liposomes, for biomedical delivery.

The review first covers how carbon dots are synthesized and why they fluoresce, then details strategies for loading them into vesicles. Hybrid systems are being tried for targeted drug delivery, imaging, tumor therapy, antibacterial work, and wound care in the literature surveyed. Loading efficiency, burst release, and what the dots do to vesicle stability remain open problems for clinical translation.
pmc-13212423:
Janith Galhenage and colleagues report in 2026 on methamphetamine use and mental illness among patients at a large psychiatry clinic in Sri Lanka. Use of the drug is rising across South and Southeast Asia, yet local evidence on who uses it and what harm follows has stayed thin.

The team studied 245 consecutive patients with questionnaires and standard diagnostic criteria. Nearly all were men, most had first been introduced to the drug by friends, and about six in ten met criteria for dependence. Nicotine and heroin use were also common, while psychosis and depression appeared in a minority. Dependence strongly predicted heavier psychiatric symptoms, supporting services that treat addiction and mental illness together.
pmc-13216323:
M. A. Helal and co-authors present a 2026 chemistry study of a new Schiff base ligand and the metal complexes built from it, tested as possible anticancer and antimicrobial agents. Schiff bases grip metal ions at several points, which makes them versatile drug scaffolds.

The ligand, assembled from a pyridine building block and a benzene-diol partner, was combined with copper, cobalt, manganese, nickel, and palladium ions. Spectral evidence showed it binding through two oxygen and two nitrogen atoms, with most complexes taking octahedral shapes and the palladium one square planar. The compounds inhibited the tested fungi more strongly than the bacteria. Cell tests against the MCF-7 breast cancer line showed notable antitumour activity, and docking simulations suggested plausible fits to cancer-related protein targets.
pmc-13217823:
Nilesh Kumar Sinha and co-authors present a 2026 imaging case report of a rare inner ear malformation in a four-year-old boy with delayed speech and severe-to-profound hearing loss in both ears. The defect, incomplete partition type 3, is tied to X-linked deafness and makes implant surgery risky.

High-resolution CT showed the signature picture: a corkscrew-shaped cochlea with its central bony pillar entirely absent and a wide-open connection to an enlarged internal auditory canal. MRI confirmed a normal cochlear nerve and no further labyrinth problems. Naming the anomaly before surgery matters because the open channel can release a gusher of fluid during cochlear implantation. The authors use the case to teach the distinguishing scan features against the other incomplete partition types.
pmc-13218123:
Linhao Hou and colleagues report a 2026 bioadhesive hydrogel sensor that keeps working at temperatures down to minus 30 degrees Celsius. Hydrogel sensors are soft and body-friendly for monitoring wounds, but standard versions freeze in the cold, stick poorly to wet tissue, and do little to shape the wound environment. The team built its gel from polyethylene glycol, a glycerol-water solvent, and carboxylated carbon nanotubes.

Hydrogen bonding in the glycerol-water mixture blocks ice formation, while the nanotube network carries current and strengthens the gel. The sensor adhered to wet tissue and kept its conductivity and strain sensitivity at minus 30 degrees, giving fast, stable readings as it stretched. In diabetic mice with full-thickness skin wounds, readings accompanied much faster healing, with wounds closed by day twelve and new tissue resembling early developmental skin. Tests on pig heart wounds showed the sensor also follows moving tissue in real time.
pmc-13218723:
Saule Spokaite and colleagues report a 2026 study that uncovers a second, ancient binding site for the RAB5 protein on a sorting machine. The VPS34 complex II builds identity signals that drive endosomal sorting, the eating of particles by cells, and the shutdown of receptors. RAB5 switches it on. Textbooks placed RAB5's grip on one helical insertion of the complex. A sister complex used for autophagy preferred a switch.

A cryo-electron microscopy structure of complex II revealed an extra RAB5 contact on the VPS15 subunit's solenoid region. The team argues this is the original site inherited from eukaryotes. Mutating the classic site in the human complex abolished RAB5 binding. Mutating the matching region in baker's yeast broke cargo sorting and the complex's association with its RAB5 counterpart. The authors suggest evolution added a grip to strengthen membrane binding as cells' transport systems grew more complex.
pmc-13220823:
Qiang Tan and colleagues read five years of disease surveillance from Chongqing, China, for trends in lung disease in a 2026 study. The Chongqing Chronic Disease Surveillance System captured a million new cases and over 1.2 million cases of COPD, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema among residents aged fifteen and over between 2020 and 2024, plus 239,000 deaths. Age-standardized rates were computed against the 2000 census.

Standardized prevalence doubled for COPD and tripled for emphysema and chronic bronchitis across the period, which the authors attribute to better case finding rather than an explosion of disease. COPD and emphysema stayed male-predominant, while chronic bronchitis flipped to female-predominant after 2023, a divergence they flag for prevention. Rural areas carried the heavier burden. The success story is diagnostic: the share of COPD cases confirmed by spirometry jumped from seven percent in 2022 to twenty-six percent in 2024, and the urban-rural gap in that rate vanished.
pmc-13221123:
Amal Rammah and co-authors follow more than 415,000 London-born children in a 2026 cohort study of air pollution and bronchiolitis admissions. Fine particles and nitrogen dioxide were estimated at home addresses during pregnancy and the first year of life. Evidence on longer exposure windows for this chest illness had been limited.

Overall results were inconclusive, though some windows hinted at raised risk. Signals appeared for pregnancy exposure in the first month after birth, and for exposures late in infancy. Confidence ranges were wide, so no firm claim is made. The authors call for work covering emergency and primary care cases, not only hospital admissions.
pmc-13222223:
Anne-Mari Mustonen and colleagues profile blood proteins in knee osteoarthritis around the time of joint replacement, in a 2026 proteomics study. Serum came from eight healthy controls and eight patients with end-stage disease, sampled again twelve months after knee surgery. Mass spectrometry catalogued the proteins, and statistical models linked them to pain and function.

Patients showed 151 raised proteins and five lowered ones at baseline, tied to immunity, clotting, inflammation, and tissue remodeling. One protein, complement factor I, stood out as a biomarker candidate. Several proteins predicted cartilage loss, pain sensitivity, and physical function. Changes persisted a year after surgery, suggesting the disease leaves a lasting systemic signature.
pmc-13226023:
A. S. Aderibigbe tracks a 2026 poultry research note comparing stress in fast-growing and slow-growing broiler chickens raised on pasture. Feather samples store corticosterone, a stress hormone, giving a noninvasive record over time. Two commercial genotypes, Cornish and Freedom Ranger, were followed for five weeks in the same outdoor system.

Feather hormone levels did not differ significantly between the fast and slow growers at any point. Levels did shift significantly across the five weeks for both types, showing that time and changing conditions registered in the birds even when breed did not. Under these pasture conditions, genotype alone did not explain stress, a result relevant to welfare claims made for slower-growing birds.
pmc-13226123:
Merzu Belete and colleagues build a 2026 prediction tool for head and neck cancer patients receiving immunotherapy, where only a minority benefit and the usual PD-L1 score predicts poorly. Their model fuses three kinds of information: clinical data, gene-activity signatures from the tumour, and features from digital pathology images. Artificial intelligence combined them into a single risk signature.

Immune-related gene patterns, especially those tied to T cells and organised immune clusters called tertiary lymphoid structures, tracked with longer time before the cancer progressed. The combined model beat any single data type in real-world patient groups. Its survival-aware design also highlighted which tissue regions drove each prediction, keeping the output interpretable for clinicians.
pmc-13227323:
Tom Chun Wai Tsoi and colleagues set out a 2026 trial protocol for an online coaching programme aimed at Hong Kong family carers of older adults. Carers often develop anxiety and depression, yet most studies of digital coaching stop at those symptoms. This three-arm randomised trial also asks whether self-directed learning can build resilience and overall well-being, especially for carers whose needs are still mild.

Participants will receive either the full module set, a partial set, or control access through an online platform. Modules cover lifestyle habits, family relationships, and emotion regulation. Standard scales measure anxiety and depression as primary outcomes, while quality of life, caregiving burden, self-care confidence, and unmet needs fill out the wider picture.
pmc-13232723:
Yael Riahi and colleagues identify in 2026 glucosamine as the missing link between high blood sugar and a growth switch that harms diabetic tissue. Chronic sugar excess keeps the switch, called mTORC1, stuck on in pancreas and kidney, driving stress and cell decline. Tracing labeled glucose in diabetic rodents showed tissue sugar and glucosamine rising in lockstep.

The same tie appeared in human blood data and grew stronger as insulin-making function worsened. Small glucosamine doses switched the pathway on in dish tests through a sugar-tagging step. Dimming the switch genetically in insulin cells, or lowering sugar with a common drug class, eased cell stress and restored function. The pathway offers a fresh target for protecting both pancreas and kidney.
pmc-13232823:
FuGuo Liu and colleagues build in 2026 a structure-aware model that predicts what viral proteins do from messy wastewater samples. Fast viral change makes look-alike proteins drift into new jobs, which breaks tools that read letter sequences alone. Their framework mixes short sequence chunks with meaning tags drawn from a protein database.

Training used more than sixty-six thousand coronavirus samples pulled from wastewater sequencing records. Scores in repeated testing ran high for sorting proteins by function, and a slimmed student model kept nearly all that skill while training much faster. Attention peaks in the model landed on known working parts of the spike protein, which makes its calls easier to trust. Earlier wastewater warnings for new variants are the intended payoff.
pmc-13233323:
Alexander Tyshkovskiy and colleagues published a 2026 study hunting for shared molecular signs of ageing across mammals. The team integrated more than 11,000 gene activity profiles from over 25 tissues in mice, rats, macaques, and humans. From these data they built clear markers that estimate age in years and expected mortality, and that respond to lifespan-changing interventions.

Ageing-related gene changes proved conserved across species and cell types, with genes such as CDKN1A and LGALS3 standing out. Their protein levels also tracked death and multiple illnesses in UK Biobank data. Damage models in cells and animals echoed the same signatures, while reprogramming and other rejuvenation steps reversed them. Separate clocks for pathways like inflammation and mitochondrial function showed that diseases and diets age different systems at different speeds.
pmc-13233923:
Sibel Bozgeyik-Bagdatli and colleagues published a 2026 cross-sectional study of symptom burden across the severity grades of knee osteoarthritis. Eighty-two patients were sorted into grades two, three, and four on the Kellgren-Lawrence X-ray scale. They were then compared on pain, sleep, daily function, walking and standing tests, and leg strength. Age and body mass were accounted for.

The most advanced grade carried the heaviest burden. Grade four patients reported worse constant pain than grade two patients. They moved more slowly on the timed up-and-go test. Their thigh muscle was weaker in the sore knee, and they rated knee function lower. Differences between grades two and three, and between three and four, were much narrower. Sleep scores did not differ significantly. The authors say the top grade marks a clear step up in suffering.
pmc-13234023:
Dorsa Manavi and co-workers issued a 2026 mixed-methods study on living with fibromyalgia alongside body-wide autoimmune diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. Surveys came from 1,269 adults, backed by talks with 19 patients and 21 doctors. About a quarter of the adults reported fibromyalgia, and over half of those doubted the diagnosis was right.

People with the dual label reported lower wellbeing, less trust in their doctors, less faith in getting help, and a worse view of their care than peers without fibromyalgia. Talks traced the doubt to overlapping symptoms and the lack of a decisive blood test, with uneven doctor habits feeding mistrust. Feeling dismissed or wrongly labeled added stigma and delays. Accepting the label, by itself, changed few outcomes.
pmc-13234323:
Eva Niessen and colleagues introduced in 2026 a new laboratory task for studying whether people notice their own mistakes. Theories of cognitive control hold that behaviour adjusts more strongly after errors that a person has detected. Older tasks produce few undetected errors, which limits comparison between the two kinds. The Speeded Inference Task was built to create many errors of both types at a steady rate.

Two small studies with about twenty adults each tested the task in practice. The first study confirmed the desired error pattern over time. Exploratory results there suggested post-error slowing and accuracy gains were not clearly tied to awareness. Changing one task feature in the second study shifted error detection without changing the overall error rate. Researchers can now use the task to probe brain and behaviour links more cleanly.
pmc-13235523:
Ganglong Duan and colleagues proposed in 2026 a system that detects distress in posts on Weibo, a major Chinese social platform, and responds with supportive content. Their approach first judges the emotional polarity of a post, then classifies negative posts by the cause behind the feeling. Positive content matched to that cause is then recommended to the user. Weakly supervised learning reduces the need for hand-labelled training examples.

Tests on a real Weibo dataset reached high accuracy for recognizing emotional polarity in posts. Sorting negative posts into cause categories proved harder, with accuracy in the low eighties. Recommendation performance was also reported as strong in the experiments described. The authors frame automatic emotional support as a scalable complement to counselling, which faces staff, distance, and stigma limits. Further validation would be needed before any mental health deployment is claimed.
pmc-13236523:
Emmeline Monique T. Ngo and co-authors described in 2026 an autoimmune cause of extreme insulin resistance in a 20-year-old woman. She arrived with diabetic ketoacidosis and blood sugar that stayed dangerously high despite enormous insulin doses. Antibodies in her blood were attacking her own insulin receptors, a rare condition called type B insulin resistance. Testing confirmed the diagnosis alongside other autoimmune markers in her profile.

Supportive diabetes drugs, including a GLP-1 medicine, cut her daily insulin need from thousands of units to a few hundred. Immune-suppressing treatment with rituximab and azathioprine then allowed insulin to stop entirely within a week. As antibody levels fell, the same antibodies began causing low blood sugar episodes during fasting. Steroids and another drug managed that second phase under continuous glucose monitoring. The authors highlight the swing between extremes as a signature of the disease.
pmc-13237323:
Mohammad N Kheshfeh and colleagues ran a randomized trial at the University of Damascus in 2026 comparing two orthodontic wire designs for pulling upper canine teeth backward after premolar removal. Thirty-eight patients aged 18 to 25 with Class II bite problems were split evenly. One group used a bi-dimensional wire, rectangular at the front and round at the back, while the other used a conventional rectangular wire throughout.

Monthly retraction was faster with the bi-dimensional wire, at roughly 1.17 millimeters per month against about 0.82 in the conventional group. The trial also tracked tooth rotation, tilt, anchor-tooth drift, bite depth change, and root shortening on scans and X-rays, with assessors kept blind to group. The authors present the mixed wire as a more efficient sliding system for this common extraction treatment.
pmc-13239123:
Maximilian Reuber, Christian Coachman, and Daniel Engler-Hamm reported in 2026 a 62-year-old woman whose collapsed bite and obstructive sleep apnea were treated together with an implant-supported jaw advancement. She had lost her occlusal height badly, a situation where ordinary mouthpieces for apnea have nothing to grip. A digital workflow planned six implants across both jaws and a same-day provisional prosthesis that held her lower jaw forward.

The bite was raised by five millimeters, and the provisional went in on the day of surgery. After three months of healing, final telescopic crown prostheses restored function and appearance. She reported that her snoring eased and her sleep improved markedly. The authors present prosthetic-driven implant therapy as an expanding answer where dentistry meets sleep medicine.
pmc-13239223:
Moamen Al Zoubi and colleagues reported in 2026 a 70-year-old man whose spreading brain lesions, first feared to be cancer, proved to be infection by the free-living amoeba Balamuthia mandrillaris. He had recently worked with soil in rural Mexico. Extensive testing for infection, cancer, and autoimmune disease found nothing, and brain biopsy showed dense granulomatous inflammation with no organism visible on ordinary stains.

A gene-amplification test on the brain tissue finally named the amoeba, a diagnosis the national disease control agency confirmed. Treatment with a multidrug regimen including miltefosine and the investigational drug nitroxoline damaged his kidneys and liver, and after brief radiological improvement the disease advanced and he died. The authors stress molecular testing when conventional work-ups fail on rare pathogens.
pmc-13239623:
Qi-Hua Yu and colleagues review recent work on piperine, the pungent compound in black pepper, as a possible cancer drug source in a 2026 article. Interest is high, yet the natural supply is small and the compound dissolves poorly in water, limiting how much reaches tumours in the body.

Covering studies from 2012 to 2025, the review explains the molecule's structure, how chemists build it in the laboratory, and how living systems produce it. Most attention goes to modified versions, especially changes at one end of the molecule that add new chemical groups. Those derivatives often killed cancer cells more strongly while keeping favourable behaviour.
pmc-13240523:
Ngawang Norbu and co-authors report a 2026 survey of white birch forests in the Nyang River Basin on the southeastern Tibetan Plateau. Plots ranged across a wide band of elevation. The study examines how woody plant variety changes with height and soil conditions.

Field teams recorded dozens of woody species across the survey plots and sorted the stands into four plant groupings. Richness and diversity measures fell as elevation rose, while dominance by a few species increased. Statistical analysis pointed to elevation plus soil nitrogen, organic matter, and phosphorus as the main influences on community makeup. The results give managers baseline data for protecting alpine forest under climate change.
pmc-13240923:
Li and colleagues in Luoyang linked the stress hyperglycemia ratio to delirium risk across two thousand ninety-three intensive care patients. The ratio compares acute blood sugar against a patient's usual level. Logistic models, curve fitting, and threshold analysis probed the shape of the link. Subgroup checks tested whether severity scores modified it.

Risk stayed flat until the ratio passed roughly two-thirds, then climbed steeply. Beyond that bend, delirium odds nearly doubled with each step upward. The association strengthened in patients with higher severity scores and inflammation markers. Li proposes the ratio as an early flag for targeted glucose management.
pmc-13241423:
da Silva and colleagues in Rio de Janeiro asked how little enlargement root canal retreatment can get away with. Fourteen extracted lower molars with severely curved canals were filled, then retreated. A paired design tested conservative and conventional protocols inside the same roots. Micro-CT scans gauged leftover filling at three stages.

The conservative protocol cleared more material early, removing ninety-five percent at the first pass. After final shaping, both approaches ended near complete removal. Less than five percent of filling stayed either way. The authors endorse the smaller preparation for sparing root dentin.
pmc-13241523:
Brandy Ndirangu and colleagues publish a 2026 review of breast artery calcification as a clue to heart disease risk in women. Calcium deposits in breast arteries show up often on screening mammograms. Unlike plaque that narrows arteries, this calcification stiffens the artery wall.

Studies link the finding to heart attack, stroke, and heart failure. Standard risk calculators often underestimate danger in women, so an extra marker already visible on routine scans is attractive. New artificial intelligence tools can measure the deposits automatically and at scale. The authors argue that standardized measurement and reporting are the missing steps. Widespread use could flag at-risk women without any extra testing.
pmc-13242023:
Chenchen Li and co-authors report a 2026 study of a protein modification that worsens brain injury when blood flow returns after stroke. The protein, PKCγ, gains a phosphate tag at one specific site following the injury. A small share of the tagged protein moves into mitochondria, the cell energy centers.

Versions of the protein that mimic the tagged state suppressed a protective gene switch, raised harmful oxygen species, and pushed neurons toward death. A version that cannot be tagged did the opposite. Silencing the protein in mice shrank damaged brain areas and improved movement outcomes. The authors propose blocking this single tagging site as a stroke treatment strategy.
pmc-13242323:
Terui-Kohbata's team in Tokyo let five lay reviewers rewrite a survey about children's genomic data before fielding it. Japanese teens re-consent at sixteen for new samples, while earlier data stay usable regardless. Four involvement stages structured the public feedback. Every change was logged under the GRIPP2 standard.

83 percent of first-round comments were adopted, then 87 percent in round two. Wording, opt-out notes, and parent-child framing all sharpened. The five disagreed productively on allowed side uses of data. The report ranks among Japan's first ordered accounts of structured patient input.
pmc-13242423:
Pureum Sun and co-authors asked whether extracts from three traditional herbs could help mice resist Toxoplasma gondii, a widespread parasite. Their paper appeared in Acta Parasitologica in 2026. One extract came from Gypsophila oldhamiana, a plant long used in herbal medicine. Mice received the extracts by mouth before and after infection, and the team tracked parasite loads and immune responses in the spleen.

Only the Gypsophila extract clearly limited the infection, leaving treated mice with far fewer parasites than the other groups. It pushed dendritic cells to mature and release interleukin-12, which in turn expanded killer T cells that produce interferon-gamma. At the same time it raised checkpoint proteins that keep the response from overshooting. The authors present the plant as a preventive candidate worth further study.
pmc-13242623:
Yu Rao wrote a short piece marking the first approval of a PROTAC drug. It appeared in Cancer Innovation in 2026. On May 1, 2026, United States officials approved vepdegestrant, sold as Veppanu, for some advanced breast cancers with ESR1 changes. Arvinas built the drug with Pfizer after more than twenty years of work.

Most drugs block a protein only while they sit on it. A PROTAC instead tags its target so the cell destroys it. Rao argues the approval proves this event-driven idea can pass review and reach the market. It also gives the many degrader drugs now in testing a path to point to. He sets degraders beside antibodies, gene therapies, and RNA drugs as one more small-molecule tool. For Rao, a lab idea has become a real treatment.
pmc-13242823:
Abdukadir Mohamed Hassan and Abdiwali Mohamed Hussein report a 2026 case of a maternal death during transfer in Somalia, framed by conflict-related service collapse. A 22-year-old first-time mother labored at home with a traditional attendant in a remote nomadic community. The nearest district facility had been shut for about six months because of insecurity.

Her labor became obstructed, and her condition worsened before the family attempted the long trip to a regional hospital. She died in transit before arrival. The authors map the failure onto the three delays model of maternal death. They urge protected emergency obstetric care, stronger referral transport and communication, and community teaching on danger signs for remote populations.
pmc-13243123:
Fang Yang and colleagues report a 2026 case of severe side effects from a new lung cancer drug. Their patient was a 72-year-old man with stage IV squamous lung cancer and an EGFR gene change. Soon after his first dose of ivonescimab with chemotherapy, he developed a lasting high fever.

Blood tests showed very high levels of IL-6, a protein that fuels inflammation, and steroid drugs calmed the fever fast. A second dose brought a worse reaction, plus heavy urine output that pointed to a hormone problem near the brain. Care with steroids and other drugs eased his symptoms over time. The team urges early hormone checks and close IL-6 tracking when fever will not settle.
pmc-13244423:
Feiyuan Ding and Kezhou Yang build ultra-clean graphene devices to carry spin signals in 2026 work. Graphene can move spin over long distances, yet rough contacts and dirt at interfaces cut coherence short. Whether the thickness of the boron nitride layer beneath helps or hurts was tangled with other effects.

The team made Hall bar devices resting on boron nitride layers of two thicknesses. Surfaces came out extremely flat, with no trapped bubbles between layers. Spin coherence lengths neared the width of the channel itself. Extra layer thickness changed screening but added no disorder, so spin behavior stayed much the same. Clean stacking like this could serve future low-power spin logic.
pmc-13247423:
Chen and co-authors record a complication they believe is the first of its kind in this 2026 Case Reports in Critical Care article. Intraosseous access, drilling a needle into bone to deliver emergency fluids and drugs, is considered safe and routine in resuscitation. A sixty-seven-year-old woman, however, crashed with severe heart failure on both sides shortly after such a line was placed and resuscitation began.

Scans showed a new, large fat embolism in her lungs, fat forced from the bone marrow into circulation, which had not been present a day earlier. Emergency heart-lung support and suction removal of the clot improved her circulation dramatically. Tragically she had already sustained anoxic brain injury and care was withdrawn. The authors urge awareness of this rare, lethal possibility.
pmc-13248323:
Bektas-Dag and colleagues analyzed personal memories written by people with anorexia nervosa, in a 2026 qualitative study. Participants answered cue words linked to disgust toward themselves or moral disgust. The team compared forty-three adults with anorexia against twenty healthy adults, coding one hundred eighty-nine short memory accounts in all.

Three themes emerged: wounds dealt by other people, constant watchfulness in relationships, and a disturbed sense of identity. Memories in the anorexia group told of betrayal, shame, and harm from treatment itself, and the feelings stayed unresolved. The authors suggest therapy should rebuild trust in others and a steadier sense of self.
pmc-13249423:
Gao and a large Chinese team report that capsaicin, the heat in chili peppers, can shield the stomach from alcohol damage, in a 2026 eLife study. Alcohol burns the stomach lining partly through oxidative stress. Using binding assays and cell tests, the team showed capsaicin slips into the KEAP1 protein and loosens its grip on NRF2, the master switch for antioxidant defenses.

Freed NRF2 switched on protective genes in stomach cells, and the effect vanished in cells or mice lacking the relevant gene. Rats given capsaicin, including a nanoparticle version that dissolves better, suffered far less inflammation after alcohol dosing. The authors propose capsaicin as a gentler template for antioxidant drugs, since it does not bind permanently.
pmc-13249923:
Son and an international team printed a living graft that grows its own blood vessels, in a 2026 Angiogenesis study. Blocked circulation starves limbs of oxygen, and injected cells usually wash away. Their graft combines a printed microvascular pattern with stem cell spheroids placed in a planned layout, tuned so the balls of cells release more vessel-growing signals and invite host capillaries in.

In mice with critically starved hind legs, the grafts doubled host vessel infiltration compared with simpler designs. Sixty percent of treated limbs were saved, a four-and-a-half-fold improvement over conventional grafts, and the new vessels joined smoothly with the animal's own. Muscle damage shrank accordingly. The authors propose the design for ischemic disease therapy.
pmc-13250323:
Ari Solomon, Laura Roberson, and Karim Jreije describe an unusually large pancreatic tumour in this 2026 case report. The tumour type, acinar cell carcinoma, makes up only about one to two percent of pancreatic cancers, and most are five to ten centimetres wide.

Their patient, an 82-year-old man, had the mass spotted on a scan done for another cancer. It measured 15 centimetres and sat against the stomach. Surgeons removed it whole, together with the tail of the pancreas and the spleen, and the patient went home four days later. Lab tests confirmed the type, with clean edges and no spread to lymph nodes, and no return was seen at two months.
pmc-13250623:
Musab Hamed Saeed and a large team test dental filling materials in this 2026 lab study. Dentists sometimes use bonding glue as a shaping liquid on soft fillings, but whether that changes how germs stick to the finished surface was unclear.

Five filling materials were made with and without the glue layer, seven samples each. The main cavity germ was grown on them, and surfaces were viewed under a powerful microscope. Glued surfaces were rougher and more uneven. Germ counts rose with glue for three materials but fell for two. Since the effect cuts both ways, the authors urge caution with the shortcut.
pmc-13250723:
Henrik Åberg and co-authors test a precise way to track broken hip bones in this 2026 study. Flat X-ray pictures can understate how far fragments of a hip fracture have shifted in three dimensions, which matters when judging a repair.

Fifteen patients with fractures near the top of the thigh bone received CT scans before and after surgery and at follow-up; twelve had complete sets. The CT-based motion analysis repeated measurements to within less than a millimetre. It showed the initial shift was large, surgery cut it sharply, and fragments then moved only slightly as they healed, mostly by shortening. The method looks reliable for follow-up checks.
pmc-13250923:
Xiao and co-authors review how an aging immune system may drive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a scarring lung disease of older adults. Their 2026 Journal of Inflammation Research paper treats the disease as age-related, with worn-out cells and a tired immune system feeding steady low-grade inflammation. The authors searched the literature through October 2025 for the clearest studies.

The review walks through recent findings on immune aging in this disease and the roles of specific immune cell groups. It also gathers candidate blood markers that might help doctors diagnose and track the condition earlier. Treatment ideas aimed at immune aging get surveyed as a fresh direction beyond current drugs. The authors call for deeper mechanism work and better tools to turn these leads into care.
pmc-13251023:
Kim and a large team are the authors of this 2026 Publisher Correction in Genome Biology, attached to their whole-genome study of lung function and COPD. The original paper analyzed sequences from more than forty-four thousand participants of many ancestries. A typesetting error dropped several figure legends from the published version.

The missing legends belonged to figures one, two, three, and five, covering fine-mapping summaries, ancestry comparisons, regional association plots, and the analysis workflow. The correction prints the four legends in full so readers can interpret the figures as intended. The journal confirms that the original article has been corrected. No data, results, or conclusions are altered by this notice.
pmc-13251223:
Xiaoming Shi and colleagues introduce a special journal issue on climate change and infections in this 2026 article. A warming world is shifting where germs spread and how they pass between people, animals, and food, yet turning that evidence into action has lagged.

The editors sum up new findings on climate-sensitive diseases and propose four strategies. They call for stronger health adaptation, fresh and combined control measures, health systems that are both climate-proof and low-carbon, and fairer global governance. Policy makers, researchers, and clinicians must work together, they argue, if the growing disease burden from climate change is to be cut.
pmc-13251823:

pmc-13257623:

pmc-13257823:

pmc-13257923:

pmc-13259323:

pmc-13259423:

pmc-13260523:

pmc-13271423:

pmc-13273023:

pmc-13273123:

pmc-13273223:

pmc-13273523:

pmc-13273623:

pmc-13273923:

pmc-13275123:

pmc-13275523:

pmc-13275723:

pmc-13276223:

pmc-13276523:

pmc-13276723:

pmc-13277823:

The design is a one-time survey, so it shows links rather than proof that the campaign caused the difference.
pmc-13278023:

pmc-13278623:

pmc-13278723:

pmc-13279723:

pmc-13281923:

pmc-13282323:

pmc-13282423:

pmc-13283523:

pmc-13284123:

pmc-13284423:

pmc-13284523:

pmc-13285323:

pmc-13286223:

pmc-13286523:

pmc-13287223:

pmc-13287323:

pmc-13287823:

pmc-13288723:

pmc-13289323:

pmc-13289823:

pmc-13290123:

pmc-13290523:

pmc-13290823:

pmc-13291023:

pmc-13291123:

pmc-13291223:

pmc-13292023:

pmc-13292323:

pmc-13292823:

pmc-13293623:

pmc-13294423:

pmc-13294923:

pmc-13295223:

pmc-13295823:

pmc-13295923:

pmc-13296123:

pmc-13296623:
Hossein Omidian, Erma J. Gill, and Umadevi Kandalam review smart hydrogels for rebuilding craniofacial tissues in a 2026 article. pmc-13297523:
Haitao Xie and colleagues present a search method for assigning computing tasks across fog networks, the local servers that sit between devices and the cloud, in a 2026 paper. pmc-13297823:

pmc-13299323:

pmc-13299823:

pmc-13301323:

pmc-13301723:

pmc-13301823:

pmc-13302523:

pmc-13302623:

pmc-13303723:

pmc-13305523:

pmc-13306223:

pmc-13306723:

pmc-13306823:

pmc-13307023:

pmc-13307423:

pmc-13307523:

pmc-13308723:

pmc-13308823:

pmc-13309023:

pmc-13311323:

pmc-13312023:

pmc-13312823:

pmc-13313223:

pmc-13314323:

pmc-13314423:

pmc-13314923:

pmc-13315023:

pmc-13315523:
