The review tours sample preparation and detection platforms, with liquid chromatography at the center, and weighs where each method strains. A closing section maps clinical uses that better measurement could unlock.
pmc-13397523:
Jessica Berns, Justin L Anderson and Detlev Erdmann reviewed the portal messages sent to one plastic surgeon at Duke University Hospital. Their 2026 study spans 18 months, from July 2023 through December 2024. Secure messaging helps patients stay in touch, but each note adds work, and plastic surgeons also face pressure from public ratings.

Every message was logged by topic, timing and patient details, then stored in a secure REDCap database for study. Patterns in the inbox show what patients most often ask before and after surgery. Spotting the common themes points to clearer handouts and pre-visit guidance, which could trim message load while keeping patients informed and doctors less strained.
pmc-13397823:
Jianqing Li and a large team scan the protein-coding genome for genes that shape the retina and its diseases. Their 2026 study uses whole-exome data from 356,982 UK Biobank participants. The retina is a reachable outpost of the brain, yet the coding variants behind its structure, its function and its blinding diseases were only sketchily known.

Gene-level tests of rare variants found 22 strong links across 16 genes, 12 of them new, with most backed in a second cohort of 245,388 people. Common variant scans added 243 independent signals in 126 genes. Three genes (CFI, C3 and RIOX1) touched structure, function and disease alike, and a new gene, FYB2, was picked for lab follow-up.
pmc-13399323:
Pattara Kanoksing and colleagues genotyped adults with asthma to see which cytokine gene variants track with the disease's inflammatory patterns, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Asthma driven by type 2 inflammation depends heavily on interleukin-4, interleukin-5, and interleukin-13. These proteins drive allergy responses and eosinophil production. Inherited changes in their genes influence asthma, but links to specific patterns needed clarifying.

The study enrolled 125 adults and tested seven variants across the IL33, IL4, IL5, and IL13 genes. One IL5 variant, rs2069812, stood out. Each extra copy of its T version raised eosinophil counts in a dose-like pattern and lowered post-bronchodilator lung function. Carriers faced more than double the prevalence of blood eosinophilia in the reported analysis. An IL13 variant, rs1800925, was tied to higher Th2 cell counts and fixed airflow obstruction. The authors propose both variants as markers for sorting asthma patients into precise treatment groups.
pmc-13399523:
Haein Kim, Seungwon Shin, and Kuo-Cherh Huang analyzed a decade of national insurance claims to show how South Korea's long-term care hospitals have quietly become end-of-life settings, in a 2026 study. The team built three views from claims filed between 2014 and 2023: yearly inpatient trends, profiles of newly admitted patients, and the final trajectories of patients who died.

Deaths involving a long-term care hospital stay climbed from 68,357 in 2014 to 112,157 in 2023. New patients typically arrived in their early eighties, at a median age of 81, and 62.1 percent were women in the admission profile. Those who died had spent a median of 79 days as inpatients, and 68.5 percent of them died inside the hospital itself. The authors call for palliative care and advance planning to be built into these hospitals.
pmc-13400223:
Hidemasa Yoneda and colleagues built a planning method that lets surgeons, without an engineer's help, measure the three-dimensional twist in a child's elbow that healed crooked, in a 2026 methods study. Their framework mirrors the healthy humerus from CT and superimposes the proximal segments. It defines coordinate systems from a centroid plus anatomical landmarks, then computes the deformity three ways: as a wedge osteotomy rotation, as a full 3D rotation, and as a coronal-plane-only correction.

Validation used CT scans from five patients with extra-articular malunion. The full 3D methods barely cared which landmarks were picked: across all twenty-one landmark pairings from seven candidate points, median within-patient ranges stayed below 0.02 degrees for every rotational component. The coronal components matched the simple single-plane method within three degrees in all patients. The authors conclude the method is robust enough for routine surgical decision-making.
pmc-13400423:
Mohammad Iqbal Nouyed and colleagues test, in 2026, how well ChatGPT handles mental health warning signs hidden in skin complaints. People with skin disease often face anxiety or depression, and some beliefs about infestation reflect psychosis. An overly agreeable chatbot might miss danger or even reinforce false beliefs.

The team fed the chatbot 50 short patient stories, section by section, and repeated each run three times. Psychiatrists had judged which stories needed referral. Focusing on 28 clear cases, the chatbot voiced concern in most chats yet advised mental health follow-up in only about half. It almost always advised skin follow-up instead. In some delusional cases it even suggested collecting specimens, which could entrench false beliefs.
pmc-13400523:
Abdulmohsin J Alamoudi reviews, in 2026, plant compounds that may calm overactive NMDA receptors in the brain. These receptors help learning and memory, but overstimulation floods nerve cells with calcium. That excitotoxic process drives damage in stroke, epilepsy, brain injury and degenerative disease.

Compounds from several plant families are surveyed, including vitexin, ginsenosides, quercetin, resveratrol, huperzine A and bilobalide. Studies suggest they can block the receptor directly, target one of its subunits, or lower its production. Many also ease inflammation, oxidative stress and cell death pathways downstream. The author presents these natural products as a rich source for future brain-protective drug design, while noting most evidence is early and experimental.
pmc-13400723:
Ulrich Schreiber, Ivan Bobkov and Marc Nowaczyk report, in 2026, unusual light responses in isolated photosystem II complexes from a heat-loving cyanobacterium. Photosystem II is the water-splitting core of photosynthesis. A new fluorometer let them watch chlorophyll glow changes during ultra-short bright flashes in two ways at once.

Freshly prepared complexes showed exceptionally high fluorescence ratios, near the theoretical ceiling. Regular oscillations with periods of four and two flashes appeared under certain chemical conditions, reflecting the stepwise cycle of the water-splitting machinery. A fast quenching process briefly lowered the glow and relaxed within microseconds. The authors dissect that quenching into donor-side and pigment triplet parts, refining how such signals should be read.
pmc-13400923:
Elizabeth Y X Leong and colleagues report, in 2026, a difficult case of orbital apex syndrome caused by several microbes at once in a woman with a weakened immune system. The syndrome strikes the nerves passing the eye socket tip, threatening vision and eye movement. Causes range from tumors to infection, and fungal disease is easy to miss.

The 70-year-old arrived with one-sided eye pain, headache and an early nerve palsy, then worsened over two weeks to complete eye paralysis and vision loss. Investigation found skull base bone infection reaching the orbital apex and cavernous sinus. Cultures grew four organisms, including a fungus and three bacteria. Six to eight weeks of targeted antimicrobial drugs followed, and the authors stress early imaging and tissue diagnosis.
pmc-13401323:
Ann-Christin Eliasson and a large team of co-authors present a 2026 study protocol called Full Speed Ahead, testing Frame Running plus goal-directed training for young children with cerebral palsy. Frame Running uses a wheeled support frame that lets children with limited walking move fast and train hard.

Early, intensive intervention matters while gross motor skills are developing, but solid evidence for early mobility programmes is still thin. The protocol uses a repeated-measures design with baseline, intervention, and follow-up phases. At least 18 children aged two to five years with cerebral palsy will take part. Outcomes centre on mobility in everyday life and cardiovascular health. The study aims to show whether combining the running frame with goal-directed gross motor practice improves daily activity at this young age.
pmc-13401523:
Seguchi and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether being treated by a board-certified medical oncologist improves survival in metastatic colorectal cancer, using Japan's SCRUM-Japan MONSTAR-SCREEN genomic screening cohort from 2019 to 2022. Among 2,184 patients overall, standard treatment uptake was nearly identical between the two physician groups, at 97.0 and 96.9 percent, setting up a test of what specialist care adds beyond protocol.

In the 358 patients with metastatic colorectal cancer, enrollment by a certified oncologist was associated with median survival of 36.5 months against 30.7 months for the others, a hazard ratio of 0.66 before fuller adjustment. The advantage persisted after adjusting for clinical factors, metastatic burden, and RAS and BRAF mutation status. They used molecular targeted therapy more often, in 89.5 percent of cases versus 80.4 percent for the others. The platform overall has enrolled over 10,000 patients across roughly 29 institutions.
pmc-13401723:
İbrahim Vasi and co-authors measure interleukin-40, a recently identified immune signal made mainly by activated B cells, in systemic sclerosis. B-cell dysfunction is central to this disease, yet this marker's behaviour in it was undefined. Their 2026 study compares blood levels in 41 patients and 29 matched healthy controls.

Levels differed significantly across three groups. Patients receiving immunosuppressive treatment had markedly lower interleukin-40 than both untreated patients and controls, while untreated patients resembled controls. The marker showed no significant link to skin subtype, lung involvement, swallowing problems, or disease activity, and the treatment pattern held regardless of activity status. The authors conclude interleukin-40 reflects treatment exposure and immune modulation rather than how active the disease is, while cautioning that only longitudinal studies can prove cause and effect.
pmc-13402023:
Meihan Guo and David Montero report in 2026 that whether raising the head during sleep boosts red blood cell production remains unknown, despite a plausible theory. More red blood cells raise oxygen delivery and endurance performance, and the authors had proposed that low chest blood volume during head-up sleep might trigger the hormone erythropoietin.

They tested twelve weeks of sleeping with the bed head raised forty centimetres, combined with increased water drinking, against increased drinking alone in healthy adults. Night-time heart rate rose in the early sleep hours for the head-up group, suggesting the intended reflex was engaged. Yet blood volumes, total red cell volume, and haemoglobin mass did not change in either group. Resting stroke volume rose in both groups. The authors conclude the intervention did not enhance red cell production under these conditions, so the question in their title stays open.
pmc-13402723:
Ting Xie and a large team survey the microbes living on tossed cigarette butts in city parks across 35 Chinese cities, treating the litter as a new urban habitat. Butts are everywhere yet barely studied as living space. Sampling butts alongside leaf litter and soil, the team combined long-read gene sequencing, metagenomics, and transcript readings to compare community makeup, function, and evolution across the three homes.

Butt communities proved strikingly uniform across cities, ruled by firm deterministic forces, and rich in Proteobacteria, especially the Pseudomonadaceae family. Their strategy leaned fast and responsive, unlike the slower, resource-gathering style of litter microbes. Genes in butt Pseudomonas showed stronger positive selection, and lab exposure of a model strain switched key functional genes upward. The authors frame butts as a human-made niche actively reshaping microbial life and evolution.
pmc-13402823:
Lin, Wang, Wilson, and Zhang present, in 2026, TraceBind, a computational framework that cleans up transcription factor footprinting from ATAC-seq data. It corrects the cutting bias of the Tn5 enzyme separately for every sample. Footprints, the protected shadows proteins cast in open-chromatin data, drown in false positives because Tn5 prefers certain DNA sequences. The team shows that bias varies between samples, a hidden batch effect.

TraceBind fine-tunes a cleavage model on each sample's mitochondrial DNA reads, then detects footprints across scales with false discovery control. Against the tool TOBIAS, its false positive rate fell by more than 60-fold on average in benchmark comparisons. Sensitivity stayed high against naked DNA controls, matched ChIP-seq and CUT&RUN data, and factor-degradation experiments. The footprints improved transcription factor activity inference and cell age prediction from single-cell data, and many high-confidence footprints escaped DNA foundation models.
pmc-13403023:
Peter O'Reilly and co-authors check whether final-year radiography students judge chest X-ray quality as consistently as experienced radiographers. Repeat exposures cost radiation, so shared quality standards matter. Working from 70 de-identified chest films taken during the COVID-19 pandemic at a Sydney teaching hospital, both groups scored positioning, sharpness, and visibility across pathology types. A consensus read by two radiologists set the reference.

No significant differences separated students from veterans in any domain or disease category. Bland-Altman checks showed students scoring a touch lower with narrow agreement limits, a caution bias rather than real discord. Overall reliability landed at an ICC of 0.90, in the good-to-excellent band. The authors, noting the single-center setting, conclude training already instills the structured criteria well by graduation.
pmc-13403523:
Huairuo Shi and co-authors studied in 2026 what dim blue light at night does to the spleen in mice fed a fatty diet. Light at night is now a common strain on body rhythms and immune health. Male mice lived under dim blue light in their dark phase for 12 weeks.

Their spleens shrank, immune cell growth slowed, and stress hormone levels climbed. Alarm and cell-stress signals in the spleen rose as protective signals fell. Drugs that blocked the stress hormone or its sensor eased part of the change. The work links night light, diet, and immune strain in one model.
pmc-13404623:
Anne J J The heads the Dutch-TIMELINESS project, a 2026 protocol to speed gallbladder surgery after bile duct stone treatment across the Netherlands. National guidance since 2016 advises removing the gallbladder within 72 hours of the duct-clearing procedure called ERCP. In practice, waits often run longer and complications follow.

All 61 Dutch hospitals doing this work take part. First, cases from January to March 2023 set a benchmark for each site. Each hospital then writes its own plan to meet the guideline, guided by its benchmark figures. A final phase from December 2025 to March 2026 checks the new routines with live monitoring. The goal is adherence of 85 percent or higher nationwide.
pmc-13404923:
Haley I Tupper, Yulei Angelina Gao and Amy L Cummings map lung cancer screening in California in a 2026 landscape analysis. Low-dose CT screening lowers deaths, yet California posts some of the lowest uptake in the United States. Gaps fall hardest on racial and ethnic minorities and poorer communities.

Their review of published and grey literature follows scoping review guidance and covers policy, care systems, delivery sites and risk patterns. Lung screening, they find, lacks supports that older programmes for breast, bowel and cervical cancer enjoy, such as firm federal frameworks and quality systems. Safety-net services carrying the highest-risk patients feature throughout. The report aims to show officials where investment could close the equity gap.
pmc-13405623:
Isabelle G Henshall and colleagues remove a major surface protein from the malaria parasite to test its true role, in 2026 work. PfMSP2 coats Plasmodium falciparum merozoites, the forms that invade red blood cells, and vaccine makers have long targeted it. Its actual job in invasion was unproven.

Gene editing deleted the protein from two parasite lines with no loss of growth or invasion ability in the lab. Surprisingly, antibodies against other invasion proteins then worked better, hitting their targets more strongly. Adding purified PfMSP2 blocked antibody binding to PfAMA1 in a dose-related way. The authors suggest the abundant protein shields the parasite from immune attack rather than driving invasion.
pmc-13406623:
Maria Kirillova and a large team expose rats to repeated low oxygen and examine their colons, in a 2026 study. Animals differ in natural tolerance to oxygen shortage, judged by three hypoxia genes in blood cells. Whether that tolerance shapes gut barrier and microbe changes was the question.

Rats breathed thin air equivalent to 5,000 or 7,000 metres altitude for one hour daily over twenty-one days. Under normal air, oxygen-sensitive rats already carried more mucus-producing goblet cells and fewer Parabacteroides bacteria. Exposure then pushed the colon and microbiome in different directions depending on starting tolerance and dose. Tissue staining and genetic microbe checks supply the evidence.
pmc-13407823:
Garrett R. Jackson and co-authors review, in 2026, using a camera probe inside the shoulder to investigate pain after shoulder replacement surgery. Pain, stiffness, or suspected infection after joint replacement is a hard problem. Keyhole inspection offers a low-invasive way to look and sometimes to treat. It applies across total, reverse, and partial replacements.

Reported uses span loose socket components, worn plastic, rotator cuff and biceps problems, stiffness, impingement, and suspected joint infection. Outcomes suggest relief for selected patients, especially after socket removal, biceps procedures, and releases of scar tissue. Tissue samples taken through the scope beat needle aspiration and blood markers for diagnosing infection. The authors detail entry strategies that protect the implant, while noting the scope cannot replace revision when failure is clear-cut.
pmc-13408123:
Dimitra Kanopoulou and co-authors review, in 2026, modern therapy for balance in children with Down syndrome, whose muscle, sensory, and nerve differences undermine postural control and everyday mobility. Searching two sources for randomised trials from 2015 to 2025, the team gathered fourteen trials with 462 patients testing everything from trampoline jumping to horse riding.

Options spanned isokinetic training, Pilates, dual-task exercise, whole-body vibration, foot strengthening, swimming, taping, and vestibular stimulation. Balance outcomes improved across a broad range of them, especially when layered onto standard therapy. Study quality ran fair to high. The authors back technology-assisted, task-oriented practice while demanding larger, longer, higher-quality trials before firm prescriptions, since follow-up in the current literature is short.
pmc-13409323:
Edward Lau and colleagues link Australian census and prescription records in 2026. They ask how often the other medicines an older person with dementia takes collide with a newly started antipsychotic, and what that costs. Over nine thousand people aged sixty-five and over who began one of five common antipsychotics were followed for ninety days. Interaction checking used a standard commercial database and counted severity and mechanism.

Three quarters of patients were exposed to at least one interaction, and nearly all of those were classed major in severity, most often involving other nervous-system drugs. One or more interactions came with a forty-three percent higher risk of death within ninety days. Two or more pushed the increase to about eighty percent. The authors argue interaction screening deserves the same seriousness as the decision to prescribe the antipsychotic itself.
pmc-13409823:
Rita Rocío Márquez-Díaz and colleagues present in 2026 a new scale that measures how caregivers feel about baby-led weaning. In that feeding style, babies feed themselves soft family foods instead of taking purées from a spoon. No checked tool existed for these views, so the team built one and tested it with Spanish caregivers.

Building the scale used past studies, expert review, and trial runs with caregivers. A group of 256 caregivers then completed the final version, while 92 more repeated it later to check stability. The 16 items fell into three groups: openness to the method, confidence in feeding, and hands-on skills. Scores held up well across checks of consistency and repeat testing.
pmc-13410923:
Yassir Lekbach and colleagues traced in 2026 how a signal protein, CXCL14, rallies immune defenders against genital herpes. The paper compares immune cells from women with and without symptoms, tests human vaginal lining cells, and follows mice lacking the signal after vaginal infection with herpes simplex virus type 2.

Mice without CXCL14 suffered worse sores, higher virus levels, and lower survival, while their recruitment of killer cells and memory T cells fell short. The paper points to CXCL14 as a possible lever for vaccines or treatments that strengthen local defense where herpes first takes hold.
pmc-13411023:
Eunhye Kim, Jae Hun Choi, Dae Soo Jung, and Yun Chan Kang report in 2026 a three-dimensional host that tames lithium metal in batteries. Lithium metal stores huge energy, yet it grows needle-like spikes and swells during charging, which ruins cells. A porous host can spread the metal out evenly.

Their host mixes carbon nanotubes, soft carbon, and evenly scattered silica, made by spray heating then baking. The blend conducts well and welcomes lithium, so deposits formed smoothly without spikes. A protective skin rich in a helpful lithium compound also formed. Test cells ran over 1,300 hours with steady voltage, and full cells paired with a common cathode kept capacity well across 600 cycles.
pmc-13411223:
Apolline Blazer and a large team set out in 2026 a study plan for judging a program that helps breast cancer survivors return to work. Treatment leaves many women facing barriers from fatigue to inflexible jobs. The FASTRACS program aims to ease and sustain that return, and realism asks what works, for whom, and under which conditions.

Interviews will trace the paths of women in the program plus key people around their return. Focus groups with the professionals delivering it will probe workplace practice. Findings will be woven with trial numbers across five domains, from personal situation to how tools were used. Funding arrived in 2022, with final analyses due by the end of 2026.
pmc-13411323:
Jaqueline Martins Ramos and colleagues watch in 2026 nurses at work in women's health visits in Brazil, hunting for prevention skills in action. Sixty-nine taped visits by 22 nurses in four towns were scored for moves that promote health and ward off disease.

Birth control was offered in about three in ten visits, while advice on infections passed through sex appeared in under three percent. Screening followed set rules in nearly half the visits, and lifestyle advice in about a quarter. No steps to prevent later harm appeared at all, and no printed handouts were used. Better training and stronger backup are the fixes proposed, since nurses cannot carry prevention on goodwill alone.
pmc-13412023:
Macarena González-Dossi and colleagues confirm in 2026 that a parasitoid wasp, Campsomeriella whitelyi, lives farther south in Chile than records previously showed. Scoliid wasps hunt soil-dwelling beetle larvae, which makes them useful allies against farm pests. Earlier Chilean sightings of this species rested on mistaken identifications, so the team rechecked specimens by detailed body features and modelled where the climate and land suit it.

Confirmed records now place the wasp in the semi-arid farming landscapes of north-central Chile, among irrigated crops and sandy soils. The authors argue that careful name-checking, paired with habitat modelling, sharpens biodiversity maps. Verified presence also supports counting this native wasp in sustainable pest management plans.
pmc-13412123:
Chengqi Yu and colleagues report a 2026 case where emergency radiation bridged a critically ill woman toward chemotherapy for a rare heart lymphoma. The 66-year-old arrived with heart failure and a lung clot, and a large tumor in the right atrium ruled out first-line chemotherapy at the outset.

After five of ten radiation sessions her breathlessness and swelling eased, oxygen levels rose from 86 to 95 percent, and follow-up scans showed a deep metabolic response. The case gives heart and cancer teams a precedent for using radiation as a bridge when a patient is too ill for standard drugs.
pmc-13412323:
Ariel Zylberberg and colleagues reanalyze food-choice experiments in 2026 to test whether attention shapes decisions while they form, or merely mirrors them afterwards. Popular models claim looking at an item multiplies its value during choosing, which makes two testable predictions about final fixations and conflicted choices. The team checked those predictions against several existing eye-tracking datasets from snack choice tasks.

Neither prediction held up in the data they re-examined. A rival account, in which gaze patterns largely reflect a choice already made, explained the last-fixation bias, the gaze cascade, and how overall value speeds responses. One link between looking time and choice still escaped that account, so the authors conclude both processes probably run together.
pmc-13414423:
Luca Galassi and co-authors review in 2026 how to stop plaque squeezing through carotid stent struts during stenting, a mechanism behind strokes around the procedure. This prolapse pushes soft atherosclerotic material into the bloodstream exactly where filters may miss it. Drawing on registries, comparative cohorts, and vessel-wall imaging studies, the narrative review maps what drives prolapse risk: plaque character, procedural choices, and above all the stent's design.

Dual-layer micromesh stents emerge as the most advanced defence in their synthesis. Combined with embolic protection, pooled data put thirty-day stroke near 1.4 percent for that technology. Optical imaging confirms less prolapse than single-layer designs show. The authors ask for shared imaging definitions and properly powered randomized trials with hard endpoints.
pmc-13414723:
Pengxuan Zhao and co-authors build a nanoparticle aimed at glioblastoma, the most aggressive common brain tumor, in a 2026 study. Their lipid particle wears a coat made from glioblastoma cell membrane, which helps it home to similar tumor cells. Inside sit gene editing tools and a messenger RNA piece.

The editing tools switch off IDO1, an enzyme that helps tumors suppress immune attack through tryptophan breakdown. The RNA piece produces part of gasdermin B, which can burst tumor cells in a fiery death called pyroptosis. Together the two actions stirred strong antitumor immunity in their system. The design offers a fresh route for brain tumor immunotherapy.
pmc-13415823:
Saja A. Althobaiti and colleagues prove a test that finds traces of the antibiotic cefixime left on lab glass, in 2026. This drug can cause strong allergy, so labs must prove their wash works. Their method splits cefixime from its close kin on a packed tube with a mild mix of acetate and alcohol.

A set light beam read the drug at low levels fit for glass checks. Spiked tests showed the method finds what a plain wash leaves. Soap traces hide from the beam, so the team read rinse water by its charge flow too. The pair of checks is green and fits rule based lab work.
pmc-13416623:
Seonyeong Park, Gangwon Jeong, Umberto Villa, and Mark A. Anastasio build a virtual imaging testbed for optoacoustic breast tomography, in 2026. This imaging method pulses light into tissue and listens to the resulting sound waves, revealing blood rich tumors. Virtual trials are cheaper than building prototype scanners for every design idea.

Their framework extends computer generated breast phantoms with varied skin tones and both benign and malignant lesions. Full simulation includes the sound detectors' spatial and electrical responses. A case study compares two scanner designs end to end. Over one thousand phantoms with matching measurement data were released publicly for other researchers.
pmc-13417023:
Xue Ting Tan and colleagues pool world data on thrush infections in people living with HIV, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Candida yeast can infect the mouth, throat, and food pipe when immunity falls. Fifteen studies fed the pooled estimates for how common these infections are and what raises the risk.

Across studies, about 39 percent of patients had one of these infections, though rates varied greatly. Risk ran higher in men, in people with very low CD4 cell counts, and in those not on strong antiretroviral therapy. Early spotting of these groups could cut illness, the authors argue, alongside steady HIV treatment.
pmc-13417723:
Strickland and colleagues built in 2026 a pigskin model to test treatments for eyelid margin disease called blepharitis. The team grew mature biofilms of a common skin germ on intact pigskin pieces kept outside the body. Biofilms are sticky germ layers that resist treatment, and samples were treated for a day before counting live bacteria.

Plain salt solution left the most bacteria after treatment. Two standard clinical treatments, povidone iodine and hypochlorous acid, cut bacteria counts clearly but left many germs alive. An antibiotic, gentamicin, did no better than the salt solution in this model. A prototype mix of natural antimicrobials plus a biofilm breaker cut bacteria to undetectable levels, beating every other treatment. The authors say the model lets teams screen eye treatments before human use.
pmc-13419323:
Xiaolan Zhao and co-workers traced an epigenetic chain in 2026 that drives placental cell death in preeclampsia, a risky high-blood-pressure disorder of expecting mothers. Using a mouse model and stressed placental cells, the team traced a gene-tagging enzyme, SETD7, through a long RNA to a transcription factor and a cell-death switch.

High SETD7 raised a histone mark on the XIST gene, whose RNA broke down FOXA1 signals, cutting a protective protein and igniting inflammasome-driven cell death. Silencing SETD7 eased disease signs. The paper names SETD7 as a treatment target for protecting the placenta in preeclampsia.
pmc-13419623:
Kurdi and colleagues track prescribing of psychotropic medicines in United Kingdom primary care through the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 national interrupted time-series analysis. The team used national dispensing data from March 2019 to March 2023 across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. Four medicine classes were followed monthly: antidepressants, anxiety and sleeping medicines, antipsychotics, and antidementia drugs, measured per head of population and tested against the two national lockdowns.

Antidepressant use rose by 24.6 percent across the UK over the period, the largest rise among the classes studied. Antipsychotics rose by 2.7 percent, while anxiety and sleeping medicines diverged by nation, climbing 7.3 percent in Scotland yet falling 9.5 percent in Wales across the same years. Time-series analysis showed most change was gradual rather than a jump at lockdowns. Kurdi concludes prescribing growth mostly continued pre-existing trends instead of reacting directly to restrictions.
pmc-13420123:
Kevin Chung and colleagues validated a simpler PET method in 2026 for measuring blood-brain barrier leakiness and brain blood flow with a single tracer. Standard methods need a second flow tracer, adding complexity and burden, so the team used fast one-second frames and kinetic modeling of fluorodeoxyglucose scans in 18 volunteers.

Single-tracer permeability estimates differed from dual-tracer values by only 3.7 percent on average, with blood-flow estimates agreeing strongly between tracers. Researchers gain a leaner protocol for studying barrier transport across brain disorders without a dedicated flow scan in routine practice.
pmc-13420923:
Morton and colleagues build the first questionnaire that measures how chronic pain affects people at work, in their own terms. Pain's work costs were known by anecdote but no tool captured their range. Their 2026 study runs in stages. Focus groups with fifty workers and stakeholders name the domains that matter. Expert panels refine questions through two Delphi rounds. Then 919 people complete it, while nine think aloud to check the wording makes sense.

Factor analysis sorted the questions into three scales. They cover wider life impacts of working in pain, day to day impacts, and the job supports that help people stay working. The scales hung together well and repeated scores weeks apart stayed steady, with test retest values in the strong range. The WORC-PAIN tool, the authors argue, gives employers and clinicians a measure for judging which adjustments help workers in pain keep their jobs and health.
pmc-13421223:
Majewska and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how common pain drugs affect plants and algae in waterways. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs, are among the most detected drug pollutants in rivers and lakes. The review gathers experimental studies from 2020 to 2025, a period of higher contamination than earlier reviews covered.

Across studies, NSAIDs damaged photosynthesis, the process plants use to make food from light. They harmed chloroplasts, the green structures where photosynthesis runs, and disturbed cell breathing and energy output. Exposure triggered oxidative stress, with excess reactive oxygen and damage to cell fats. Growth, root shape, mineral balance, and the making of secondary compounds also shifted in many species. The authors argue these results give a more realistic picture of ecological risk under current pollution.
pmc-13421423:
Humberto Guanche Garcell leads a twelve-author team reviewing, in a 2026 study from Qatar, infections after tummy-tuck surgery at The Cuban Hospital. Abdominoplasty counts as clean elective surgery, yet wound infection remains a real risk that grows with combined procedures and patient factors.

Records covered 323 operations between January 2022 and July 2025. Patients averaged about forty years old, most were women, and roughly one in seven had diabetes. Seventeen infections gave an overall rate of 5.3 percent, with the highest share in 2025. Combined operations, such as tummy tuck plus liposuction, carried roughly double the infection rate of simple ones. The study also audited preventive antibiotic practice, consumption and costs.
pmc-13421523:
Zhiyun Wang and seven colleagues show, in a 2026 study, that PVC microplastics help the bacteria behind urinary tract infections do more damage. Plastic particles under five millimetres reach many body sites, and PVC is a special concern because patients meet it directly through medical materials.

The particles collected uropathogenic E. coli on their surfaces and ferried the bacteria into bladder cells by an unusual route, worsening both acute and chronic infection in mice. Inside bladder cells, the plastic disturbed mitochondria, triggering a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis that sheds the bladder lining and shelters chronic infection. The authors frame microplastics as active mediators of infection rather than passive dirt.
pmc-13421823:
Yongfu Liang, Xiaomei Deng, Meixia Chen and Xun Zhang pool the head-to-head trial evidence, in a 2026 meta-analysis, between two injected eye drugs for swelling of the retina after a vein blockage. Ranibizumab and bevacizumab both block a growth signal that leaks fluid into the macula, yet direct randomised comparisons were few and small.

Four trials with 759 participants met their criteria. At six months the two drugs differed by less than a letter on standard vision charts, with a confidence range spanning small effects either way. Retinal thickness changes and the share of eyes gaining fifteen letters were likewise comparable. Side-effect profiles looked broadly similar, though rare whole-body events were too few to judge. The authors rate certainty moderate for vision outcomes.
pmc-13422923:
Malou Crasborn leads a large Dutch team asking, in a 2026 qualitative study, how doctors experience two ways of consulting across the primary-secondary care divide. One way is written teleconsultations, answered in the gaps of the day. The other is live joint consultations. Both are meant to keep patients with their own GP while borrowing specialist brains.

Thirty-seven professionals — fourteen GPs and twenty-three specialists — were interviewed in an urban region. Teleconsultations were prized for quality, speed, flexibility and better access. Four theme areas organised the findings: the intervention itself, professional collaboration, the imagined patient view, and what lasting implementation requires. The authors map the barriers and facilitators to guide services weighing the same redesign.
pmc-13424023:
Muhanned Faisal Towfig and six colleagues systematically review what predicts the return of atrial fibrillation after catheter ablation, a procedure that burns or freezes faulty heart tissue to restore rhythm. Recurrence is common and varies widely between patients, so dependable predictors would sharpen follow-up planning.

Following standard review guidance, the team searched five sources for studies from 2016 to 2026 and screened thousands of records down to 21 studies with multivariable models. Recurring predictors included older age, the persistent form of the rhythm disorder, a larger left atrium, and higher pressure inside it. Because studies differed too much to pool, findings were combined narratively, with bias and certainty graded formally.
pmc-13424123:
Wu and colleagues release a long-run crop calendar in this 2026 dataset paper, mapping when maize passes eight key growth stages across Northeast China, one of the world's great corn belts. Knowing stages from emergence to maturity at field scale guides fertilizer timing, irrigation, pest control, and yield forecasts, but existing products cover few stages.

The dataset spans 2001 to 2024 at 500-meter spatial resolution with daily time steps, built by coupling satellite vegetation data with weather drivers in a gradient-boosted model. Validation against records from 91 agrometeorological stations for 2009 to 2024 gave timing errors under five days on average, with agreement scores above 0.63 for every stage in the reported checks. The maps preserve sensible regional gradients and year-to-year wobbles, offering a benchmark for crop model calibration and climate impact studies.
pmc-13424323:
Qingpeng Han and five colleagues assess nineteen heavily fished species in China's Bohai Sea using five assessment methods designed for data-poor fisheries. The Bohai fleet, like small-scale fleets worldwide, lacks the long catch records that standard models need, so the team leaned on fish length data instead and graded each stock's condition.

Five stocks, 26%, rated sustainable with no risk. Seven more, 37%, were acceptable but need targeted management, while the rest need stronger action: 16% are overfished and 21% face high risk. Advice is matched to status, from effort and quota control to larger minimum landing sizes and wider net mesh. The authors argue such graded management can rebuild stocks, as seen elsewhere.
pmc-13424423:
Naoki Yago, Masami Saito, and Hiroki Yago report a refined flap operation for severe anal stenosis, including the Whitehead deformity, where scarring leaves the opening too narrow. Their method, developed with plastic surgeons, moves nearby skin inward on a deep fat pedicle whose pivot point is shifted toward the midline, letting the flap advance without twisting or tension.

Fifty-two consecutive patients treated between 2021 and 2025, median age sixty-seven, mostly had scarring from earlier surgery or chronic fissure. Of forty-nine who completed six months of follow-up, 48 passed the success test, a dilator of at least 22 millimetres. No flap died. Wound splitting in nine patients healed without surgery within about four weeks.
pmc-13424523:
Lurquin and colleagues examine in 2026 whether ABO blood group changes the risk of microangiopathy, damage to the smallest blood vessels, in type 2 diabetes. Blood group was already known to shift the risk of large-vessel disease.

The single-center study covered 1,006 patients with type 2 diabetes, just over half of whom had some microvascular complication. Patients outside blood group O showed lower insulin sensitivity and weaker beta-cell function, along with higher long-term blood sugar exposure. Overall microvascular damage ran about a quarter higher in non-O patients, and nerve damage showed an even larger gap. After accounting for diabetes duration, blood sugar, smoking, cholesterol remnants, and blood pressure, group A patients still carried clearly higher odds of microvascular damage. The comparison was against group O patients.
pmc-13424623:
Rangxi Jin and seven colleagues test whether training the trunk on unstable surfaces sharpens elite air pistol shooting more than the same training on firm ground. Twenty national-level shooters were randomised for eight weeks. Half used unstable tools such as Swiss balls and balance discs; half trained on stable surfaces. Pressure plates and a laser system measured body sway and gun steadiness in the final second before each shot.

The unstable group improved more on nearly every measure. Sway area shrank by about 11% against about 2%, and scores rose about twice as fast. Steadiness inside the top scoring ring jumped sharply. After strict correction for multiple testing, only the finest stability measure and muzzle control stayed significant, so the authors label the rest exploratory.
pmc-13424723:
Hu and a large team studied two diabetes-linked genes, MYT1 and ST18, that act as gene regulators in human insulin-producing beta cells, asking how they protect those cells from failure. They silenced each gene in donated human islet cells, then measured survival, insulin release, and gene activity in culture and in mice under obesity-related stress.

Silencing MYT1 killed beta cells outright, while silencing ST18 weakened glucose-stimulated insulin secretion by reducing calcium entry into the cells. Under obesity stress in transplanted tissue, ST18 silencing also caused cell death, showing the two regulators back each other up differently. Each gene controlled distinct stress, mitochondria, and ion-channel gene sets in the expression data. Genes regulated by either factor were enriched 2.05-fold for type 2 diabetes risk locations, tying the pair directly to inherited disease susceptibility.
pmc-13425023:
Hörold and colleagues present a protocol for building a survivorship care program. It serves people living with metastatic melanoma, who report unmet needs even as modern treatments extend life. The LeMela project follows the UK Medical Research Council framework and an intervention mapping approach. It builds the program with patients rather than for them.

Phase A combines a scoping review of existing evidence with interviews and focus groups. Those involve survivors, relatives, and health workers. Partners including physicians, psycho-oncologists, nurses, epidemiologists, and health services researchers then merge their knowledge. They use a joint process to shape a theory-based program. Phase B will test whether the program can work, through a pilot study with structure and process review. That will guide whether a full randomized trial is warranted. The project and its short protocol were both pre-registered on the Open Science Framework.
pmc-13426023:
Ross and colleagues bred 55 inbred lines of the dengue mosquito Aedes aegypti in 2026 to test how inbreeding affects fitness and the bacterial community the insects carry. Inbreeding shrinks genetic variety and can sap vigor, which matters for mosquito control programs that rear and release insects. Whether it also reshapes the microbes inside the mosquito was unclear.

Lines were raised from two founding populations and scored for life traits, genetic diversity, and gut bacteria. Fitness costs varied widely: many lines suffered badly, while others held up despite equally low diversity. Bacterial mixes differed a lot between lines but did not track fitness or origin. The authors conclude inbreeding harms fitness unevenly while leaving the microbiome largely to other forces.
pmc-13426123:
Jeongeun Choi and colleagues used a national South Korean survey to study how confidence with digital tools shapes satisfaction with digital change. The survey covered 4,155 adults aged 40 and over, split into middle-aged and older groups.

Older adults reported lower digital confidence, weaker social ties, and less satisfaction than the middle-aged group. Confidence in one's digital skills linked to higher satisfaction in both groups, and the link ran stronger for people with few social ties. Schooling and digital skill also lifted satisfaction, while income mattered only for the middle-aged. Choi urges training that builds digital confidence, above all for older adults with small social networks.
pmc-13427723:
Zhao and colleagues built in 2026 a game-theory model of how attackers and defenders adapt to each other on a network, and how that contest decides whether the network survives disruption. Modern systems are so interlinked that one local failure can cascade, and many failures come from opponents reacting to each other, not from chance. Static defense plans miss that back-and-forth.

In the model, both sides revise their strategies round by round based on past payoffs. The outcome turns on network shape: on uneven networks, where a few hubs hold many links, attackers gain the upper hand, while on even networks defenders prevail. The best attack strategies settled at the network's percolation threshold, the tipping point where it falls apart, across artificial and real networks. The authors argue topology, not just effort, governs resilience.
pmc-13428023:
Kgokolo and colleagues reported in 2026 a patient with pemphigus vulgaris, a blistering disease where the immune system attacks the glue between skin cells, whose mouth sores refused standard care. Skin lesions and mouth lesions do not always answer treatment alike. In this case, high-dose steroids cleared the skin, but the mouth disease stayed stubborn.

The turning point was rituximab, an antibody drug that wipes out B cells, the white cells that make the harmful antibodies. After rituximab, the mouth disease finally entered remission. The authors set the case against trial evidence in which most rituximab patients reached full remission off treatment, far more than on steroids alone. They stress tailoring therapy by site, and note a second gain: rituximab spares patients long steroid exposure and its damage to bones, metabolism, and mood.
pmc-13428123:
Barnes and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how giant cell arteritis affects quality of life, how steroid treatment adds to the burden, and how patient-reported measures capture it. The disease inflames large arteries, mostly in women over fifty, and can blind if missed. High-dose steroids control it but add weight, mood, and bone problems of their own.

General health surveys used in trials have shown gains from newer drugs. Symptom scales reveal that about half of patients suffer anxiety and a third depression. Disease-specific and steroid-specific questionnaires have now been validated so patients can describe impact in their own terms, which the authors say improves shared decision making in clinic. Digital versions promise faster triage, but they risk shutting out older patients with low digital access.
pmc-13429023:
Cate V. Cheney and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, an overlooked link between gut microbes and the most common childhood blood cancer. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia now sees survival above 90 percent in children, yet its harsh treatment leaves lasting harm. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids, small molecules that feed gut lining cells and tune immunity. Evidence in other cancers ties these molecules to treatment response and side effects.

Direct evidence in this leukemia remains sparse, which the authors state plainly. They assemble plausible routes from related fields: the molecules might blunt treatment toxicity, shape immune recovery, and even touch early-life factors tied to leukemia risk. Their aim is to provoke targeted experiments and clinical studies. Supportive care that spares children late effects is the prize motivating the agenda.
pmc-13429123:
Camille Bosc and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, three artificial lens designs that share the same springy double-loop frame. These toric lenses, implanted at cataract surgery, correct astigmatism, the uneven focusing caused by a misshapen eye front. Sixty-nine eyes received one of three optic designs built on the shared frame, with 23 eyes in each group. Vision, refraction, and lens rotation were checked three months after surgery.

Sharp distance vision was excellent across all three designs, and every lens stayed within ten degrees of its intended angle. One design put every eye within a tight half-diopter of the target refraction. Another gave the finest corrected acuity on average, a small but measured edge. Rotation stayed near one to two degrees in all groups. Surgeons choosing among optic styles on this frame can expect steady positioning either way.
pmc-13429223:
Dilşat Tepe and co-authors review, in a 2026 study, a stubborn breast inflammation and the germ increasingly tied to it. Granulomatous mastitis causes painful breast lumps and abscesses that mimic cancer and resist simple treatment. Records covered 165 women treated at a university hospital between 2018 and 2023. The team compared patients whose samples grew Corynebacterium bacteria with those whose did not.

The germ appeared in about 15 percent of cases, most often the species kroppenstedtii, which hides inside fatty tissue. Positive cases formed more abscesses and needed more procedures. Combined treatment with steroids, antibiotics, and sometimes surgery gave the best outcomes overall. Fat-loving antibiotics paired with steroids looked helpful, though the edge fell short of statistical proof. About 16 percent of patients relapsed, especially those whose symptoms had dragged on before treatment.
pmc-13429523:
Doua Elamin and colleagues examine, in a 2026 database study, the rare practice of removing part of the stomach and transplanting a kidney in one operation. Obesity blocks many kidney failure patients from transplant lists, and sleeve gastrectomy can restore eligibility. Doing both at once is tempting but risky. A national bariatric surgery database from 2020 to 2023 held over 580,000 sleeve operations, of which only 22 included a simultaneous kidney transplant.

Those 22 patients were older, more often male, and far sicker at baseline, with more diabetes, high blood pressure, and dialysis dependence. Their operations ran longer and their hospital stays stretched further. Serious complications and readmissions ran higher, and about 9 percent died within thirty days, against about a tenth of a percent for sleeve surgery alone. Adjusted analysis kept the combined operation as the strongest predictor of harm. The authors urge extreme care in selection.
pmc-13429923:
Wenqian Ren, Jing Liang, and Xu Peng warn, in a 2026 study, that China's electric vehicle boom can backfire at the power plant. Electric cars cut street-level emissions, yet charging draws on a grid still dominated by coal. Panel data covered Chinese regions from 2017 to 2022. Statistical methods designed to separate cause from correlation linked vehicle sales growth to power sector emissions.

A 10 percent rise in electric vehicle sales came with about a 0.4 percent rise in power plant carbon emissions. The effect also spilled across plant networks, with plants influencing one another regionally. Scenario modeling showed the picture flips when renewable growth keeps pace with electrified transport. Paired together, clean power and electric driving deliver the deep cuts each promises alone. The authors argue for sequencing the two transitions as one policy, not two.
pmc-13430023:
Qin Wang leads a large team that pins, in a 2026 study, a new inherited brain disorder on faults in a chromatin-shaping gene. Chromatin remodelers open and close DNA to time gene activity, and their failure often disrupts brain development. The gene DMAP1 helps run several of those processes yet had no linked human disease. The team gathered 20 affected people from 16 families, each carrying two damaged copies of the gene.

Fruit flies with the matching gene silenced in the brain died early or showed shrunken learning centers, stunted nerve branches, odd social behavior, and seizures. Adding back the healthy human gene mostly rescued the flies, while patient versions rescued weakly or not at all. Two downstream genes emerged whose boost repaired the damage. A chemical fingerprint on DNA then identified one more patient. Genetic testing panels for developmental disorders gain a new entry.
pmc-13430323:
Chon and colleagues tested whether a liver MRI measure called iron-corrected T1, which reflects liver inflammation and scarring combined, also predicts cancers outside the liver in the general population. They followed 24,003 cancer-free UK Biobank participants with liver imaging and complete data over a median of 4.28 years during the study.

During follow-up, 1,144 participants developed an extrahepatic malignancy, meaning a cancer arising outside the liver itself. Each standard deviation rise in the MRI measure carried a hazard ratio of 1.116 for future cancer after adjustment for demographic, metabolic, and liver factors. People above the 771 millisecond cutoff showed a cumulative incidence of 6.1 percent, versus 4.6 percent below it in the cohort. Older age and male sex also predicted risk, while liver fat fraction pointed the opposite way, leading the authors to suggest the marker captures systemic processes.
pmc-13430523:
Li and colleagues isolated in 2026 three rare sugar-bearing indole compounds from a microbe that lives inside sugarcane. The new finds also corrected the known structure of a relative. The microbe is an actinomycete, a thread-like bacterium prized for new chemistry. Its products carry a cyano group seldom seen in this family.

Two of the compounds, named sugarnitriles A and B, had never been described before. The team worked out their flat structures with mass measurements and magnetic resonance spectra, then pinned down the shape of their sugar parts by comparing signal patterns and light-twisting readings. Those data forced a revision of the structure long assigned to the known relative, SF-2140, in the older literature. Two of the three compounds showed modest to weak power against E. coli in lab tests.
pmc-13430823:
Brice Even and colleagues argue that weight-loss drugs may push big food firms toward poorer countries. GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound are spreading fast in rich countries, with clear effects on shopping and eating.

Early United States household data show grocery spending falling about 5 percent within six months of a household member starting a GLP-1 drug. Falls ran bigger for richer households, and bigger still for snacks and energy-dense foods. Firms already sell smaller packs and GLP-1-friendly brands. The paper warns that if rich-world demand for ultra-processed food softens, firms may hedge by marketing harder where regulation is weaker.
pmc-13432523:
Santi Nolasco, Jaime Bernaola, and Parameswaran Nair asked a pointed question in 2026. Could starting targeted biologic drugs early in asthma lift the odds of full calm, or does the hope run ahead of proof? Such drugs aim at key sparks of one asthma type. Calm, by agreed marks, blends quiet symptoms, steady lung tests, and no flare-ups or daily steroid pills.

Across drug kinds, calm stalls at a fifth to two fifths of patients. Wider tests to pick the right drug may push the share higher. Long disease runs cut the odds of calm, since harm and side faults pile up over years. The authors press on weak spots in the early-start case. Calm on the surface may not mean the deep disease has cleared. Mild asthma may never march toward severe forms at all.
pmc-13433823:
McGregor and colleagues build a statistical model for a stubborn problem in microbiome science: samples never catch every species, so diversity counts come out low. Diversity sums up how many species live in a sample and how evenly they share it. Their 2026 paper uses a hierarchical Pitman-Yor process, a flexible probability model. The model can guess the unseen tail of rare species. The team fits it across several populations at once with a sampling algorithm.

Simulations show the fitting method works. Diversity estimates from the fitted model beat naive counts that use only what was seen. The gain is biggest when samples are small, exactly where naive counts fail worst. The team derives a formula for Hill numbers, the family of diversity measures, inside the model. An infant gut dataset shows the method in action. Ecologists gain a way to compare diversity without pretending the sample saw everything.
pmc-13434223:
Jiao Liu and colleagues map in 2026 how a germ builds and exports Psl, a sugar coat that helps it form sticky films on surfaces. The germ is Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common cause of hard to treat lung illness. The sugar coat moves out through a guarded path that spans the cell wall.

Cryo electron images of two linked proteins show a sealed channel from inside to outside the cell. A third protein likely sits in the channel and links sugar units one by one. Side ports may feed new units in while the chain grows. The model may fit many germs that use the same export route.
pmc-13434423:
Xiaocui Li and a large team settle a puzzle about flaws in perovskite crystals in 2026. These crystals bend at room heat in a way that should need free sliding flaws. Older images showed stuck flaws instead, which clashed with the bendy behavior. A pulsed electron beam let the team view crystals with less beam harm.

With pulses, the true flaws show the free sliding split form that models predict. Steady beams push flaws into the stuck form, and the end shape depends on which atoms line the flaw core. The fix in method matters for any soft crystal study. Device makers gain a truer picture of how these crystals deform.
pmc-13434623:
Hossain and a collaboration report a charge density wave inside a material that should not host one. A charge density wave is a ripple in electron density that repeats. The material, alpha-Bi4Br4, is a band insulator with no Fermi surface. A Fermi surface is the usual breeding ground for such waves. Low-temperature topographic and spectroscopic imaging showed the state in the bulk and at the surface.

The one-way charge pattern appears below 40 kelvin. It breaks the crystal's translational symmetry across regions. It opens an energy gap on top of the compound's existing insulating gap. That deepens the behavior at low temperature. Transport tests showed nonlinear current flow. That sliding behavior is usually tied to incommensurate charge density waves in metals. The authors present this as a charge density wave of a different type. It forces a rethink of where electron states like these can arise.
pmc-13435423:
Büşra Karadağ's team compared eye scans in 2026 among people with early to mid glaucoma, people with high eye pressure but no glaucoma, and healthy controls. Using OCT angiography, they measured macular ganglion cell thickness and small-vessel density near the center of vision in 150 eyes from glaucoma and high-pressure patients plus 50 healthy eyes. Scans were taken at a glaucoma unit in Istanbul over two months in 2022.

High-pressure eyes looked much like healthy eyes on both measures, while glaucoma eyes showed clear drops that grew with disease stage. Vessel loss hit surface layers harder than deep layers, and in early glaucoma, cell layer thinning stood out more than vessel loss. Eye doctors get a staged picture of which retinal change leads, useful for tracking early disease.
pmc-13435523:
André Pereira's team surveyed flea-borne pathogens in Portugal in 2026, screening 1,261 fleas from dogs and cats across the mainland. Fleas plague pets and can carry germs that sicken animals and people, yet nationwide pathogen data were thin. Lab tests targeted Bartonella, Rickettsia, and the tapeworm Dipylidium, with positive samples sequenced and linked to host, flea species, lifestyle, and region.

About a quarter of fleas carried at least one pathogen. Rickettsia appeared in about sixteen percent and Bartonella in about eight percent, the latter more common in fleas from cats, especially strays and shelter animals. Three Bartonella species were named. Vets and public health workers get a national baseline for flea control and for watching spillover risk from pets.
pmc-13435823:
Lonergan and colleagues explore training placements for occupational therapy and physiotherapy students inside research teams, a rarely used setting. Universities struggle to find enough placements as enrolments rise, and research roles could host students if the fit is right. Their 2026 study interviews thirty people: students, therapists who work in research jobs, and university educators, and sorts the transcripts into themes about gains, worries, and barriers.

Views ran positive overall. Placements in research built confidence with evidence, sparked interest in research careers, and still met core skill goals. But some educators doubted every research setting could satisfy accreditation rules, the formal standards a placement must meet. Students feared missing hands on client time, and researchers feared harm to study quality. Seven themes in all were mapped. The authors call for placement models built jointly by universities and research teams, then trialed and judged on real results.
pmc-13436023:
Guanghui Chen, Yang Zou, and Keqian Chen caution that cutoff values for Sporothrix fungi may rest on flawed test heat in 2026. Standard broth tests run at thirty five degrees, which pushes the fungus to shift form mid test. Mixed forms skew the drug levels that set wild type cutoffs.

Yeast form fungi can read eight fold lower drug levels than the thread form. Rejected data sets ran seventeen to thirty percent for one species, the letter notes. A terbinafine cutoff for a second species rests on just thirty eight isolates with a split pattern. The authors urge retesting at thirty degrees before cutoffs harden into clinic rules.
pmc-13436423:
Kei Furui Ebisawa and coauthors test an AI app that reads Gram stains from blood cultures in 2026. Specialists are not always on hand, which delays care. Phone photos from two hospitals cover 126 aerobic and ninety anaerobic samples for the head to head test.

Specialists hit about ninety one percent accuracy on both bottle types. The app reached about seventy five to seventy seven percent, short of parity. Errors clustered on a few tricky germ types, while most common germs read well. Off hours cover is the prize if accuracy climbs. The authors flag the weak germ classes for retraining.
pmc-13436923:
Takashi Wada and co-authors followed surgical patients to learn how often throat growths linked to breathing tubes appear after long operations. Their 2026 study enrolled forty adults at one hospital whose planned surgery was expected to last at least five hours. Most had heart surgery, and the group had a median age of 73 years.

Scope checks of the voice box were done the day after the tube came out, then again at one week, one month, and three months. Growths were found in ten of forty patients at one week, and most cleared on their own within a month. Two grew larger and needed two months of inhaled steroid treatment. Tubes left in for thirteen hours or more raised the risk, as did wider double-lumen tubes. The authors urge care with tube choice and early checks for high-risk patients, though the small single-center group limits firm claims.
pmc-13437323:
Saara Krishnamurthy and colleagues mapped what research says about favorite colours among people with common mental health disorders. Colour has been used as a healing aid for centuries, yet hard evidence stays scarce. Their 2026 scoping review searched four databases for studies that asked diagnosed patients which colour they preferred. Sixteen studies qualified, most using a standard colour test, coloured cards, or screen displays.

Patterns differed by diagnosis. People with depressive disorders leaned toward blue, those with anxiety-related disorders toward grey, and those with schizophrenia toward black. Healthy participants never favored the flat colours black or grey. Healthy groups also varied by region, with Europeans preferring blue and Asian participants red and yellow, while patient groups showed no such geographic pattern. The authors read colour choice as a soft clue tracking diagnosis more than culture among patients, and they stress how thin the research base remains for clinical use.
pmc-13437623:
Anil Kumar Monga and colleagues reviewed real-world records for a paired nasal spray used against allergic rhinitis, the allergy-driven sneezing, blocked, itchy nose. Current guidance backs a steroid plus antihistamine spray as a first choice for moderate to severe cases. Their 2026 study drew on 4,500 patient records from 424 ear, nose, and throat clinics across India, tracking symptom scores and any harms during treatment.

Scores improved quickly and firmly. Nasal symptom totals fell by about two points at day seven and by over three and a half at day fourteen, with eye and other symptoms easing in parallel. No patient was hospitalized, suffered a serious side effect, or stopped treatment. The authors conclude the mometasone and azelastine spray pair relieved symptoms well and was tolerated smoothly in daily practice. They present the work as real-world backing for guideline advice, drawn from routine records rather than a controlled trial.
pmc-13438623:
Tamir Edri and colleagues found the missing link between folic acid and the birth defects it famously prevents. Folic acid supplements cut neural tube defects, failures of the early spine and brain to close, yet nobody could say how, and some cases resist it. Their 2026 study names an enzyme, ALDH1L1, as the bridge. The vitamin works only because this enzyme helps turn vitamin A into retinoic acid, a signal the embryo needs.

Folic acid feeds a pathway whose messenger is retinoic acid; without the bridging enzyme the supplement cannot deliver. That insight reframes old arguments over dose: a pregnancy could take folic acid faithfully and still fall short if vitamin A supply runs low. They present the mechanism as a way to sharpen a prevention that already ranks among public health's clearest wins.
pmc-13439023:
Buşra Tozduman and İrem Zengi report a 2026 choice study on what draws public health specialist doctors to one post over another. Public health specialists shape health promotion policy and support care at every level, yet posts in remote areas often stay hard to fill. The authors asked 183 specialists to weigh job features against each other and to show which trade-offs they would accept.

Five of six job features shaped choices in the survey. Being close to family and friends ranked first, ahead of the working setting, pay, how developed the workplace area was, and holding a manager role. Pay mattered most for manager posts among younger specialists with no past manager experience. Readers learn that fair pay alone will not fix staffing gaps, while posts near home and supportive workplaces may do more.
pmc-13439723:
Skinner and colleagues test whether early liver injury from alcohol feeds back into drinking behavior in this 2026 mouse study. The liver-brain connection is suspected in alcohol use disorder, but the behavioral effects of early liver disease were largely unexplored. Female mice were fed an alcohol liquid diet to induce early fatty liver. They were then allowed to choose freely between alcohol and water. Meanwhile, their memory and anxiety were tested.

The alcohol-fed mice developed fatty, enlarged livers, and then drank significantly more than controls in the choice test, with intake rising in step with the degree of liver fat. Their spatial working memory was impaired, though recognition memory and anxiety-like behavior were unchanged in the tests used. The injured livers later recovered their fat but showed lingering inflammation, and a brain growth factor and its receptor were reduced in the hippocampus.
pmc-13439923:
Yen and co-authors build a gene drive that rewrites mosquito populations from inside a native gene. Their 2026 paper describes nanosd, an integral gene drive inserted into the nanos gene of Anopheles gambiae, the main malaria mosquito. Integral drives use the host gene's own control sequences, shrinking the added machinery compared with earlier designs.

The drive inherited at striking rates, 98.4 percent through females and 99.5 percent through males. Females carrying two copies paid a price, with reduced fertility and underdeveloped ovaries, linked to lowered nanos expression and shifts in other fertility genes. Broader gene activity stayed largely undisturbed, and infected mosquitoes remained as susceptible to malaria parasites and a second virus as wild types. In cages, the drive spread efficiently, kept supplying its cutting enzyme after resistant variants appeared, and mobilised a separate antiparasitic modification.
pmc-13441823:
Sanchun Wang and colleagues compare a through-the-mouth plasma ablation surgery against open neck surgery for chosen voice box cancers, reporting in 2026. Saving the larynx matters when curing the cancer. Thirty-one patients with early supraglottic or selected glottic cancers treated by transoral plasma radiofrequency ablation were matched against thirty-six treated with open partial surgery. Survival, disease control, and recovery details were compared after matching balanced the groups.

Ablation patients stayed a median of eight days, needed no simultaneous windpipe opening, and suffered no postoperative bleeding. Swallowing recovery ran faster, and routine feeding tubes were avoided, though temporary coughing on swallowing and tissue overgrowth appeared in a minority. Five-year disease-specific survival, disease-free survival, and local control all landed within a few points of the open surgery figures, with no significant gaps. The authors back the transoral route for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13442923:
Nakhaei and colleagues review whether old, approved drugs can rescue temozolomide, the standard chemotherapy for glioblastoma, the most aggressive brain tumor in adults. Tumors resist the drug by repairing its DNA damage and by switching on survival pathways. Repurposed drugs already have known safety records, so they could reach patients faster than new compounds. Their 2026 narrative review weighs a dozen candidates tested in tumor models and early clinical work.

Candidates range from chloroquine and valproic acid to metformin, aspirin, melatonin, and an old antipsychotic, chlorpromazine. In cell and animal studies, several boosted the killing effect of temozolomide by blocking DNA repair, forcing cell death, or cutting survival signals. Yet clinical proof stays thin and mixed. The authors list hard barriers: getting enough drug past the blood brain barrier, dosing, side effects, and the wide variety among tumors. Careful trials must come before any routine use.
pmc-13443523:
Fallah and colleagues recounted in 2026 how research was organized across Africa during the mpox outbreaks, and what that effort taught about preparing for the next epidemic. A research pillar inside the continent's incident team, led by the Africa CDC, set out to generate evidence fast enough to guide the response. Studies spanned behavior, spread, diagnostics, vaccines, and treatments.

The team built a shared continental platform, launched studies across several countries, and mapped research already under way. Those gains came against hard friction: slow bureaucracy, late funding, ethics approval bottlenecks, tangled coordination, and gaps in case surveillance all delayed work. The authors argue for continuous tracking of study progress and for sharing findings in real time from the first community contact, so evidence turns into action. Their lessons aim at faster research in future outbreaks.
pmc-13443823:
Ackerman and colleagues reviewed procedural sedation and pain relief practice in 2026 at a regional hospital emergency department in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Patients ranged from toddlers of eighteen months to adults of eighty-seven years, mostly young adults without other illnesses. Ketamine was the main sedative, often paired with opioid pain relief. Monitoring followed national guidance, and documented problems were mild and brief, with no aspiration or vomiting. The authors offer the audit as a baseline for South African departments.
pmc-13444123:
Xin Wang and colleagues solve how a ginseng kin makes a key scaffold yet misses a prized product line in a 2026 study. A lost hydroxylase step blocks the next rung toward RK goods in the plant. Rebuilt in tobacco kin, the full path made ginsenosides Rk1, Rk2, and Rk3 from scratch.
pmc-13444223:
Ze-Mei Chen and colleagues name two new Ophiocordyceps fungi that grow on wasps and kin in Yunnan, China, in a 2026 paper. These fungi parasitize insects of the Hymenoptera order. Shape checks plus five-gene family trees placed the finds in the Hymenostilbe branch of the genus.

pmc-13444323:

Their frame, Alternating Neural Integrators, swaps steps between the fixed old code and a learned correction.

The split follows operator-splitting rules, so each half does what it does best. Chaotic systems regained lost coupling under the patch in their tests. Turbulence runs used the patch as a fine-grid fix where old models wander. In neat settings, symbol distillation squeezed the patch into compact formulas that fed back into the old code. The authors pitch the frame as a gray-box upgrade path for labs stuck with legacy tools.
pmc-13444623:
Tatsumi Tanaka and colleagues test two small RNA molecules, miR-126-3p and miR-140-5p, as a joint injection for knee osteoarthritis pain in rats, in a 2026 study. Cartilage wear did not improve, so the gain reads as pain relief rather than joint repair, and more safety work is still needed.
pmc-13445523:
Hamid Eshaghi and colleagues report a sixteen-month-old boy in Iran whose brain shunt let a skin fungus reach his brain, published in 2026 with a review of past cases. The fungus, Neoscytalidium dimidiatum, usually stays on skin and nails, and brain infection is rare and often fatal. The boy had been healthy before a head injury led to the shunt.

The first drug mix failed, so care shifted to drugs picked by lab sensitivity tests, among them drug delivery straight into the brain fluid spaces. pmc-13445923:
Jin-Hui Yi and coauthors develop a 2026 machine learning model to tell apart pancreas cancer from swelling in chronic pancreas swelling patients with focal lesions, a famously hard call. pmc-13447623:
Wendemi Daniel Ouedraogo and colleagues assess a 2026 evaluation of Burkina Faso's national malaria control program from 2020 to 2024, a period of progress shadowed by elimination hurdles. Using program time-series data and change theory, the team tracked coverage, availability, use, incidence, and forecasts to 2030.

Cases fell from 537.5 to 446.4 per 1,000 yearly, yet forecasts warn incidence could rebound toward 473 by 2030 amid supply and resource gaps. Sustained funding and tailored strategies remain essential.
pmc-13447823:
Ziyu Tao and coauthors propose a 2026 rule-driven method fixing broken-chain errors when mapping 3D rock mock results into control information models. Gaps in data structure, layout, traits, and storage often sever trait flow and shape links, spoiling viewing and analysis.

A pile-base case in Southwest China showed fixed layout, calmed mess and self-crossing, and kept nodal traits. Cross-platform rock workflows gain a reliable transfer path.
pmc-13449223:
Dinkar Regmi and co-authors build an integrated Raman spectroscopy platform with embedded artificial intelligence for real-time cancer detection during surgery. Raman scattering reads a tissue's molecular fingerprint, but workflows are fragmented across proprietary tools and ad hoc scripts. Their 2026 paper unifies instrument control, data collection, cleaning, processing, and classification in one auditable system.

Validation used a painkiller product and tissue samples from around human laryngeal tumours, and results matched commercial software and previous algorithms. Across fifty independent runs it averaged about eighty-nine percent accuracy and produced predictions in under three seconds from signal acquisition, with the device itself taking most of that time. The authors stress that the end-to-end audit trail, archiving every intermediate output, is as important as the classifier itself.
pmc-13449323:
Dominik Martinát and colleagues published a 2026 paper turning a membrane database into linked open data. MolMeDB gathers curated records of how compounds interact with biological membranes, information that matters for predicting whether a drug reaches its target. In its original relational form, however, the data were hard to combine automatically with other sources.

The new schema draws on standard vocabularies already used by PubChem and ChEMBL, so federated queries can reach across databases at once. Researchers can now ask structural and cross-database questions that the old tables could not answer directly.
pmc-13449523:
Kazi Md Azman Hossain and colleagues compared two group exercise plans for older adults in a 2026 trial. Aging erodes activity, strength, fall safety, and quality of life, and exercise is a standard way to fight back. Yet proof comparing sense-and-balance training with strength training in local settings was thin.
