Activity, function, fall confidence, and quality of life were scored before and after. Both plans raised scores over time, with the sense-and-balance plan showing larger gains in activity. Local centers gain a head-to-head basis for picking between the two plans.
pmc-13449623:
Granek and colleagues study how talk between clinicians shapes access to specialist pediatric palliative care for children with cancer in Canada. That care eases symptoms and supports families through serious illness, yet referrals often come late. Their 2026 study draws on deep interviews with 66 health providers at four Canadian children's cancer centers, spanning doctors, nurses, and psychosocial staff, and codes the transcripts for patterns.

Some oncologists, meaning cancer doctors, avoided the talk or used coded, indirect language that confused families. What helped was the opposite: clear, full explanations, age fitting ways to involve the child, joint meetings, shared care plans, and prompt exchange of updates between teams. Fuzzy roles between teams risked split care, the authors warn.
pmc-13449923:
Janna Teigeler, Yannik Stegmann, and Matthias Gamer examine in 2026 how the body braces for a threat it can dodge versus one it cannot. Forty-eight volunteers watched naturalistic images while cues warned of a painful or mild electric stimulus that was either avoidable or inevitable. The team recorded brain waves, heart rate, skin conductance, pupil size, and eye movements, looking for the attentive immobility state that readies a person to act.

Eyes centralized more strongly before avoidable threats, a signature of action preparation. Skin conductance mostly mirrored how intense the coming shock would be, regardless of escape. Heart rate, the drop in visual alpha rhythm, fixation length, and pupil dilation answered to both intensity and escapability at once. pmc-13450123:
Zhang and a large team test the timing of Chinese medicine rehabilitation after stroke in this 2026 prospective study in Hong Kong. Acupuncture and herbal medicine are widely used in post-stroke recovery across Southeast Asia, but the best timing was unproven. Five community centers enrolled survivors aged 35 to 90, all receiving individualized treatment three times weekly for 24 weeks, totaling 72 sessions.

Of 398 patients recruited, about 87 percent completed at least three-quarters of the sessions, a strong adherence rate for a long program. Daily-living scores improved by about six points on average, and thinking scores and a traditional symptom score also improved significantly over the treatment period. Starting within six months of the stroke doubled the odds of a good response. Matched comparisons confirmed the pattern. Early starters gained significantly more daily-living ability.
pmc-13450523:
Reethi Padmanabhan and Lauryn Falcone describe a 2026 case of a stubborn skin reaction confined to one arm that at last cleared with a biologic drug. Their patient, a woman aged 32, had red patches and bumps on her left arm and hand for a month. Steroid courses eased the rash for a short while, then it came back each time.

pmc-13451423:
Christine Heinrich and others tested hamstring-to-quadriceps strength ratios across menstrual cycle phases in 2026, in physically active women. Muscle balance around the knee may vary with hormones, affecting injury risk, but evidence across cycle phases at different speeds was thin. Thirty eumenorrheic women were tested in early follicular, ovulatory, and mid-luteal phases.

Isokinetic peak torque for leg extension and flexion was measured at sixty and one hundred twenty degrees per second, with five maximal repetitions per test. The hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio did not differ significantly across phases at either speed, nor did flexion peak torque differ between phases in the reported results. Coaches and clinicians gain reassurance that knee muscle balance stays stable across the cycle in active women.
pmc-13452123:
Manfred Dopfner and a very large team test in 2026 a step-up care plan for German school children with mild to mid ADHD. Later steps then matched each child's reply, from booster calls to therapy, or therapy plus drugs.

pmc-13453023:

pmc-13453723:

Treated adults showed more of the syndrome's classic features and more often carried other diagnoses that can look like Rett syndrome. Baseline health burdens otherwise ran similar. The authors read the low uptake as a wide unmet need among adults, whose care often fragments after childhood.
pmc-13454623:

pmc-13454823:

pmc-13455223:

Both child self-report and parent proxy versions of the KINDL questionnaire were used, alongside comprehensive clinical assessment of caries, hygiene, gingival health, and enamel defects. pmc-13455423:

pmc-13456823:

The analysis covered publication trends, countries, journals, keywords, and themes across the field.

pmc-13457023:

pmc-13457123:

pmc-13457223:

pmc-13457523:

The authors offer this as a biomarker and drug target pairing.
pmc-13457623:

pmc-13457723:

pmc-13458523:

pmc-13458823:

pmc-13459023:

The authors stress repeated checks of germs, immune state, and organ function to guide each change.
pmc-13459223:

pmc-13459323:

pmc-13459623:

pmc-13459923:

pmc-13461123:

Confidence in these results ranged from moderate to low, tempering firm rankings.
pmc-13461323:

The strongest signals of non-response were more severe pain itself, worse period-linked symptoms such as bloating and dull pelvic ache, and greater sleep disturbance. Their models still explained only a modest share of who responds.
pmc-13461623:

The case was found in Kunming, Yunnan, in 2025 through routine flu-like illness monitoring. Health workers gathered medical and exposure details, then tested samples from the patient, contacts, animals, and the home. They aimed to trace the source and check for spread.

Tests found the N2 flu type in lung tissue from the dead pig, while other samples were negative. The patient recovered and left hospital. pmc-13461823:

pmc-13462023:
Taku Maruki and co-authors checked whether a bipolarity score matches the drug choices that keep depression patients stable for years. pmc-13462123:

pmc-13463523:
Zhao and colleagues examined in 2026 how the muscles of Tibetan sheep adapt to thin plateau air. Low oxygen on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau challenges every grazing animal there. The team compared thigh muscle from sheep at high and lower altitudes. They measured fiber size in the tissue. They also mapped a network of competing genetic regulators that fine-tune gene activity.

pmc-13463623:

pmc-13463823:
Koshiol and a binational team described in 2026 the design of a case-control study of gallbladder cancer in Chile. The study tackles a stubborn puzzle. pmc-13464923:
Maochun Lei and colleagues ran a masked multicentre trial in 2026 of dialectical behaviour skills training for depressed patients who injure themselves without suicidal intent. Medication changes were not tracked, so drug effects cannot be ruled out, yet the brain link backs skills training for teens in particular.
pmc-13465223:
Sillers and colleagues mapped the immune receptors of garden strawberry in 2026. The NLR genes let plants detect certain pathogens and trigger defense. It appeared in other rose-family species but in no species outside that family. Nearly all hybrid genes switched on or off when microbes attacked. pmc-13465323:
Marco Antonio Hernández-Valenzuela and five co-authors hunt for dangerous Staphylococcus epidermidis strains hiding on healthy skin. Healthy skin, the authors conclude, can quietly stock device-ready pathogens.
pmc-13465423:
Suleyman Yaman, Hasan Guler, and Abdul Hafeez-Baig present MAF-SleepNet, a neural network that sorts sleep disorders from overnight recordings. Under the loose test the same model neared ninety-nine percent, which exposes how much loose testing flatters scores. The authors push strict testing as the honest yardstick for clinic-ready claims.
pmc-13465923:
Thanaporn Kaewpradup and colleagues pool research findings on green leafy vegetables and heart disease risk, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Standard tools graded bias risk separately for each study design. Random-effects models handled the wide variation between studies. The synthesis gives readers a single place to judge whether the leafy-greens advice rests on habit data, trial data, or both.
pmc-13466123:
Minjie Ou and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 16-year-old girl whose bladder tumour mimicked a paraganglioma, a hormone-secreting growth. She arrived with intermittent visible blood in urine, and scans showed a richly vascular bladder wall mass with strong enhancement and mild hormone-receptor uptake. Suspicion of paraganglioma led to blood pressure blockade before surgery.

pmc-13466323:
Ruchi Naik and colleagues review how cytomegalovirus wakes from dormancy after kidney transplantation, in a 2026 article. The virus hides for life inside blood-forming and marrow-lineage cells, held down by chemical silencing of its genes and steady immune watch. After transplant it can reactivate, harming the graft and raising rejection and death risks.

Surgical stress, oxygen deprivation followed by restored flow, and inflammation release signals that switch on the virus's master promoter. Transplant drugs weaken the immune watch at the same time, and some directly favor viral activity. The review ties these threads into one account of the latency-to-activity switch, aiming at better prevention for recipients.
pmc-13466523:
Anwar and colleagues trained a machine learning system in 2026 to spot multiple sclerosis from eye scans alone. MS damages nerves body-wide, and the retina thins measurably as it progresses. Models were tuned per patient, and explanation tools showed which features drove each call.

One layer alone performed strongly. Ganglion cell layer sectors reached an F1 score, a combined accuracy measure, of about 94 percent. The nerve fiber layer alone scored lower, near 88 percent. Combining both layers gave the best result: an F1 near 96 percent with precision above 97 percent. Every measured sector of both layers was thinner in MS patients, a highly significant pattern. The authors argue eye scans could offer a cheap, painless screening route for MS.
pmc-13466623:
Forszt and colleagues present a 2026 review of saliva as a diagnostic fluid for stroke patients. Saliva is easy to collect, non-invasive, and cheap to store, and many markers measured in blood also appear in it. Markers found in patients' saliva include antioxidants such as glutathione and uric acid, damage products of oxidation and nitrosative stress, and inflammatory cytokines of both directions. Levels of many markers track disease severity and organ complications, which is what a useful test must do. A spit sample cannot replace brain imaging in an emergency, but it could serve follow-up and rehabilitation monitoring, especially where blood draws and labs are hard to reach.
pmc-13466823:
Shibo Zhang and colleagues map the invasive front edge of liver tumors, where growth pushes into healthy tissue and outcomes turn worst, in a 2026 study. Layered molecular data showed two proteins, SPARC and IGFBP7, running high in that edge zone. The edge neighborhood looked remodeled and short on immune cells, with signals favoring further invasion.

Computer experiments that simulated disturbing the edge program, crossed with drug response data, nominated three existing cancer drugs as candidates against it. The authors are explicit that these picks are predictions awaiting bench proof.
pmc-13466923:
Shen Li, Xin Liu, and Yong Hu simulate reactor accidents to study how hydrogen moves in chromium-coated zirconium fuel cladding, in a 2026 study. Such coatings are meant to make fuel safer in a loss-of-coolant accident, but hydrogen behavior under those conditions had been little examined. The finding tempers enthusiasm for the coating with a failure mode designers must now engineer around.
pmc-13467023:

pmc-13467123:
Krzysztof Granatyr and colleagues test a fly ash geopolymer concrete as a thin protective skin over asphalt pavement, in a 2026 laboratory study. The program ran a long battery: pressure water entry, abrasion, skid grip, wheel rutting, bending fatigue, strength, freeze-thaw cycles, and salt scaling. Alone, the geopolymer let pressurized water through fully, yet the layered specimen over asphalt leaked nothing in the same three-day test. The authors judge the pairing, not the skin alone, as the workable system.
pmc-13467823:
Tiţa and co-authors fortify yogurt with cherry plum powder and watch what changes. The aim is a functional dairy product whose nutritional upgrade does not cost it consumer appeal.

Antioxidant activity edged up only slightly. Texture firmed during storage, with firmness reaching about 170 grams by day fourteen and consistency rising in parallel, while cohesiveness wandered without a trend. pmc-13467923:
Chen and colleagues review esketamine as a treatment for depressive states in people with cancer, in 2026 psycho-oncology research. pmc-13468223:

pmc-13469123:

pmc-13469223:

pmc-13470123:
Jing Niu and colleagues built a lightweight steering predictor in 2026 for robots navigating complex scenes. pmc-13471723:
David Kumar Yesudoss and colleagues probe in 2026 how water moves when trapped between the atomic layers of transition metal carbides and nitrides, materials known as MXenes. Pure carbide layers sat between the two extremes. The deciding factor was not how much water the layers held. pmc-13472023:

Questions covered CPR training, readiness to intervene on a stranger, and awareness of where the nearest defibrillator sits. pmc-13472223:

The authors call the rewiring a real vulnerability, provided combinations and marker validation hold up.
pmc-13472923:

pmc-13473023:
Unzueta-Roch and colleagues review in 2026 how new technologies and artificial intelligence might humanize care in pediatric intensive care units, where very sick children are treated. pmc-13473423:
Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study linking immune activity, brain wiring, and thinking problems in bipolar disorder. Cognitive impairment is a major cause of social disability in this illness. pmc-13473523:
Dong Hua and five colleagues developed in 2026 a forecasting system that predicts wind power across many sites and horizons at once. pmc-13474623:

pmc-13474823:

pmc-13478223:

pmc-13478323:

pmc-13479423:

pmc-13479923:
Adrienne Kish published a 2026 opinion piece, as sole author, reframing how science describes life at the edges of what the world allows. Extreme-loving microbes that thrive in boiling acid, deep ice, or radiation are usually sorted by the harsh setting they endure. Kish argues the better lens is chemistry: what damage each stress does to the cell's building blocks.

Four rules frame decades of research. Life ends when damage to the building blocks mounts, not when the setting itself crosses a line. The cell's parts differ in how easily each stress harms them. The stuff right around the cell changes that damage. Most of all, different stresses often cause the same wounds inside the cell, and cells fight them with the same defenses. The new frame gives life scientists, chemists, and planet scientists one shared tongue for life's limits.
pmc-13481823:

pmc-13485023:

pmc-13485223:

pmc-13485623:

pmc-13487923:
Pingluo Xu and co-authors catalog a gene family in Paulownia fortunei, a fast-growing timber tree, in a 2026 genome-wide study. The 14-3-3 proteins help plants respond to stress and infection. Paulownia faces drought, salty soil, and a phytoplasma disease that causes abnormal branching called witches' broom, so the team searched the genome and tracked gene activity under each stress.

Fourteen family members were found, split into two broad groups. Individual genes switched on or off in distinct patterns, one rising under drought and another under salt. Lab tests showed two proteins binding partners in a key signaling pathway and triggering defense responses in test leaves. The work offers targets for breeding tougher trees.
pmc-13488123:
Qing Li and colleagues describe four cases of psittacosis pneumonia found with advanced testing in rural China in a 2026 case series. The germ Chlamydia psittaci spreads from birds and causes community pneumonia that county hospitals often miss. Lung wash fluid from each patient went to a central laboratory for targeted sequencing, a test that hunts DNA from hundreds of respiratory germs at once.

All four patients had high fever, cough, and contact with birds, from market visits to a pet parrot at home. Standard antibiotics failed, while switching to doxycycline or a fluoroquinolone after confirmation cleared fever within days. Scans were clear by three months. Sending samples out worked well, the authors argue.
pmc-13490923:
Shafiei and her dental team in Iran asked in 2026 how the way a glue is applied changes the strength of filled upper premolar teeth. They used 108 pulled teeth, split them into nine groups, and filled large three surface holes with resin composite. Each group used a set etching plan, meaning a brief acid step, with or without an extra resin coat. All teeth then went through load cycles, water storage, and heat and cold cycles to mimic months in the mouth.

The best plan paired short dentin etching with a water free resin coat set with light before the fill. Those teeth bore the top load before they broke, at about twelve hundred newtons of force. Adding a resin coat helped in most plans, and the best groups also broke in ways that could still be fixed.
pmc-13491623:
Yan Yu and nine colleagues recount in 2026 the case of a thirteen-year-old boy with a rare inherited connective tissue disorder, kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. The condition brings loose joints and spinal curvature, and its blood vessel risks are easy to overlook. The boy also had blue-tinted eye whites and a sunken chest, and he died when his aorta ruptured.

Standard gene sequencing and copy-number screening first found nothing, and Marfan syndrome genes were ruled out as well. Re-examining the sequencing data revealed a missing stretch covering exons fifteen and sixteen of the PLOD1 gene on both copies, later confirmed by a targeted test. The authors warn that routine pipelines can miss such small deletions, delaying diagnosis and counseling, and urge vigilance for vessel problems in this syndrome.
pmc-13491723:
Li-Jiuan Lai and Tzuhui Angie Tseng build and validate in 2026 a questionnaire that measures food literacy in older elementary school children in Taiwan. A national food and agriculture education law made the topic a policy priority, but no tested instrument existed for this age group. The scale rests on the law's six principles and a framework separating functional, interactive, and critical literacy.

Expert review, pilot testing, and a survey of 400 students in twelve schools across the island produced a thirty-six-item final scale. Reliability scores cleared the accepted threshold for every dimension, and factor analyses supported the scale's structure. Children scored highest on cherishing food, cutting waste, and food culture, and lowest on balanced diet ideas and buying local. Scores also varied with school type, region, and family food habits.
pmc-13492423:
Luigi Spadafora and Massimiliano Camilli systematically review in 2026 whether sacubitril/valsartan, a proven heart failure drug pair, can shield the heart during anthracycline chemotherapy. Anthracyclines cure cancers but can quietly injure heart muscle. Searching four databases through January 2026 produced 753 records, of which only three randomized trials, covering 352 mostly breast cancer patients, fit the prevention question.

Definitions of heart damage differed so much between trials that the reviewers refused to pool a single summary number. In one trial no treated patient developed cardiac dysfunction while about a quarter of standard-care patients did, with all events detected by sensitive strain imaging rather than pumping fraction. A second trial found moderate or severe damage rare in both arms. The authors call the signal promising but the underlying data far too small and inconsistent.
pmc-13492723:
Sina A Al-Nomi and four colleagues measure in 2026 how often appendicitis turns complicated in Taiz, Yemen, and what pushes patients toward gangrene, perforation, or abscess. The prospective study enrolled 207 appendectomy patients at two hospitals between February 2024 and February 2025, classifying severity from what surgeons found during the operation.

Forty-nine patients, just under a quarter, had complicated disease. Delay before reaching hospital showed a powerful raw association with complicated disease, and its ingredients were separately damning. Being misdiagnosed at the primary care level multiplied the odds many times over, and so did visiting a traditional healer first or failing to grasp how serious the symptoms were. Other illnesses and a stone blocking the appendix also raised risk. In-hospital delays, notably, did not. The authors push for earlier recognition and referral in conflict-affected Yemen.
pmc-13493823:
Bodinier and colleagues introduce LEAP, a tool meant to forecast how lab disease models will respond to gene knockouts and drugs before the experiments are run. Such screens, which disturb cells systematically and measure the fallout, generate huge datasets, but models trained on them often fail on new cell lines or resist interpretation. LEAP, described in 2026, layers together many predictors, each trained on a different compressed view of gene activity.

Across tasks, the layered ensemble consistently beat single predictors on cell lines the models had never seen, lifting correlation scores by a few points. One lean version combined LEAP with simple per-drug models and nearly matched the best performance while staying fast. The team also distilled the ensemble to highlight which biological pathways drive its predictions. They argue the method can prioritise which lab experiments are worth doing first.
pmc-13493923:
Wu and co-authors ask which parts of a long-span cable-stayed bridge matter most for the comfort of people driving across it. Using the Linyu Yangtze River Bridge in China as their case, the 2026 team simulated traffic crossing while the bridge flexed. They then virtually softened each major component in turn: the main girder, the stay cables, and the towers.

Each component ruled a different behaviour. Cable stiffness mainly governed how far the deck sagged vertically. Girder stiffness shaped rotation at the girder ends and the jolts vehicles felt. Tower stiffness tied to overall stability-type deformation. Road surface roughness, meanwhile, dominated passenger comfort more than any stiffness change did. The authors offer the framework as a planning layer that tells engineers whether a comfort complaint points at the deck surface or at a structural part.
pmc-13495323:
Nicole T Cacho leads a large team setting out, in a 2026 protocol, the GAIN study of early feeding for newborns born with gastroschisis. In this birth defect the gut sits outside the belly wall and moves sluggishly after repair. Babies often rest the bowel for long spells and depend on vein feeding, with risks of infection, poor growth, and long stays. Custom varies widely between hospitals.

The two-site, single-group study will test whether an early plan can be carried out. The plan removes the stomach suction tube within a day of belly closure and starts tiny human milk feeds within two days, advancing by a shared pathway. Success will be judged by enrollment, sticking to the plan, and dropout, with stay length, time to full feeds, and growth as early signals. Safety checks watch for feeding harm and infection. The team hopes to set up a full trial.
pmc-13495423:
Phebe De Heus and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a white blood cell measure can serve as a stress gauge in ponies handled again and again for research. Stress is expected to raise cortisol and shift blood cell ratios, while weakening the burst of germ-killing oxygen from neutrophils. That burst, measured as leukocyte coping capacity, was tracked in nine university ponies over a 42-day vaccine study.

The coping measure and cortisol both drifted down over the study, which might signal growing strain. Yet the cell ratio did not follow the same course, and the coping measure tied only weakly or moderately with the other markers. Its per-cell version showed no ties at all. The authors conclude the markers likely tap different arms of the stress response. They urge bigger studies adding behavior watching before the coping test earns a place as a horse stress gauge.
pmc-13495523:
Hyun Woo Yu, Pretty Manyimo, and John I MacArtney gather, in a 2026 scoping review, how palliative care writing describes dying as normal, ordinary, or natural. The World Health Organization's own definition calls dying a normal process, and such words carry weight in ideas of a good death. The team searched six databases for real-world studies that used these terms plainly.

Twenty-one studies qualified. The words were often swapped for each other in a single loose claim, and writers themselves worried the ideas lacked clear edges. What counted as normal or natural dying varied widely with person, place, and culture. Some proof suggested the framing can ease the dying experience, yet no study used ordinary dying explicitly enough to judge it at all. With definitions this tangled, the authors counsel care before the words harden into practice or policy.
pmc-13495823:
Büsra Akay Hacan leads a Turkish Oncology Group team searching, in a 2026 prospective study, for blood markers that predict who benefits from bevacizumab in metastatic colorectal cancer. The drug targets blood vessel growth, yet doctors have no validated test to pick patients. Eighty-eight people with inoperable spread disease gave blood before treatment for vessel-growth factors, nitric oxide, and immune cell counts, with drug levels checked during therapy.

Higher starting levels of three vessel-growth factors, VEGF, PDGF-B, and endothelin-1, went with longer survival, the reverse of the usual guess. Combining the three into an Angiogenesis Index predicted both time without progression and overall survival. Drug levels above a threshold on day fourteen also tracked with longer life, and patients starting with fewer regulatory T cells tended to fare better. The authors offer the trio for refining patient selection, pending confirmation.
pmc-13496023:
Qing Zeng, Xianping Yuan, and Xing Wei pool evidence in 2026 on hernia risk after a major cancer operation that combines tumour removal with heated chemotherapy inside the abdomen. A hernia here means the surgical cut later weakens and bulges. Published rates varied widely, so the authors set out to give a single estimate and list the factors that raise risk.

Searching three large databases, they combined 12 studies covering 2,170 patients and used standard quality checks. About one patient in eight developed such a hernia, with study rates spread from low to much higher values. Older age, obesity, chemotherapy around surgery, bowel joining or stoma work, and problems after surgery each raised the odds.
pmc-13496323:
Charles Weschler and William Nazaroff review in 2026 the hydroxyl radical as an indoor oxidant, a highly reactive molecule that transforms other chemicals in air. Outdoors it rules air chemistry, while indoors ozone was long thought to do nearly all the oxidizing.

Gathering models, lab work, and field measures, they place typical indoor levels of the radical far below sunny outdoor air but near outdoor night levels. It forms mainly when ozone meets scent compounds from wood, cleaners, and skin, and sunlight splitting a nitrogen compound can add more. The same compounds also consume it, which steadies its level. The authors argue its quiet work on indoor air and surfaces deserves far more measurement.
pmc-13498523:
Navid Radfar and colleagues argue in 2026 that stroke prevention for atrial fibrillation, a common irregular heartbeat, should move beyond one standard risk score. That score treats each risk factor as simply present or absent and misses how much abnormal rhythm a person actually carries. New trials and imaging tools now allow a finer, more personal estimate of clot risk versus bleeding risk from blood thinners.

Measures of the upper heart chamber, including its size, stretch, and the shape of a small pouch where clots form, can sharpen risk estimates, especially for patients in the middle range. Blood markers of heart stress and inflammation may add further detail. Recent trials cited by the authors support judging each patient individually, with wearable devices and computer models offering a path to wider use.
pmc-13499723:
Bogdan Muresan and colleagues use German insurance claims in 2026 to count injuries to the ureter, the tube carrying urine from kidney to bladder, during abdominal and pelvic surgery. They also price the aftermath of such injuries. Such injuries are a feared complication that can drive long stays and repeat admissions. Anonymised claims covered adults who had at-risk surgery between 2014 and 2021, with one year of follow-up costs and care use.

Among roughly one hundred sixty thousand patients, just over two hundred suffered the injury, a small fraction overall. Gut and gynaecological operations contributed most cases, with rectal removal carrying the highest rate. Injured patients stayed in hospital about twice as long at first and cost far more over the following year, driven mainly by inpatient care, with many more repeat admissions and emergency visits. The authors press for targeted prevention in high-risk operations.
pmc-13499823:
Altés and co-authors ask whether Spain's health service gets its money's worth from semaglutide injections for obesity. Their 2026 economic model took effectiveness data from the STEP 1 trial. It projected costs and health over forty years, comparing the injection plus diet and exercise support against lifestyle support alone. Benefits were counted in quality-adjusted life years, which combine length and quality of life.

Adding semaglutide bought a modest extra slice of healthy life per person while raising lifetime healthcare costs by a few thousand euros. That produced a cost per healthy year in the mid twenty-thousands of euros. The figure sat below the thirty-thousand-euro threshold the authors use for value, and stress tests never pushed it above the line. They conclude the drug is cost-effective for Spain under current assumptions, driven largely by avoided diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
pmc-13500723:
Abdul Razaq and four co-authors present a 2026 method for building secure substitution boxes, the nonlinear parts of symmetric ciphers that scramble data during encryption. Their construction starts with the action of the modular transformation group on a projective line over a finite field with 257 elements. That action produces Schreier graphs, and the cycle structure of those graphs forms an initial 8 by 8 substitution box. A non-abelian permutation group then rearranges the box positions to refine the design.

The finished box was checked against standard cryptographic tests, including nonlinearity, differential uniformity, the strict avalanche test, bit independence, and linear approximation odds. It also performed well in an image encryption trial judged by texture measures such as contrast, correlation, energy, homogeneity, and entropy from gray-level co-occurrence matrices. The authors argue the graph-based route gives strong random-looking scrambling for encryption and image work.
pmc-13500823:
Alexander Ukhov leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 reconstruction of the Hayli Gubbi volcano eruption in the Afar region of Ethiopia. The volcano, which had no recorded eruptions in the Holocene record, exploded on 23 November 2025. Hazard assessment afterwards needs quick estimates of how much ash and sulfur dioxide were released and at what heights. The team ran the WRF-Chem atmospheric model and traced air parcels backward from TROPOMI satellite plume observations.

The trajectory-based ash source, scaled to 0.8 million tonnes, reproduced the main ash corridor. It also matched the timing of coarse particles recorded at a monitoring station in Oman. Sulfur dioxide emissions came to roughly 0.15 million tonnes, and a hand-adjusted time-height profile fit the observed plume better than the first automatic estimate. About 6 percent of the fine ash settled within 28 hours, some falling into the southern Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
pmc-13501623:
Yan Jiang leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 study of suspected pulmonary hypertension among people on long-term haemodialysis in China. Raised pressure in the lung arteries strains the heart and is common in kidney failure, yet published prevalence figures vary wildly. The single-centre review covered 948 dialysis patients who had a heart ultrasound between January 2023 and December 2024. Suspected disease was defined objectively as an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure above 35 millimetres of mercury.

Prevalence came to 29.7 percent, covering 282 of the 948 patients. Those affected had lower haemoglobin and albumin and much higher brain natriuretic peptide, a heart strain marker. After adjustment, independent predictors were a larger left atrium, with an odds ratio of 1.292 per unit, a lower ejection fraction, and previous vascular access surgery: thrombectomy carried an odds ratio of 2.450 and angioplasty a ratio of 1.511 on those measures. The authors link the condition mainly to left-heart remodelling.
pmc-13501723:
Ha Young Jo leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 family case where a rare skeletal disorder hid behind a growth hormone diagnosis. An adolescent boy with slowing growth and borderline hormone test results was treated as growth hormone deficient and received three years of recombinant hormone with negligible benefit. During puberty a short trunk and flattened vertebrae with hump-shaped endplates emerged on imaging, pointing instead to X-linked spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia tarda, a cartilage disorder caused by faults in the TRAPPC2 gene.

Standard exome sequencing found nothing. Whole-genome sequencing then uncovered a new deep intronic variant in TRAPPC2, first labelled uncertain, which family segregation testing upgraded to likely pathogenic. His younger brother showed earlier spinal changes yet responded favourably to the hormone, while his sister, a healthy carrier, had a normal spine. The authors stress genome sequencing and family testing when growth treatment fails.
pmc-13501823:
Hansen Shi leads an eight-author team reporting a 2026 study of the immune checkpoint CD274, better known as PD-L1, in liver cancer. Its prognostic meaning in hepatocellular carcinoma has been disputed. Mining the TCGA and GTEx databases, the team compared gene activity in tumour and normal tissue, ran survival models, and stained tissue microarrays for the protein. They measured blood levels by ELISA in untreated patients and controls.

Tumour tissue expressed CD274 less than normal liver, yet patients whose tumours expressed more of it lived longer, and models confirmed it as a protective factor for disease-specific survival. The protein staining showed no tumour-versus-normal difference. Blood told the opposite story to tissue: median serum PD-L1 was 349.6 picograms per millilitre in patients against 181.3 in controls on those assays. The authors describe a low-in-tissue, high-in-blood pattern and propose serum testing as a forecasting tool.
pmc-13502923:
Hamad A Alhussain leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 survey of what patients want their doctors to wear at primary healthcare centres in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Between April and May 2026, 1,176 adult visitors at centres in the Riyadh Second Health Cluster completed a bilingual questionnaire. It rated male and female physician outfits and eleven statements about trust, respect, and willingness to return. Appearance mattered to 80.8 percent of respondents across every demographic subgroup.

The white coat won decisively for both sexes of physician, chosen by 85.5 percent for men and 78.4 percent for women, while jeans and expensive clothing were rejected. For female doctors, the niqab or veil and the skirt also ranked high, reflecting local modesty norms, and niqab preference shifted significantly with respondent age. Preferred attire travelled with higher perceived respect, satisfaction, intention to follow up, and expected treatment compliance. The authors advise dress codes that take these preferences seriously.
pmc-13503923:
Zengler argued in 2026 that engineering soil microbes is one of the most promising, and most stubborn, routes to sustainable farming and carbon storage. Soil covers only about a fifth of Earth's surface yet grows about ninety-five percent of the world's food, and land ecosystems soak up a third of carbon emissions. Its microbes drive both crop nutrition and that carbon capture.

New molecular tools now allow targeted work: editing single microbes, dosing soils with helpful microbes or their feed, or breeding plants that recruit the right partners. Zengler traces why field success lags behind lab promise, citing cost and the poor survival of introduced microbes. He weighs modest near-term paths, such as tuning plant-microbe partnerships, as likelier to pay off soon.
pmc-13505023:
Anitha Jeyagurunathan leads a team measuring partner violence among women treated for mental illness in Singapore, in a 2026 study. Partner violence is common worldwide, and women with mental illness face added risk. Local rates and their ties to quality of life were unmapped.

The study enrolled 255 women with psychosis or depression at a tertiary hospital. Half reported partner violence on a world-standard scale, spanning mental, physical, and sexual forms. Women with stronger positive psychotic symptoms faced higher odds of each violence form. Those who faced mental abuse scored lower on social and environmental quality of life, while physical abuse tracked with lower physical quality of life. The authors call for routine screening in psychiatric care.
pmc-13505123:
Hai Wang and colleagues report a single-child case in which two genome-wide methods were combined to explain a rare disorder of sex development. The child, aged about eighteen months, had a male appearance but a 46,XX karyotype, along with an unfused scrotum and hypospadias. Standard tests had not shown how Y-chromosome material came to sit on the X chromosome.

Copy-number sequencing flagged losses on both the X and Y short arms, while optical genome mapping traced the actual structure. Mapping showed a piece of Yp inserted into Xp22.33, with three rejoining events, a deleted stretch, and a local inversion. The kept segment held SRY, the gene that drives male development, which fits the child's condition. The authors argue the two methods add different detail and can sharpen genetic counselling, including growth checks linked to the X deletion.
pmc-13508423:
Hasan Nawaz Tahir leads a nine-author review comparing full intravenous anesthesia with gas-based anesthesia for robot-assisted belly surgery, in 2026 work. Robot surgery changes anesthesia needs, and the choice of method may shape pain, sickness, and pressure inside the eye after surgery. The team searched databases for randomized trials from 2017 to mid-2024. Eligible operations included prostate, womb, kidney, gallbladder, and bladder procedures done by robot through the abdomen. Only six trials with 340 patients in total met the rules, a thin base the authors state openly.

Just one trial measured post-surgery pain, and it favored intravenous anesthesia. The eye pressure measure named in the review plan rests on few data as well. With evidence this sparse, the authors avoid firm verdicts and map what is missing. Their message is that robotic surgery has outrun its anesthesia evidence, and larger head-to-head trials are the pressing need.
pmc-13509223:
Zhivkova and colleagues tested whether herbal feed additives can protect rabbits from ochratoxin A, a mold toxin that contaminates animal feed, in 2026 animal research. The trial used 48 New Zealand White rabbits aged 37 days over an 80-day period. Some rabbits received the toxin alone at 2 parts per million in feed. Others also got supplements such as ashwagandha, milk thistle, gotu kola, or silymarin at doses reaching 25,000 parts per million.

Rabbits on the toxin alone lost body weight and showed the worst damage, concentrated in the liver, kidneys, and spleen, with milder injury in the heart, gut, and lungs. Blood markers of organ strain and measures of oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive molecules, also peaked in that group. Rabbits given herbal additives showed the same pattern in milder form, with protection strongest in the kidneys and liver. Zhivkova concludes the supplements blunted, but did not remove, the toxin's harm.
pmc-13509323:
Bing Song leads a seven-author team examining which immune cells help cause frozen shoulder, a painful condition where the shoulder joint grows stiff, in work published in 2026. The group combined genetic data for 731 immune cell traits with gene readings from shoulder capsule tissue taken from patients and controls. They also tested whether steroid drugs known as glucocorticoids change the same immune patterns.

The genetic analysis flagged seven immune traits that may raise risk and seventeen that may protect against the condition. Tissue readings confirmed five of these traits at higher levels, tied to swelling, scarring, and new blood vessel growth in the capsule. Steroid drugs showed no direct causal link to the disease, yet they lowered one protective immune trait, a trade-off the authors say deserves closer study.
pmc-13512623:
Juan Pablo Carvajal and Fred Gustavo Manrique-Abril tested whether morning cortisol, a stress hormone in blood, matches burnout scores in Colombian health workers. The study covered 69 staff in Boyacá and paired fasting blood samples with a standard burnout survey.

Almost all workers, 96.6 percent, had cortisol in the normal range, and full burnout was rare at about 5 percent. About 68 percent scored as engaged, though 16.9 percent showed high emotional exhaustion, a warning sign worth watching. No link appeared between cortisol levels and any burnout dimension, with all tests far from significance. Carvajal advises watching the exhausted subgroup early and studying stress with several body markers over time.
pmc-13514623:
Ziyang Yu, Shuaiwang Huang, and Xiyang Peng compare exercise therapies for regaining movement after acute ischaemic stroke in a 2026 systematic review and network meta-analysis. Stroke survivors often keep lasting weakness, and clinicians face a crowded menu of rehabilitation methods with little guidance on which suits which deficit. Searching four databases through late 2025, the authors pooled sixty-six trials covering 3,675 patients and used Bayesian ranking to compare methods across several recovery domains.

Different winners emerged for different goals. Tilting postural training and one-sided strength work ranked high for balance, robot-assisted Tai Chi and home guidance for daily living, and robot hand training paired with electrical stimulation for standard motor scores. Visual feedback training led for walking endurance. Yu's team stresses that no single method tops every domain, so prescriptions should match the patient's main deficit.
pmc-13514823:
Simon Wagner and eight colleagues report, in a 2026 lab study, a drug pairing that pushes colorectal cancer cells toward death. Colorectal cancer often survives by dodging the cell's built-in suicide programme, often through the protective protein Bcl-2. The team combined dimethyl fumarate, a redox-shifting drug already approved for multiple sclerosis, with venetoclax, which blocks Bcl-2 directly. Experiments centred on a widely used colorectal cancer cell line, HCT-116.

Dimethyl fumarate hobbled the cells' mitochondria, draining their energy currency and triggering recycling responses and cell-cycle arrest. Together, the two drugs deepened that stress, slowed growth, and held cells in a lasting arrest phase while switching off the cyclin proteins that drive division. Cell death rose most clearly when both drugs were given. Wagner's group frames the pairing as attractive because both drugs already exist in clinical use for other diseases.
pmc-13515323:
Junlin Dong and colleagues studied how bacterial communities in reservoir water and mud shift with the seasons in dry northwest China. They sampled eight reservoirs in Guyuan, Ningxia, in April, July, and October 2025 and read bacterial genes.

Mud communities held far more kinds of bacteria than water ones and barely changed across the year. Water communities swung strongly with the seasons, tracking temperature, acidity, and nutrient levels as they changed. Chance-like processes shaped the water communities most, while mud ones followed firmer environmental selection. Links among mud bacteria formed the richest networks, peaking in July, Dong reports, when nutrients ran high.
pmc-13516423:
Yahia AL-Helih and five colleagues compare how well nurses keep resuscitation skills after training in a 2026 prospective study. CPR skill fades without practice, and ward setting may shape the fade. The team assessed 265 registered nurses right after basic life support training. Each nurse was then retested once, at one, three, or six months, so the design compares groups across time points rather than tracking each nurse throughout.

Knowledge scores sat lower at every later check in both critical care and general care nurses. The slide looked clearer among general care nurses. Hands-on skills told the same story: more nurses needed remediation at later checks, again worst in the general care group. AL-Helih's team backs refresher training aimed at each setting's exposure level. They caution that the design cannot prove why the gap opens.
pmc-13516923:
Liu and colleagues improved in 2026 a candidate drug for autism spectrum disorder so it can reach the brain. Their earlier work showed XAV939, a tankyrase blocker, eased social problems in two autism mouse models by damping Wnt and sugar-burning pathways. But the drug crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly and has low bioavailability. The team created ester versions, called prodrugs, and coated the best one in cell membrane for brain targeting.

Of three ester versions, one named XAV939-L1 kept the dual pathway blocking in cells and in neurons from Shank3b-mutant mice. Injected plainly, it improved social behaviour in those mice but caused liver side effects. Coating it in a hybrid neuron-astrocyte membrane greatly increased brain accumulation. The authors present membrane-coated prodrugs as a route to brain delivery for autism drug candidates that otherwise cannot cross.
pmc-13517123:
Uğur Ergün leads a thirty-six-author survey of healthcare workers' history and knowledge of shingles in a 2026 Turkish study. The virus behind chickenpox sleeps in nerves for life and can wake as painful shingles, especially with age or weak immunity. A strong recombinant vaccine exists and was licensed in Türkiye in 2024. Over five thousand health workers, nearly half of them physicians, answered an online questionnaire.

About one in ten reported having had shingles themselves. Nearly nine percent knew nothing of the disease, and only about forty percent knew a vaccine exists. One in five would refuse to pay for it. Being a physician roughly doubled the odds of solid knowledge, and having heard of shingles tripled it. Ergün's team concludes that staff education must come first, since uninformed health workers cannot protect themselves or steer vulnerable patients toward vaccination.
pmc-13518223:
Hélène Martini leads a twenty-nine-author study of how aged cells fuel their own inflammatory chatter in a 2026 paper. Senescent cells stop dividing but broadcast a cocktail of signals, the SASP, that damages tissue over time. Leaked mitochondrial DNA was known to flip the alarm switch. This team found the second half of the circuit: the same powerhouses supply the raw material that lets the alarm be transcribed.

Senescent mitochondria ramp up a pyruvate-to-acetyl-CoA pipeline, and that molecule feeds the chemical tagging that opens SASP genes for reading. Blocking the citrate exporter that feeds the pipeline closed those genes down. In aged mice the same block softened inflammation and improved healthspan measures. Martini's team calls it a metabolic checkpoint: signalling proposes the inflammatory programme, but metabolism decides whether the cell can afford to run it, a distinction drug hunters can target.
pmc-13518523:
Ahmet Emre Eşkazan leads an eighteen-author survey comparing what leukaemia patients and their doctors prioritise in a 2026 Turkish study. Chronic myeloid leukaemia on modern targeted pills now allows near-normal lifespans, so conversation quality steers switching and adherence. One hundred twenty-nine haematologists answered online and one hundred twenty patients by phone through the national society.

Both sides agreed on what must be explained at the start, then ranked it differently: patients wanted disease course, daily-life impact, and whether treatment works; doctors stressed safety and monitoring. On switching, patients again chased effectiveness while doctors chased manageable side effects. A quarter of patients admitted imperfect adherence, mostly forgetfulness, and follow-ups ran about ten minutes every few months. Patients also felt sunnier about daily life with the disease. The team urges shared decision-making to close the gap.
pmc-13518623:
Jawad Fares and seven colleagues report a 2026 case of a brain tumor in a 19-year-old woman who came to care after a first seizure. Imaging showed a small lesion in the right frontal lobe that looked like a low-grade glioma. Tissue study found mixed glial and neuronal elements with low growth activity. Standard tests found no IDH1, IDH2, or BRAF changes, while methylation profiling matched no known tumor class.

RNA sequencing then found a CLIP2::MET fusion as the only harmful change present. Fares and the team argue that the fusion may mark a separate molecular group within glioneuronal tumors. Readers gain a worked example of broad genomic testing, plus a reminder that MET fusions can guide treatment because approved inhibitors already exist for other cancers.
pmc-13518823:
Baqer M. Merzah leads a seven-author team introducing BioPars in 2026, a large language model built for Persian biomedical text. General chatbots remember medical facts well yet stumble on deeper real-world questions, and Persian medical question answering had no dedicated model. The team assembled training material from over 10,000 articles, textbooks, and medical websites.

Their benchmark, BioParsQA, holds 5,231 Persian medical questions and answers. BioPars scored a ROUGE-L of 29.99 on that set, edging GPT-4 by 1.0 point in their reporting, with a BERTScore of 90.87 using one ranking method. MoverScore and BLEURT also topped the three rival models tested. Fine-grained reasoning, the authors note, still needs work.
pmc-13518923:
Madison Caballero and colleagues offered a new way to find autism risk genes whose effects are too modest to stand out alone. Published in 2026, the study drew on 10,795 families from the SPARK collection and looked for gene pairs that raise risk only when inherited together. The idea rests on a threshold view of autism, in which many small genetic and life factors add up until they cross into the condition.

The search found 97 modest genes forming 50 pairs with a strong joint link to autism, though no single gene crossed the line alone. Checks against control groups sharpened the result, and gene-activity patterns in brain tissue backed the biological fit of the pairs. The authors argue that paired genes help explain why autism varies so much from person to person. The work opens fresh paths for research and, in time, for more targeted forms of support.
pmc-13520423:
Nilufer Zorlutuna Kaymak and colleagues review in 2026 vitrectomy surgery for eye inflammation from many causes, covering why surgery was chosen and how vision fared afterward. Inflammation inside the eye can detach the retina or cloud diagnosis, and removing the gel can treat both problems.

Records spanned 32 eyes in 30 patients treated from 2019 to 2025 with fine-gauge surgery. Detachment repair and diagnostic sampling were the leading reasons. Retinal reattachment succeeded in nearly all detachment cases, vision gains held at one year, and nearly half the eyes gained at least two chart lines. No severe post-surgery inflammation occurred in the series.
pmc-13520523:
Hoshiko Furusawa and colleagues test in 2026 whether a DNA methylation blocking drug called decitabine can calm spine and joint inflammation in a mouse model of spondyloarthritis. Gene silencing by methylation may fuel immune imbalance in this chronic disease, yet its role was unclear.

Arthritis was triggered in susceptible mice, with weekly drug dosing thereafter. Treated mice showed milder joint disease and better tissue scores, including less lining overgrowth. Immune profiling focused on Th17 responses, a cell type that drives inflammation. Tissue sequencing pointed to raised VIPR1, a receptor gene freed by reduced methylation, as part of the mechanism.
pmc-13521323:
Sharmin Sultana and colleagues search in 2026 for respiratory germs other than COVID virus among adults with flu-like illness at a Bangladesh teaching hospital during the pandemic. Testing focused heavily on COVID at the time, leaving negative cases unexplained despite ongoing symptoms.

Swabs from 165 adults between July and December 2022 were tested with a broad panel covering viruses and bacteria. At least one germ appeared in about 36 percent of patients, split between viral and bacterial finds. Statistical checks confirmed that germ types were unevenly distributed rather than random. Co-infection patterns were also tested, giving clinicians a fuller local picture for future flu seasons.
pmc-13521523:
Zhikui Wei and colleagues link in 2026 wrist-measured sleep patterns with fat-hormone levels in older adults from a long-running Baltimore ageing study. Sleep and fat hormones both steer metabolic health, yet their interplay late in life was poorly mapped.

Participants numbered 350 people aged sixty or older, averaging about 75 years, with roughly a week of wrist sleep recording plus fasting blood tests. Longer wake bouts inside sleep tracked with lower adiponectin and leptin at baseline. Longer total sleep predicted adiponectin gains over time, while short sleep predicted decline. Links varied by sex and belly fat level in subgroup checks.
pmc-13521923:
Srihari Srinivasan and colleagues adapt in 2026 a large vision transformer for two jobs at once, depth estimation and human segmentation, using tiny trainable plug-in modules instead of full retraining. Full fine-tuning for dense prediction is costly, so cheap adaptation matters for small teams.

Only about 150,000 new parameters were trained inside the decoder of a depth model. Segmentation scores reached competitive levels against leading dedicated models, with strong average precision and overlap scores on filtered public datasets. Depth accuracy of the base model stayed intact. Dual output from one adapted backbone suits robotics and editing tools with tight compute budgets.
pmc-13522523:
Funda Ersoy Atalay and colleagues made clean, intact microcapsules from walnut pollen for future medical delivery. Published in 2026, the study worked with Juglans regia pollen, whose tough outer shells, called sporopollenin exine capsules, suit drug carrying but normally retain allergy-triggering proteins. Sequential chemical washes stripped proteins, while a PEG-4000 step repaired shells that collapsed during acid treatment.

Lab checks found no detectable protein bands and faded protein signals, showing allergen content below detection limits. PEG treatment restored round shape in about five sixths of capsules examined and raised surface area, with roughly one quarter of material recovered as product. The authors present the capsules as sustainable natural carriers. Readers get a verified recipe, still awaiting tests with real drug loads.
pmc-13522623:
Reza Nouri, Erfan Ayubi, Shiva Borzouei, and Sajjad Farashi apply machine learning to predict thyroid cancer recurrence in a 2026 retrospective study. Three hundred fifty-five patients with differentiated thyroid cancer were followed for ten years after thyroid removal and radioactive iodine treatment. Records supplied tumor, treatment, and blood marker data, and six learning algorithms were compared head to head.

One boosted-tree model performed best, reaching accuracy near ninety-eight percent with an almost perfect discrimination score. The strongest predictors were prior recurrence count, a stimulated blood marker level in the first year, spread to neck nodes, and first response to treatment. The authors also propose reserving whole-body scans for high-risk patients, which could spare low-risk patients unnecessary testing while keeping close watch where recurrence is likely.
pmc-13523223:
Ruth Namazzi and colleagues show that a sickle cell drug distorts a bedside kidney test in Ugandan children in a 2026 analysis nested in a clinical trial. Two hundred forty-eight children with sickle cell anemia had creatinine, a kidney marker, measured by a point-of-care device and by a reference laboratory method. About half started hydroxyurea during a year of follow-up as part of routine care.

At enrollment the two methods agreed well. At follow-up, children on hydroxyurea showed device readings notably higher than laboratory values, with some results crossing into the abnormal range, while untreated children showed no such gap. Drug levels in blood explained most of the variation in device readings. The authors warn that the interference can misclassify kidney function and mislead care decisions.
pmc-13523323:
Pramana Adhikari and Mahesh Bhatta explore the hidden social burden of infertility in a 2026 review. Beyond its biology, it interacts with stigma, gendered expectations, and unfair systems. Peer-reviewed studies were read through three lenses: how people cope with stress, how stigma works, and how overlapping disadvantages intersect, producing three linked themes.

It was commonly felt as a threat to identity, relationships, and future plans, producing intense turmoil. Coping differed by gender, with peer support and therapy helping some, while shutting it out and denial harmed others. Stigma eroded gendered self-image, with men linking infertility to lost manhood and women cast as failures, and racial bias in medicine deepened the harm. System-wide gaps worsened every layer. The authors call for mental health support that fits local culture, cheaper treatment, and anti-stigma campaigns.
pmc-13523423:
Elena Campilii leads a team building an automatic engagement meter for children in robot-assisted walking therapy in a 2026 study. Twenty children with cerebral palsy were monitored across multiple sessions on a robotic gait system. Heart rate changes, facial heat imaging, and movement data from the robot frame were collected to capture body and behavior signals linked to engagement, which an expert clinician rated in three classes.

Combining all signal types with one ensemble model gave the best result, with a moderate combined score across classes. The system distinguished the clearly disengaged and clearly engaged states best, while most errors confused neighboring classes, especially the neutral middle. Feature analysis supported the value of mixing body and movement inputs. The authors aim at neutral, scalable engagement monitoring for children's recovery care.
pmc-13523523:
Lotte Nijhuis and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, whether nicotinamide, a form of vitamin B3, can calm inflammation in juvenile idiopathic arthritis, the most common rheumatic disease of childhood. The disease involves chronic joint inflammation with an imbalance between regulatory T cells, which restrain immunity, and effector T cells. Nicotinamide helps make a molecule central to cell energy and immune control.

In laboratory work, nicotinamide raised the share of regulatory-type T cells in blood and joint fluid cells from patients and increased suppressive capacity in healthy control cells. In a small pilot phase, six patients took high-dose nicotinamide by mouth for three days, and similar levels appeared in blood plasma and joint fluid, showing the vitamin reaches inflamed joints. The authors call for larger studies on dose and long-term place in care.
pmc-13524623:
León and colleagues presented in 2026 a computer method that labels ten tissue types in microscope slides of oral cancer. Pathologists now mark these slides by hand, which is slow, and rare tissue types get few examples to learn from. The method aims to cut that hand work while keeping the labels sharp at tissue borders.

The team grouped nearby pixels into small clusters called superpixels, and used them both to build training labels and to clean up the final maps. They trained on slides from ten patients and tested on slides from two more. Across nine model setups, their best runs reached mean accuracy near 92 percent, with strong overlap scores even for rare tissue classes. The tool plugs into the free QuPath program, so labs can rebuild whole-slide maps with it.
pmc-13525623:
Aisha Krieger-Hussain, Zaineb Ahmad, Lejla Hodzic and Besher Kabak published this 2026 case report of one patient, a 67-year-old man whose high-grade B-cell lymphoma first announced itself through two emergencies at once. They were acute confusion and cardiac tamponade, fluid crushing the heart. He arrived from a group home with altered mental state and breathlessness. A head scan cleared stroke but revealed a large fluid collection around the heart plus fluid around the lungs.

Heart ultrasound confirmed tamponade, and emergency drainage removed 2.2 litres of bloody fluid from the pericardial sac. His course grew complicated, with respiratory failure needing a ventilator and abnormal heart rhythms. Testing of the lung fluid then revealed the lymphoma cells. Surgeons cut a pericardial window for the fluid. He improved, came off the ventilator, and was discharged to begin chemotherapy. The authors urge clinicians to consider hidden blood cancers behind bloody pericardial fluid.
pmc-13526123:
Josef Zahner leads a large team in a 2026 dosimetry analysis asking whether hormone blocking drugs change radiation doses from PSMA-targeted therapy in advanced prostate cancer. Androgen receptor signaling inhibitors improve results and might raise PSMA expression and tumor dose. Patients got one of two lutetium-177 PSMA radioligands.

The retrospective analysis at one center covered fifty men at their first treatment cycle, half also taking abiraterone or enzalutamide and half on radioligand therapy alone. Imaging at three time points after dosing fed dose math for 148 tumor lesions and for kidney, spleen, and liver. Median tumor dose was comparable between combination and control groups for both radioligands, with no significant differences. Organ doses were also comparable in the results noted, which the authors call preliminary.
pmc-13526523:
Kim and colleagues reported in 2026 that a stress protein called GRP78, also known as BiP, helps drive liver cancer growth. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide, so new drug targets are badly needed. The team found GRP78 enriched in lab-grown liver cancer spheroids, small balls of tumor cells, and linked high levels in tissue near tumors to worse outcomes after surgery.

Blocking GRP78 slowed cancer cell growth and weakened their response to DNA damage. The protein peaks during cell division and sits in the midbody, the bridge between two new cells at the final step of division. Extra GRP78 held onto another protein, PLK1, and kept it stable in the midbody, so cells failed to finish dividing and ended up with several nuclei. The authors argue that blocking GRP78 could become a new treatment route for liver cancer.
pmc-13526723:
Ananthika Vijayan and others build, in a 2026 study, an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory scaffold from hydroxyapatite taken from bovine bone waste. Hydroxyapatite, the mineral of bone, was mixed with polyethylene glycol, zinc oxide nanoparticles, and ascorbic acid, better known as vitamin C. The goal was a material safe for bone that also calms inflammation and lets zinc out slowly.

Tests confirmed the zinc particles and vitamin C were mixed in and that the polymer changed crystal size and order. Adding ascorbic acid gave stronger antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity than the version lacking it, while germ-killing action came mainly from zinc oxide. Macrophage cell tests showed the scaffold fit well with cells at low doses, with viability above ninety percent, but marked toxicity at higher concentrations. Dose control is therefore central to any use.
pmc-13528023:
Ristha Kamar and nine colleagues report a 2026 genomic survey of MRSA carried by healthy people in Qatar. MRSA is a drug-resistant staph germ usually studied in hospitals. The team swabbed noses and armpits of 576 residents with no recent hospital care or antibiotics. Lab tests confirmed the germ and its resistance genes. Whole genomes were read for a subset.

Sixty people carried staph, and twenty-one of those strains were MRSA. That gives a carriage rate near four percent. Most carriers were men aged eighteen to forty-five. Resistance to common antibiotics was frequent, and seventy-one percent of MRSA strains resisted several drug classes. Only one strain carried the PVL toxin gene. Genome family trees showed four separate clusters. The authors urge community surveillance and careful antibiotic use.
pmc-13528323:
Elmer Victor Bernstam, Todd R. Johnson, and Fares Alahdab weigh academia against industry in the AI age in a 2026 review. Industry holds the biggest computers, the largest datasets, and most AI doctorates. Top models now come from firms. Academic medical centers still run research, teaching, and care, the trio note. Their edge lies elsewhere.

Centers steward rich health data, a key fuel for medical AI. That asset only pays off with investment. Data quality, tidy management, and easy reuse all need work. Rules should lower hurdles for sharing while guarding the public interest. The authors cast centers as careful stewards rather than racers. Used well, their data could shape health AI more than raw computing power. Neglect would hand the field to industry by default.
pmc-13531923:
Liwei Liao and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol comparing two biopsy routes for unexplained fluid around the lung. A newer ultrasound elasticity-guided biopsy promises high yield with less invasion than camera surgery inside the chest. Five Chinese centers will randomize 420 patients whose fluid tests came back negative.

Half start with the guided biopsy and move to camera surgery only if no diagnosis emerges. The other half go straight to camera surgery. Diagnostic yield leads the outcomes, with a five-point non-inferiority margin. Safety, hospital days, drainage time, avoided surgeries, and costs follow behind.
pmc-13532823:
Mhandu and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how researchers set the loads placed on hearts removed from the body and kept beating in the lab. Such isolated heart setups, including the Langendorff and working-heart models, are a basic tool for studying heart mechanics and energy use. Preload means the stretch on the heart as it fills, and afterload means the resistance it pumps against, and both must be set with care to mimic real life.

Mhandu gathers the physical and software methods used to present, control, and vary these loads, whether by pressure or by flow resistance. The review also covers how models copy the body's blood flow patterns inside a working-heart rig. The authors look ahead to a smart afterload device that adjusts resistance beat by beat, which would copy living conditions more closely and fix limits of current setups.
pmc-13534623:
Lei Fan and colleagues test in 2026 how sky view factor, the share of sky visible from a spot, shapes body and brain responses in urban settings. Standard comfort models treat people as passive heat systems and miss brain processing. Volunteers moved from a calm baseline through a stress step to places with varied sky openness.

Brain waves, heart measures, and skin temperature were tracked together. Main effects of sky openness on brain power and heart rate did not reach significance in this modest sample. A trend toward higher calm-linked brain activity in open-sky spots hints that openness may buffer heat stress.
pmc-13536723:
Jin Suh Yu and colleagues propose a biology-first approach to cervical cancer screening in a 2026 review. Nearly all cervical cancers follow lasting infection with high-risk human papillomavirus, leaving a long window for prevention. Current options each have trade-offs in accuracy, judgment, and access, especially where clinics and labs are scarce. The review sorts tools by the biological target they measure rather than by device type.

Four target groups are covered, from virus markers and host cell-cycle proteins to small chemical signals and marker-free light-based methods paired with computer reading. Attention goes to bedside-ready tests, sampling without invasive exams, and layered risk sorting that fits large programs. The authors frame the scheme as a path toward screening that is both precise and widely reachable.
pmc-13538823:
Sungho Bea and colleagues weigh severe low blood sugar risk when a heart rhythm drug joins a common diabetes pill in a 2026 Korean claims study. The rhythm drug slows liver breakdown of the diabetes pill, plausibly raising its levels. Among 12,730 adults with type 2 diabetes starting rhythm therapy while on the pill class, starters of the drug in question were weighted against starters of three rival rhythm drugs.

After weighting, starting the drug in question carried nearly double the hazard of severe low blood sugar needing hospital or emergency care versus the rivals. The elevation persisted across sensitivity and subgroup checks. The authors urge caution and close monitoring when the two medicines combine, given how widely the pill class remains used.
pmc-13539823:
Tesfay Gebreslassie Gebrehiwot and nine co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, suicidal thoughts and attempts among young people in Tigray, Ethiopia, after the region's war ended. School pupils and students aged 15 to 24 answered validated questionnaires about mood, trauma, and violence exposure.

Among 599 respondents, about one in five reported suicidal thoughts and roughly one in ten reported an attempt. Depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress raised the odds of both outcomes, while sexual abuse and witnessing violence also mattered. Physical activity appeared protective against thoughts of suicide. The authors argue that post-war schools need mental health support built into recovery programs.
pmc-13540223:
Jennifer Brown and colleagues present a modelling study, published in 2026. It estimates avoidable heart-related deaths in the United States. The comparison is between two pills for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Zanubrutinib and ibrutinib are both targeted pills for this blood cancer. Ibrutinib carries a higher cardiac risk. No real-world head-to-head death comparison exists.

The model applied trial-based risk numbers to real prescribing data. Five years of data were used. About eighty-one avoidable cardiac deaths were estimated in later-line treatment. About one hundred forty were estimated in first-line treatment over five years. The numbers rise over a decade of use. The estimates rest on model assumptions and trial populations, the authors caution.
pmc-13540823:
Malgoda Gamage Nimesha Madushani Amarasinghe leads a 2026 survey of job satisfaction among married female nurses at a district general hospital in Sri Lanka's Southern Province. Married nurses juggle ward duties with family demands that may colour how they feel about work.

A random sample of 306 nurses received a questionnaire built around a validated satisfaction scale, and 251 replied. Overall satisfaction scored high. Professional recognition drew the warmest ratings, while recognition tied to pay scored lowest. Age, the ward or unit where a nurse worked, and education level each showed significant links with satisfaction. The authors ask for wider research into the forces behind these patterns.
pmc-13540923:
Lizzy Winstone and colleagues study social media feeds in a 2026 project. They asked how recommendation algorithms shape teen mental health. Most research blames screen time or personal weakness. The commercial machinery that picks the content gets less attention. The team built a grounded theory from teen accounts.

Twenty-seven British teens took part in interviews. Their ages ran from fourteen to nineteen. Each shared screenshots from TikTok and Instagram feeds. The algorithms organised what appeared, and how often. They also set the emotional punch of the feed. Three loops kept exposure going. Teens fought back with savvy tricks, yet those tricks were unevenly shared.
pmc-13542123:
Jorge Jonathan Nué-Martinez and colleagues mapped how a hopeful parasite drug grips parasite DNA. Published in 2026, the study used magnet-based resonance to solve the structure of JNII40 bound to a DNA double strand with four AT repeats. JNII40 kills Leishmania parasites in animals and homes in on AT-rich DNA in their energy hubs.

The drug sank deep into the DNA minor groove, held by direct and water-aided H bonds, among them direct links from drug amidine parts to DNA phosphate oxygens. Two ordered water units bridged drug and DNA, keeping the complex shape true, while drug entry narrowed the groove. These contacts explain the drug's tight grip and AT pickiness seen in heat and magnet tests. The authors offer the structure as a blueprint for designing choosy DNA-targeting drugs against kinetoplastid parasites.
pmc-13542223:
Frederik Schliephake, Isabella Lurje, and Georg Lurje reply to critics in 2026. Their trial tested hypothermic oxygenated machine perfusion. That cold, oxygenated rinse protects donor livers. Their study showed the treatment improving bile chemistry. The letter answers a commentary on that work. Bile duct scarring is the point at issue.

Critics asked why better bile brought no visible drop in strictures. The trial held only twenty-six patients. This donor type rarely develops such strictures at all. Too few events occurred to judge the question. Trials in higher-risk donation showed scarring roughly halved. The authors also discuss glands around the bile ducts. They propose long warm perfusion of discarded livers next.
pmc-13543623:
Satoru Hagiwara and co-authors published a 2026 study of liver cancer returning after hepatitis C was cured with modern direct-acting antivirals. Clearing the virus does not erase cancer risk, especially in patients who already had a tumour. Records of 279 patients who reached sustained viral clearance after 2014 were reviewed for who developed cancer. The twenty-eight recurrences were sorted into spread within the liver, reawakened dormant tumour, or genuinely new cancer.

Thirty-three patients developed cancer after cure, and a prior cancer history was the only independent predictor, multiplying risk about fourteenfold. Recurrences split fairly evenly among the three patterns. Because follow-up was strict, nearly all recurrences were caught at the earliest stages, and curative treatment proved possible in twenty-seven of twenty-eight patients. Whatever form recurrence takes, the authors conclude, vigilant surveillance after viral cure keeps it treatable.
pmc-13543923:
Shazia Sarela and colleagues report a study of mnemonic-based teaching led by near-peers for third-year medical students, testing whether the memory tricks students swap informally actually work when taught on purpose. Over eight months, twenty-three peer-led sessions on commonly examined clinical topics wove mnemonics into every class. Students answered single-best-answer questions and rated their confidence before and after each session, and later rated how useful the mnemonics felt and whether they would use them again.

Scores improved significantly after teaching, especially on questions tied to the taught mnemonics, and confidence rose as well. Students left more likely to use mnemonics in future, and the students whose confidence grew most were the keenest adopters. Formalising a folk study technique, the authors conclude, pays off twice: the peer format and the memory aids each earn their place in the timetable.
pmc-13545423:
Douglas J Marr and colleagues set out in 2026 to explain how a small switch protein called ARL11 turns on phospholipase D1. That enzyme makes a signaling fat linked to cancer and brain disease. Earlier work knew ARL11 could activate the enzyme, but not how the two fit together. The team combined test-tube activity assays with computer-predicted structures of the pair.

ARL11 stimulated the enzyme only when loaded with GTP, the usual on signal for such switches. Mutations at the predicted contact surface broke the activation, confirming the model's layout. Parts of a loose loop on the enzyme appear to fold into shape against ARL11, giving three neighboring contact zones that together explain the activation.
pmc-13546523:
Yan Ming and co-authors compared in 2026 the two classic forms of stomach cancer, intestinal and diffuse, once the disease has already spread. Their analysis drew on a large United States cancer registry and included 4,696 patients with metastatic disease. Statistical matching balanced the two groups so that differences in spread patterns and survival could be read more fairly.

Intestinal-type tumors reached the liver more often, while diffuse-type tumors reached bone more often. Diffuse-type disease also carried a worse outlook for both overall and cancer-specific survival, even after matching. Among spread sites, patients whose cancer reached the liver lived relatively longer than those with bone, brain, or multiple sites of spread. The authors say the subtype should inform risk discussions.
pmc-13546723:
Šimon Halás and a large team fed dairy cows humic substances, natural compounds from decomposed organic matter, in 2026 to see whether they ease the difficult weeks around calving. Sixty pregnant Slovak spotted cows were split into groups, with the treated group receiving the additive daily from two months before calving through the first week of lactation. Rumen fluid, blood, milk, and udder health were monitored.

Treated cows showed a friendlier rumen pattern, with higher pH, relatively more acetate, and less ammonia, alongside lower urea in blood and milk. Their milk carried more protein and fewer somatic cells, and fewer udder quarters were infected shortly after calving. Immune measures calmed as well. The authors propose the additive as part of a herd health program.
pmc-13547723:
