Prichayudh and co-authors studied a 2026 test problem in children with cyanotic congenital heart disease, where low blood oxygen drives haemoglobin unusually high. That compensation hides iron deficiency, because standard measures look normal even when iron runs out. One hundred and ten patients aged six months to fifteen years were enrolled.

Twenty-eight children, about a quarter, proved iron depleted by ferritin or transferrin measures between September 2022 and September 2023. Haemoglobin and haematocrit matched between depleted and sufficient groups, confirming they cannot separate the two states. Prichayudh found two red cell measures did separate them: wider spread of red cell sizes and lower haemoglobin inside young red cells. Combined, the pair reached about eighty-five percent diagnostic accuracy, a practical option where full iron studies are unavailable.
pmc-13548523:
Hafiz Bilal Ahmed Jilani and colleagues pool randomized trials of omega-3 fatty acid supplements for people on hemodialysis, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Heart disease kills more dialysis patients than any other cause, and fish-oil fats have shown heart benefits in the wider population. The team searched three databases through November 2025 for trials comparing these supplements against placebo.

Across the pooled trials, supplements did not lower deaths from all causes. Deaths from heart causes fell by nearly half, however, and heart attacks and problems with dialysis access sites also became less common. The authors support omega-3 as an add-on protective treatment, while warning that one large trial supplies most of the data. They call for further big trials before firm guidance can follow.
pmc-13548723:
Yi Wang and colleagues trace how pancreatic cancer prepares the liver for invasion using tiny parcels shipped from the tumor, in a 2026 study. The liver is this cancer's favorite distant target, and a fibrotic landing pad forms there before tumor cells arrive. Comparing tumor and normal tissue gene activity, then testing in cells and mice, the team singled out a transcription factor, RUNX1, whose levels tracked with liver spread.

Silencing RUNX1 in mouse tumors cut liver metastasis dramatically. The factor switches on a sticky surface protein, ITGB1, which tumor cells pack into their extracellular vesicles. Liver support cells swallow those parcels and, through an inflammatory pathway, start laying down scar-like matrix and calling in other cells, building the fibrotic niche. Blood vesicle levels of the protein also marked patients with liver spread and poor outlook, suggesting a diagnostic use.
pmc-13550023:
Dieter Seifert traces how German psychiatry and criminal law renamed intellectual disability across a century, in a 2026 German-language article. Words carry attitudes, and the terms used between lawyers and psychiatrists shape real legal outcomes. The old word Schwachsinn was once a diagnosis, but it hardened into an insult. Yet it survived inside the criminal code's insanity paragraph until the end of 2020. Another outdated phrase, for deep personality deviation, survived with it.

Seifert walks through how diagnostic labels for people with reduced intelligence shifted across classification editions and why each generation renegotiates the line between normal and disordered. He notes stubborn public prejudice, including surveys where many people reject neighbors with schizophrenia. His plea is for careful, current wording in statutes and diagnoses alike, so that law keeps pace with psychiatric knowledge and language stops branding the people it describes.
pmc-13551323:
Ahmed Sohaib and seven colleagues test whether dropping the 5-fluorouracil bolus harms patients with metastatic colorectal cancer. The bolus adds worry about blood toxicity in modern multidrug regimens, yet its value is uncertain. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covers 267 patients treated from June 2020 to June 2024 in Egypt. Patients got bolus-free nbFOLFOX or standard mFOLFOX6, with or without targeted therapy.

Bolus omission gave a small but significant progression-free survival gain, with mean 10.029 months versus 9.319 months. Overall survival was similar, at mean 21.7 months versus 20.7 months. High-grade neutropenia fell from 25.4 percent with the bolus to 14.9 percent without it. Omitting the bolus thus cuts blood toxicity without giving up survival, aiding choices during drug shortages.
pmc-13551923:
Min Jiang, with five colleagues, published a 2026 study of a metabolic index and death in acute myocarditis. Myocarditis is sudden inflammation of the heart muscle. Records covered 1,373 adults at three districts of one hospital. The index, called TyG, blends triglycerides and glucose as a stand-in for insulin resistance. The team related it to death in hospital. Curve methods allowed bent, not just straight, links.

The index stood as an independent risk factor for death in hospital. The link bent in a U-like shape. Both very high and very low values tied to more deaths. Heart size and function measures also shifted across index levels. No subgroup changed the main link. The team proposes the cheap index as a short-term warning sign in myocarditis.
pmc-13554223:
Juan Pablo Cisneros-Barba leads a five-author team field-testing a cheap printed sensor that reads soil acidity nonstop in a 2026 study. Soil acidity steers crop health, yet dense readings are hard to gather with pricey lab gear. Their printed carbon strip uses a dye whose electrical signal shifts with acidity. Tests spanned wet and dry soils, loose and packed ground, and several soil types.

Readings stayed steady across all those changes, with no fresh calibration needed. Mounted on a small board with a low-power reader, the sensors logged data alone for months outdoors. Weatherproofing kept the setup running through field conditions. The authors see cheap, dense acidity maps guiding fertilizer choices field by field, rather than by rough averages.
pmc-13555223:
Yoonha Lee and colleagues report long-term outcomes for Korean children with lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia, a rare steroid-making disorder, publishing the multicentre study in 2026. Faults in the STAR protein block cholesterol transport inside hormone-making cells, crippling cortisol, aldosterone, and sex-hormone production. The team followed 31 patients from ten centres, nearly all with the classic form diagnosed in infancy.

Salt wasting affected about six in ten patients, and darkened skin was the most common feature, seen in over seven in ten. Most classic patients carried the same East Asian founder variant, and those reaching adulthood attained near-average height on hormone replacement. The authors call for continued follow-up of puberty and fertility, since ovarian cysts and varied pubertal timing appeared in the cohort.
pmc-13556023:
Jiahui Qi and ten colleagues tested in 2026 whether simple combined blood indices can flag people at high risk of heart and metabolic disease. They built two scores from routine glucose and lipid measures. One score uses six factors and the other uses seven. Both were checked against disease records in a large United States survey and a Chinese ageing cohort. Machine learning models measured how well each score predicted illness.

Both scores rose alongside risk across nine disease groups and fourteen specific conditions, plus death, with thyroid overactivity the lone exception. The six-factor version predicted about as well as the seven-factor one for most diseases, especially heart and metabolic conditions. Follow-up data linked higher six-factor scores, and scores that stayed high over time, to new cardiovascular disease and diabetes. A short panel of routine tests may thus serve long-term risk monitoring.
pmc-13556523:
Nanako Yamada and colleagues investigated how thin nerve fibres in the brain and spinal cord survive for so long without proper myelin insulation. Mice lacking a protein called teneurin-4 develop severe faulty myelination of small fibres, the kind of damage seen in multiple sclerosis, yet the animals live beyond a year. Microscopy and protein profiling were used to find what keeps those bare fibres alive.

Staining showed abnormal spread of structural proteins inside the fibres, and electron microscopy confirmed that small fibres survived to one year of age despite having no compact myelin. Protein analysis found four members of the 14-3-3 family raised in the damaged tissue. When drugs blocked those proteins, fibre damage advanced. The team concludes that 14-3-3 proteins act as survival factors for unmyelinated fibres, a lead for treatments in demyelinating disease.
pmc-13558323:
Zehra Naseem and colleagues tested whether improving liver blood tests can predict that a bile-duct stone has already passed, publishing the retrospective study in 2026. Guidelines use static lab values to judge the odds of a stone, but doctors hoped falling bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase might safely spare patients an ERCP, which carries real risks. The team reviewed 198 patients who underwent ERCP for suspected stones between 2002 and 2018.

Stones were found at nearly identical rates whether labs had normalised or not, and even fully normal labs still hid stones in over half the cases. Final lab values predicted stones barely better than chance, while the normalised group suffered more post-procedure pancreatitis. The message is plain: when suspicion stays high, ERCP should proceed regardless of improving labs.
pmc-13558623:
Apoorva Sherigar and five colleagues optimised in 2026 a bacterial process that eats PET plastic, the polymer of drinks bottles. A bacterium pulled from a Chennai waste dump, Glutamicibacter mysorens ASR14, had already shown it could break the plastic down at room temperature. The team screened twenty trial conditions, then applied response surface statistics across twenty-five runs of four chosen variables to hunt for the best recipe.

Untuned, the bacterium removed about a quarter of the plastic's weight in a month. The optimised recipe more than doubled the pace, reaching about three quarters weight loss in sixty days. Enzyme checks confirmed strong activity from two fat and ester cutting enzymes. Surface erosion, falling crystallinity, and a rich yield of the plastic's building block acid completed the picture. The authors claim the first fully optimised process report for this organism.
pmc-13558723:
Zhe Sun and ten colleagues found in 2026 a side door into cancers driven by the MYC oncoprotein, a driver long considered undruggable because of its shapeless structure. A genome-wide screen from the team's earlier work flagged a cell surface receptor, EphB4, whose loss hurts only MYC-high cells. Testing that lead in MYC-driven triple-negative breast cancer, they removed or blocked the receptor in cell lines and in mouse tumours.

Blockade triggered strong self-destruction in MYC-high cancer cells while sparing MYC-low ones, and it worked without the p53 safeguard that many breast cancers lack. Pairing the blockade with a drug that releases a second death brake produced synergy and tumour shrinkage in animals. Mechanistically, silencing the receptor starved the cell's protein shredder by switching off one of its core parts, overloading MYC's busy protein factories. The authors name the axis a distinct, actionable weakness.
pmc-13560723:
Pisut Pongchaikul and colleagues review infection inside the womb, a leading cause of early birth and harm to mother and baby. Their survey covers naming, diagnosis, treatment, and the lab tools used to find the germs involved.

Standard culture tests are slow and miss germs that are hard to grow in the lab. Newer DNA tests can name single species or read a broad bacterial gene, catching organisms that culture misses. Whole-genome and sweep-all sequencing go further, spotting bacteria, viruses, and fungi at once, plus resistance and attack genes. The catch is that womb fluid holds few germs, so stray DNA and the mother's own DNA can muddy results.
pmc-13562323:
Mercè Sitjà-Rabert and colleagues studied why frail older adults in Barcelona stick with, or drop out of, a community program meant to prevent disability. The + AGIL Barcelona program mixes exercise, nutrition, medication review, and social support for people showing early frailty. In this 2026 qualitative study, researchers ran focus groups with 22 participants averaging 82 years old and 18 primary care professionals.

Warm, personal communication, exercise plans tailored to each person, and a sense of group belonging kept people going, the interviews showed. Caregiving duties, tight budgets, and scarce local resources pulled the other way. Lasting success, the authors conclude, depends less on the program's contents than on steady staffing and close links between clinics and community services.
pmc-13562623:
Sergio Barbero and two colleagues explain an optical puzzle: why the starburst spikes around a night light come in countable patterns. When a bright point is viewed in dim light, faults in the eye's optics fold light into caustic patterns on the retina, and those patterns often show rotational symmetry. The number of spikes varies between viewers and occasions. The 2026 study builds a theory from the mathematics of the eye's wave aberration, written as a sum of Zernike shapes.

Counting special fold points in that surface, called cusps of Gauss, predicts how many peaks appear and how they arrange. A round aberration mixed with a three-lobed one yields a three-peak starburst. Swapping in a four-lobed term yields four-fold patterns with four or eight peaks. The authors add that the link runs backward too: a measured starburst could betray facts about a person's eye aberrations.
pmc-13562723:
Jiachen Wang and three colleagues pool trials on a familiar frustration: weight lost through diet, drugs, or surgery tends to creep back. Their 2026 review, registered in advance and run to standard reporting rules, searched five databases to October 2025. Eleven randomised trials with 568 adults covered exercise started after successful weight loss, during the maintenance phase when regain usually strikes. Bias was scored with the standard Cochrane tool.

People assigned to exercise regained 2.81 kilograms less than controls on average, a small edge with no statistical scatter between trials. Fat mass told a murkier story: the main analysis missed significance and the trials disagreed with each other, at 69 percent heterogeneity. The authors call the maintenance benefit real but modest. They ask for longer trials with standard exercise doses, honest adherence tracking, and uniform body-composition measures before stronger claims are made.
pmc-13563723:
Nigatu Admasu Desta and three colleagues investigate a sharp malaria outbreak that hit Meinit Goldia District in southwest Ethiopia in 2025. Cases spiked in week 13 of the year, and the response lagged. Their study, run from late March to June, checked the district line list: 3,630 confirmed cases across eight villages, an attack rate of 274.7 per thousand people. A case-control arm compared 145 confirmed patients with 145 neighbours, found by house-to-house checks, on home conditions, net use, and malaria knowledge.

Never using a bed net carried nearly five times the odds of illness, and patchy use more than doubled it. Living near broken glass bottles that hold water, or near an open deep well, raised risk sharply, as did poor knowledge of how malaria spreads. Long clothing at night protected. The authors aim the findings at targeted control: nets, water-point fixes, and teaching where the outbreak burned hottest.
pmc-13563923:
Patrick O'Donnell and colleagues mapped what helps and hinders the recruitment of rural patients into cancer trials. Distance from major cancer centres is only part of the story, and researchers do not even agree on how to define rural. Their scoping review searched five databases for studies since 2004, screened 29,160 papers, and kept 27, most of them from the United States, with a few from Australia and Canada.

Travel burden, patchy local services, and inconsistent definitions of rurality emerged as recurring barriers, while partnerships between academic centres and rural clinics showed promise as a lever. The authors argue that solutions must span the wider determinants of health, and they call for collaborative research networks that bring trials closer to where rural patients live.
pmc-13569523:
Eline Tobback and co-authors develop, in a 2026 study, a scoring tool for judging the quality of written medication review reports from Belgian community pharmacists. The service has run nationally since 2023. Criteria from an existing framework were adapted with detailed instructions, then tested by student assessors on ninety-eight real reports, with a larger round involving sixty-one final-year students.

Each report was scored on its own by several assessors so agreement could be measured with standard reliability statistics, and timing checks showed whether scoring was practical. No validated tool existed for this report type before. Pharmacy teachers and regulators get a tested way to audit report quality in a steady way instead of relying on impression.
pmc-13573423:
Qiheng Yuan, with nine colleagues, reports a 2026 gene study of plasmids that carry drug resistance across borders. These small DNA rings hold genes for OXA-48-like enzymes, which break last-resort antibiotics called carbapenems. Tracking the rings, not just the bacteria, shows how resistance hops between species and places.

The team mined 747 complete plasmid sequences from a public database, the largest such set yet. The rings turned up in 50 countries on six continents, with one gene form leading in Europe and others in South Asia. Sixteen spread units were defined, and one traced to the Netherlands around 2005 before fanning out worldwide. Rings often carried extra resistance to other drug families at once. High-risk forms showed up in non-clinical settings too, which widens the watch list for health teams.
pmc-13575123:
Yongjiang Zhang leads a 2026 study of heavy metals in soils where mining meets farmland in China's manganese triangle, near Xiushan in Chongqing. Metals there come from rock, industry, and farm inputs, yet how they stack up with depth was poorly known. The team compared paired soil profiles from mining and smelting ground.

Smelting soils were less acidic than mining soils. Antimony and cadmium stood out as the main pollutants, driving most of the ecological risk in each setting. For human health, swallowing soil particles drove cancer risk, while skin contact drove most non-cancer risk. Breathing in dust mattered little. The authors argue cleanup plans should match each metal's depth pattern.
pmc-13575223:
Chunwang Zhu and four colleagues build a video detection system tuned for soccer broadcasts in a 2026 paper. Broadcasts switch cameras often, which breaks many tracking tools: frames jump suddenly, and players look tiny in wide shots yet detailed in close-ups. A single fixed strategy struggles at both extremes.

Their system, ViewAdapt-Det, adds two modules. One senses shot changes and dials down the use of past frames at those moments, while keeping the boost during smooth sequences. The other guesses the current view type and adjusts feature handling to match. Tests on three soccer datasets, including one the team built for broadcast switching, beat rival methods. Robustness held up best when shots changed abruptly, the authors report.
pmc-13578323:
Emma J. Diethorn and colleagues traced a developmental cause of social-recognition failure in a mouse model of autism. Mice lacking Shank3, a gene tied to autism and Phelan-McDermid syndrome, fail to recognise familiar peers, but why that failure starts in development was unknown. Their 2026 study examined the CA2 region of the hippocampus, a hub for social memory, across development in Shank3B knockout mice.

Mutant mice built up excess perineuronal nets, mesh-like coats around neurons, in CA2, trapping the guidance cue semaphorin-3A and overgrowing incoming fibres. Trimming those nets in development restored the cue, the inputs, and social recognition into adulthood, partly normalising CA2 activity. The authors present early net excess as a reversible cause, not a fixed defect.
pmc-13579223:
Hammad and colleagues presented in 2026 a platform for building living materials that grow their own fibers, mining natural proteins to make the fibers stronger and more useful. Engineered living materials use bacteria to produce the fabric they live in. One known fiber system, curli, comes from gut bacteria and limits what can be built. The team searched nature for better fiber proteins.

They screened more than thirty-three thousand look-alike proteins and used structure prediction and simulation to pick stable candidates with extra repeat units. Reprogrammed bacteria then produced fibers up to nine times heavier than the natural version. Gels made from the fibers were about three times stiffer, and the fiber mesh shielded cells inside from ultraviolet light, raising survival five-fold. The materials could also be printed in three dimensions.
pmc-13586323:
Confidence Dordoe and colleagues review growth factors as a possible repair therapy after ischemic stroke. Such a stroke blocks blood flow to part of the brain, and the only approved drug must be given within hours, which many patients miss. Fibroblast growth factors, a family of signaling proteins, have shown in lab models that they can protect nerve cells, calm inflammation, guard the blood-brain barrier, and grow new vessels.

The 2026 review weighs that promise against a hard record in human trials, where dosing and side effects have tripped up progress. Timing and context seem to matter: the same factor may help early and hinder late. The authors also note that growth factor readings in blood might help pick who could benefit. Their prescription is better delivery systems, clearer treatment windows, and smarter trial design before these proteins can earn a place in stroke care.
pmc-13589123:
W.Y. Son and eight colleagues test two kitchen-chemistry tricks for upgrading chicken breast protein into a better food ingredient. Plain chicken protein dissolves poorly and forms weak emulsions, limiting its use in powders and processed foods. Their 2026 study compared four versions: untouched protein, protein linked to a tea polyphenol called EGCG, enzyme-chopped protein, and protein given both treatments in sequence.

Chopping loosened the protein and exposed reactive groups; EGCG bonding then consumed some of those and clouded the mixes further. Both treatments raised water holding, oil absorption, and emulsifying power, and together they produced the strongest defense against oxidation. Chopping alone weakened emulsion stability, which EGCG then restored. Digestion in a test system improved with chopping and held up when EGCG followed. The authors recommend the sequence for functional protein ingredients.
pmc-13591223:
Ting Liu and Yaomin Hu review how skeletal muscle ages, arguing that loss of bulk alone does not explain frailty in later life. Strength and speed often fall faster than mass. Drawing on recent single cell and multi layer studies, they frame aging muscle as a loss of resilience across many parts at once. Fibers, stem cells, immune and vessel cells, and nerve links all change together.

Faults in protein house keeping, cell power stations, and long term low grade swelling sit at the core, the review says. Signals from the liver, fat, gut, and brain add further pressure. Exercise and diet stay the proven base of care. Liu and Hu weigh newer ideas, from power station repair to clearing worn out cells, as still in testing.
pmc-13592323:
Jun Hyeon Lee, Minlang Yang, and Takuma Yasuda grow, in 2026, three pure color light emitters for displays from a single starting platform in one pot. Their emitters belong to a boron based family prized for razor thin color bands in organic screens. Stretching that sharpness into red has long proved hard. Rival reaction paths in the pot yield one, two, or reshaped boron insertions, giving green, yellow, and red emitters side by side.

Each color stayed under a 25 nanometer band width with near perfect light yield in doped films. Test screens hit top efficiency above 35 percent. Lee and the team present the forked one pot route as a unified way to stock a full color set from one precursor.
pmc-13592823:
Julie M. Schallhorn and Alekya Rajanala report, in 2026, on a phase four registry tracking the light adjustable lens in people implanted in both eyes. The lens is unique: after cataract surgery, ultraviolet light can fine tune its power in the clinic, then lock it in place. That promise matters most for eyes with prior corneal refractive surgery, where standard lens math often misses. The registry enrolled people with and without that history across many sites.

Entry required sharp corrected vision after implant and completed light treatments, and one visit one to three months after lock in gathered the outcome data. Records spanned September 2021 to January 2025. Schallhorn and Rajanala frame the registry as a real world check on whether adjustability delivers the targeting that fixed lenses struggle to reach.
pmc-13594423:
Xiaowei Ma leads a seventeen-author trial of near-infrared light therapy aimed precisely at the angular gyrus on both sides of the brain in Alzheimer's disease. Earlier work shone the light over the whole head with mixed results. This randomized, sham-controlled study instead treated thirty-six patients with confirmed Alzheimer's biomarkers. Each side received twenty minutes daily over fifteen days.

The targeted group improved in cognition, memory, language, attention, and executive function, and their psychiatric symptoms eased. Brain scans showed stronger connections inside the default mode network, the system active at rest, and better teamwork between that network and attention and emotion systems. A combined stimulation and recording method found richer information flow, especially at the front and back of the brain. The authors present targeted light therapy as a precise, promising way to re-tune large brain networks in Alzheimer's disease.
pmc-13597523:
Ying Liu and colleagues read ancient DNA from lake sediments around Siberia and Alaska. They watched Arctic plant communities change across the last twenty-four thousand years. Shrubs and trees advanced into tundra during that span. Nine lake cores preserved the DNA of past vegetation, and statistical null models separated true plant-to-plant interactions from mere shared habitat preferences.

During the ice age, interactions leaned positive, with plants sheltering and helping each other. As the Holocene warmed and woody plants took over, interactions flipped toward competition, and the community grew taller with longer roots on average. The authors propose a feedback: climate enabled the woody advance, the new arrivals intensified competition, and that competition further squeezed native low plants, shrinking their ranges even as diversity between sites rose. They offer the deep-time pattern as an analogy for today's Arctic greening.
pmc-13600623:
Sara Hana Weisz leads a nine-author team testing a simple risk score in patients with infective endocarditis, an infection of the heart's inner lining. Their 2026 study asks whether the ACEF score, built from just age, a kidney blood marker, and the heart's pumping fraction, can flag patients headed for poor outcomes. The team reviewed 143 patients treated at one infectious diseases hospital between January 2023 and February 2025.

Thirty patients died during follow-up. In adjusted analysis, a higher ACEF score tracked with worse survival, alongside diabetes, infection with Staphylococcus aureus, and cases where heart surgery was advised but never done. A score of 1.30 or above marked the higher-risk group in both operated and non-operated patients. The authors suggest ACEF as a quick bedside tool for sorting newly diagnosed patients by risk, since it needs only three routine values and no lengthy calculation.
pmc-13600923:
Preeti Gupta leads a seven-author team presenting a 2026 deep learning system that reads ventilator waveforms with near-perfect accuracy. Ventilators push air into critically ill lungs, and harm can follow when the machine's rhythm fights the patient's own breathing. Spotting that mismatch requires marking exactly where each breath begins and ends, a job rule-based software often fumbles in noisy recordings.

The team trained a one-dimensional attention-gated U-Net network on 9,719 breaths from 33 patients. It beat published rule-based methods, scoring above 0.99 at detecting breath starts and ends within a tenth of a second. Performance held on mismatched breaths, scoring at least 0.98 there. When used to count patient-ventilator mismatches, the model matched human reference counts, while rule-based methods drifted widely. Visual maps showed which waveform features guided the model. The authors offer it as a fast base for studying ventilator interactions at scale.
pmc-13612423:
Xiaoqian Fu leads a four-author team reviewing how mitochondria handle calcium inside eggs and ovaries. Brief calcium pulses into mitochondria switch on energy production; sustained overload triggers cell death. The review walks the molecular machinery: the uniporter channel with its MICU1, MICU2, and EMRE regulators taking calcium in, and the NCLX exchanger pushing it back out. It then connects that machinery to reproduction.

Contact sites where the endoplasmic reticulum touches mitochondria funnel calcium signals straight into metabolism. Evidence from mice, pigs, birds, fish, frogs, and sea urchins ties mitochondrial calcium to follicle cell survival, egg maturation, and the first embryonic divisions. Obesity, aging, freezing, heavy metals, and oxidative stress all disturb the balance. The authors are candid about weak spots: blunt drug tools, poorly calibrated sensors, and almost no direct human egg data. They call mitochondrial calcium a promising biomarker candidate, not yet a clinical target.
pmc-13612823:
Tobias Rindfleisch, Emilie Fjeldberg Taule, Markus S Miettinen, and Jarl Underhaug publish a 2026 reference dataset of NMR chemical shifts. It covers 275 common dipeptides, the short two-unit chains found in loose, flexible proteins. NMR, a method that reads how atoms respond in a magnetic field, can map proteins atom by atom. For disordered proteins the signals overlap badly, so firm reference values for the building blocks are rare and much needed.

The dataset holds 11,571 checked data points covering nearly all the dipeptides that occur in disordered proteins, plus the spectra used to assign them. It also tracks how shifts change when two acidic units gain or lose protons. Labs can use the set to train and test software that picks peaks and assigns spectra with far less hand work.
pmc-13614923:
Yiping Lu and colleagues report a 2026 study of how a blue-green bacterium grabs phosphate, the nutrient it needs to live, using two different binding proteins. In nutrient-poor water, matching phosphate intake to the cell's needs is vital. Crystal pictures at very fine detail showed both proteins, called PstS1 and SphX, holding a phosphate ion with a web of hydrogen bonds, 14 in one and 15 in the other.

Despite the similar webs, SphX held phosphate 26 times more weakly. The difference came down to one part of the protein: a threonine that takes a proton in place of a special strong bond used by its cousin. Changing single parts of the protein one by one confirmed each piece's role. The work explains how one cell can run a tight, high-grip system and a looser one side by side.
pmc-13616323:
Dimitra Mantzara, Richard Whitfield, Glen R. Jones, Nghia P. Truong, and Athina Anastasaki report the first controlled version of a reaction that unbuilds polymers made by a popular controlled method. In that method, called atom transfer radical polymerisation, chains grow in a managed way because most sit dormant at any moment. Recycling those materials, though, has been all-or-nothing: chains unzip completely with no say over the stopping point.

By raising catalyst levels and lowering the heat, the team tipped the balance toward putting chains back to sleep over letting them run. Molecular weight then fell in a straight, even line, proving the chains shortened uniformly on demand. Controlled unbuilding opens a path to recovering graded feedstock from plastic waste, or to trimming a polymer to a chosen size instead of shredding it to monomer.
pmc-13617223:
Amy L. Sweeny and six colleagues report a 2026 analysis of what makes intravenous cannula insertion painful for children in an emergency department. Research staff observed one hundred ninety-eight insertion attempts in one hundred thirty children under sixteen, scoring pain with a faces scale. A secondary analysis of that prospective study then searched for child, clinician, and situational factors tied to high pain scores.

More than two in five children hit the high pain range. Younger age raised the odds, and so did needing three or more attempts, a past bad cannulation experience, a child who fought the procedure, and choosing the inner elbow site first. The authors argue the first attempt matters most: teams should optimize it and use proven pain-reducing strategies, especially for younger children and those already fearful from earlier experiences.
pmc-13617523:
Kristina Goryunova and Yunis Gahramanli compare the main ways to make porous geopolymers, a class of cement-like materials built from industrial by-products rather than energy-hungry Portland cement. Pores decide whether these materials insulate buildings, filter water, or carry catalysts, yet earlier reviews treated each foaming method in isolation. The authors line the methods up inside one processing, structure, and properties framework.

Direct foaming emerges as the most practical and scalable route for low-density insulation, while lightweight fillers give the best balance of strength and density. Emulsion templating, replica processing, and sacrificial templates better create the connected pore networks that adsorption, catalysis, and filtration need. Printing offers the finest architectural control but remains slow and costly, and microwave foaming is fast yet hard to scale. The review closes with a selection guide that starts from the pore architecture a job requires.
pmc-13617623:
Somaya Al Kiswani and six colleagues report a rare case of Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome, a vascular malformation condition marked by abnormal capillaries, veins, and lymph vessels plus overgrowth of a limb. Their patient, a thirty-seven-year-old Yemeni man, arrived with blood in his urine with clots, rectal bleeding, and back pain radiating into his leg. Two separate pelvic masses raised fears of cancer.

Careful teamwork across clinical examination, imaging, endoscopy, and pathology showed the masses were vascular malformations involving both the urinary bladder and the rectosigmoid colon, not malignancy. Internal organ involvement is uncommon in this syndrome, and pelvic disease can announce itself through exactly these bleeding symptoms. The syndrome is usually managed conservatively, with lifelong follow-up aimed at bleeding control and complication prevention. The authors stress that a full multidisciplinary workup protects patients from misdiagnosis and unneeded aggressive treatment.
pmc-13619323:
Stefan Sieber led a 2026 study of how cleaner air and more schooling might have cut low birth weight in Spain between 2010 and 2018. Low birth weight, below 2,500 grams at term, carries risks across life, and both pollution and maternal education shape its odds. The team analyzed administrative records for 1,409,084 term births, pairing each with fine-grained estimates of fine particles and nitrogen dioxide exposure. They then modeled what would change under cleaner-air targets or universal higher education.

Each 10-microgram rise in fine particles was tied to about 6 percent higher odds of low birth weight, and nitrogen dioxide to about 1 percent higher odds. Lower maternal education carried much larger odds, at 1.32 times for secondary and 1.76 times for primary education against tertiary education. Meeting stricter particle limits might have prevented roughly two thousand cases, while universal tertiary education might have prevented more than nine thousand.
pmc-13621623:
Jin-Yang Yu and eleven colleagues profiled the genetics of inherited ataxias across more than two thousand Chinese patients, building the HARMONY cohort from two Yangtze River Delta centers. These coordination disorders come in dozens of flavors, and the local mix shapes how testing should be ordered. The team combined diagnoses with systematic testing and sorted results as definitive, probable, unclear, or undiagnosed.

Nearly eighty-five percent of the 2,096 patients received a molecular answer. One subtype towered over the rest: spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 accounted for about sixty percent, trailed by types 2 and 1 in single digits. Beyond those giants stretched a long tail of rare causes, and five candidate genes turned up empty. The authors convert the landscape into a stepwise testing algorithm tuned for their region, testing the common expansions first. They argue such maps speed diagnosis, sharpen counseling, and point therapy developers to the subtypes that matter most.
pmc-13621823:
David Aini and co-authors report the case of a sixty-six-year-old man whose month of pain in the lower right belly led to a very rare finding. Scans showed an enlarged appendix with no signs of inflammation around it. Surgeons removed the appendix through small incisions, and his symptoms cleared within three weeks.

Under the microscope, the appendix tissue showed lipomatosis, a harmless overgrowth of fat cells inside the organ wall. The authors note that only five earlier cases of this appendix condition had been reported, which makes firm guidance hard to give. The case adds one more documented example, with the patient's history, scan measurements, and tissue results laid out in full. For doctors, the lesson is that fat overgrowth belongs on the list of causes when an appendix looks enlarged without infection.
pmc-13624023:
Toshiaki Taoka and colleagues published a 2026 review arguing for a new reading of a popular brain scan measure, the DTI-ALPS index. The index uses diffusion MRI, which tracks water movement in tissue, and it was sold as a gauge of the glymphatic system, the brain's waste-washing flow. Years of use have complicated that simple story.

The authors point out that the index samples water movement at one fixed spot and says nothing direct about whole-brain flow. Its value bends with the local white matter itself: fibre direction, crossing fibres, the spaces between cells, and plain ageing all shift it. Two brains can also reach the same low index by opposite internal changes. The review proposes calling it a fixed-point biomarker of the tissue environment instead, bundling fibre structure, vessels, and fluid dynamics. Used that humbler way, they argue, it still serves brain health research well.
pmc-13625023:
Marlene M Meyer, Marina Proft, Jan Engelmann, and Hannes Rakoczy test whether three-year-olds know when they do not know. Older work said clear judgments about one's own knowledge arrive near school age, yet those tests asked children alone. Across four pre-registered studies with 195 children, this team placed three- and five-year-olds in a social task where a partner depended on the child's advice despite partial views of a hidden setup.

Even the three-year-olds spoke up about doubt when they had seen only part of the picture, and they stayed confident when they had seen it all. Two control studies gave mixed clues about why the social setting helped. Knowing may be voiced earlier when a child must guide someone else.
pmc-13625123:
Britanny Stark and colleagues built a 3D-printable, electrically conductive gel for heart and vessel repair. After a heart attack, adult hearts barely regrow muscle and lose electrical signalling, yet drugs replace neither muscle nor conduction. Their 2026 study made a light-cured gel from modified hyaluronic acid linked to a conductive thiophene compound, printable into tissue scaffolds.

The new gel conducted electricity far better than plain modified hyaluronic acid, though it softened somewhat. Heart and vessel cells stayed active in both gels, and stem-cell-derived heart muscle cells kept their cardiac marker and kept beating spontaneously. Stark and colleagues present the gel as a step toward printed heart patches.
pmc-13625723:
Tim Hensen and co-authors build personal computer models of whole-body metabolism to test how gut microbes may stir the blood chemistry of Alzheimer's disease. Earlier modeling in healthy older adults had forecast microbe-driven changes, unproven in real patients. The team therefore built models for thirty-four patients with Alzheimer's dementia, fifty-one with mild cognitive trouble tied to the disease, and 298 healthy controls, each tuned to that person's gut microbe mix.

The models foresaw greater capacity to make five blood compounds, including creatine and taurine, in Alzheimer's patients. Two Bacteroides species carried most of the blame for the shift, and the forecasts also tied to variants of the APOE risk gene in healthy people. Computer twins like these may expose testable links between gut and brain.
pmc-13626223:
Hafiz Syed Zaigham Ali Shah and co-authors describe a typhoid emergency that hid behind a birth defect. A 33-year-old man arrived with six days of fever, fierce upper belly pain, vomiting, and septic shock, and X-rays showed free air, so a burst stomach ulcer topped the working diagnosis. Typhoid perforation usually declares itself low on the right side, where the end of the small bowel normally sits.

Surgery told another story. The belly was heavily soiled, and a two-centimeter typhoid hole gaped in the small bowel. The bowel's end sat high in the upper belly, because the gut had never finished its fetal rotation. Surgeons diverted the bowel through the skin, blood tests confirmed typhoid, and he healed well enough to have the diversion reversed. Odd anatomy, the case warns, can scramble classic signs.
pmc-13628523:
Davide Auricchio and three colleagues examined how drugs designed for one unusual DNA shape behave toward its mirror-image partner. Their 2026 study concerns G-quadruplexes, knots formed in guanine-rich DNA, and i-motifs, folded structures on the matching cytosine-rich strand that may also help switch cancer genes on or off.

The team screened four well-known quadruplex-binding compounds against a small, well-defined i-motif using magnetic resonance and light-based methods. One compound, TMPyP4, bound a specific region of the i-motif and gradually unfolded the structure as it attached. Knowing exactly where such a ligand grips should help chemists design molecules that tune i-motif stability on purpose, a step toward drugs that act on both DNA shapes at once.
pmc-13629323:
Federica Bruno and two colleagues give a step-by-step protocol for infecting lab mice with a rodent malaria parasite. The parasite is Plasmodium chabaudi. People in malaria regions are infected again and again across a life. The protocol copies that pattern. Researchers can then study how immunity builds, and what it costs the host.

The method covers a first infection and full natural recovery. No malaria drugs are used. A second infection follows. Each stage is set out in detail. Letting the mice clear the parasite themselves is the point. It mirrors how partial immunity forms in humans. Hidden costs come with it, such as lasting anaemia. The authors frame the method as a shared platform. Labs studying long-term responses to repeated malaria can all use it.
pmc-13630823:
Liang-Chen Lin and five colleagues ran a split-face trial of skincare support after laser treatment for sun-aged skin. The study appeared in 2026. Thirty-five Asian patients received three picosecond laser sessions a month apart. One cheek got a standard soothing serum and sunscreen. The other got an added three-product regimen. It included an antioxidant serum and a lipid cream.

The laser alone improved pores, brown spots, and moisture on both sides. The supported side gained extra ground on wrinkles and texture. Patients rated it more satisfying. Temporary redness appeared in about a third of patients. Most reported no side effects at all. The authors conclude that integrated skincare meaningfully boosts laser results.
pmc-13632123:
Adam W Potter and six colleagues published this 2026 study measuring a gap between heart risk and treatment in United States adults.
